Category 1, Part A — Debug This Query: Logic Bugs
This is the classic interview opener — the interviewer slides a query across the screen (or pastes it into
the shared editor) and says "this is returning wrong results, find the bug." No table sizes, no execution
plan, just SQL and the symptom. Part A focuses on logic bugs — queries that run cleanly without errors
but produce the wrong output: missing rows, extra rows, duplicated rows, or rows in the wrong order.
The bugs here are about how SQL semantics differ from how the candidate read the query in their head.
Parts B and C cover NULL/coercion bugs and aggregation/window bugs respectively. For each scenario
below, the structure is the same: scenario setup, the buggy SQL, expected vs actual, a "thinking out
loud" walkthrough that mirrors how you should narrate your debugging on a live screen-share, the
diagnosis, the fix, and the common follow-up the interviewer will ask next.
Scenario1 · LEFT JOIN Silently Turned Into INNER JOIN
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Flipkart, Razorpay, Swiggy, Zomato · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
You're asked to list every user along with their total order count. Users who have never placed an
order should still appear with a count of zero. The query below runs fine but the analytics team
says brand-new signups are missing from the report.
SELECT u.user_id, u.name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS total_orders
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY u.user_id, u.name;
Expected: All users, with total_orders = 0 for users with no completed orders. Actual: Users with
zero completed orders are missing entirely from the result.
Thinking out loud (what to say while you stare at the screen): 1. "It's a LEFT JOIN, so all users from the
left side should survive — let me re-read why they're not." 2. "The WHERE clause references 
o.status — for users with no orders, o.status is NULL after the LEFT JOIN." 3. "NULL =
'completed' is unknown, which WHERE treats as false, so those rows get dropped after the join." 4. "That
effectively converts my LEFT JOIN back into an INNER JOIN."
The diagnosis: The LEFT JOIN preserves users without orders by filling order columns with NULL. The
WHERE clause then evaluates NULL = 'completed', which is UNKNOWN, which WHERE treats the
same as false. Those preserved rows are filtered out, and you end up with INNER JOIN semantics.
The fix:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 2 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 3
SELECT u.user_id, u.name,
       COUNT(o.order_id) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'completed') AS total_orders
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.user_id
GROUP BY u.user_id, u.name;
Or, move the status predicate into the join condition:
SELECT u.user_id, u.name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS total_orders
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON o.user_id = u.user_id
 AND o.status  = 'completed'
GROUP BY u.user_id, u.name;
Why this works: Predicates in the ON clause are evaluated before the outer join decides whether to
preserve the left-side row, so non-matching users still survive with NULL on the right.
What NOT to say: - "I'll just add OR o.status IS NULL to the WHERE" — that works by accident
and breaks if you ever add another status filter. - "LEFT JOIN doesn't work in this database" — it does;
the bug is in your filter placement.
Common follow-up: "What if I also need to filter to orders placed in the last 30 days? Where does that
predicate go?"
Scenario2 · Inner Join Where Outer Was Needed
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: PhonePe, Paytm, Meesho · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A merchant dashboard should show every merchant alongside their last payout amount.
Merchants who have never been paid out should show as zero. The report is silently dropping
new merchants who haven't seen a payout cycle yet.
SELECT m.merchant_id, m.business_name, p.amount AS last_payout
FROM merchants m
JOIN payouts p ON p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id
WHERE p.payout_date = (
  SELECT MAX(payout_date) FROM payouts WHERE merchant_id = m.merchant_id
);
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 3 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 4
Expected: Every merchant in the result, with NULL or zero for those without payouts. Actual: Merchants
with zero payouts are absent.
Thinking out loud: 1. " JOIN without LEFT means INNER — a merchant with no row in payouts is gone
immediately." 2. "Even if I correlate the subquery, the outer join is the wrong one." 3. "I need to preserve
all merchants and let payouts be optional."
The diagnosis: The plain JOIN is INNER. New merchants have zero rows in payouts and therefore
zero rows in the join output. The correlated subquery is a red herring — it filters the matched payout row,
but the row had to exist first.
The fix:
SELECT m.merchant_id, m.business_name, COALESCE(p.amount, 0) AS last_payout
FROM merchants m
LEFT JOIN payouts p
  ON p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id
 AND p.payout_date = (
   SELECT MAX(payout_date) FROM payouts WHERE merchant_id = m.merchant_id
 );
Why this works: LEFT JOIN preserves every merchant; the correlated subquery still picks the latest
payout when one exists; COALESCE shows zero when none does.
What NOT to say: - "I'll UNION the missing merchants" — wasteful and easy to get wrong. - "Just add 
WHERE p.merchant_id IS NOT NULL OR TRUE" — meaningless noise.
Common follow-up: "Rewrite this without a correlated subquery — use a window function or DISTINCT
ON."
Scenario3 · Duplicate Rows From One-to-Many Join
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Zerodha · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
You're computing revenue per order. Each order has multiple line items, and the join is producing
rows that, when summed, inflate revenue 3-4x. The CFO is asking pointed questions.
SELECT SUM(o.order_total) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.created_at >= '2026-01-01';
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 4 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 5
Expected: Sum of distinct order totals for the period. Actual: Each order's total is summed once per line
item, inflating revenue.
Thinking out loud: 1. " SUM(o.order_total) — order_total is on the orders table, but the FROM has
a 1-to-many join." 2. "For an order with 4 items, that order_total shows up 4 times in the joined row set."
3. "Either remove the join (if I don't need item data), or sum line items instead, or de-dupe before
summing."
The diagnosis: The join multiplies each order row by its number of items. Summing the order-level total
across multiplied rows inflates the result. Classic fan-out bug.
The fix: If you don't need item data at all:
SELECT SUM(order_total) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01';
If you need it for another part of the query:
SELECT SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.created_at >= '2026-01-01';
Why this works: Either we drop the join that caused the duplication, or we sum at the line-item grain
where each row genuinely contributes once.
What NOT to say: - "I'll just divide by the average items per order" — terrifying. - "Use SELECT
DISTINCT" — DISTINCT on aggregated rows doesn't fix this and hides the real issue.
Common follow-up: "Now compute revenue and item count in a single query."
Scenario4 · ORDER BY With LIMIT, Non-Deterministic Order
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Swiggy, Zomato, Dunzo · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
"Top 10 most recent orders" page is showing a different set of 10 orders every time the
dashboard reloads, even though no new orders are coming in during the test window.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 5 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 6
SELECT order_id, user_id, created_at, status
FROM orders
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 10;
Expected: A stable set of 10 most recent orders. Actual: Same created_at value on many orders;
the 10 returned shuffle between requests.
Thinking out loud: 1. "ORDER BY is there, so the order key is deterministic — but if many rows share the
same created_at, ties are broken arbitrarily." 2. "If a hundred orders share the same second, any 10
of them might surface." 3. "I need a tiebreaker, ideally something unique."
The diagnosis: created_at likely has duplicates (same second, or same default-precision
timestamp). When the ORDER BY key has ties, SQL is free to return any ordering of the tied rows, and
that ordering can change across executions.
The fix:
SELECT order_id, user_id, created_at, status
FROM orders
ORDER BY created_at DESC, order_id DESC
LIMIT 10;
Why this works: Adding a unique tiebreaker (order_id is the PK) makes the ordering total, so the
same 10 rows surface every time.
What NOT to say: - "Pagination is broken in our database" — your ORDER BY is broken. - "Add ORDER
BY 1, 2, 3, 4" — random columns don't guarantee uniqueness either.
Common follow-up: "What if I want pages 2, 3, 4 of this list and the data is being written to
continuously?"
Scenario5 · LIMIT Without ORDER BY
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Ola, Uber India, Rapido · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A new dev wrote "give me 100 sample users for a CSV export". The query works, but the same
100 users don't come back twice in a row, and they're not even close to a random sample — they
all seem to be from one city.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 6 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 7
SELECT user_id, name, email, city
FROM users
LIMIT 100;
Expected: A consistent or at least clearly-defined set of 100 users. Actual: Set varies between runs;
heavily biased toward whatever rows the storage engine returns first.
Thinking out loud: 1. "LIMIT without ORDER BY returns any 100 rows the planner finds first." 2. "That
depends on physical storage order, current index choice, parallel workers — none of it is stable." 3. "If the
user wants 'first 100 by signup', say so in SQL. If they want random, say that in SQL."
The diagnosis: LIMIT does not imply any order. The engine returns whichever rows are cheapest to
surface — often the first physical page, which clusters by insertion or by some index. The result is
unstable and biased.
The fix: For deterministic "first 100 by signup":
SELECT user_id, name, email, city
FROM users
ORDER BY signup_date, user_id
LIMIT 100;
For a random sample (Postgres):
SELECT user_id, name, email, city
FROM users TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI (1)
LIMIT 100;
Why this works: The first version defines exactly which 100 rows; the second uses an actual sampling
mechanism instead of relying on physical order.
What NOT to say: - "Add ORDER BY RAND()" — works on small tables, melts your CPU on large
ones. - "LIMIT is broken" — LIMIT is fine; the missing ORDER BY is on you.
Common follow-up: "How would you take a reproducible 1% sample week after week, with the same
users each time?"
Scenario6 · DISTINCT Applied Too Late
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Cred, Razorpay, Jupiter · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 7 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 8
A "unique customers who paid today" tile is slow and returning a too-high number. The query
uses DISTINCT but is being run against the joined transactions-and-payments view.
SELECT DISTINCT t.user_id, u.name, u.email
FROM transactions t
JOIN payments p ON p.transaction_id = t.transaction_id
JOIN users    u ON u.user_id        = t.user_id
WHERE t.txn_date = CURRENT_DATE;
Expected: Unique paying customers. Actual: Count is plausible at first glance but reconciliation against
payments-only shows it's slightly too high; query is also slow because the joins fan out before the de-
duplication.
Thinking out loud: 1. "DISTINCT is at the top — it dedupes the final result set, which is correct for the
rows we project." 2. "But the joins multiply rows before the dedupe, so we're doing extra work and the
join with users could double-fire if there are dirty user rows." 3. "Better to dedupe earlier — at the
transactions level — and join users afterward."
The diagnosis: DISTINCT works on the final projected rows. If the join with payments produces
multiple payment rows per transaction (partial payments, retries), the user_id is repeated, then de-duped.
If there's any dirty data in users (duplicate emails for same user_id), DISTINCT can hide it or, if you
include such a duplicate column, expose it. Pushing the dedupe earlier is cheaper and clearer.
The fix:
WITH paying_users AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT t.user_id
  FROM transactions t
  JOIN payments p ON p.transaction_id = t.transaction_id
  WHERE t.txn_date = CURRENT_DATE
)
SELECT pu.user_id, u.name, u.email
FROM paying_users pu
JOIN users u ON u.user_id = pu.user_id;
Why this works: We dedupe at the smallest grain (user_id only), then enrich. The final join with users
happens against a tidy unique set.
What NOT to say: - "DISTINCT is always bad" — it isn't, it just needs to be applied at the right grain. -
"Add GROUP BY everywhere" — that hides the issue rather than fixing it.
Common follow-up: "What if users itself has duplicate rows per user_id — how would your query
behave?"

Scenario7 · GROUP BY Missing A Column
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Myntra, Nykaa · Dialect: Postgres / SQL Server (MySQL
behaves differently)
The scenario:
A report "orders per city per status" works on the dev's MySQL laptop but blows up on the prod
Postgres database with an error about non-aggregated columns. The dev says "it works for me."
SELECT u.city, o.status, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders o
JOIN users  u ON u.user_id = o.user_id
GROUP BY u.city;
Expected: Per-city per-status counts. Actual (Postgres): ERROR: column "o.status" must
appear in the GROUP BY clause. (MySQL with relaxed mode): runs but returns one arbitrary
status per city.
Thinking out loud: 1. "I'm selecting o.status but only grouping by u.city — every selected non-
aggregate column must be in GROUP BY." 2. "MySQL with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY off picks a random
status per group, which is why it 'worked' on the laptop." 3. "Add o.status to GROUP BY."
The diagnosis: Standard SQL (and Postgres/SQL Server by default) requires every non-aggregate
column in the SELECT list to be in GROUP BY. MySQL historically allowed it and returned arbitrary
values, which is almost always a silent bug.
The fix:
SELECT u.city, o.status, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders o
JOIN users  u ON u.user_id = o.user_id
GROUP BY u.city, o.status;
Why this works: Now each output row corresponds to exactly one (city, status) pair, and the count is
meaningful.
What NOT to say: - "Turn off ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY in prod" — that hides the bug; don't do it. -
"Use ANY_VALUE(o.status)" — only valid when you genuinely don't care which status is picked,
which is almost never.
Common follow-up: "What if I want city totals plus per-status breakdown in one query? GROUPING
SETS?"

Scenario8 · WHERE Used Where HAVING Is Required
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Paytm · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A query meant to list cities with more than 100 orders is throwing "column COUNT(*) does not
exist" or "aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE".
SELECT u.city, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders o
JOIN users  u ON u.user_id = o.user_id
WHERE COUNT(*) > 100
GROUP BY u.city;
Expected: Cities with more than 100 orders. Actual: Syntax/semantic error about aggregates in WHERE.
Thinking out loud: 1. "WHERE filters input rows before grouping. COUNT() is only defined after
grouping." 2. "The filter on an aggregate has to be in HAVING."*
The diagnosis: WHERE runs row-by-row before aggregation; aggregates aren't available yet. HAVING
runs after GROUP BY and is allowed to filter on aggregate results.
The fix:
SELECT u.city, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders o
JOIN users  u ON u.user_id = o.user_id
GROUP BY u.city
HAVING COUNT(*) > 100;
Why this works: HAVING evaluates after the aggregation, so COUNT(*) is defined and can be
compared.
What NOT to say: - "Wrap it in a subquery" — works but unnecessarily indirect for this case. - "WHERE
and HAVING are interchangeable" — no, they really aren't.
Common follow-up: "When would you use a subquery anyway, despite HAVING being legal?"
Scenario9 · HAVING Used Where WHERE Is Better
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Meesho, Snapdeal · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 10 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 11
The scenario:
Query is correct but painfully slow. It aggregates the entire orders table by city and then filters out
cities outside India. The filter on country should have happened earlier.
SELECT u.city, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders o
JOIN users  u ON u.user_id = o.user_id
GROUP BY u.city, u.country
HAVING u.country = 'IN' AND COUNT(*) > 50;
Expected: Cities in India with more than 50 orders. Actual: Result is right but the query scans and
groups every row globally, then discards non-IN groups.
Thinking out loud: 1. " u.country = 'IN' is a non-aggregate predicate — it doesn't depend on
COUNT." 2. "In HAVING, it runs after the giant aggregation. Moving it to WHERE shrinks the input
dramatically." 3. "COUNT() > 50 must stay in HAVING — that one is genuinely an aggregate."*
The diagnosis: HAVING is meant for aggregate filters. Non-aggregate predicates belong in WHERE so
they shrink the input before grouping happens.
The fix:
SELECT u.city, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders o
JOIN users  u ON u.user_id = o.user_id
WHERE u.country = 'IN'
GROUP BY u.city
HAVING COUNT(*) > 50;
Why this works: WHERE narrows the input, the aggregation runs on a much smaller set, and HAVING
only handles the aggregate predicate.
What NOT to say: - "It's fine, HAVING does the same thing" — semantically yes, but the planner can't
always push it down. - "Add an index on city" — useful, but not the bug.
Common follow-up: "Show me the execution plan before and after the change."
Scenario10 · ON Vs WHERE In Outer Joins
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Cred, Jupiter, Niyo · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 11 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 12
Two versions of a query return different numbers. The candidate insists they're equivalent
because "filter is filter." The interviewer asks them to walk through why a particular customer
disappeared.
-- Version A
SELECT u.user_id, b.booking_id
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN bookings b
  ON b.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE b.status = 'confirmed';
-- Version B
SELECT u.user_id, b.booking_id
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN bookings b
  ON b.user_id = u.user_id
 AND b.status  = 'confirmed';
Expected: One of these preserves all users; the other doesn't. Actual: Version A behaves like an INNER
JOIN; Version B preserves users with no confirmed booking (and NULL booking_id for them).
Thinking out loud: 1. "In a LEFT JOIN, predicates in ON apply before the outer-join decision." 2. 
"Predicates in WHERE apply after the join, so they can filter out the preserved NULL-padded rows." 3. 
"Version A's WHERE on b.status drops the NULL rows — losing users with no confirmed booking."
The diagnosis: For outer joins, ON and WHERE are not interchangeable. ON shapes the match; WHERE
shapes the final filter. Filtering the right-side table in WHERE silently converts the outer join into an inner
one.
The fix: Use the appropriate semantics. Version B keeps all users. If the goal is to keep only users with a
confirmed booking, an INNER JOIN is more honest:
SELECT u.user_id, b.booking_id
FROM users u
JOIN bookings b
  ON b.user_id = u.user_id
 AND b.status  = 'confirmed';
Why this works: You're now expressing the intent explicitly — "I want users who have a confirmed
booking" — rather than writing LEFT JOIN you didn't mean.
What NOT to say: - "ON and WHERE are the same thing" — for outer joins, they're materially different. -
"Just use WHERE for everything, it's simpler" — simpler-looking, harder bug.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 12 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in

Common follow-up: "Now write me a query that returns every user and the count of their confirmed
bookings, including users with zero."
Scenario11 · Self-Join Missing The Exclusion
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Zerodha · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
Finding pairs of transactions on the same user, same amount, within a 5-minute window — meant
to flag possible duplicates. Output is dominated by rows where each transaction is paired with
itself.
SELECT a.txn_id AS a_id, b.txn_id AS b_id, a.user_id, a.amount
FROM transactions a
JOIN transactions b
  ON a.user_id = b.user_id
 AND a.amount  = b.amount
 AND ABS(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (a.created_at - b.created_at))) < 300;
Expected: Pairs of distinct transactions. Actual: Every transaction is paired with itself (a=a), and each
genuine pair appears twice (a-b and b-a).
Thinking out loud: 1. "Self-join — every row matches itself trivially because all conditions are equal to
themselves." 2. "And every pair (a, b) shows up as (b, a) too." 3. "Add a.txn_id < b.txn_id — kills
both birds."
The diagnosis: A self-join joins the table with itself, so every row trivially matches itself when the join
columns are equal to themselves. Symmetric pairs (a-b and b-a) also both appear unless you impose an
ordering predicate.
The fix:
SELECT a.txn_id AS a_id, b.txn_id AS b_id, a.user_id, a.amount
FROM transactions a
JOIN transactions b
  ON a.user_id = b.user_id
 AND a.amount  = b.amount
 AND ABS(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (a.created_at - b.created_at))) < 300
 AND a.txn_id  < b.txn_id;
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 13 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 14
Why this works: a.txn_id < b.txn_id excludes the self-match (where they're equal) and the
duplicate orientation (a-b is kept, b-a dropped).
What NOT to say: - "Use a.txn_id != b.txn_id" — still gives you the duplicate orientation. -
"Add DISTINCT" — wasteful and doesn't kill self-matches cleanly.
Common follow-up: "What if you need to find triples instead of pairs?"
Scenario12 · Missing Join Condition Produces Cartesian Product
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: any startup with junior devs · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
"Pull all orders along with the user's mobile number." The query runs for ages and returns billions
of rows on a tiny dev dataset.
SELECT o.order_id, u.mobile, o.amount
FROM orders o, users u
WHERE o.amount > 0;
Expected: One row per order. Actual: Every order × every user. Cartesian product.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Comma syntax cross-joins by default — there's no ON condition." 2. "The only
predicate is on amount; nothing links orders to their users." 3. "Need to add the join condition on
user_id."
The diagnosis: Comma in the FROM clause is a CROSS JOIN. Without a predicate linking the two
tables, you get the full cartesian product. The amount filter doesn't help — it just narrows the cartesian
rows.
The fix:
SELECT o.order_id, u.mobile, o.amount
FROM orders o
JOIN users  u ON u.user_id = o.user_id
WHERE o.amount > 0;
Why this works: Explicit JOIN ... ON ... makes the linkage obvious and forces you to think about
it. Each order matches exactly one user.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 14 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 15
What NOT to say: - "The database is slow today" — no, you wrote a cross join. - "Add LIMIT 1000"
— masks the bug and gives wrong results.
Common follow-up: "Why do we still see this bug in 2026? Should the linter catch it?"
Scenario13 · Implicit Cross Join With Three+ Tables
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Infosys, Wipro, TCS Digital · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
Old-style comma joins across three tables. The query almost works because two of the three are
linked, but the third sneaks in as a cross join.
SELECT o.order_id, u.name, p.payment_method
FROM orders o, users u, payments p
WHERE o.user_id = u.user_id;
Expected: One row per order with the user's name and the payment method. Actual: Each order-user
row is multiplied by every row in payments.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Three tables, comma-joined. Two are linked via the user_id predicate. Payments
has no join predicate." 2. "That makes payments a cross join against the other two." 3. "Need 
p.order_id = o.order_id (or whichever link exists)."
The diagnosis: With comma joins, every pair of tables must have its linking predicate in WHERE. Miss
one, and you get a partial cartesian. With explicit ANSI joins, the structure forces you to write the linkage
table-by-table.
The fix:
SELECT o.order_id, u.name, p.payment_method
FROM orders o
JOIN users    u ON u.user_id  = o.user_id
JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.order_id;
Why this works: ANSI JOIN syntax binds each predicate to a specific table pair, so it's structurally
impossible to forget one without a syntax error or obvious gap.
What NOT to say: - "Comma joins are equivalent to JOIN ON" — they are, but only when you remember
every predicate. - "Old syntax is fine" — fine for one table, dangerous for many.

Common follow-up: "Convert this codebase from comma joins to ANSI joins — how would you scope
the change?"
Scenario14 · Scalar Subquery Returning Multiple Rows
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Niyo · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A query that ran fine last quarter just started failing in prod with "more than one row returned by a
subquery used as an expression." Test data had one row per user; prod has more than one for
some users.
SELECT u.user_id,
       u.name,
       (SELECT amount FROM payments WHERE user_id = u.user_id) AS latest_payment
FROM users u;
Expected: One value per user. Actual: Error when a user has more than one payment.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Scalar subquery — must return at most one row." 2. " payments can have many
rows per user, especially in prod." 3. "Need to either aggregate (MAX, SUM) or order-and-limit to one
row."
The diagnosis: A subquery in the SELECT list must return at most one row and one column. With
multiple payments per user, the engine doesn't know which one to pick and raises an error.
The fix: For latest payment by date (Postgres):
SELECT u.user_id,
       u.name,
       (SELECT amount
        FROM payments
        WHERE user_id = u.user_id
        ORDER BY paid_at DESC
        LIMIT 1) AS latest_payment
FROM users u;
For total payments:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 16 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 17
SELECT u.user_id,
       u.name,
       (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0)
        FROM payments WHERE user_id = u.user_id) AS total_payments
FROM users u;
Why this works: Either we collapse multiple rows into one with an aggregate, or we pick exactly one
with ORDER BY + LIMIT.
What NOT to say: - "Add DISTINCT inside the subquery" — only works when the amounts happen to be
identical. - "It was fine in dev, must be a database bug" — your dev data was too thin.
Common follow-up: "Rewrite this with a LEFT JOIN and a window function instead of a correlated
subquery."
Scenario15 · IN Subquery Contains NULLs
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Walmart Labs India, Myntra · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A query "users who have placed at least one order" is mysteriously returning zero rows in one
environment. Same query, same data shape, fewer matches than expected.
SELECT user_id, name
FROM users
WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders);
Expected: All users who appear in orders. Actual: In one environment, returns no rows.
Thinking out loud: 1. "IN works fine even with NULLs if there's at least one matching non-NULL row." 2. 
"But if orders.user_id has any NULL, and the candidate value doesn't match any non-NULL row, IN
returns UNKNOWN, which WHERE treats as false." 3. "For positive IN it's usually okay — the bug is more
famous for NOT IN. But there can still be edge cases here."
The diagnosis: Positive IN mostly behaves intuitively even with NULL values in the subquery because
any true match short-circuits the comparison. The classic failure mode is when the outer value is itself
NULL, in which case NULL IN (...) is UNKNOWN and the row is dropped. If the report is looking at
"users with NULL user_id" (data-quality investigation), this scenario surfaces.
The fix:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 17 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 18
SELECT u.user_id, u.name
FROM users u
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.user_id
);
Why this works: EXISTS evaluates a clean boolean per row and is not confused by NULL columns in the
inner query.
What NOT to say: - "Just WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL" — fixes the symptom, not the habit. - "IN
doesn't work in this database" — it does, but its NULL semantics bite.
Common follow-up: "Now show me the NOT IN version of this bug, which is much worse."
Scenario16 · NOT IN With Subquery Containing NULL
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Cred, Razorpay, Jupiter, Niyo · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
"Users who have not placed any order" returns zero rows. The team is staring at it because they
know for a fact there are inactive users in the table.
SELECT user_id, name
FROM users
WHERE user_id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders);
Expected: Users with no orders. Actual: Empty result. Always.
Thinking out loud: 1. " NOT IN against a subquery — if the subquery has even one NULL, every NOT
IN comparison turns into UNKNOWN." 2. "WHERE drops UNKNOWN rows, so we get nothing." 3. 
"Three-valued logic strikes again. NOT EXISTS doesn't have this problem."
The diagnosis: x NOT IN (a, b, NULL) becomes x != a AND x != b AND x != NULL.
The last comparison is UNKNOWN. AND with UNKNOWN is at best UNKNOWN, never true. So the row
is dropped. One NULL in the subquery's projected column wipes out the entire result.
The fix: Use NOT EXISTS:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 18 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 19
SELECT u.user_id, u.name
FROM users u
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.user_id
);
Or filter NULLs out of the subquery, but NOT EXISTS is safer:
SELECT user_id, name
FROM users
WHERE user_id NOT IN (
  SELECT user_id FROM orders WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL
);
Why this works: NOT EXISTS uses per-row existence checks, which are clean booleans. The second
form removes the NULLs before NOT IN sees them.
What NOT to say: - "NOT IN is just like NOT EXISTS" — they differ exactly when NULLs are involved,
and that's the bug. - "Add IS NOT NULL to the outer WHERE" — wrong side; the NULLs are inside.
Common follow-up: "Why does NOT EXISTS not have this problem semantically?"
Scenario17 · EXISTS Vs IN Semantic Mismatch
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Paytm · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A dev rewrote an IN query as EXISTS for "performance" and now the results differ. They
swear the queries are equivalent.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 19 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 20
-- Original
SELECT user_id, name
FROM users
WHERE user_id IN (
  SELECT u2.user_id
  FROM users u2
  JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u2.user_id
  WHERE o.amount > 5000
);
-- Rewrite
SELECT user_id, name
FROM users u
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM orders o
  WHERE o.amount > 5000
);
Expected: Users with at least one order above 5000. Actual: The rewrite returns all users, because the
EXISTS subquery is uncorrelated.
Thinking out loud: 1. "EXISTS works on a correlated subquery — it has to reference the outer row." 2. 
"The rewrite has no o.user_id = u.user_id link; it just asks 'does any high-value order exist
anywhere?'" 3. "If even one exists, EXISTS is true for every outer row."
The diagnosis: EXISTS without a correlation predicate is equivalent to "is the subquery non-empty?" —
a global yes/no, not a per-user yes/no.
The fix:
SELECT u.user_id, u.name
FROM users u
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o
  WHERE o.user_id = u.user_id AND o.amount > 5000
);
Why this works: The correlation o.user_id = u.user_id makes the EXISTS check per-user.
What NOT to say: - "EXISTS is always faster than IN" — sometimes; not always; not the point here. -
"Add DISTINCT to the outer query" — doesn't fix anything.
Common follow-up: "When would you actually prefer IN over EXISTS, and vice versa?"

Scenario18 · CASE Without ELSE Silently Returns NULL
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: any analytics interview · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A status-bucketing query is showing NULL for some orders. The dev expected the unhandled
cases to fall into a default like 'other'.
SELECT order_id,
       CASE
         WHEN status = 'paid'      THEN 'success'
         WHEN status = 'refunded'  THEN 'reversed'
         WHEN status = 'failed'    THEN 'failure'
       END AS status_group
FROM orders;
Expected: Every order has a status_group. Actual: Orders with status like 'pending' or 'partial_refund'
get NULL.
Thinking out loud: 1. "CASE without ELSE returns NULL when nothing matches." 2. "I never wrote a
catch-all bucket." 3. "Need an explicit ELSE clause."
The diagnosis: A CASE expression returns NULL for any input that doesn't match any WHEN branch.
There's no implicit "else default" — you have to write one.
The fix:
SELECT order_id,
       CASE
         WHEN status = 'paid'      THEN 'success'
         WHEN status = 'refunded'  THEN 'reversed'
         WHEN status = 'failed'    THEN 'failure'
         ELSE 'other'
       END AS status_group
FROM orders;
Why this works: The ELSE branch guarantees a non-NULL value for every row, so downstream code
doesn't have to special-case NULL.
What NOT to say: - "I'll wrap it in COALESCE" — works but hides the intent; ELSE is more obvious. -
"There shouldn't be any other status values" — there always are, eventually.
Common follow-up: "How would you flag rows that hit the ELSE branch so the data team can
investigate?"

Scenario19 · BETWEEN Endpoints Confusion
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Wipro, Infosys, Capgemini · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A candidate inserted "BETWEEN 18 AND 25" for age, expecting 19-24. Output includes 18 and
25, leading to confusion downstream.
SELECT user_id, name, age
FROM users
WHERE age BETWEEN 18 AND 25;
Expected (per dev's mental model): 19-24. Actual: 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25.
Thinking out loud: 1. "BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends in SQL." 2. "If I want strict bounds, I need to
use > and < explicitly."
The diagnosis: SQL's BETWEEN x AND y is shorthand for >= x AND <= y — both endpoints
included. This is a constant source of off-by-one bugs because mathematical "between" is often read as
exclusive.
The fix:
SELECT user_id, name, age
FROM users
WHERE age > 18 AND age < 25;
Or, if 18 was the actual lower bound intent:
SELECT user_id, name, age
FROM users
WHERE age >= 18 AND age < 26;
Why this works: Explicit operators leave no ambiguity about endpoint behavior.
What NOT to say: - "BETWEEN should be exclusive, this is a SQL bug" — it's defined behavior. - "Use
NOT BETWEEN to invert" — fine for inverting, not relevant here.
Common follow-up: "Now do the same for a date range — what's the gotcha there?"

Scenario20 · Date Range Off-By-Day With Timestamps
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Swiggy · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A "March transactions" report shows 31-day numbers that don't match Finance's reconciliation.
Finance says we're including one extra day on the end, or missing one at the start, depending on
which month.
SELECT SUM(amount) AS march_total
FROM transactions
WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-03-01' AND '2026-03-31';
Expected: All March transactions. Actual: Misses transactions on 31 March after midnight (because 
'2026-03-31' is implicitly '2026-03-31 00:00:00').
Thinking out loud: 1. " created_at is a timestamp. '2026-03-31' casts to 2026-03-31
00:00:00." 2. "BETWEEN is inclusive but only up to that instant — anything after 00:00:00 on 31 March
is excluded." 3. "Need to use a half-open interval up to 1 April."
The diagnosis: Comparing a timestamp column to a date literal anchors the comparison at midnight of
that date. Inclusive BETWEEN misses everything that happens during the last day. The robust pattern is
a half-open interval >= start AND < next_day.
The fix:
SELECT SUM(amount) AS march_total
FROM transactions
WHERE created_at >= '2026-03-01'
  AND created_at <  '2026-04-01';
Why this works: Half-open intervals scale to any precision (date, timestamp, timestamptz) without subtle
inclusion bugs.
What NOT to say: - "Use BETWEEN '2026-03-01' AND '2026-03-31 23:59:59'" — misses anything in
the last second, and .999999 precision games are fragile. - "Cast created_at to DATE" — works
but kills index usage on created_at.
Common follow-up: "Now do this in the user's local timezone instead of UTC."

Scenario21 · Week Starts Monday Vs Sunday
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Cred, Swiggy, Dunzo · Dialect: Postgres / MySQL differ
The scenario:
A weekly cohort report buckets transactions by week. Numbers look off by one day at the
boundary, depending on the database.
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('week', created_at) AS wk, SUM(amount)
FROM transactions
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('week', created_at);
Expected (Finance): weeks start Sunday in their model. Actual (Postgres): weeks start Monday.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Postgres DATE_TRUNC('week', ...) follows ISO 8601 — weeks start
Monday." 2. "MySQL's WEEK() defaults to Sunday-start in many configurations." 3. "If Finance reports
against Sunday-start weeks, I need to align."
The diagnosis: Different databases (and different settings within MySQL) use different week-start
conventions. ISO 8601 says Monday; US convention often uses Sunday.
The fix (Postgres, simulate Sunday-start):
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('week', created_at + INTERVAL '1 day') - INTERVAL '1 day' AS wk_start,
       SUM(amount)
FROM transactions
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('week', created_at + INTERVAL '1 day');
Or document and standardise on ISO Monday-start and educate Finance, which is honestly cleaner.
Why this works: Adding a day before truncation shifts the week boundary by one day, then subtracting it
back gives a Sunday-anchored bucket.
What NOT to say: - "Postgres is buggy" — it's just opinionated. - "Use EXTRACT(DOW, ...) and
group on that" — doesn't bucket by week, only by day-of-week.
Common follow-up: "How would you make this configurable per tenant?"
Scenario22 · Timezone Mismatch: UTC In DB, IST In Business
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Cred · Dialect: Postgres
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 24 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 25
The scenario:
A daily revenue dashboard shows the wrong day's numbers between midnight IST and 5:30am
IST. Sales recorded "today in India" land in "yesterday in UTC", or vice versa.
SELECT DATE(created_at) AS dt, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM transactions
GROUP BY DATE(created_at);
Expected: Daily totals in IST. Actual: Daily totals in UTC, which puts post-midnight-IST transactions
onto the previous day.
Thinking out loud: 1. " created_at is timestamptz stored in UTC. DATE() casts to UTC date."
2. "India is UTC+5:30. Anything created between 18:30 UTC and 23:59 UTC is 'tomorrow' in IST." 3. 
"Need to convert to IST before truncating."
The diagnosis: By default, casting a UTC-stored timestamp to date uses UTC. Without an explicit
timezone conversion, your day boundary is in UTC, not in the user's or business's timezone.
The fix (Postgres):
SELECT (created_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date AS dt_ist,
       SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM transactions
GROUP BY (created_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date;
Why this works: AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata' shifts the stored timestamp into IST wall-clock
before we truncate to a date, so the day boundaries align with the business calendar.
What NOT to say: - "Just add 5.5 hours to created_at" — works around DST issues for India today, but
fragile. - "Store everything in IST instead" — terrible idea for multi-region apps.
Common follow-up: "What if you have customers in Singapore (UTC+8) and Dubai (UTC+4) and need
per-customer-local daily totals?"
Scenario23 · Boolean Column In WHERE Without Explicit Compare
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: any · Dialect: Postgres vs SQL Server differ
The scenario:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 25 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 26
A migration moves a query from Postgres to SQL Server. It refuses to run with "An expression of
non-boolean type specified in a context where a condition is expected."
SELECT user_id, name
FROM users
WHERE is_active;
Expected: Active users. Actual (SQL Server): error. (Postgres): works fine.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Postgres has a real boolean type; is_active alone is a valid condition." 2. 
"SQL Server doesn't have a native boolean — BIT columns need explicit comparison." 3. "Write it as 
is_active = 1 (or whatever truthy value the schema uses)."
The diagnosis: Boolean handling is not uniform across SQL dialects. Postgres allows a boolean column
as a WHERE condition directly; SQL Server requires an explicit equality against the BIT representation.
MySQL allows it because BOOLEAN is an alias for TINYINT.
The fix (portable):
SELECT user_id, name
FROM users
WHERE is_active = TRUE;   -- Postgres, MySQL
-- or
WHERE is_active = 1;      -- SQL Server (BIT)
Why this works: Explicit comparison removes the ambiguity and works consistently across dialects (with
the value adjusted per dialect).
What NOT to say: - "SQL Server is broken" — it's just stricter. - "Cast it to boolean" — SQL Server still
won't accept a non-boolean expression in a condition context.
Common follow-up: "How would you keep this portable across Postgres and SQL Server in the same
codebase?"
Scenario24 · LIKE Without A Wildcard
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: any · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 26 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 27
A search field uses LIKE but is behaving as exact match. "ravi" returns one Ravi instead of all the
Ravis.
SELECT user_id, name
FROM users
WHERE name LIKE 'ravi';
Expected: Names starting with or containing 'ravi'. Actual: Only exact match 'ravi' (case-sensitive too on
some collations).
Thinking out loud: 1. "LIKE without % or _ is functionally =." 2. "Need 'ravi%' for prefix, 
'%ravi%' for substring, '%ravi' for suffix." 3. "And consider case-insensitivity — ILIKE on
Postgres, LOWER() everywhere else."
The diagnosis: LIKE only filters by pattern; without wildcards there's no pattern to match, so it behaves
as equality. Add the wildcard you actually meant.
The fix:
-- Substring search, case-insensitive (Postgres)
SELECT user_id, name
FROM users
WHERE name ILIKE '%ravi%';
-- Portable
SELECT user_id, name
FROM users
WHERE LOWER(name) LIKE '%ravi%';
Why this works: The wildcard enables substring matching; ILIKE or LOWER() handles case
folding.
What NOT to say: - "Replace LIKE with =" — that's what it's already doing, badly. - "Add wildcards on
both sides always" — kills index usage; only do it when needed.
Common follow-up: "How would you make this search fast on a 10-million-row table?"
Scenario25 · Operator Precedence: AND Vs OR
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Flipkart, Swiggy · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 27 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 28
A query "high-value orders in Mumbai or Bangalore" is returning every Mumbai order regardless
of value, plus only the high-value Bangalore ones.
SELECT order_id, city, amount
FROM orders
WHERE city = 'Mumbai' OR city = 'Bangalore' AND amount > 10000;
Expected: High-value orders in Mumbai or Bangalore. Actual: All Mumbai orders + only Bangalore
orders above 10000.
Thinking out loud: 1. "AND binds tighter than OR." 2. "That parses as city='Mumbai' OR
(city='Bangalore' AND amount>10000)." 3. "I need explicit parentheses around the OR group."
The diagnosis: SQL's operator precedence puts AND above OR. Without parentheses, OR's branches
don't share predicates the way the dev intended.
The fix:
SELECT order_id, city, amount
FROM orders
WHERE (city = 'Mumbai' OR city = 'Bangalore')
  AND amount > 10000;
Or, cleaner:
SELECT order_id, city, amount
FROM orders
WHERE city IN ('Mumbai', 'Bangalore')
  AND amount > 10000;
Why this works: Parentheses force the OR to be evaluated first; IN makes the intent obvious and avoids
the trap entirely.
What NOT to say: - "SQL evaluates left-to-right" — no, it respects precedence. - "Always wrap
everything in parentheses" — fine instinct, but clean grouping is better.
Common follow-up: "Rewrite this with a CASE to bucket the cities and amounts."
Scenario26 · String Concatenation With NULL
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: any · Dialect: Postgres/MySQL/SQL Server differ
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 28 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 29
The scenario:
A "full name" column for a CRM export is mysteriously empty for users with no middle name. The
dev used || (or + in SQL Server) and didn't handle NULL.
-- Postgres
SELECT user_id, first_name || ' ' || middle_name || ' ' || last_name AS full_name
FROM users;
Expected: 'Ravi Kumar Sharma', or 'Ravi Sharma' if no middle name. Actual: NULL for any user with a
missing middle name (or first or last).
Thinking out loud: 1. " || propagates NULL — anything concatenated with NULL is NULL in standard
SQL." 2. "Need COALESCE per field, or use CONCAT (which treats NULL as empty in Postgres and
MySQL), or CONCAT_WS for cleaner separators."
The diagnosis: The || and + concatenation operators (and CONCAT in some dialects) treat NULL
as a poison value — any NULL operand makes the whole expression NULL. CONCAT in Postgres and
MySQL treats NULL as empty string. CONCAT_WS is even cleaner because it skips NULLs entirely.
The fix:
-- Postgres / MySQL
SELECT user_id,
       CONCAT_WS(' ', first_name, middle_name, last_name) AS full_name
FROM users;
-- SQL Server (uses + and ISNULL)
SELECT user_id,
       CONCAT_WS(' ', first_name, middle_name, last_name) AS full_name
FROM users;
Why this works: CONCAT_WS ignores NULLs and uses the separator only between actual values,
producing clean names regardless of which middle fields are missing.
What NOT to say: - "NULL is empty string, my fault for forgetting" — NULL is not empty string; that's
the bug. - "Wrap each field in COALESCE(field, '') and use ||" — works, but you'll get double-
spaces when middle_name is missing.
Common follow-up: "What if last_name is also nullable and you want it formatted as 'Last, First'?"

Scenario27 · DELETE / UPDATE Without WHERE
Tags: Difficulty: Easy (to spot), Hard (to recover from) · Asked at: every senior screen · Dialect: vendor-
agnostic
The scenario:
A migration script intended to mark inactive users ran without a WHERE clause, and every user in
the table now has is_active = false. The interviewer wants to know (a) how this could
happen, (b) how to prevent it, and (c) what's the recovery story.
-- The catastrophic version
UPDATE users SET is_active = false;
-- The intended version
UPDATE users SET is_active = false WHERE last_login_at < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '180 days';
Expected: Inactive users flagged. Actual: Every user is now flagged inactive.
Thinking out loud: 1. "UPDATE without WHERE updates every row. DELETE without WHERE deletes
every row." 2. "The query is syntactically valid; the engine has no way to know intent." 3. "Recovery
depends on backups, point-in-time recovery, or transaction logs — and prevention is far cheaper than
recovery."
The diagnosis: SQL statements update or delete the rows that match the WHERE clause. Omit WHERE
and the predicate is implicitly true, which matches every row. This is the most common cause of "I just
nuked prod" stories.
The fix (prevention, not retroactive): 1. Always write the SELECT first, verify the row set, then convert to
UPDATE/DELETE. 2. Wrap DDL/DML in an explicit transaction so you can ROLLBACK before COMMIT.
3. Configure the client to require WHERE clauses (MySQL Workbench's safe_update mode; psql
custom scripts; ORM guardrails). 4. Use LIMIT with UPDATE/DELETE (MySQL/Postgres extension) as
a belt-and-braces during ad-hoc fixes. 5. Reviewable migrations — never run ad-hoc DML in prod
consoles.
BEGIN;
SELECT count(*) FROM users WHERE last_login_at < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '180 days';
-- verify the count matches expectation
UPDATE users SET is_active = false WHERE last_login_at < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '180 days';
-- inspect a sample
SELECT user_id, is_active FROM users WHERE last_login_at < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '180 days' LIMIT 10;
COMMIT;  -- or ROLLBACK if anything looks wrong
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 30 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 31
Why this works: The transaction makes the operation reversible until COMMIT; the SELECT-first habit
verifies the predicate before destructive action; the safe-update setting in clients adds an extra net.
What NOT to say: - "I'd just restore from backup" — recovery is the last resort; if the WAL isn't archived
you'll lose data; and you'll lose every transaction between backup and disaster. - "It's the database's
fault for allowing this" — every relational DB allows this by design.
Common follow-up: "Walk me through your prod-database access policy at your last job — who had
write access, what review existed, what guardrails were in place?"
Category 1, Part B — Debug This Query: NULL & Type &
Cardinality Bugs
Part B focuses on the trickiest bug class — NULL semantics, implicit type coercion, and join cardinality
surprises. Where logic bugs are obvious once you see them (a wrong operator, a missing GROUP BY
clause), these need closer reading. The query parses, runs, returns a result, and the result looks
plausible. Then someone reconciles it against another system and the gap shows up. Each of the 27
scenarios below is a real shape that has shipped to production at an Indian product company — the kind
round-2 interviewers ask precisely because they separate candidates who can read SQL from candidates
who can debug it.
Scenario28 · The signup count that drops half the users
Asked at: Razorpay · Meesho · Difficulty: Easy · Topic: NULL bug · COUNT(col) vs COUNT(*)
The scenario: A growth analyst pings you on Slack — the daily signup dashboard shows 12,400 new
users on Monday but the product team's own onboarding log shows 22,800. Half the users are
vanishing. The query feeding the dashboard is this:
SELECT signup_date, COUNT(referral_code) AS signups
FROM users
WHERE signup_date = '2026-05-25'
GROUP BY signup_date;
Expected vs Actual: Expected 22,800 signups. Got 12,400.
Thinking out loud: 1. "COUNT with a column name only counts non-NULL values of that column — not
rows. That is the standard behaviour across every dialect." 2. " referral_code is almost certainly
nullable — most users sign up without a referral. So we are counting only referred users, not all signups."
3. "22,800 minus 12,400 is 10,400, which is exactly the kind of number you'd get if roughly 45% of users
come in organic with NULL referral_code." 4. "The query author probably wrote 
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 31 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 32
COUNT(referral_code) thinking it meant 'count this group' — a very common mistake when you
started SQL with COUNT(*) and got told 'use a column name, it is more efficient'."
Diagnosis: COUNT(expression) skips NULL values of that expression. To count rows regardless of
NULL, use COUNT(*). To count distinct non-NULL referrals, use COUNT(DISTINCT
referral_code). The query as written is asking "how many signups had a non-NULL referral_code",
not "how many signups".
Fix SQL:
SELECT signup_date, COUNT(*) AS signups
FROM users
WHERE signup_date = '2026-05-25'
GROUP BY signup_date;
Why this works: COUNT(*) counts rows — it does not look at any specific column, so NULL values
are irrelevant. This is also the path most query planners optimise hardest because it can be answered
from the index without touching the heap rows.
What NOT to say: - "COUNT(*) is slower than COUNT(column)" — false on every modern engine; often
the opposite. - "Add ISNULL around referral_code" — that just maps NULL to a sentinel, still doesn't
restore the semantics if the sentinel matches a real value.
Common follow-up: "When would COUNT(column) actually be the right call?" — when you genuinely
want the count of non-NULL values, e.g. how many users have set a profile picture.
Scenario29 · The average order value that ignores the freebies
Asked at: Flipkart · Zepto · Difficulty: Easy · Topic: NULL bug · AVG excludes NULLs
The scenario: Pricing team is debating whether to retire the free-trial SKU. They asked for the average
order value last month. Your query returns ₹847. The finance team's report says ₹612. Same time
window, same orders table.
SELECT AVG(order_value) AS avg_order_value
FROM orders
WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2026-04-01' AND '2026-04-30';
Expected vs Actual: Expected ₹612 (matches finance). Got ₹847.
Thinking out loud: 1. "AVG ignores NULLs the same way COUNT does. So if free-trial orders have
order_value = NULL, they drop out of the numerator AND the denominator." 2. "Finance is treating free
orders as ₹0 in the average, which lowers the mean. Our query is averaging only paid orders." 3. "Both
numbers are technically correct — but they answer different questions. The ambiguity sits in NULL vs 0."
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 32 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 33
4. "For 'business-level AOV' the free orders should be ₹0, not absent. We have to decide which
interpretation the dashboard owner wants."
Diagnosis: AVG(order_value) computes SUM(non-null values) / COUNT(non-null
values). NULL rows are silently dropped from both. If business defines AOV as "total revenue divided
by total orders including freebies", you have to coerce NULLs to 0.
Fix SQL (assuming finance's definition is the business truth):
SELECT AVG(COALESCE(order_value, 0)) AS avg_order_value
FROM orders
WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2026-04-01' AND '2026-04-30';
Why this works: COALESCE converts NULL to 0 before AVG sees the value. Now free orders count in

What NOT to say: - "AVG is broken" — it is doing exactly what the spec says. - "We should filter out free
orders" — that changes the business question entirely.
Common follow-up: "What if order_value is sometimes NULL because the row is mid-checkout, not
because it's a freebie?" — then you have a data quality problem, not an aggregate problem, and
COALESCE will mask it.
Scenario30 · The SUM that returned NULL instead of zero
Asked at: Cred · PhonePe · Difficulty: Easy · Topic: NULL bug · SUM over all-NULL set
The scenario: A merchant onboarding flow shows "Lifetime refunds: NULL" on the dashboard instead of
"₹0" for new merchants. The frontend now crashes because it tries to render NULL as a currency string.
SELECT merchant_id, SUM(refund_amount) AS lifetime_refunds
FROM refunds
WHERE merchant_id = 8821
GROUP BY merchant_id;
Expected vs Actual: Expected ₹0 for a merchant with no refunds. Got NULL — or worse, no row at all if
the merchant has zero refunds.
Thinking out loud: 1. "SUM over an empty or all-NULL set returns NULL across every major dialect —
not 0. That's the SQL standard." 2. "If the merchant has no rows in the refunds table at all, the GROUP
BY produces zero rows. The frontend sees a missing row, not NULL." 3. "If the merchant has rows but
every refund_amount is NULL, SUM returns NULL. Two different bug paths, same symptom." 4. "Right fix
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 33 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 34
has two parts: COALESCE the SUM, and make sure we return a row even when there are no refunds.

Diagnosis: Two NULL traps stacked. SUM of an empty/NULL set yields NULL; missing GROUP key
produces no row at all. Frontend treats both as errors.
Fix SQL:
SELECT m.merchant_id,
       COALESCE(SUM(r.refund_amount), 0) AS lifetime_refunds
FROM merchants m

WHERE m.merchant_id = 8821
GROUP BY m.merchant_id;
Why this works: LEFT JOIN guarantees a row for the merchant even if no refunds exist. COALESCE
turns the NULL SUM into 0. Frontend gets a clean ₹0.
What NOT to say: - "SUM should return 0 by default" — argue with the standard, not the interviewer. -
"Add IF EXISTS" — that's procedural thinking, not SQL.
Common follow-up: "How would you do this if your engine doesn't have COALESCE?" — ISNULL
(SQL Server), NVL (Oracle), or IFNULL (MySQL). Same semantics, different name.
Scenario31 · The dedup that didn't dedup
Asked at: Swiggy · Myntra · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: NULL bug · NULL = NULL is NULL
The scenario: You're cleaning up a customer table that was loaded twice. You write a "find duplicates"
query joining the table to itself on the natural key. It returns far fewer dupes than the count of suspicious
rows. Manual inspection shows obvious duplicates the query missed.
SELECT a.customer_id, b.customer_id
FROM customers a
JOIN customers b
  ON a.email = b.email
 AND a.phone = b.phone
 AND a.dob   = b.dob
WHERE a.customer_id < b.customer_id;
Expected vs Actual: Expected ~14,000 duplicate pairs (count of suspicious rows). Got ~6,200.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Duplicates we are missing all share one trait — they have NULL in at least one of
email, phone or dob." 2. "In SQL, NULL = NULL is not TRUE, it is NULL. A join predicate that
evaluates to NULL is treated as FALSE for the purpose of including the row." 3. "So any duplicate where
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 34 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 35
both rows have NULL phone is silently dropped from the join." 4. "Fix is IS NOT DISTINCT FROM in
Postgres, or a manual (a.x = b.x OR (a.x IS NULL AND b.x IS NULL)) in dialects that lack
it."
Diagnosis: SQL uses three-valued logic. NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, which join
predicates treat as "no match". Genuine duplicates that share NULL phone/dob/email never pair up.
Fix SQL (Postgres):
SELECT a.customer_id, b.customer_id
FROM customers a
JOIN customers b
  ON a.email IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.email
 AND a.phone IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.phone
 AND a.dob   IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.dob
WHERE a.customer_id < b.customer_id;
Why this works: IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is NULL-safe equality. NULL matches NULL, and any
value matches itself. Standard SQL since SQL:2003, supported in Postgres natively, and MySQL has the
equivalent <=> operator.
What NOT to say: - "Just put NOT NULL on the columns" — fine for new data, doesn't fix the dirty rows
you already have. - "Use COALESCE to map NULL to empty string" — works but breaks down when
empty string is itself a valid value (it usually is for phone).
Common follow-up: "In MySQL, what's the operator?" — <=>, the NULL-safe equal. Same behaviour,
ugly syntax.
Scenario32 · The "!=" filter that hides half the bugs

The scenario: Compliance team asks for "all orders where the order status is not CANCELLED" — they

Thinking out loud: 1. " status != 'CANCELLED' evaluates to NULL when status IS NULL. Three-
valued logic again — NULL in a WHERE clause is treated as FALSE, so those rows drop out." 2. 
"Compliance asked for 'not cancelled', which in English includes 'no status yet'. SQL doesn't agree." 3. 
"Fix is to be explicit — status IS DISTINCT FROM 'CANCELLED' in Postgres, or (status !=

What NOT to say: - "The data is wrong, fix the data" — sometimes true, but the query has to be
defensible regardless. - "NOT IN is safer than !=" — opposite is true; NOT IN with a NULL in the list
returns nothing.
Common follow-up: "What's the bug with WHERE status NOT IN ('CANCELLED', NULL)?" —
returns zero rows. NOT IN with a NULL is equivalent to FALSE for every row.

Scenario34 · The foreign key that doesn't enforce anything

The scenario: A new junior dev claims "our orders.customer_id has a foreign key to customers, so every

in customers — guests drop out." 3. "Fix is a LEFT JOIN if guest orders are expected, or a NOT NULL

Scenario35 · The unique index that allowed three NULLs
Asked at: Salesforce · Microsoft India · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: NULL bug · UNIQUE allows multiple
NULLs (dialect-specific)
The scenario: A migration team is moving customer data from SQL Server to Postgres. The Postgres
side has a UNIQUE index on email. They successfully load a dataset that has 12,000 rows with NULL
email. The same load on SQL Server fails with a unique constraint violation on the second NULL.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 38 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 39
CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE
);
-- Insert 12,000 rows with email = NULL. 
-- Works fine on Postgres + MySQL + Oracle.
-- Fails on SQL Server after the second NULL.
Expected vs Actual: Engineer expected UNIQUE behaviour to be consistent across engines. It is not.
Thinking out loud: 1. "This is one of the most famous dialect divergences. Most engines treat NULL as
'unknown', so two NULLs are not 'equal' and don't violate uniqueness." 2. "SQL Server is the odd one
out — its default unique index treats NULL as a value and allows only one NULL row. Filtered indexes can
change this." 3. "Postgres 15+ added the NULLS NOT DISTINCT clause to flip the behaviour the other
way. So you can configure it either side." 4. "For migration scripts, the safe move is to make email NOT
NULL with a sentinel — or to be explicit about the desired NULL semantics."
Diagnosis: SQL standard says NULLs are not equal, so a UNIQUE index should permit multiple NULLs.
Postgres / MySQL / Oracle / SQLite follow the standard. SQL Server historically deviates — only one
NULL allowed per unique index.
Fix SQL (Postgres-style — explicit):
-- Standard behaviour (multiple NULLs allowed)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX customers_email_uniq ON customers (email);
-- Strict behaviour (only one NULL row)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX customers_email_uniq ON customers (email) NULLS NOT DISTINCT;
For SQL Server, a filtered index gets the standard behaviour:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX customers_email_uniq
  ON customers (email)
  WHERE email IS NOT NULL;
Why this works: Explicit NULL handling at index creation time makes the semantics match across
engines.
What NOT to say: - "Postgres is broken" — it follows the standard; SQL Server doesn't. - "Just don't
allow NULL emails" — sometimes that's the right call, but you have to know it's a choice.
Common follow-up: "What's the right design — allow NULL emails or force a sentinel?" — usually allow
NULL, because email is genuinely optional for many users.

Scenario36 · The dedup join that needed IS DISTINCT FROM
Asked at: Atlassian · Postman · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: NULL bug · NULL-safe equality fix
The scenario: A data engineer is auditing a CDC pipeline that compares "current snapshot" against
"previous snapshot" to detect changes. The pipeline reports zero changes for some rows, but manual
inspection shows the rows were updated — the change was specifically that a nullable column went
from NULL to 'something' or vice versa.
SELECT cur.id
FROM current_snapshot cur
JOIN previous_snapshot prev ON cur.id = prev.id
WHERE cur.middle_name = prev.middle_name
  AND cur.address_line2 = prev.address_line2;
-- Pipeline says: "These rows are unchanged."
-- Reality: middle_name was NULL in prev, now 'Kumar' in cur.
Expected vs Actual: Expected to detect "no change" when columns truly match. Actually flagging "no
change" any time a NULL flip happens, because NULL = anything is NULL (treated as false), and
the row falls out of the "unchanged" set — but the bigger sibling query that flags "changed" rows uses
the same = operator and also misses them. Both halves of the diff lose these rows.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Plain equality on nullable columns is broken in both directions — = says 'not
equal' when one side is NULL, even if the other side is also NULL." 2. "The right operator for CDC diffs is 
IS DISTINCT FROM / IS NOT DISTINCT FROM. It treats NULL = NULL as 'same' and NULL =
value as 'different'." 3. "Without it, you have to write (a = b OR (a IS NULL AND b IS NULL))
for every nullable column — verbose and easy to forget." 4. "This pattern shows up in any data-quality /
replication / diff-detection scenario where nullable columns flip."
Diagnosis: = is not NULL-safe. CDC pipelines that diff snapshots with nullable columns must use IS
DISTINCT FROM / IS NOT DISTINCT FROM to avoid silent miscounts.
Fix SQL:
-- Rows that are genuinely unchanged across all monitored columns:
SELECT cur.id
FROM current_snapshot cur
JOIN previous_snapshot prev ON cur.id = prev.id
WHERE cur.middle_name    IS NOT DISTINCT FROM prev.middle_name
  AND cur.address_line2 IS NOT DISTINCT FROM prev.address_line2;
Why this works: IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is NULL-safe. (NULL, NULL) → same. (NULL,
'Kumar') → distinct. ('A', 'A') → same.
What NOT to say: - "Just COALESCE everything to empty string" — collisions with real empty strings. -
"It's an edge case" — for nullable columns, NULL flips are the common case in CDC.

Scenario37 · The COALESCE that doesn't exist on this engine
Asked at: Oracle India · TCS BFSI · Difficulty: Easy · Topic: Dialect mismatch · COALESCE vs ISNULL
vs NVL
The scenario: A team is porting a Postgres reporting query into an Oracle environment. The query
parses fine on Postgres but throws ORA-00904: invalid identifier: ISNULL on Oracle. The

-- Original (Postgres-leaning):
SELECT customer_id, ISNULL(loyalty_points, 0) AS points

Expected vs Actual: Expected the same NULL-default function name everywhere. It does not exist.
Thinking out loud: 1. "NULL-default functions are one of the worst dialect tangles in SQL. Every engine
ships its own name." 2. "COALESCE is the standard, supported across Postgres, MySQL, Oracle, SQL
Server, BigQuery, Snowflake. Always pick COALESCE for portability." 3. "ISNULL is SQL Server. IFNULL

standard.

SELECT customer_id, COALESCE(loyalty_points, 0) AS points
FROM customers;
Why this works: COALESCE is in the SQL standard and supported by every major engine — Postgres,
MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server, SQLite, BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift.
What NOT to say: - "ISNULL works everywhere" — only on SQL Server and as a different operator in
Postgres (expr IS NULL returns boolean). - "Use a CASE statement, more portable" — actually less
so, since CASE is portable but so is COALESCE, and CASE is verbose.
Common follow-up: "What's the difference between COALESCE and NVL in Oracle?" — NVL is 2-arg
only and forces type coercion of both args; COALESCE short-circuits and is N-arg.

Scenario38 · The NULLIF that erased the wrong rows
Asked at: Walmart Labs · Target India · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: NULL bug · NULLIF direction
The scenario: A report wants to treat discount_pct = 0 rows as "no discount" (NULL) so they're
excluded from AVG. The query author writes:
SELECT product_id, AVG(NULLIF(discount_pct, 0)) AS avg_real_discount
FROM line_items
GROUP BY product_id;
A reviewer says "this looks backwards — NULLIF returns NULL when the column IS NULL, right?"
Confusion follows.
Expected vs Actual: Both devs are unsure which direction NULLIF goes. The query is actually correct,
but the discussion reveals a common mental model bug. The reviewer wants to use NULLIF to replace
NULLs with a sentinel — which is the wrong function entirely.
Thinking out loud: 1. "NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL when a equals b; otherwise returns a. It is the
OPPOSITE of what people often expect from the name." 2. "NULLIF(discount_pct, 0) means 'treat 0 as
NULL'. That is what the report wants — exclude zero-discount rows from AVG." 3. "What the reviewer is
thinking of is COALESCE, which fills in NULLs. NULLIF creates NULLs." 4. "The mnemonic: NULLIF(a, b)
= NULL if a = b. Read it as a conditional, not a fallback."
Diagnosis: The query is correct; the reviewer's mental model of NULLIF is wrong. NULLIF creates NULL
when two values match; COALESCE replaces NULL with a default. They are inverses.
Fix SQL (it is already correct, but spelled out):
-- "Treat zero as missing" — for AVG that should ignore zero discounts:
SELECT product_id, AVG(NULLIF(discount_pct, 0)) AS avg_real_discount
FROM line_items
GROUP BY product_id;
-- "Fill missing with zero" — for SUM that needs zero-default:
SELECT product_id, SUM(COALESCE(discount_pct, 0)) AS total_discount
FROM line_items
GROUP BY product_id;
Why this works: NULLIF and COALESCE are complementary. NULLIF is for masking a known sentinel;
COALESCE is for filling in missing values.
What NOT to say: - "NULLIF is for replacing NULLs" — exactly backwards. - "We need both NULLIF
and IFNULL on every column" — not without a reason; default to COALESCE.
Common follow-up: "What does NULLIF(NULL, NULL) return?" — NULL. Because NULL is never equal
to NULL, the comparison fails, and NULLIF returns the first arg, which is NULL.

Scenario39 · The CASE that drops UNKNOWN cases
Asked at: Adobe India · Intuit · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: NULL bug · Three-valued logic in CASE
The scenario: A loyalty programme classifies customers into Gold / Silver / Bronze based on 
lifetime_value. The categorisation query returns three buckets but a separate count shows 4,200
customers that don't appear in any bucket.
SELECT customer_id,
       CASE
         WHEN lifetime_value >= 100000 THEN 'Gold'
         WHEN lifetime_value >= 25000  THEN 'Silver'
         WHEN lifetime_value >= 0      THEN 'Bronze'
       END AS tier
FROM customers;
Expected vs Actual: Expected every customer to land in one tier. 4,200 rows return NULL tier — they
have lifetime_value IS NULL (never made a purchase).
Thinking out loud: 1. "CASE evaluates conditions top-down. The first one that's TRUE wins." 2. "If 
lifetime_value IS NULL, then NULL >= 100000 returns NULL, not TRUE. Same for the other
two branches." 3. "With no TRUE branch and no ELSE, CASE returns NULL. So nulls leak through." 4. 
"Fix is an ELSE clause to catch them — usually 'Unranked' or 'New'."
Diagnosis: Three-valued logic. NULL >= anything is NULL, not TRUE. CASE with no matching WHEN
and no ELSE returns NULL.
Fix SQL:
SELECT customer_id,
       CASE
         WHEN lifetime_value IS NULL    THEN 'New'
         WHEN lifetime_value >= 100000  THEN 'Gold'
         WHEN lifetime_value >= 25000   THEN 'Silver'
         WHEN lifetime_value >= 0       THEN 'Bronze'
         ELSE 'Other'
       END AS tier
FROM customers;
Why this works: Explicit NULL check first; explicit ELSE catches negative or unexpected values. Every
row gets a non-NULL label.
What NOT to say: - "Add WHERE lifetime_value IS NOT NULL" — drops the customers entirely, which is
worse for the report. - "CASE is non-deterministic with NULL" — it is deterministic; it's just that NULL
falls through.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 43 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 44
Common follow-up: "Why does ELSE matter even if you think you've covered every case?" — defensive
coding. ELSE catches the bugs you didn't anticipate (negatives, NaN in some engines, unexpected
NULL).
Scenario40 · The ORDER BY that puts NULLs in the wrong place
Asked at: Snowflake India · Databricks · Difficulty: Easy · Topic: NULL bug · NULLS FIRST/LAST default
differs
The scenario: A dashboard built on Postgres got ported to Oracle. The "latest signups" list shows new
users sorted by signup date desc. On MySQL it showed real users at the top. On Oracle the top 50 are
all "NULL signup date" placeholder rows.
SELECT customer_id, signup_date
FROM customers
ORDER BY signup_date DESC
LIMIT 50;
Expected vs Actual: Same query, two engines, different sort. Postgres puts NULLs last by default with
DESC; Oracle puts NULLs first by default with DESC.
Thinking out loud: 1. "ORDER BY's NULL handling default varies by engine. Postgres treats NULLs as
'larger than anything', so DESC sorts them first. Oracle does the same. MySQL treats NULLs as
'smaller'." 2. "Wait — Postgres puts NULLs first with DESC, last with ASC. MySQL is the opposite. SQL
Server is yet another flavour." 3. "Always be explicit with NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST when sorting
nullable columns. Don't trust the default." 4. "For 'latest signups', we want real dates first and NULLs last
— so NULLS LAST."
Diagnosis: NULL ordering default is dialect-specific. The portable fix is to specify NULLS FIRST or 
NULLS LAST explicitly.
Fix SQL:
SELECT customer_id, signup_date
FROM customers
ORDER BY signup_date DESC NULLS LAST
LIMIT 50;
Why this works: NULLS LAST forces NULL rows to the bottom regardless of dialect default.
Supported by Postgres, Oracle, SQLite. MySQL doesn't support the keyword but ORDER BY
signup_date IS NULL, signup_date DESC achieves the same result.
What NOT to say: - "NULLS LAST works everywhere" — MySQL needs a different syntax. - "Just
exclude NULL rows" — changes the semantic; the dashboard might still want to count them.

Common follow-up: "What's the MySQL workaround?" — ORDER BY signup_date IS NULL ASC,
signup_date DESC. The first key sorts NULLs to the end (since NULL IS NULL = 1, non-NULL IS
NULL = 0).
Scenario41 · The integer join key that became a string
Asked at: ThoughtWorks · Infosys · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Type bug · Implicit cast int → varchar
disables index
The scenario: A reporting query that used to run in 80ms now takes 14 seconds after a schema
migration. The migration moved customer_id from INT to VARCHAR in the new 
customer_events table (to support multi-tenant IDs). The join in the report still works but is dog
slow.
SELECT c.customer_name, e.event_type, e.event_time
FROM customers c
JOIN customer_events e ON c.customer_id = e.customer_id
WHERE c.region = 'IN';
-- customers.customer_id is INT
-- customer_events.customer_id is now VARCHAR(64)
Expected vs Actual: Expected the existing index on customer_events.customer_id (varchar) to
handle the join. Actual plan shows a full scan of customer_events with implicit cast on every row.
Thinking out loud: 1. "When the join column types differ, SQL coerces one side to the other. MySQL and
SQL Server typically coerce silently (column side cast to varchar or int — which kills the index). Postgres
actually errors out (operator does not exist: integer = character varying) unless an
explicit cast is provided." 2. "That cast happens per row of the table being scanned. If the cast is on the
indexed side, the index becomes unusable for the join." 3. "Postgres explain plan will literally show 
(customer_id)::integer = c.customer_id — that ::integer wraps the indexed column." 4. "Fix
is to cast on the unindexed side, or align the column types at the schema level."
Diagnosis: Implicit type coercion in join predicates often disables index usage because the indexed
expression is wrapped in a cast that the planner can't match to the raw index.
Fix SQL (short-term):
SELECT c.customer_name, e.event_type, e.event_time
FROM customers c
JOIN customer_events e ON CAST(c.customer_id AS VARCHAR(64)) = e.customer_id
WHERE c.region = 'IN';
Long-term fix is to align column types — either both INT or both VARCHAR — and rebuild the index.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 45 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 46
Why this works: Casting the smaller, unindexed side (customers.customer_id) preserves the index on
the larger side (customer_events.customer_id).
What NOT to say: - "Implicit casts are free, the planner handles it" — they are not free; they force per-
row evaluation and disable index seeks. - "Add a function-based index" — sometimes works but is a
workaround for a schema bug.
Common follow-up: "How would you detect this without staring at the plan?" — look for Seq Scan
(Postgres) or Full Table Scan (Oracle/MySQL) on a column that has an index.
Scenario42 · The varchar filter that triggers a full scan
Asked at: Goldman Sachs · Morgan Stanley · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Type bug · varchar → int
implicit cast
The scenario: A user-facing report filters on account_number = 12345 where account_number
is VARCHAR(20). The query is slow despite a B-tree index on account_number. Engineer claims
"the index isn't being used".

FROM accounts
WHERE account_number = 12345;
-- account_number is VARCHAR(20), indexed
Expected vs Actual: Expected index seek (sub-ms). Got full table scan (8s).
Thinking out loud: 1. " account_number is varchar but the literal is an int. SQL has to coerce one
side. Standard rule: string is promoted to int." 2. "That means every row gets

account_number can't parse as int (e.g. 'A12345') will throw at runtime in some engines, or silently drop
in others." 4. "Fix is to quote the literal: account_number = '12345'. Index seek restored."
Diagnosis: Implicit varchar → int coercion. Engine wraps the indexed column in a cast, disabling the
index. Also a correctness risk if any rows fail to parse.
Fix SQL:
SELECT *
FROM accounts
WHERE account_number = '12345';
Why this works: String literal matches string column directly. No cast, index is usable, sub-ms seek.

What NOT to say: - "The engine should know what we mean" — engines do exactly what the spec says.
