Scenario43 · The SUM that overflowed an INT
Asked at: Tata 1mg · Pharmeasy · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Type bug · Numeric overflow on aggregate
The scenario: A revenue report that ran cleanly for two years started returning negative numbers in
January 2026 after a strong holiday quarter. The dev checks the query — it's a plain SUM over a
transactions table. There are no negative transactions.
SELECT SUM(amount_paise) AS total_revenue_paise
FROM transactions
WHERE quarter = '2025-Q4';
-- amount_paise is INT (4 bytes, signed)
-- Q4 total exceeded 2^31 - 1 = 2.147 billion paise = ₹21.47 crore
Expected vs Actual: Expected ~₹35 crore total revenue. Got a negative number — classic 32-bit signed
integer overflow.
Thinking out loud: 1. "INT in most engines is 4 bytes, signed — range about ±2.1 billion. Summing many
positive INTs can exceed that range." 2. "In paise, ₹21.47 crore is the overflow point. We just crossed it."
3. "Postgres throws an integer overflow exception. MySQL silently wraps to negative. SQL Server's
behaviour depends on ARITHABORT setting." 4. "Fix: cast to BIGINT before SUM, or use
SUM(amount_paise * 1.0) to promote to NUMERIC. BIGINT is cleaner."
Diagnosis: SUM of INT stays INT in many engines (MySQL especially). Aggregate can overflow the INT
range. Some engines warn / throw, some silently wrap.
Fix SQL:
SELECT SUM(CAST(amount_paise AS BIGINT)) AS total_revenue_paise
FROM transactions
WHERE quarter = '2025-Q4';
Why this works: Each value is promoted to 8-byte signed integer (range ±9.2 × 10^18) before the
running total accumulates. No realistic financial sum reaches that range.

What NOT to say: - "SUM auto-promotes to BIGINT" — true on Postgres for SUM(int) → bigint, but not
universally; MySQL keeps the type. - "We should never store paise as INT" — long-term yes, but the bug
is in the query right now.
Common follow-up: "How would you store currency safely going forward?" — DECIMAL(19,4) or
BIGINT for paise, never FLOAT. And cast on aggregate to be defensive.
Scenario44 · The division that lost the decimal
Asked at: Zoho · Freshworks · Difficulty: Easy · Topic: Type bug · Integer division precision loss
The scenario: A success-rate report computes successful_orders / total_orders. The result
is always 0 or 1, never a fraction. Dev expected percentages like 0.87 or 0.92.
SELECT product_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'SUCCESS' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*) AS success_rate
FROM orders
GROUP BY product_id;
Expected vs Actual: Expected 0.0 to 1.0 floats. Got 0 or 1 (integer truncation).
Thinking out loud: 1. "Both numerator and denominator are integers. Integer / integer in most engines
returns integer with truncation." 2. "In Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server — integer division drops the
decimal. Only when one side is float/numeric does the result include decimals." 3. "Fix: multiply
numerator by 1.0, or cast one side to NUMERIC." 4. "A common trap because the SQL parses fine and
returns plausible-looking values. Test on a known product first."
Diagnosis: Integer division. To get a fractional result, one operand must be a non-integer type.
Fix SQL:
SELECT product_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'SUCCESS' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 1.0 / COUNT(*) AS success_rate
FROM orders
GROUP BY product_id;
Or explicit cast:
CAST(SUM(...) AS NUMERIC) / COUNT(*) AS success_rate
Why this works: Multiplying by 1.0 promotes the numerator to NUMERIC; the division then returns
NUMERIC with the decimals intact.

What NOT to say: - "Just round to 2 decimals" — there are no decimals to round; the truncation already

Common follow-up: "What's the difference between NUMERIC, DECIMAL and FLOAT for this?" —
NUMERIC/DECIMAL are exact; FLOAT is binary approximation and inappropriate for money or rates that

Scenario45 · The DATE column that won't match the TIMESTAMP
Asked at: Airbnb India · Booking.com · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Type bug · DATE vs TIMESTAMP
mismatch
The scenario: A check-in report joins bookings.check_in_date (DATE) to events.event_ts
(TIMESTAMP) on the assumption that they represent the same day. It returns zero matched rows even
though the data clearly aligns.
SELECT b.booking_id, e.event_type
FROM bookings b
JOIN events e ON b.check_in_date = e.event_ts;
-- check_in_date is DATE: 2026-05-25
-- event_ts is TIMESTAMP: 2026-05-25 14:32:11
Expected vs Actual: Expected matches on same calendar day. Got zero rows.
Thinking out loud: 1. "DATE has no time component, TIMESTAMP does. When SQL compares them,
DATE gets promoted to TIMESTAMP at 00:00:00." 2. "So 2026-05-25 becomes 2026-05-25
00:00:00. An event at 2026-05-25 14:32:11 is not equal to that. No match." 3. "Fix is to truncate
the TIMESTAMP side to DATE before comparing — DATE(e.event_ts) in MySQL/Postgres, 
CAST(e.event_ts AS DATE) portable." 4. "Beware of timezone — DATE(event_ts) uses the session
timezone, which may not be IST."
Diagnosis: Comparing DATE and TIMESTAMP promotes DATE to midnight TIMESTAMP. Real-time
events never match midnight exactly.
Fix SQL:
SELECT b.booking_id, e.event_type
FROM bookings b
JOIN events e ON b.check_in_date = CAST(e.event_ts AS DATE);
Why this works: Both sides are now DATE. Calendar-day matching works. Trade-off: the cast on 
event_ts will disable any index on that column unless you have a functional index on 
CAST(event_ts AS DATE).

hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 50
What NOT to say: - "DATE and TIMESTAMP are interchangeable" — they are not; only the date part
overlaps. - "Concatenate the date with ' 00:00:00'" — same wrong result, more typing.
Common follow-up: "How would you index this join efficiently?" — CREATE INDEX ON events
((CAST(event_ts AS DATE))); — a functional index on the cast expression.
Scenario46 · The timezone bug that shifted Diwali sales to Thursday
Asked at: Nykaa · Tata CLiQ · Difficulty: Hard · Topic: Type bug · Timezone arithmetic
The scenario: A festival-sales report shows the Diwali campaign starting on Thursday instead of
Wednesday. Marketing insists they pushed it live on Wednesday at 8pm IST. The SQL uses naive 
TIMESTAMP (no timezone).
SELECT campaign_id, COUNT(*) AS clicks
FROM clicks
WHERE click_ts >= '2026-11-04 00:00:00'
  AND click_ts <  '2026-11-05 00:00:00'
  AND campaign_id = 'DIWALI-2026';
-- Server is UTC. Click events are stored in UTC TIMESTAMPs.
-- Marketing pushed at 2026-11-04 20:00:00 IST = 14:30:00 UTC.
-- The first hour of clicks (until midnight IST) bleeds into the next UTC day.
Expected vs Actual: Expected Wednesday Nov 4 to show 8pm onwards. Wednesday looks empty;
clicks appear on Thursday.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Click timestamps are stored UTC. The filter uses literal '2026-11-04 00:00:00'
which the engine interprets as UTC (server tz). So the bucket is Nov 4 UTC = Nov 4 5:30am IST onwards.
Marketing started at 8pm IST = 14:30 UTC, which is in the Nov 4 bucket — but ends at Nov 5 18:29:59
IST." 2. "The 'Wednesday in India' window the marketing team means is 2026-11-04 00:00:00 IST
to 2026-11-05 00:00:00 IST = 2026-11-03 18:30:00 UTC to 2026-11-04 18:30:00
UTC. The query filters a different window." 3. "Fix is to convert IST literals to UTC explicitly, or to use
TIMESTAMPTZ everywhere and let the engine handle the conversion." 4. "For India this is a 5h30 offset
bug — half a day's data lands in the wrong bucket if your filter window doesn't account for it."
Diagnosis: Naive timestamps + UTC-stored data + IST-meaning filter literals. The arithmetic looks right
but applies to the wrong day boundaries.
Fix SQL (Postgres with TIMESTAMPTZ):
SELECT campaign_id, COUNT(*) AS clicks
FROM clicks
WHERE click_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2026-11-04 00:00:00' AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata'
  AND click_ts <  TIMESTAMP '2026-11-05 00:00:00' AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata'
  AND campaign_id = 'DIWALI-2026';
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 50 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 51
Why this works: Filter literals are explicitly anchored in IST and converted to UTC for comparison
against the UTC-stored column. Day boundaries align with India's calendar day.
What NOT to say: - "Just add 5.5 hours to the literal" — works once, breaks for DST transitions in other
countries, and breaks if the server timezone changes. - "Store in IST" — creates the opposite problem
for users in other timezones; UTC is the right storage choice.
Common follow-up: "Why use TIMESTAMPTZ over TIMESTAMP for new tables?" — TIMESTAMPTZ
stores a UTC instant and lets each session render in its own timezone; TIMESTAMP is naive and prone to
exactly this class of bug.
Scenario47 · The CHAR column that won't match the VARCHAR
Asked at: Bank of America · IBM India · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Type bug · CHAR padding
The scenario: An old core-banking table uses CHAR(10) for IFSC codes. A newer microservice uses 
VARCHAR(20). A join between the two returns surprisingly few matches in some dialects, even though
the IFSC values are correct in both.
SELECT a.account_no, b.branch_name
FROM accounts a
JOIN branches b ON a.ifsc_code = b.ifsc_code;
-- accounts.ifsc_code is CHAR(10), padded with spaces: 'HDFC0001234'
-- branches.ifsc_code is VARCHAR(20), no padding:     'HDFC0001234'
Expected vs Actual: Some IFSC matches drop, depending on dialect. Behaviour is dialect-specific and
dangerous.
Thinking out loud: 1. "CHAR(n) is fixed-width — values shorter than n are padded with trailing spaces.
VARCHAR stores the exact length." 2. "In Postgres, comparison of CHAR(10) with VARCHAR strips the
CHAR padding silently — usually you get a match." 3. "In MySQL, the default behaviour also pads. In
SQL Server, it depends on the comparison context and ANSI_PADDING setting." 4. "The unsafe bet is to
assume any dialect handles this transparently. Trim explicitly when joining CHAR with VARCHAR."
Diagnosis: CHAR padding semantics vary by engine. Some strip on comparison, some don't. Cross-
engine portability requires explicit trimming.
Fix SQL:
SELECT a.account_no, b.branch_name
FROM accounts a
JOIN branches b ON RTRIM(a.ifsc_code) = b.ifsc_code;
Or convert the schema:

ALTER TABLE accounts ALTER COLUMN ifsc_code TYPE VARCHAR(11);
Why this works: RTRIM strips trailing spaces explicitly, making the join behave identically across
engines. Schema-level fix removes the trap entirely.
What NOT to say: - "VARCHAR is always better than CHAR" — for fixed-length codes (IFSC, country
codes), CHAR can be marginally more efficient if used consistently. - "Comparison ignores trailing
spaces by SQL standard" — true for the LIKE operator but not always for = across engines.
Common follow-up: "What's the difference between CHAR(10) and VARCHAR(10) storage in Postgres?"
— Postgres internally stores both as varlena; the only difference is the padding semantics, not storage.
Scenario48 · The case-sensitive join that misses 'Mumbai' vs 'mumbai'
Asked at: Make My Trip · Goibibo · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Type bug · Collation mismatch
The scenario: A reporting query joins searches.destination_city to cities.city_name.
The result set is much smaller than expected. Manual check shows that the source data has cities in
mixed case ('Mumbai', 'mumbai', 'MUMBAI') while the lookup table is title case ('Mumbai').

JOIN cities c ON s.destination_city = c.city_name;

that key — so for hot joins, a case-insensitive collation or generated lowercase column is better."
Diagnosis: Collation determines case sensitivity at the column or expression level. Default behaviours
differ across engines and even across MySQL versions.
Fix SQL:
SELECT s.search_id, c.country
FROM searches s
JOIN cities c ON LOWER(s.destination_city) = LOWER(c.city_name);

Scenario49 · The emoji in the customer name that breaks the join
Asked at: WhatsApp India · ShareChat · Difficulty: Hard · Topic: Type bug · Encoding mismatch (utf8 vs

The scenario: A MySQL-based customer service tool joins WhatsApp display names to internal user

Thinking out loud: 1. "MySQL's utf8 charset is the historical bug — it supports only the basic

Scenario50 · The double-counted GMV from a one-to-many join
Asked at: Flipkart · Tata Neu · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Cardinality bug · SUM inflated by join
The scenario: A weekly business review shows GMV at ₹84 crore. Finance reconciliation says it should
be ₹42 crore. Exactly double. The query joins orders to order_items to compute per-category
GMV — but rolls up to total without thinking about cardinality.
SELECT SUM(o.order_total) AS total_gmv
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_date BETWEEN '2026-05-19' AND '2026-05-25';
Expected vs Actual: Expected ₹42 crore (sum of order totals). Got ₹84 crore — every order has on
average 2 items, and the join duplicates order_total by the number of items.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Joining orders to order_items multiplies rows. A 3-item order produces 3 rows in
the joined set. SUM(o.order_total) then sums the order total 3 times." 2. "The query author probably
wanted per-category breakdown and forgot that summing parent-level metrics across a one-to-many join
double-counts." 3. "Fix depends on what they want — for total GMV, drop the join. For per-category
GMV, sum item-level amounts, not order_total." 4. "This is the most common 'looks right but is doubled'
bug in SQL reporting. Always check the join cardinality before summing."
Diagnosis: Joining a parent table to a child on one-to-many duplicates the parent's columns. Summing
the parent's columns across the joined set multiplies by the child count.
Fix SQL (for total GMV):
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 54 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 55
SELECT SUM(o.order_total) AS total_gmv
FROM orders o
WHERE o.order_date BETWEEN '2026-05-19' AND '2026-05-25';
For per-category GMV, sum item-level prices:
SELECT oi.category, SUM(oi.line_amount) AS gmv
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_date BETWEEN '2026-05-19' AND '2026-05-25'
GROUP BY oi.category;
Why this works: For totals, the parent table alone has every order once. For per-child breakdowns, you
sum child-level amounts. Don't mix scopes.
What NOT to say: - "Use DISTINCT" — SELECT SUM(DISTINCT order_total) is wrong because
two different orders might genuinely have the same total. - "JOIN bug, switch to LEFT JOIN" — doesn't
change the duplication.
Common follow-up: "How would you debug this without recomputing manually?" — SELECT
order_id, COUNT(*) FROM (joined query) GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
— confirms duplication.
Scenario51 · The many-to-many that exploded to 12 million rows
Asked at: LinkedIn India · Naukri · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Cardinality bug · M:N row explosion
The scenario: A recruiter analytics query joins candidates to applications to interviews
and the result set is 12 million rows from 50,000 candidates. The query takes 4 minutes and then crashes
the dashboard. Each candidate has on average 8 applications and 6 interviews — 50,000 × 8 × 6 ≈ 2.4
million, but they're seeing 12 million.
SELECT c.candidate_id, c.name, a.role, i.interview_round
FROM candidates c
JOIN applications a ON a.candidate_id = c.candidate_id
JOIN interviews   i ON i.candidate_id = c.candidate_id;
-- All three joins on candidate_id only.
-- The applications join produces 50k × 8 = 400k rows.
-- The interviews join cross-products with applications, producing 400k × 6 = 2.4M.
-- Actual observed is higher because the average is heavy-tailed.
Expected vs Actual: Expected one row per interview (~300k). Got 12M — a Cartesian-style explosion
because applications × interviews is a cross-product per candidate.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 55 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 56
Thinking out loud: 1. "Joining candidates → applications gives one row per application. Joining that to
interviews on candidate_id gives every (application, interview) pair for the same candidate." 2. "That is a
cross-product within each candidate. If candidate A has 8 applications and 6 interviews, the result
contains 48 rows for that candidate — even though interviews are not tied to specific applications in this
join." 3. "The right join key is 
interviews.application_id = applications.application_id, assuming interviews are
scheduled per application. With that, you get one row per interview." 4. "Without it, the engine has no
choice but to enumerate every pair."
Diagnosis: Joining three tables only on the common ancestor key creates a many-to-many Cartesian
within each group. Need the secondary FK to constrain the join.
Fix SQL:
SELECT c.candidate_id, c.name, a.role, i.interview_round
FROM candidates c
JOIN applications a ON a.candidate_id  = c.candidate_id
JOIN interviews   i ON i.application_id = a.application_id;
Why this works: interviews.application_id ties each interview to a specific application. The
join is now one-per-interview, not all-pairs-per-candidate.
What NOT to say: - "Use SELECT DISTINCT to dedup" — masks the bug, doesn't fix it, and is
expensive on 12M rows. - "Add LIMIT 1000" — hides the explosion, lies about the data.
Common follow-up: "What if interviews don't have an application_id?" — then your schema can't
answer "which application is this interview for" — you have a data model problem, not a query problem.
Scenario52 · The LEFT JOIN to a subquery that duplicates parents
Asked at: Razorpay · Stripe India · Difficulty: Hard · Topic: Cardinality bug · Subquery returns multiple
rows per outer row
The scenario: A "latest payment" report uses a LEFT JOIN to a derived table that's supposed to return
one payment per customer. But the report shows some customers appearing multiple times.
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, p.payment_id, p.payment_ts
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT customer_id, payment_id, payment_ts
    FROM payments
    WHERE status = 'SUCCESS'
) p ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id;
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 56 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 57
Expected vs Actual: Expected one row per customer, with their latest payment (or NULL if none). Got
many rows per customer — one per successful payment.
Thinking out loud: 1. "The subquery returns every successful payment per customer, not the latest. The
LEFT JOIN then expands to one row per payment." 2. "The author probably thought 'latest' was implied
by some ordering. SQL has no implicit ordering; you have to explicitly pick the latest." 3. "Fix: use a
window function (ROW_NUMBER) to pick the latest per customer, then filter to row 1. Or use DISTINCT
ON in Postgres." 4. "Or — if the goal is 'show the latest', use a correlated subquery with (SELECT
MAX(payment_ts) FROM payments WHERE customer_id = c.customer_id)."
Diagnosis: A "latest per group" intent expressed without a deduplication step. The subquery returns N
payments per customer; the LEFT JOIN duplicates the customer N times.
Fix SQL (Postgres DISTINCT ON):
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, p.payment_id, p.payment_ts
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id) customer_id, payment_id, payment_ts
    FROM payments
    WHERE status = 'SUCCESS'
    ORDER BY customer_id, payment_ts DESC
) p ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id;
Portable form (any dialect):
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT customer_id, payment_id, payment_ts,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY payment_ts DESC) AS rn
    FROM payments
    WHERE status = 'SUCCESS'
) p ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id AND p.rn = 1
Why this works: The deduplication happens inside the subquery so each customer has exactly one
payment row (or zero), and the LEFT JOIN preserves the one-row-per-customer cardinality.
What NOT to say: - "Use MAX(payment_ts) GROUP BY customer_id" — gives you the timestamp but
not the payment_id of that latest payment. - "Add LIMIT 1 to the subquery" — that limits the entire
subquery to 1 row globally, not 1 per customer.
Common follow-up: "What if you wanted the top 3 payments per customer instead of just the latest?" —
same ROW_NUMBER pattern with WHERE rn <= 3.

hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in

Scenario53 · The wrong join key that returned zero rows
Asked at: Stripe India · Pine Labs · Difficulty: Easy · Topic: Cardinality bug · Wrong join key
The scenario: A merchant reconciliation query joins transactions to merchants. It used to
work; after a schema migration, it returns zero rows.
SELECT t.txn_id, t.amount, m.merchant_name
FROM transactions t
JOIN merchants m ON t.user_id = m.user_id;
-- After migration:
-- transactions.user_id is the END USER who paid.
-- merchants.user_id no longer exists; the new field is merchants.owner_user_id.
-- Old query used merchants.user_id = the merchant's owner_user_id.
-- The correct relationship is transactions.merchant_id = merchants.merchant_id.
Expected vs Actual: Expected every transaction to resolve to a merchant. Got zero rows or an
"unknown column" error depending on engine.
Thinking out loud: 1. "The join key is wrong. We are matching the paying user's ID to the merchant's
owner user ID. Different things." 2. "Pre-migration, the schema happened to have both fields named 
user_id, so the join 'worked' by accident — until business added a check that revealed it was joining
wrong rows the whole time." 3. "Post-migration, the column was renamed and the query now errors.
Lucky — the migration exposed the bug." 4. "The right join key is transactions.merchant_id =
merchants.merchant_id."
Diagnosis: Wrong join key. Two columns happened to share a name (user_id) but represent different
entities. The join silently produced incorrect results until a rename forced the bug into the open.
Fix SQL:
SELECT t.txn_id, t.amount, m.merchant_name
FROM transactions t
JOIN merchants m ON t.merchant_id = m.merchant_id;
Why this works: Joining on the proper foreign key that actually models the "transaction belongs to
merchant" relationship.
What NOT to say: - "Restore the old column name as a backwards-compat alias" — preserves the bug,
papers over the rename. - "Join on multiple keys for safety" — confuses cardinality further.
Common follow-up: "How would you catch this kind of bug in code review?" — name your foreign key
columns by the entity they reference (merchant_id, not user_id), and avoid generic names like 
user_id that can mean different roles in different tables.

Scenario54 · The self-join that counted every friend pair twice
Asked at: Bumble India · ShareChat · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Cardinality bug · Self-join without
ordering predicate
The scenario: A "mutual friends" analysis self-joins the friendships table to find pairs of users who
are friends. The output count is exactly double the expected (each pair appears as (A, B) and (B, A)).
SELECT f1.user_id AS user_a, f2.user_id AS user_b
FROM friendships f1
JOIN friendships f2 ON f1.friend_id = f2.user_id
                   AND f1.user_id  = f2.friend_id;
-- friendships table stores (user_id, friend_id) — symmetric, both directions.
-- The self-join finds reciprocal pairs but counts each pair twice.
Expected vs Actual: Expected N pairs. Got 2N rows — each pair appears as (A, B) and (B, A).
Thinking out loud: 1. "Classic self-join symmetry bug. If (A, B) qualifies, so does (B, A) under the same
predicate." 2. "Standard fix is to add WHERE f1.user_id < f2.user_id — only one ordering of
each pair survives." 3. "This is the same pattern as 'find duplicate emails' or 'find users in same city' —
any predicate that's symmetric across two copies of the same table produces doubled output." 4. "The 
< predicate also conveniently excludes self-matches where user_id = friend_id."
Diagnosis: Symmetric self-join without an ordering predicate. Both orderings of each pair satisfy the join,
doubling the row count.
Fix SQL:
SELECT f1.user_id AS user_a, f2.user_id AS user_b
FROM friendships f1
JOIN friendships f2 ON f1.friend_id = f2.user_id
                   AND f1.user_id  = f2.friend_id
WHERE f1.user_id < f2.user_id;
Why this works: f1.user_id < f2.user_id keeps only the (A, B) ordering where A's ID is smaller.
(B, A) where B > A is rejected. Each pair appears once.
What NOT to say: - "SELECT DISTINCT" — works on (a, b) tuples but if you compute counts later, you
still need ordering. - "Use UNION instead of JOIN" — different shape; doesn't address the symmetry.
Common follow-up: "What if you want self-friendships (user is friends with self) included?" — change 
< to <=. That keeps (A, A) once.

Scenario55 · GROUP BY Missing a Non-Aggregated Column
Tags: aggregation, group-by, sql-standard, postgres-strict, mysql-lenient
Scenario: A junior engineer at a Pune-based edtech firm writes a query to show the latest enrolment per
course. It runs on the staging MySQL box, returns plausible numbers, and ships. A week later the
product team complains the dashboard shows random instructor names against each course.
SQL:
SELECT
  course_id,
  instructor_name,
  MAX(enrolled_at) AS latest_enrolment
FROM enrolments
GROUP BY course_id;
Expected vs Actual: Expected one row per course with the correct instructor. Actual: instructor_name is
picked arbitrarily — sometimes the right one, sometimes a stale row.
Thinking out loud: 1. The query groups by course_id but selects instructor_name which isn't
in the GROUP BY and isn't aggregated. 2. ANSI SQL says this is illegal. MySQL with 
ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY off will accept it and return any value from the group — undefined behaviour.
3. Postgres would have rejected this at parse time with column "instructor_name" must appear
in the GROUP BY clause. 4. Even if instructor and course are 1:1, the engine doesn't know that —
it returns the first row it happens to see.
Diagnosis: Non-deterministic column selection because of lenient MySQL mode. The query is
functionally dependent in business logic but not declared as such to the engine.
Fix:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 60 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 61
SELECT course_id, instructor_name, MAX(enrolled_at) AS latest_enrolment
FROM enrolments
GROUP BY course_id, instructor_name;
Why this works: Adding instructor_name to GROUP BY makes the engine partition by both
columns, which is safe when each course truly has one instructor. If a course can have multiple
instructors, you instead want a window function or a join-back pattern (covered in Scenario14).
What NOT to say: "MySQL just picks randomly so add ORDER BY." ORDER BY does not fix selection
within a group — it only orders the final result set.
Common follow-up: "What if the same course has had two instructors over time?" Then GROUP BY
both, or use ROW_NUMBER partitioned by course_id ordered by enrolled_at DESC and filter to rn=1 to
get the latest instructor.
Scenario56 · HAVING vs WHERE Confusion
Tags: having, where, aggregation, evaluation-order
Scenario: A Bengaluru fintech analyst writes a query to find merchants who processed more than ₹10
lakh in successful transactions in April. The query returns merchants who never had any successful April
transactions at all.
SQL:
SELECT merchant_id, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM transactions
GROUP BY merchant_id
HAVING status = 'success'
  AND txn_date >= '2026-04-01'
  AND SUM(amount) > 1000000;
Expected vs Actual: Expected merchants whose successful April sums cross ₹10L. Actual: merchants
whose total (across all statuses and dates) crosses ₹10L, filtered weirdly because status =
'success' in HAVING is treated against an arbitrary row.
Thinking out loud: 1. HAVING runs after GROUP BY on aggregate-aware predicates. Row-level filters
like status = 'success' belong in WHERE. 2. In some engines 
HAVING status = 'success' either throws or evaluates against an undefined row in the group. 3.
The SUM is over all transactions for the merchant, not just successful April ones, because the row filter
was never applied. 4. The fix is to move row predicates to WHERE and keep only the aggregate
predicate in HAVING.
Diagnosis: Row-level filters placed in HAVING are either ignored, rejected, or applied at the wrong stage.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 61 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 62
Fix:
SELECT merchant_id, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM transactions
WHERE status = 'success'
  AND txn_date >= '2026-04-01'
GROUP BY merchant_id
HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000000;
Why this works: WHERE filters rows before aggregation, so SUM only adds successful April amounts.
HAVING then filters the aggregated groups.
What NOT to say: "HAVING and WHERE are interchangeable for performance." They are not
interchangeable for correctness, and putting row filters in HAVING is always slower because the engine
aggregates rows it should have discarded.
Common follow-up: "When would you put a non-aggregate in HAVING?" Almost never. The one valid
case is when you've already grouped and the column is a GROUP BY key — but even then WHERE is
clearer.
Scenario57 · COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column) NULL Handling
Tags: count, nulls, aggregation
Scenario: A Hyderabad SaaS team tracks support tickets. PM asks "how many tickets did we close last
week with a resolution note?" Engineer writes COUNT(*) and gets 4,200. Manual sample suggests it
should be closer to 3,100.
SQL:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS resolved_with_note
FROM tickets
WHERE status = 'closed'
  AND closed_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7 days';
Expected vs Actual: Expected count of closed tickets that have a non-null resolution_note. Actual:
count of all closed tickets, including those with NULL notes.
Thinking out loud: 1. COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of NULL. 2. COUNT(resolution_note)
counts rows where that column is NOT NULL. 3. The question asked for "with a resolution note" — that's
a NULL filter, not a row count. 4. Either switch to COUNT(resolution_note) or add AND
resolution_note IS NOT NULL to WHERE.
Diagnosis: COUNT(*) ignores NULL semantics; the analyst conflated "row exists" with "column has a
value".
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 62 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 63
Fix:
SELECT COUNT(resolution_note) AS resolved_with_note
FROM tickets
WHERE status = 'closed'
  AND closed_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7 days';
Why this works: COUNT(column) silently skips NULLs, which is exactly the semantic we want here.
What NOT to say: "COUNT(*) and COUNT(1) are different." They are identical in every modern engine.
Common follow-up: "What if the column is sometimes an empty string?" Empty strings are not NULL —
COUNT(col) would still count them. You'd need COUNT(NULLIF(resolution_note, '')) or a
WHERE filter for trimmed length.
Scenario58 · COUNT(DISTINCT) on a 200-Million-Row Table
Tags: count-distinct, performance, approximate-functions
Scenario: A Mumbai-based OTT platform runs COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) over a 200M-row event
table to estimate weekly active users. The query takes 14 minutes and locks up the BI warehouse during
morning standup hours.
SQL:
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS wau
FROM events
WHERE event_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7 days';
Expected vs Actual: Expected sub-minute response for a dashboard. Actual: 14 minutes, blocks other
queries.
Thinking out loud: 1. COUNT(DISTINCT) needs to hold every unique value in memory or spill to disk —
it doesn't scale. 2. Most modern warehouses (BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift, DuckDB) have an
approximate variant — APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT or APPROX_DISTINCT — with 1-2% error and a
fraction of the cost. 3. For an internal dashboard, 1% error on WAU is invisible. 4. If we truly need exact,
partition the query by date and roll up via HyperLogLog sketches.
Diagnosis: Using exact distinct when approximate suffices — a classic warehouse cost trap.
Fix (dialect-dependent):
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 63 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 64
-- BigQuery / Snowflake
SELECT APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT(user_id) AS wau
FROM events
WHERE event_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7 days';
-- Postgres (no native; use the hll extension or pg_stat sampling)
-- Redshift
SELECT APPROXIMATE COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS wau FROM events WHERE ...;
Why this works: HyperLogLog sketches give cardinality estimates with bounded error in constant
memory.
What NOT to say: "Just add an index on user_id." Indexes don't help COUNT(DISTINCT) materially
because the engine still has to scan every distinct value.
Common follow-up: "What if finance needs an exact count for monthly reporting?" Run the exact query
offline on the weekend or maintain a daily distinct sketch that you UNION.
Scenario59 · SUM(CASE WHEN ...) Returns 0 vs NULL
Tags: conditional-aggregation, nulls, coalesce
Scenario: A Delhi-based D2C brand wants the count of refunds per order. Analyst joins orders with
refunds and aggregates. Orders with no refunds show 0 in one query and NULL in another, and
downstream filtering breaks.
SQL:
SELECT
  o.order_id,
  SUM(CASE WHEN r.refund_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS refund_count
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY o.order_id;
Expected vs Actual: Expected 0 for unrefunded orders. Actual: 0 — which is fine here, but the 
neighbouring query that did SUM(r.amount) returned NULL for unrefunded orders and broke a 
WHERE refund_total > 0 filter elsewhere.
Thinking out loud: 1. SUM over an empty set returns NULL in SQL standard, not 0. 2. SUM(CASE
WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) returns 0 because the ELSE 0 makes it a non-empty sum when there's
any row — and the LEFT JOIN produces at least one row (with r.* as NULL). 3. SUM(r.amount) returns
NULL because every joined row has NULL for amount. 4. The fix is COALESCE(SUM(...), 0) when you
want 0 for empty groups.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 64 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 65
Diagnosis: SQL's SUM semantics return NULL for "no rows", and LEFT JOIN preserves the outer row
but with NULL columns. Without ELSE or COALESCE, you get NULL.
Fix:
SELECT
  o.order_id,
  COALESCE(SUM(r.amount), 0) AS refund_total,
  COUNT(r.refund_id) AS refund_count
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY o.order_id;
Why this works: COALESCE turns NULL totals into 0. COUNT(r.refund_id) handles the row-count side
cleanly because COUNT(col) skips NULLs.
What NOT to say: "Use ISNULL." ISNULL is SQL Server only — COALESCE is portable.
Common follow-up: "Why not just inner join?" Inner join would drop orders with no refunds entirely,
which we need for the dashboard's "refund rate per order" metric.
Scenario60 · AVG Over Filtered Subset — Wrong Denominator
Tags: avg, denominator, filtering, semantics
Scenario: A Chennai-based food delivery startup reports "average delivery time for late orders" as 47
minutes. The CEO asks why the same metric drops to 32 minutes when computed with a different filter
clause. Both queries claim to use the same data.
SQL (the wrong one):
SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN delivered_at > eta THEN delivery_minutes END) AS avg_late_time
FROM orders;
Expected vs Actual: Expected the average over late orders only. Actual: SQL's AVG ignores NULL, so
the function looks correct — but the analyst expected the denominator to be total orders, not late orders,
leading to confusion when this number was compared with a SUM/COUNT version that used the wrong
denominator.
Thinking out loud: 1. AVG(CASE WHEN cond THEN val END) gives average over rows where cond is
true — NULLs are skipped. 2. SUM(CASE WHEN cond THEN val ELSE 0 END) / COUNT() gives average
over all rows* — different denominator. 3. The two formulas answer different questions. Pick the one
matching the business definition. 4. Always spell out the denominator in code review.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 65 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 66
Diagnosis: Ambiguous "average" — average of late delivery times, vs. expected delivery time across the
whole order base.
Fix (explicit):
-- Average over late orders only
SELECT
  AVG(delivery_minutes) AS avg_late_time
FROM orders
WHERE delivered_at > eta;
-- Average lateness contribution over all orders
SELECT
  SUM(CASE WHEN delivered_at > eta THEN delivery_minutes - eta_minutes ELSE 0 END) * 1.0 / COUNT(*) AS avg_lateness_per_order
FROM orders;
Why this works: Each form spells out exactly which rows are in the numerator and denominator.
What NOT to say: "AVG always handles NULL correctly." Correctly by SQL standards, yes — but that's
often the opposite of what the business meant.
Common follow-up: "How would you compute weighted average?" SUM(value * weight) /
SUM(weight) — and watch for SUM(weight) being zero.
Scenario61 · Median via AVG — Statistically Wrong
Tags: median, percentile, statistical-functions
Scenario: A Gurgaon-based jobs platform reports "median salary offered" but the dashboard shows
₹14.7L when the recruitment team insists the true median is closer to ₹9L. The query is being defended
in a review meeting.
SQL:
SELECT AVG(salary) AS median_salary
FROM offers
WHERE offered_at >= '2026-04-01';
Expected vs Actual: Expected the middle value (50th percentile). Actual: the arithmetic mean — heavily
skewed by a few ₹80L+ exec offers.
Thinking out loud: 1. AVG is mean, not median. The analyst named the column wrong. 2. True median in
SQL needs PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) or PERCENTILE_DISC(0.5) — ordered-set aggregates. 3. Postgres
and Oracle support PERCENTILE_CONT WITHIN GROUP. BigQuery has PERCENTILE_CONT as a
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 66 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 67
window/analytic. MySQL 8 has no native — needs window simulation. 4. Salary data is right-skewed —
mean will always overshoot median.
Diagnosis: Mean used as a proxy for median on skewed data — guaranteed to mislead.
Fix:
-- Postgres / Oracle
SELECT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary) AS median_salary
FROM offers
WHERE offered_at >= '2026-04-01';
-- BigQuery
SELECT APPROX_QUANTILES(salary, 100)[OFFSET(50)] AS median_salary
FROM offers
WHERE offered_at >= '2026-04-01';
-- MySQL 8 (simulation)
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT salary, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS rn, COUNT(*) OVER () AS cnt
  FROM offers WHERE offered_at >= '2026-04-01'
)
SELECT AVG(salary) AS median_salary
FROM ranked
WHERE rn IN (FLOOR((cnt+1)/2), CEIL((cnt+1)/2));
Why this works: PERCENTILE_CONT interpolates the true median; the MySQL simulation picks the
middle one or two ordered rows and averages.
What NOT to say: "Mean and median are basically the same for large samples." Only on symmetric
distributions — salary is never symmetric.
Common follow-up: "What about p95 latency?" Same pattern — 
PERCENTILE_CONT(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms).
Scenario62 · LAST_VALUE With Default Frame
Tags: window-functions, frames, last-value
Scenario: A Bengaluru analyst writes a window query to fetch the last login timestamp per user across
their session history, expecting each row to show the user's most recent login. Every row shows that
row's own login instead.
SQL:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 67 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 68
SELECT
  user_id,
  login_at,
  LAST_VALUE(login_at) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_at) AS last_login
FROM sessions;
Expected vs Actual: Expected each row's last_login to equal the user's final login_at. Actual: 
last_login = login_at on every row.
Thinking out loud: 1. The default frame in a window with ORDER BY is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED
PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. 2. LAST_VALUE on that frame returns the current row — because the
frame ends at current row. 3. The fix is to extend the frame to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING. 4. Alternative:
use FIRST_VALUE with DESC ordering.
Diagnosis: Default window frame stops at current row, so LAST_VALUE never sees future rows in the
partition.
Fix:
SELECT
  user_id,
  login_at,
  LAST_VALUE(login_at) OVER (
    PARTITION BY user_id
    ORDER BY login_at
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
  ) AS last_login
FROM sessions;
-- Or simpler:
SELECT
  user_id,
  login_at,
  MAX(login_at) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id) AS last_login
FROM sessions;
Why this works: Either explicit unbounded frame, or MAX (which doesn't need a frame because it's a
partition-level aggregate).
What NOT to say: "LAST_VALUE is just buggy in this engine." It's working as specified — the frame
default is the trap.
Common follow-up: "When would you actually want LAST_VALUE?" Almost never in interview problems
— MAX/FIRST_VALUE-with-DESC or LAG/LEAD cover most needs more clearly.

Scenario63 · Filtering on a Window Function Result
Tags: window-functions, where-clause, evaluation-order, cte
Scenario: An Indore-based logistics analyst tries to fetch only the latest event per shipment using
ROW_NUMBER. The query throws "column rn does not exist" or returns all rows depending on the
engine.
SQL (broken):
SELECT
  shipment_id,
  event_at,
  status,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY shipment_id ORDER BY event_at DESC) AS rn
FROM shipment_events
WHERE rn = 1;
Expected vs Actual: Expected one latest event per shipment. Actual: error (most engines) or unfiltered
output.
Thinking out loud: 1. WHERE is evaluated before SELECT, so the alias rn doesn't exist yet at the
WHERE phase. 2. Window functions are computed during/after SELECT, not before WHERE. 3. The fix is
to wrap in a CTE or subquery, then filter on the outer level. 4. QUALIFY (BigQuery, Snowflake, Teradata,
DuckDB) is the cleanest variant.
Diagnosis: Logical query processing order — WHERE runs before window functions are evaluated.
Fix:
-- Portable
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT
    shipment_id, event_at, status,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY shipment_id ORDER BY event_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM shipment_events
)
SELECT shipment_id, event_at, status
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1;
-- Snowflake / BigQuery / DuckDB
SELECT shipment_id, event_at, status
FROM shipment_events
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY shipment_id ORDER BY event_at DESC) = 1;
Why this works: Wrapping isolates the window evaluation; QUALIFY is syntactic sugar that lets the
engine push the filter at the right phase.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 69 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 70
What NOT to say: "Just use HAVING instead of WHERE." HAVING doesn't apply to window functions
either — both run before window phase.
Common follow-up: "When does the engine evaluate window functions exactly?" After GROUP BY/
HAVING but before final SELECT / ORDER BY / LIMIT.
Scenario64 · ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK — Wrong Pick
Tags: window-functions, row-number, rank, dense-rank, ties
Scenario: A Bengaluru gaming company runs a "top 10 scorers this week" leaderboard. Six players tie at
rank 1 with the same high score, but the leaderboard shows only one of them and ranks the next four
players as 2, 3, 4, 5.
SQL:
SELECT player_id, score,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS leaderboard_rank
FROM weekly_scores;
Expected vs Actual: Expected ties to share rank 1, then next player at rank 2 (DENSE_RANK) or rank 7
(RANK). Actual: arbitrary rank 1-6 across the six tied players, and rank 7 onward looks normal — but a
tied player at #6 got pushed off the top-10 unfairly.
Thinking out loud: 1. ROW_NUMBER always gives 1,2,3 with no ties. 2. RANK gives 1,1,1,1,1,1,7,8,9 —
gaps after ties. 3. DENSE_RANK gives 1,1,1,1,1,1,2,3,4 — no gaps. 4. For a leaderboard where ties
should genuinely share the rank, RANK is the typical pick; DENSE_RANK if you want gapless.
Diagnosis: ROW_NUMBER is non-deterministic on ties unless tiebreakers are added; wrong function for
a leaderboard.
Fix:
SELECT player_id, score,
  RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS leaderboard_rank
FROM weekly_scores;
Why this works: RANK lets ties share the same rank, which is the universally understood leaderboard
semantic.
What NOT to say: "RANK and DENSE_RANK are interchangeable." They are not — the gap behaviour
matters for "top N with ties".
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 70 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 71
Common follow-up: "How do you pick top N with ties guaranteed included?" Use RANK() (or
DENSE_RANK) in a CTE then filter WHERE rank <= 10 — this returns more than 10 rows if ties exist
at position 10.
Scenario65 · LAG Returning NULL for First Row in Partition
Tags: lag, lead, defaults, window-functions
Scenario: A Hyderabad e-commerce analyst computes the time gap between consecutive orders per
customer. The first order per customer shows NULL gap, which is correct — but downstream WHERE
gap_days > 30 filtering drops all first-order rows silently, biasing churn analysis.
SQL:
SELECT
  customer_id, order_id, order_at,
  EXTRACT(DAY FROM order_at - LAG(order_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_at)) AS gap_days
FROM orders;
Expected vs Actual: Expected first-order rows to either be included or explicitly excluded with
reasoning. Actual: silent NULL → silent drop on downstream filter.
Thinking out loud: 1. LAG defaults to NULL for the first row per partition because there's no prior row. 2.
LAG has a third argument: LAG(col, 1, default_value) — useful when you want a sentinel. 3.
NULL > 30 is NULL, which is treated as false in WHERE — so first-order customers vanish from any
"gap" filter. 4. Either set a default (e.g., the customer signup date) or handle NULL explicitly.
Diagnosis: Default NULL for first row in partition flows silently into filter and biases the result.
Fix:
SELECT
  customer_id, order_id, order_at,
  EXTRACT(DAY FROM order_at - LAG(order_at, 1, signup_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_at)) AS gap_days
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c USING (customer_id);
-- Or be explicit downstream
WHERE gap_days IS NULL OR gap_days > 30
Why this works: Either substituting signup_at as the previous-row default makes the first gap
meaningful, or being explicit about NULL handling prevents silent drops.
What NOT to say: "LAG returns 0 for missing rows." It returns NULL — always.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 71 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 72
Common follow-up: "What if you need the next gap instead?" Use LEAD with the same default-value
pattern.
Scenario66 · Running Total Broken Because No ORDER BY in OVER
Tags: running-total, cumulative-sum, window-functions
Scenario: A Pune fintech runs a daily running total of payments received per branch. The numbers are
random and inconsistent across reruns of the same query.
SQL:
SELECT
  branch_id, payment_date, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY branch_id) AS running_total
FROM payments;
Expected vs Actual: Expected cumulative sum up to each row's date. Actual: every row shows the
branch's grand total — same value on every row.
Thinking out loud: 1. SUM OVER (PARTITION BY x) with no ORDER BY is a partition-level aggregate —
same value on every row in the partition. 2. To get cumulative, add ORDER BY payment_date inside
OVER. 3. The default frame with ORDER BY is ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
— exactly what running total needs. 4. Without ORDER BY, the frame defaults to the entire partition.
Diagnosis: Missing ORDER BY inside OVER turns "running" into "total".
Fix:
SELECT
  branch_id, payment_date, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (
    PARTITION BY branch_id
    ORDER BY payment_date
    ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING
  ) AS running_total
FROM payments;
Why this works: ORDER BY inside OVER establishes the cumulative direction; the explicit frame
removes ambiguity around RANGE vs ROWS.
What NOT to say: "Just use a self-join with <=." Self-joins for running totals are O(N²) and inexcusable
when window functions exist.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 72 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 73
Common follow-up: "What if there are ties in payment_date?" RANGE and ROWS behave differently
with ties — RANGE includes all tied rows in the same frame edge, ROWS does not. Use ROWS for strict
per-row cumulative.
Scenario67 · Multiple Unnamed Windows in Same Query
Tags: window-functions, named-window, performance
Scenario: A Bengaluru analytics team's nightly report has six window functions, each with the same 
PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_at clause. Query runs for 28 minutes. The plan shows
six separate Sort operations.
SQL (problematic):
SELECT
  user_id, event_at,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_at) AS rn,
  LAG(event_at) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_at) AS prev_evt,
  LEAD(event_at) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_at) AS next_evt,
  FIRST_VALUE(page) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_at) AS landing,
  LAST_VALUE(page) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_at ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS exit_page,
  COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_at) AS events_so_far
FROM events;
Expected vs Actual: Expected a single sort. Actual: planner sorted six times because each OVER is
structurally distinct in the parser even if semantically identical.
Thinking out loud: 1. Most engines can reuse a sort when OVER clauses are textually identical — but
the LAST_VALUE one differs (explicit frame), breaking reuse. 2. Named windows via WINDOW clause
make sharing explicit and let the planner reuse the sort. 3. Splitting the LAST_VALUE into its own pass
might be unavoidable but the other five can share. 4. Always check the explain plan for sort count.
Diagnosis: Window reuse depends on textual identity; minor differences split the sort.
Fix:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 73 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 74
SELECT
  user_id, event_at,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER w AS rn,
  LAG(event_at) OVER w AS prev_evt,
  LEAD(event_at) OVER w AS next_evt,
  FIRST_VALUE(page) OVER w AS landing,
  LAST_VALUE(page) OVER w_full AS exit_page,
  COUNT(*) OVER w AS events_so_far
FROM events
WINDOW
  w AS (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_at),
  w_full AS (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_at ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING);
Why this works: Named windows are explicit reuse contracts; engines that respect WINDOW clauses
sort once per named window.
What NOT to say: "Window functions always share the sort." They share only when the OVER clause is
byte-identical (in many engines) or named identically.
Common follow-up: "Does Snowflake/BigQuery support WINDOW clauses?" Both do; MySQL 8 does;
Postgres does; some older engines don't. Check the docs for your target.
Scenario68 · Latest Record Per Group via MAX + JOIN — Duplicates on Ties
Tags: latest-per-group, join, ties, duplicates
Scenario: A Delhi-based jobs platform wants the latest application per candidate. The query joins
applications with MAX(applied_at) per candidate. Some candidates show up twice — they applied
to two roles at the exact same millisecond.
SQL:
SELECT a.*
FROM applications a
JOIN (
  SELECT candidate_id, MAX(applied_at) AS max_t
  FROM applications
  GROUP BY candidate_id
) m ON a.candidate_id = m.candidate_id AND a.applied_at = m.max_t;
Expected vs Actual: Expected one row per candidate. Actual: candidates with multi-application ties at
the same timestamp returned twice.
Thinking out loud: 1. MAX + self-join is the classic "latest per group" pattern. 2. It breaks on ties
because both rows with max timestamp match the join. 3. To tie-break, you need a secondary ordering
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 74 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 75
— but MAX can't express that. 4. The cleaner fix is ROW_NUMBER (Scenario15) or DISTINCT ON
(Scenario16).
Diagnosis: MAX + JOIN pattern has no tiebreaker, so any tie at the max value duplicates the row.
Fix (with tiebreaker):
-- Tiebreak by application_id (or any unique secondary)
SELECT a.*
FROM applications a
JOIN (
  SELECT candidate_id, MAX(applied_at) AS max_t
  FROM applications
  GROUP BY candidate_id
) m ON a.candidate_id = m.candidate_id AND a.applied_at = m.max_t
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY a.candidate_id ORDER BY a.application_id DESC) = 1;
But Scenario15's pattern is cleaner.
Why this works: We've added a deterministic tiebreaker. Still messier than ROW_NUMBER though.
What NOT to say: "Use SELECT DISTINCT at the end." DISTINCT on a.* works only if columns differ
— and with truly identical rows we still won't deduplicate something we want.
Common follow-up: "Why is this pattern still taught?" Historical — pre-window-function SQL had no
better option. Modern code shouldn't use it.
Scenario69 · Latest Record Per Group via ROW_NUMBER — The Canonical Fix
Tags: latest-per-group, row-number, canonical-pattern
Scenario: After hitting the MAX+JOIN duplication issue (Scenario14), the same team rewrites with
ROW_NUMBER. Result is clean and one-row-per-candidate.
SQL:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT a.*,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY candidate_id ORDER BY applied_at DESC, application_id DESC) AS rn
  FROM applications a
)
SELECT *
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1;
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 75 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 76
Expected vs Actual: Expected one row per candidate. Actual: exactly that, every time, even with
timestamp ties.
Thinking out loud: 1. ROW_NUMBER gives a unique sequence per partition — no ties. 2. The ORDER
BY inside OVER controls which row gets rn=1. 3. Adding a secondary key (application_id DESC)
guarantees determinism on ties. 4. Filtering rn = 1 in outer query picks exactly one per group.
Diagnosis: This is the fix to Scenario14 — the same problem solved cleanly.
Fix: As shown — and the pattern is so common it deserves a permanent name in your team's style
guide.
Why this works: Window-based ranking is partition-aware, tie-deterministic when you supply a
secondary key, and runs in a single pass over the table.
What NOT to say: "ROW_NUMBER is slower than MAX." It is usually the same speed or faster — both
require a sort by partition key.
Common follow-up: "What if I need the top-3 per candidate, not just top-1?" Same pattern, filter 
WHERE rn <= 3.
Scenario70 · DISTINCT ON (Postgres) — Clean Alternative
Tags: distinct-on, postgres, latest-per-group, dialect
Scenario: A Postgres-shop analyst at a Mumbai-based brokerage uses the ROW_NUMBER pattern and
a senior reviewer asks why they didn't use DISTINCT ON. The reviewer claims it's faster and shorter.
SQL:
SELECT DISTINCT ON (candidate_id) *
FROM applications
ORDER BY candidate_id, applied_at DESC, application_id DESC;
Expected vs Actual: Expected one row per candidate, latest application. Actual: exactly that — and the
query is half the lines of the ROW_NUMBER version.
Thinking out loud: 1. DISTINCT ON is Postgres-only syntax. The columns in DISTINCT ON define the
group; the ORDER BY decides which row wins. 2. ORDER BY must start with the DISTINCT ON
columns, then add the ordering for picking the winner. 3. It's not faster than ROW_NUMBER in all cases
— Postgres can use the same index either way — but the SQL is shorter and reads better. 4. Not
portable to MySQL, SQL Server, BigQuery.
Diagnosis: This isn't a bug — it's a dialect comparison. Pick based on portability needs.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 76 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 77
Fix: Already shown. If portability matters, stick with ROW_NUMBER. If you're Postgres-only, DISTINCT
ON is idiomatic.
Why this works: DISTINCT ON is purpose-built syntactic sugar for the "latest per group" question.
What NOT to say: "DISTINCT ON is always faster than window functions." Same plan in most cases;
readability is the real win.
Common follow-up: "What's the BigQuery / Snowflake equivalent?" QUALIFY with ROW_NUMBER —
Scenario9's pattern.
Scenario71 · Aggregating After JOIN Inflates Totals
Tags: join-multiplication, aggregation, line-items
Scenario: A Chennai-based retail chain reports a sudden 4x jump in revenue. Analyst is summing order
totals after joining with line items.
SQL:
SELECT SUM(o.total_amount) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_date = '2026-05-01';
Expected vs Actual: Expected total revenue for May 1st. Actual: revenue inflated by average items-per-
order (4x in this case).
Thinking out loud: 1. The JOIN to order_items multiplies each order row by its line-item count. 2.
SUM(o.total_amount) then counts each order's total once per line item. 3. The fix is to aggregate before
joining, or to sum at the order grain without joining. 4. Classic "fan-out" join-multiplication bug.
Diagnosis: Joining a 1:N table inflates 1-side aggregates by the N count.
Fix (multiple options):
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 77 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 78
-- Option 1: Don't join if you don't need item details
SELECT SUM(total_amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE order_date = '2026-05-01';
-- Option 2: Aggregate before joining if you do need items
SELECT o.order_id, o.total_amount, agg.item_count
FROM orders o
JOIN (
  SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS item_count FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id
) agg ON agg.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_date = '2026-05-01';
-- Option 3: Sum the line items directly
SELECT SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS revenue
FROM order_items i
JOIN orders o USING (order_id)
WHERE o.order_date = '2026-05-01';
Why this works: Each option ensures we sum at the correct grain — order-level or item-level, never
mixed.
What NOT to say: "Just SELECT DISTINCT before SUM." DISTINCT on order_id-amount might work but
breaks if two orders have the same amount.
Common follow-up: "What if you need both order count and item count in one query?" Two subqueries
joined back, or window-COUNT, but never naively SUM after JOIN.
Scenario72 · Aggregate of Aggregate — Needs Subquery
Tags: aggregate-of-aggregate, subquery, window-function
Scenario: A Bengaluru SaaS team wants "average number of orders per customer" — a single number.
Engineer tries AVG(COUNT(order_id)) and the engine throws.
SQL (broken):
SELECT AVG(COUNT(order_id))
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;
Expected vs Actual: Expected a single average. Actual: most engines reject nested aggregates without
a window or subquery.
Thinking out loud: 1. You can't nest two aggregate functions directly — SQL needs you to first
aggregate, then aggregate again. 2. Subquery is the standard fix: GROUP BY customer_id inside, AVG
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 78 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 79
outside. 3. Window function alternative: COUNT per customer using OVER, then AVG. 4. Some engines
allow AVG(COUNT(...)) OVER () as a workaround — non-portable.
Diagnosis: Aggregates can't be nested without an intermediate query level.
Fix:
-- Standard subquery
SELECT AVG(order_count) AS avg_orders_per_customer
FROM (
  SELECT customer_id, COUNT(order_id) AS order_count
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
) t;
Why this works: The inner query produces one row per customer with an order count; the outer
averages those counts.
What NOT to say: "Use a window function for everything." Window functions don't collapse rows —
you'd still need a final aggregation step.
Common follow-up: "What if you want it per region?" Wrap the per-customer count, then GROUP BY
region in the outer query.
Scenario73 · COUNT in Correlated Subquery — Slow
Tags: correlated-subquery, performance, join-rewrite
Scenario: A Hyderabad-based analytics team's nightly job has a query that times out at 4 hours. The
query counts, for each product, how many orders contain that product.
SQL (slow):
SELECT
  p.product_id,
  p.name,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM order_items i WHERE i.product_id = p.product_id) AS order_count
FROM products p;
Expected vs Actual: Expected completion in minutes. Actual: 4-hour timeout because the subquery
executes once per product row (50k products × full scan).
Thinking out loud: 1. Correlated subqueries that touch a large fact table are O(rows_outer × cost_inner).
2. Rewrite as a join + GROUP BY for a single scan. 3. Modern optimisers sometimes flatten correlated
subqueries — but don't rely on it. 4. LEFT JOIN preserves products with zero orders.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 79 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 80
Diagnosis: Correlated subquery forces per-row re-execution.
Fix:
SELECT
  p.product_id, p.name,
  COALESCE(agg.order_count, 0) AS order_count
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT product_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
  FROM order_items
  GROUP BY product_id
) agg ON agg.product_id = p.product_id;
Why this works: One pass over order_items aggregates everything; a hash join then attaches counts to
products.
What NOT to say: "Add an index on product_id." The index helps the correlated subquery only
marginally — the real win is single-pass aggregation.
Common follow-up: "When is a correlated subquery acceptable?" When the outer is small (a dozen
rows) or when it's an EXISTS / NOT EXISTS that short-circuits.
Scenario74 · GROUP BY on Expression — Index Issue
Tags: group-by, expression, function-on-column, sargability
Scenario: A Pune-based logistics analyst groups shipments by month using 
MONTH(shipment_date). The query scans the full table even though there's an index on
shipment_date.
SQL:
SELECT
  MONTH(shipment_date) AS month,
  COUNT(*) AS shipments
FROM shipments
WHERE YEAR(shipment_date) = 2026
GROUP BY MONTH(shipment_date);
Expected vs Actual: Expected index seek on shipment_date. Actual: full table scan because applying a
function to the indexed column makes it non-sargable.
Thinking out loud: 1. Function on an indexed column kills index usage on most engines. 2. Rewrite the
filter to a range that uses the raw column. 3. GROUP BY on expression is fine — it's the WHERE that
hurts. 4. Some engines (Postgres) support expression indexes if grouping is frequent.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 80 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 81
Diagnosis: Function-wrapped column predicates can't use B-tree indexes.
Fix:
SELECT
  DATE_TRUNC('month', shipment_date) AS month,
  COUNT(*) AS shipments
FROM shipments
WHERE shipment_date >= '2026-01-01' AND shipment_date < '2027-01-01'
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', shipment_date);
Why this works: Range predicate on the raw column uses the index; DATE_TRUNC in SELECT/GROUP
BY is computed after seek.
What NOT to say: "Indexes aren't useful for GROUP BY anyway." Index-organised reads massively help
when filtering before grouping.
Common follow-up: "What if I really need MONTH() in the WHERE?" Create an expression index: 
CREATE INDEX ix_ship_month ON shipments((MONTH(shipment_date))) — Postgres
syntax, slightly different on each engine.
Scenario75 · DATE_TRUNC Missing Timezone
Tags: date-trunc, timezone, aggregation, edge-of-day
Scenario: A Mumbai-based fintech reports daily transaction volumes. Volumes look about 5% lower
than expected for some Indian customers, with late-night transactions appearing on the previous day.
SQL:
SELECT
  DATE_TRUNC('day', created_at) AS txn_day,
  COUNT(*) AS txns
FROM transactions
GROUP BY 1;
Expected vs Actual: Expected IST-day grouping. Actual: UTC-day grouping because created_at is
stored as UTC and DATE_TRUNC operates without conversion.
Thinking out loud: 1. UTC and IST differ by 5h30m. A 2am IST transaction is 8:30pm UTC the previous
day. 2. DATE_TRUNC on a UTC timestamp gives a UTC day. 3. Convert to IST before truncating: 
DATE_TRUNC('day', created_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata') in Postgres. 4. Other
engines: BigQuery has DATE(created_at, 'Asia/Kolkata'); Snowflake has 
CONVERT_TIMEZONE.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 81 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 82
Diagnosis: Truncating without converting timezone aligns days to UTC, not the user's local boundary.
Fix:
-- Postgres
SELECT
  DATE_TRUNC('day', created_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata') AS txn_day,
  COUNT(*) AS txns
FROM transactions
GROUP BY 1;
-- BigQuery
SELECT
  DATE(created_at, 'Asia/Kolkata') AS txn_day,
  COUNT(*) AS txns
FROM transactions
GROUP BY 1;
-- Snowflake
SELECT
  DATE_TRUNC('DAY', CONVERT_TIMEZONE('UTC', 'Asia/Kolkata', created_at)) AS txn_day,
  COUNT(*) AS txns
FROM transactions
GROUP BY 1;
Why this works: Each engine has a way to anchor the truncation to the target timezone's day boundary.
What NOT to say: "Just store everything in IST." That breaks when you scale to multiple timezones —
keep storage in UTC, convert at query time.
Common follow-up: "What about daylight saving?" India doesn't observe DST, so IST is fine. But for
global businesses, prefer named timezones over fixed offsets.
Scenario76 · Active Users — At Least One Event vs Total Events
Tags: active-users, distinct-vs-count, semantics
Scenario: A Bengaluru SaaS team reports 8.4 lakh "active users this month" but their MAU on the
investor pitch deck is 2.1 lakh. Both numbers come from the same database.
SQL (wrong):
SELECT COUNT(*) AS active_users
FROM events

Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 82 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 83
Expected vs Actual: Expected count of distinct users with at least one event. Actual: count of events,
which is much larger because heavy users contribute many rows.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Active users" means distinct users; the analyst counted events. 2.
COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) gives the right number. 3. If the table is huge, approximate variants are fine
