Scenario77 · Cumulative DISTINCT Users — No Native Window
Tags: cumulative-distinct, window-functions, workaround
Scenario: A Chennai-based growth team wants "cumulative unique users by day" — Day 1: users who
used the app on Day 1. Day 2: users who used the app on Day 1 or Day 2. And so on. They try 
COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) OVER (ORDER BY day) and get an error.
SQL (doesn't work):
SELECT
  day,
  COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS cumulative_users
FROM daily_active;
Expected vs Actual: Expected cumulative distinct count. Actual: most engines reject COUNT(DISTINCT)
inside OVER.
Thinking out loud: 1. SQL standard doesn't define COUNT(DISTINCT) as a window function. Some
engines (BigQuery, Postgres 16+) support it with caveats. 2. Workaround: find the first day each user
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 83 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 84
appeared (MIN per user), then count users whose first day ≤ N. 3. Equivalent to "cumulative new users"
— the cumulative distinct equals the running sum of new users. 4. This is the standard pattern.
Diagnosis: COUNT(DISTINCT) is not generally supported in OVER clauses.
Fix:
WITH first_seen AS (
  SELECT user_id, MIN(event_date) AS first_day
  FROM events
  GROUP BY user_id
),
new_per_day AS (
  SELECT first_day AS day, COUNT(*) AS new_users
  FROM first_seen
  GROUP BY first_day
)
SELECT
  day,
  SUM(new_users) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS cumulative_users
FROM new_per_day;
Why this works: Each user contributes exactly once (their first appearance); the running sum gives
cumulative distinct.
What NOT to say: "Cross-join every day with users and count." That's O(days × users) which explodes
on real data.
Common follow-up: "What if I want cumulative distinct over a sliding window, not cumulative-forever?"
Use HyperLogLog sketches per day, then UNION-merge across the window.
Scenario78 · Mode / Most Frequent Value
Tags: mode, most-frequent, group-by
Scenario: An Indore-based analyst is asked for the "most common payment method per merchant" in an
interview. They try MODE(payment_method) and the engine throws.
SQL (engine-dependent):
SELECT
  merchant_id,
  MODE() WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY payment_method) AS top_method
FROM transactions
GROUP BY merchant_id;
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 84 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 85
Expected vs Actual: Expected most-frequent method per merchant. Actual: works in Postgres and
Oracle; throws in MySQL, BigQuery, Snowflake.
Thinking out loud: 1. MODE WITHIN GROUP is Postgres/Oracle. Not standard. 2. The portable pattern
is GROUP BY + COUNT + ROW_NUMBER. 3. Tiebreaker logic must be explicit if two methods tie. 4.
APPROX_TOP_K (BigQuery, Snowflake) gives an approximate version.
Diagnosis: MODE is dialect-specific; portable code needs the window pattern.
Fix:
WITH counts AS (
  SELECT merchant_id, payment_method, COUNT(*) AS c
  FROM transactions
  GROUP BY merchant_id, payment_method
),
ranked AS (
  SELECT *,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY merchant_id ORDER BY c DESC, payment_method) AS rn
  FROM counts
)
SELECT merchant_id, payment_method AS top_method
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1;
Why this works: Count occurrences per (merchant, method), rank within merchant by count, pick rank 1.
What NOT to say: "Use MAX(COUNT(*))." That gives the count value, not the method — and joining
back to retrieve the method is more code than the window pattern.
Common follow-up: "What about top 3 methods per merchant?" Same pattern, filter 
WHERE rn <= 3.
Scenario79 · Sessionization Gone Wrong — Wrong Gap Threshold
Tags: sessionization, sessions, gap-analysis, window-functions
Scenario: A Mumbai content platform defines a "session" as page views within 30 minutes of the
previous view. The sessionization query gives suspiciously long sessions (some lasting 14 hours).
SQL:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 85 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 86
WITH gaps AS (
  SELECT
    user_id, page_view_at,
    EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM page_view_at - LAG(page_view_at) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY page_view_at)) AS gap_sec
  FROM page_views
),
flagged AS (
  SELECT *,
    CASE WHEN gap_sec > 1800 OR gap_sec IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_new_session
  FROM gaps
)
SELECT user_id, page_view_at,
  SUM(is_new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY page_view_at) AS session_num
FROM flagged;
Expected vs Actual: Expected new session after 30-minute gap. Actual: code looks right but engineers
misread the threshold — they wrote 18000 (5 hours) instead of 1800 (30 min) in production rollout.
Thinking out loud: 1. The pattern is correct: LAG for previous timestamp, flag new sessions on gap >
threshold, running sum. 2. Bug is the threshold value — 18000 seconds (5 hours), not 1800 (30 minutes).
3. Always express thresholds via named constants or CTEs: WITH config AS (SELECT 1800 AS
session_gap_sec). 4. Worth defining in code review.
Diagnosis: Magic number off by a factor of 10 — classic.
Fix:
WITH config AS (SELECT 30 * 60 AS session_gap_sec),  -- 30 minutes
gaps AS (
  SELECT
    user_id, page_view_at,
    EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM page_view_at - LAG(page_view_at) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY page_view_at)) AS gap_sec
  FROM page_views
),
flagged AS (
  SELECT g.*,
    CASE WHEN g.gap_sec > c.session_gap_sec OR g.gap_sec IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_new_session
  FROM gaps g CROSS JOIN config c
)
SELECT user_id, page_view_at,
  SUM(is_new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY page_view_at) AS session_num
FROM flagged;
Why this works: Named threshold via CTE avoids magic-number bugs and makes the intent reviewable.
What NOT to say: "Sessionization is too complex for SQL." It is one of SQL's strongest use cases when
window functions are used well.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 86 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 87
Common follow-up: "How would you compute session duration?" MAX(page_view_at) -
MIN(page_view_at) per (user_id, session_num).
Scenario80 · Recency Aggregation — Off-by-One Sliding Window
Tags: sliding-window, last-n-days, off-by-one, recency
Scenario: A Bengaluru-based ride-hailing app reports "rides in the last 7 days" but the count includes 8
days when reviewed against business records. The analyst's filter looks reasonable.
SQL:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rides_last_7
FROM rides
WHERE ride_at >= CURRENT_DATE - 7
  AND ride_at <= CURRENT_DATE;
Expected vs Actual: Expected 7 days of rides. Actual: 8 days because the inclusive range spans 
today - 7 through today, which is 8 distinct calendar days.
Thinking out loud: 1. CURRENT_DATE - 7 is exactly 7 days before today. 2. Range from today -
7 to today is 8 days inclusive (today-7, today-6, ..., today). 3. For "last 7 days including today", you
want >= today - 6 or > today - 7. 4. Also worry about timestamps vs dates — ride_at
may be a timestamp and the cast matters.
Diagnosis: Off-by-one in inclusive date ranges — most candidates hit this once.
Fix:
-- Last 7 days including today (today, today-1, ..., today-6)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rides_last_7
FROM rides
WHERE ride_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '6 days'
  AND ride_at < CURRENT_DATE + INTERVAL '1 day';
-- Or, explicit windowed: last 7 complete days, excluding today
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rides_last_7
FROM rides
WHERE ride_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7 days'
  AND ride_at < CURRENT_DATE;
Why this works: Explicit half-open intervals [start, end) are the safest way to avoid off-by-one —
and < CURRENT_DATE + 1 day handles the timestamp-vs-date trap.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 87 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 88
What NOT to say: "Just use BETWEEN." BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends, which is exactly the trap
— and worse with timestamps where BETWEEN '2026-05-19' AND '2026-05-26' excludes the
afternoon of May 26.
Common follow-up: "What about timezone for 'today'?" CURRENT_DATE returns server-default
timezone — use (NOW() AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date for IST-correct day.
Category 2, Part A — Optimize This Query: Index-Based Fixes
"This query works but takes 8 minutes" is the most universal interview prompt in the optimization
category — every product company in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and the GCC belt opens the second
round with some version of it. Part A of this category covers the 27 scenarios where the right answer is
the right index — adding a missing one, reordering an existing composite, switching from B-tree to GIN
or BRIN, dropping a redundant cousin, or building a partial index for a hot subset. Parts B and C go
further: B handles query rewrites (CTEs, EXISTS vs IN, window-function replacements), and C handles
plan-driven fixes that need EXPLAIN ANALYZE before you touch anything. Read them as a trilogy —
interviewers love jumping between the three.
Scenario81 · Add Missing Single-Column Index — The Basic Case
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Razorpay, Zoho · Dialect: ANSI / All
Scenario setup: A support engineer at a logistics startup says "our admin dashboard takes 12 seconds
to load a single user's order history." The orders table has 40 million rows. The query is straightforward
— fetch all orders for one user_id. There's a primary key on id, but no index on user_id.
SELECT id, status, amount, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE user_id = 1487291
ORDER BY created_at DESC;
Current perf vs target: 12s full table scan reading 40M rows; target is sub-100ms for a UI call.
Thinking out loud: 1. The WHERE clause filters on a column with no index — that forces a sequential
scan of every row in the orders table. Even on a fast SSD with cold cache, that's 12 seconds at this
volume; on a warm cache it's still 4-5 seconds of CPU walking pages. 2. user_id is high cardinality (one
row per user is rare, most have 5-50 orders), so an index will narrow the scan from 40M rows to roughly
20-50 rows. The index does the heavy filtering, the engine just visits the matching heap pages. 3.
Confirm the access pattern is read-heavy and that user_id doesn't change after insert — both true for
user_id on orders, so the write-amplification cost of an index is negligible. The index pages will be
appended at the user_id leaf each time a new order is placed; no page splits in unpredictable places. 4.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 88 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 89
Before recommending the index, ask: is this the only query that filters by user_id, or do we also filter by
user_id + status combined? If combined, a composite is better — covered in Scenario2. Don't add a
single-column index that will be made redundant by next sprint's composite.
The diagnosis: Missing index on orders.user_id — every dashboard load triggers a full table scan
of 40M rows.
The fix:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);
-- Postgres: prefer CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on a live table to avoid table locks
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);
Why this works: The database can now do a single B-tree lookup to find the leaf pages for that user_id,
then follow pointers to the actual heap rows. Cost drops from O(N) sequential scan to O(log N) tree
traversal plus a small number of random heap fetches. For 40M rows, the tree depth is roughly 4 levels
— five page reads to find any user_id. The ORDER BY on created_at still requires a sort, but on 20 rows
that sort is essentially free — it happens in memory in microseconds. Scenario8 covers when the sort
itself becomes the bottleneck and needs to be absorbed into the index.
What NOT to say: "Add an index on every column in the WHERE clause" — that's how you end up with
30 single-column indexes on one table and a write performance catastrophe. Index decisions are query-
pattern decisions, not column-level decisions. Also avoid saying "an index always speeds up reads" —
on tiny tables it's slower than a full scan because the planner has to descend the tree.
Common follow-up: "What's the write penalty?" — Roughly 10-15% slower INSERT/UPDATE on
user_id, because the index has to be maintained on every row insert and on any UPDATE that touches
user_id (rare). For a read-heavy admin path on an insert-heavy table, this is still net positive. If writes are
the bottleneck, batch your inserts and use unlogged or partitioned tables to amortize the index-
maintenance cost.
Scenario82 · Composite Index — Order Matters (Leftmost-Prefix)
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Myntra, Swiggy, GCC banks · Dialect: ANSI / MySQL /
Postgres
Scenario setup: A reporting query pulls all "delivered" orders for a specific user in a date range. There's
an index on (status, user_id, created_at) already, but the query still does a full scan. The team is confused
— they "have an index" but it's not being used.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 89 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 90
SELECT id, amount, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE user_id = 1487291
  AND status = 'delivered'
  AND created_at >= '2026-01-01';
Current perf vs target: 9s scan despite existing 3-column index; target sub-200ms.
Thinking out loud: 1. Composite indexes are sorted by the leading column first, then the next, then the
next — think of it like a phone book sorted by surname, then first name, then street. The index on (status,
user_id, created_at) is sorted by status first, so the tree only narrows by status before any other
dimension. 2. The query filters on user_id alongside status — but if the leading column doesn't carry
weight, the optimizer either does a partial scan or skips the index entirely. With 4 status values, the
leading column narrows the search to only 25% of the table; user_id then has to filter linearly within that.
3. The leftmost-prefix rule (sometimes called the "left-to-right rule"): an index on (A, B, C) is useful for
queries filtering on A, or A+B, or A+B+C — never B alone, never C alone, never A+C without B. The
optimizer can use any prefix that begins at the left edge. 4. The fix is reordering: lead with the most
selective equality column. user_id is most selective (millions of values), status next (4 values), created_at
is a range so it must come last. Equality columns first, then range columns last is the standard
composite-index recipe.
The diagnosis: Composite index column order is wrong — leading column is low-cardinality status (4
values), not the high-cardinality user_id (millions of values) the query actually filters on. The index can't
seek efficiently to a user_id without first scanning the status slice.
The fix:
DROP INDEX idx_orders_status_user_created;
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_status_created
  ON orders(user_id, status, created_at);
Why this works: Now the index can seek to the exact (user_id, status) prefix in one descent, then walk
forward through created_at in already-sorted order. The range filter on created_at piggybacks on the sort
order — no extra scan needed because the rows are already ordered by created_at within each (user_id,
status) group. From a tree-depth perspective, lookup goes from "find status slice, scan for user_id within
it" to "descend directly to user_id, descend to status, walk created_at."
What NOT to say: "The optimizer should figure it out" — it can't. The B-tree structure is physical; you
can't skip leading columns without scanning every value of them. Some engines call this trick "loose
index scan" or "skip scan" — Oracle has it, MySQL 8 has limited support, Postgres doesn't — but it's
slower than a properly-ordered composite in every benchmark.
Common follow-up: "Why not put created_at first since it's most selective?" — Range columns belong
last. A range on the leading column stops the index from being useful for any equality filter after it,
because the tree fans out over the range instead of pinning a single value. Equality columns first preserve
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 90 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 91
the ability to seek down to a precise point in the tree; range columns at the end let you walk a contiguous
slice from that point.
Scenario83 · Reorder Columns in Existing Composite for New Query Pattern
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Cred, Walmart Labs · Dialect: ANSI / All
Scenario setup: A payments table has a composite index on (merchant_id, captured_at) that serves the
merchant dashboard well. A new analytics query was added last sprint that filters only by captured_at
across all merchants — and it's not using the index. The team wants to add a second index but is
worried about write cost.
SELECT merchant_id, SUM(amount) AS daily_volume
FROM payments
WHERE captured_at >= '2026-05-01'
GROUP BY merchant_id;
Current perf vs target: 45s scan of 200M-row payments table; target sub-5s.
Thinking out loud: 1. The existing index leads with merchant_id, so it's useless for a query that doesn't
filter by merchant_id — exactly the leftmost-prefix problem from Scenario2 in reverse. The analytics
query has no merchant_id in its WHERE, so the optimizer falls back to a sequential scan of all 200M
rows. 2. Option A: add a second index on (captured_at). This doubles the write penalty on this hot table
— every payment insert now updates two indexes instead of one. 3. Option B: see if the existing index
can be reordered to (captured_at, merchant_id). But then the merchant dashboard query breaks because
it expects merchant_id as the leading column for its per-merchant lookups. Reordering helps one query
at the cost of the other. 4. The right move is two indexes — but only if both query patterns are truly hot.
Profile both before adding. If the analytics query runs once a day at 2 AM, you might tolerate the slow
scan and skip the second index. If it runs every five minutes from a dashboard, the second index is
justified.
The diagnosis: Existing composite cannot serve a query that skips its leading column. Need either a
second index or a redesign of the access pattern. The choice depends on query frequency and write
budget.
The fix:
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_captured_at_merchant
  ON payments(captured_at, merchant_id);
Why this works: The new index leads with captured_at (the range filter), so the engine can seek to May
1, 2026 and walk forward sequentially through the leaf pages until the range ends. Including merchant_id
as the second column lets it do an index-only scan for the GROUP BY without touching the heap — the
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 91 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 92
planner reads just the index leaves, groups by merchant_id, and sums amount from the same pages.
Covered more in Scenario4 on covering indexes.
What NOT to say: "Indexes are free, just add one for every query" — they cost write throughput,
storage, and cache pressure. The honest answer is "two indexes for two access patterns, and we'll
monitor write latency for the next week to confirm the trade-off is worth it." Also avoid "we'll add a
materialized view" without checking whether it's truly cheaper than the index — materialized views have
their own refresh overhead.
Common follow-up: "What if writes get slower?" — Drop the lower-value index. On a payments table,
captured_at is essentially append-only, so index-maintenance cost is low — the page splits happen at
the tail end of the B-tree and don't fragment older pages. Monitor with pg_stat_user_indexes to
confirm the new index is actually being scanned; if it's not, drop it after a week.
Scenario84 · Covering Index — INCLUDE / Index-Only Scan
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Microsoft, Postgres-heavy startups, Atlassian · Dialect: Postgres
11+ / SQL Server / MySQL 8
Scenario setup: A KYC verification page reads a small slice of columns from a wide users table — just
email, kyc_status, and last_login_at — for users in a specific city. There's an index on city, but the query
still does heap lookups for every matching row, and the page takes 4s.
SELECT email, kyc_status, last_login_at
FROM users
WHERE city = 'Bengaluru'
  AND kyc_status = 'verified';
Current perf vs target: 4s with heap fetches for 200k rows; target sub-500ms.
Thinking out loud: 1. The current index on city does the filtering but only returns row pointers — the
engine still has to visit the heap (the actual table pages) to read email, kyc_status, and last_login_at. For
200k matching rows, that's 200k random I/O operations against the heap, each potentially a cache miss.
2. If we include all three columns in the index itself, the engine can answer the query entirely from the
index — no heap visit at all. Postgres calls this an "index-only scan"; SQL Server calls it a "covering
index"; same concept, different vocabulary. 3. The trick: use INCLUDE for the non-key columns so they
don't bloat the B-tree key, but are still available for the result. INCLUDE columns are stored in leaf pages
only, meaning they don't affect tree depth or fanout — they just ride along. 4. Sanity-check: are these
columns mostly stable? last_login_at updates often, so including it means every login triggers an index
update — that may swing the trade-off. If last_login_at gets updated 1000 times per second across the
user base, the index churn might cost more than the read savings. Profile both sides.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 92 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 93
The diagnosis: Index returns row pointers; engine then does 200k random heap reads to fetch the actual
column values. A covering index eliminates the heap visit entirely by stuffing the needed columns into the
index leaves.
The fix:
-- Postgres 11+ / SQL Server
CREATE INDEX idx_users_city_kyc_covering
  ON users(city, kyc_status)
  INCLUDE (email, last_login_at);
-- For MySQL 8, add columns to the index key (no INCLUDE)
CREATE INDEX idx_users_city_kyc_email
  ON users(city, kyc_status, email, last_login_at);
Why this works: The leaf pages of the index now contain everything the query needs — city and
kyc_status for filtering, email and last_login_at for output. The planner sees this and uses an "index-only
scan" — zero random I/O against the heap. For a wide table where the heap row is 2KB and the index
entry is 200 bytes, you read 10x less data. In cache-cold scenarios the difference is even more dramatic
because random heap reads thrash the buffer pool.
What NOT to say: "Just add all columns to the index key" — that bloats the B-tree, increases write cost,
and slows down lookups by reducing fanout. INCLUDE columns sit in leaf pages only, which is the whole
point. Also avoid suggesting "make every index covering" — coverage is per-query; an index that covers
query A may force heap visits for query B, and you can't cover everything.
Common follow-up: "What if MySQL doesn't have INCLUDE?" — MySQL 8 has it via separate
functional indexes; older MySQL forces you to add the columns to the index key itself, which bloats the
B-tree. Calling it out shows you know the dialect difference. The Postgres + SQL Server INCLUDE clause
is genuinely cleaner because it preserves the small key while still enabling index-only scans.
Scenario85 · Partial Index for Hot Filter Values
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Zerodha, Postgres-heavy fintechs, Stripe-style teams · Dialect:
Postgres / SQL Server
Scenario setup: A transactions table has 500M rows total but only ~50k rows at any moment have
status = 'pending'. The payment processor polls "pending" rows every second to retry them. A full index
on status is bloated and ineffective because 99% of rows are 'success' or 'failed'.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 93 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 94
SELECT id, amount, retry_count
FROM transactions
WHERE status = 'pending'
ORDER BY created_at
LIMIT 100;
Current perf vs target: 800ms per poll with full status index; target sub-50ms.
Thinking out loud: 1. A B-tree on status with 500M entries pointing to 'success' is pointless — the
optimizer would skip the index anyway because the cardinality is poor. With only 3-4 status values, each
value matches such a huge chunk of the table that a full scan is cheaper than the index seek + heap
reads. 2. The hot subset is tiny — only the small slice of 'pending' rows matters for the polling workload.
A partial index that excludes the rest is essentially a 50k-row mini-table glued onto the side of the main
table. 3. The polling query reads only pending rows, so a partial index WHERE status = 'pending'
covers 100% of its workload while skipping 99% of the data. The index can include other columns (like
created_at) sorted in poll-order for free. 4. Bonus: the partial index is small enough to live in RAM, so
polls become memory-resident reads — a huge latency win and a near-zero cache-eviction penalty for
the rest of the database.
The diagnosis: Full index on status is bloated and selectivity is poor for the only column value the
application actually queries. A partial index for the hot value is dramatically smaller and faster, and is
automatically maintained as rows enter and exit the 'pending' state.
The fix:
-- Postgres / SQL Server with filtered index syntax
CREATE INDEX idx_transactions_pending
  ON transactions(created_at)
  WHERE status = 'pending';
Why this works: The index now contains only ~50k entries — about 1MB on disk vs the 5GB the full
status index would consume. Every poll hits a fully-cached index and walks the first 100 entries in
created_at order. As rows transition out of 'pending' (via an UPDATE setting status to 'success' or
'failed'), the database automatically removes them from the partial index — no manual maintenance, no
stale rows accumulating. The optimizer matches the query predicate WHERE status = 'pending'
against the index predicate directly and picks it without prompting.
What NOT to say: "MySQL has partial indexes too" — it doesn't, in the same WHERE-clause-on-the-
index sense. MySQL's KEY (col(N)) is a different feature (indexing a prefix of a string column). If
asked in a MySQL shop, propose an expression index, a separate hot-queue table, or a generated-
column workaround. Calling MySQL's prefix-key feature a "partial index" in an interview is a credibility
hit.
Common follow-up: "What if 'pending' grows to 5M rows?" — Still fine; the index stays proportional to
the hot set. The real risk is if 'pending' becomes 50% of the table, at which point a partial index has no
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 94 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 95
advantage over a regular one — the predicate filters nothing meaningful. Another follow-up: "What about
INSERT cost?" — Negligible, because rows enter the partial index only when status starts as 'pending',
and exit when status changes. Most inserts probably already start as 'pending', so it's one index update
either way.
Scenario86 · Expression / Functional Index for WHERE UPPER(col)
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Oracle shops, BFSI GCCs, Postgres startups · Dialect: Postgres /
Oracle / MySQL 8
Scenario setup: A legacy user-lookup query uppercases the email before comparing, because the
column has mixed case from years of inconsistent data entry. There's an index on email, but it's never
used — the optimizer can't match an index on email against a predicate on UPPER(email).
SELECT id, name, signup_at
FROM users
WHERE UPPER(email) = 'RAVI@EXAMPLE.IN';
Current perf vs target: 6s full scan of 20M users; target sub-50ms.
Thinking out loud: 1. Wrapping a column in a function disables any plain index on the underlying column
— the optimizer has no way to know UPPER(x) is monotonic or even deterministic, so it can't translate 
UPPER(email) = 'X' into a B-tree seek against the raw email column. 2. Two paths: rewrite the
query to compare without the function (problematic if the data really is mixed case and you can't trust
normalization), or build an index on the expression itself. The expression-index path doesn't require any
application change. 3. The expression index is the cleaner fix because it preserves the existing query and
handles every variation of case the column might contain. The engine evaluates UPPER(email) once at
insert time and stores the result in the index. 4. Side note: a better long-term fix is data cleanup —
normalize email to lowercase at write time and add a CHECK constraint enforcing it — but that's a multi-
week ticket touching the write path. The expression index is a 30-second deployment that buys you
time.
The diagnosis: WHERE clause wraps the indexed column in UPPER(), making the plain index unusable.
Need an index on the exact expression the query uses so the optimizer can match the predicate against
the indexed expression.
The fix:
-- Postgres / Oracle
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_upper ON users(UPPER(email));
-- MySQL 8+ via functional index (note the double parens for expression)
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_upper ON users((UPPER(email)));
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 95 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 96
Why this works: The B-tree now stores the uppercased form, and the optimizer can match the query
predicate UPPER(email) = 'X' directly against the index key. No function call per row, no scan —
single seek down the tree, single heap fetch. The expression is computed once at write time and cached
in the index leaves. Every read amortizes the one-time write cost across millions of lookups.
What NOT to say: "Just add LOWER() in the query and an index on LOWER(email)" — same problem if
other queries still call UPPER(). You need the index to match the predicate the application actually writes.
Also avoid "the optimizer should constant-fold UPPER" — it can fold constants, not column expressions,
because the engine has no proof that UPPER is a pure function on every value in the column.
Common follow-up: "What about citext in Postgres?" — Cleaner option for new schemas: the citext
type does case-insensitive comparison natively, no expression index needed, and the equality operator
just works. But you can't retrofit it on a 20M-row column without a rewrite, a column-type change, and
an index rebuild — usually not worth the migration risk on a working production table. The expression
index is the practical answer for existing schemas.
Scenario87 · Index on FK Column — The One Everyone Forgets
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Every product company · Dialect: MySQL / Postgres / SQL Server
Scenario setup: A teammate complains that deleting a user takes 30 seconds because of the orders
table's foreign key. The orders table has 80M rows. There's no index on orders.user_id, only the FK
constraint declaration. (MySQL InnoDB auto-creates one, but Postgres does not — and the team is on
Postgres.)
DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 99284;
-- Cascades into orders.user_id check
Current perf vs target: 30s delete (full orders scan to check FK); target sub-100ms.
Thinking out loud: 1. FK constraint just defines the relationship — it doesn't auto-create an index in
Postgres or SQL Server. MySQL InnoDB does auto-create one, which causes everyone to assume it's
universal — and then they get burned the first time they touch a Postgres database. 2. Every DELETE on
the parent triggers a scan of the child to verify no orphans exist (or to cascade the delete). Without an
index on the FK column, that's a full table scan of the child for every parent-row delete. 3. Same issue on
UPDATE if the PK changes (rare in modern schemas, but happens in legacy systems where the natural
key was originally used). Same scan cost. 4. Adding the index is essentially mandatory for any FK
column on a child table that's larger than a few thousand rows. The write-cost penalty is real but tiny
compared to the delete-cost penalty without the index.
The diagnosis: Foreign key column has no index — every parent-row delete or PK update triggers a full
scan of the child table to check referential integrity. This is one of the most common silent performance
bugs in Postgres and SQL Server schemas.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 96 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 97
The fix:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);
-- On a live large table, use CONCURRENTLY in Postgres to avoid table locks
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);
Why this works: The DELETE on users(id) now uses an index seek into orders to find dependent rows in
O(log N) instead of O(N). Cascading deletes (if configured) become proportional to the number of child
rows that actually reference the parent, not the entire child table. For a parent with 5 children, the scan
reads 5 index entries plus 5 heap rows — milliseconds, not minutes.
What NOT to say: "FK constraints are bad for performance, drop them" — that's how data integrity dies.
The constraint is fine; the missing index is the bug. Also avoid "Postgres should auto-create the index"
— that's a design choice (Oracle and Postgres deliberately don't, MySQL does); the database isn't
broken, the schema author missed a step.
Common follow-up: "How do I find all FKs missing indexes?" — In Postgres, join pg_constraint
against pg_index and filter for FK constraints whose columns aren't covered by any index. Most
DBAs have a saved query for this and run it before every schema migration. SQL Server has 
sys.foreign_keys joined to sys.indexes for the same audit; MySQL exposes the relationship
in information_schema.KEY_COLUMN_USAGE but the InnoDB auto-index usually makes this audit
unnecessary there.
Scenario88 · Index for ORDER BY + LIMIT Pattern
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Swiggy, Zomato, Dunzo, Razorpay · Dialect: ANSI / All
Scenario setup: A "recent orders" widget on the user profile page fetches the latest 10 orders for a user.
The table has an index on user_id, and the query filters by user_id and sorts by created_at DESC with
LIMIT 10. But the engine reads all of that user's orders (could be thousands), sorts them, then takes 10
— slow for power users.
SELECT id, amount, status, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE user_id = 1487291
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 10;
Current perf vs target: 1.2s for a heavy user (8k orders); target sub-50ms.
Thinking out loud: 1. The index on user_id finds the relevant rows in O(log N), but then everything inside
that user's slice has to be sorted by created_at — that's an explicit sort step on whatever number of
orders the user has. For a power user with 8,000 orders, that sort dominates the query time. 2. If the
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 97 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 98
index includes created_at as the second column, the rows are already in created_at order within each
user_id, so the sort vanishes — just walk backwards from the latest entry. The index does both jobs at
once. 3. The LIMIT 10 then becomes a top-of-tree walk: descend to the user_id, jump to the last entry in
that user's slice, take 10 going backwards, stop. Constant time regardless of how many orders the user
has — 10 orders or 10 million orders is the same wall-clock latency. 4. Important: the index must order
created_at the same direction the query asks for (or the engine must support backwards scan, which
most do, but with sometimes-worse cost estimates). Building the index DESC removes the ambiguity.
The diagnosis: Sort is happening after the index lookup because the index doesn't preserve the ORDER
BY direction. A composite index covering both filter and sort eliminates the sort entirely.
The fix:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_created
  ON orders(user_id, created_at DESC);
Why this works: The index physically stores rows grouped by user_id, and within each group ordered by
created_at descending. The query descends to user_id 1487291, walks 10 entries from the head of that
user's slice, and returns — no sort, no extra work. This is the single most common composite-index
pattern in real-world product code: filter column first, sort column second, with sort direction matching
the query. Almost every "recent X for user Y" widget uses exactly this shape.
What NOT to say: "Add a second index on created_at alone" — that doesn't help, because the filter on
user_id would force the optimizer to choose between the two indexes; it can only use one for the bulk of
the work. Index-merge plans exist but are rarely chosen and rarely faster than a properly-designed
composite.
Common follow-up: "What if the user has only 5 orders?" — Same plan, even faster. The optimizer
doesn't care about the row count under the user_id; the descent cost is O(log N) regardless. "What if the
user has 5 million orders?" — Still constant time for the first 10, because LIMIT short-circuits the index
walk. The composite shape scales gracefully across the full range of per-user activity.
Scenario89 · Index for ORDER BY DESC + LIMIT — Direction Matters
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: PhonePe, Cred, fintech GCCs · Dialect: Postgres / MySQL 8
Scenario setup: A transaction-history API returns the latest 50 transactions across all users, sorted by
created_at DESC. The team has an index on created_at ASC. The plan shows a sort step costing 80% of
total time.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 98 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 99
SELECT id, user_id, amount, created_at
FROM transactions
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 50;
Current perf vs target: 2.1s with explicit sort; target sub-100ms.
Thinking out loud: 1. An index on created_at ASC can sometimes be walked backwards by the engine
— Postgres supports this for all B-trees, MySQL supports it from 8.0 — but in older MySQL versions and
in certain plan shapes, the optimizer will fall back to a full scan + sort because the cost estimate for the
backwards walk comes out wrong. 2. Building the index in DESC order eliminates the ambiguity — the
engine walks the leaf pages forward and gets the latest rows first. The plan choice is unambiguous and
the cost estimate is straightforward. 3. Postgres has supported backwards index scan since forever, but
the cost estimator sometimes picks a sequential scan + sort if statistics are stale or if the table is small
enough that the planner thinks the full scan is cheaper. Explicit DESC removes the guesswork. 4. MySQL
8 finally supports descending indexes natively — before 8, the DESC keyword in an index definition was
silently ignored, which led to years of confusion. If you're still on 5.7, you have to live with the ASC index
and hope the backwards-scan plan gets picked.
The diagnosis: Index direction doesn't match query sort direction; engine either does extra work or
picks a worse plan. An explicit DESC index aligns physical storage with query intent and removes the
ambiguity from the cost estimate.
The fix:
-- MySQL 8+, Postgres, SQL Server
CREATE INDEX idx_transactions_created_desc
  ON transactions(created_at DESC);
Why this works: The leaf pages are now physically ordered with the latest rows first. The LIMIT 50 walks
the first 50 entries and stops — no sort step, no full scan. Plan goes from Sort (cost=high) to 
Index Scan ... LIMIT 50 with predictable cost. On a 200M-row table the difference is the
difference between 2 seconds and 2 milliseconds.
What NOT to say: "The optimizer always handles DESC" — true in Postgres, mostly true in modern
MySQL, but on MySQL 5.7 the DESC was silently ignored on indexes for years and many production
schemas still don't have explicit DESC indexes for that reason. Always test on your target version. Also
avoid suggesting "the cost is the same" — backwards scans have slightly higher cost estimates in some
planners and may lose to a sort + sequential scan if the table is small.
Common follow-up: "What if I sort by two columns, one ASC one DESC?" — Build a composite index
with matching directions: (col_a ASC, col_b DESC). MySQL 8 and Postgres handle this; older
MySQL doesn't. Without per-column direction support, you have to pick one direction for the index and
the other column always gets a sort step — usually you choose the leading column's direction to match
the most common query.

Scenario90 · Index for Sort + Filter Combined
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Myntra, retail GCCs · Dialect: ANSI / All
Scenario setup: A product-listing page filters orders by warehouse_id and sorts by created_at DESC for
an inventory dashboard. Indexes exist on warehouse_id (alone) and created_at (alone). The plan picks
one, scans, sorts the result — slow at 200ms per page load.
SELECT id, sku, qty, created_at
FROM inventory_movements
WHERE warehouse_id = 17
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 100;
Current perf vs target: 200ms with sort step; target sub-30ms.
Thinking out loud: 1. Two separate indexes can't be combined into a single sorted scan — the engine
picks one and pays the cost of sorting (or filtering) the other dimension. The planner might use index-
merge in some engines, but the merge step is expensive and rarely competitive with a proper composite.
2. The composite trick: leading column is the equality filter (warehouse_id), next column is the sort key
(created_at DESC). Rows within each warehouse are stored already sorted by created_at descending, so
the engine just walks the slice in order. 3. This is the same shape as Scenario8 — filter column first, sort
column second with matching direction — and it's the pattern that comes up in every list-with-filter UI in
production. Master it once and you'll use it weekly. 4. The leftmost column must be the equality (not the
range/sort), otherwise the index can't seek directly to it. If you ever see someone put created_at first
because "it's more selective," gently educate them on the leftmost-prefix rule.
The diagnosis: Two single-column indexes can't satisfy filter + sort together; the engine picks one and
does extra work on the other dimension. A composite with filter-then-sort columns in matching direction
does both in one walk.
The fix:
CREATE INDEX idx_inv_movements_warehouse_created
  ON inventory_movements(warehouse_id, created_at DESC);
-- Optionally drop the now-redundant single-column index
DROP INDEX idx_inv_movements_warehouse;
Why this works: The descent finds warehouse_id = 17 in log time, lands on the slice already sorted by
created_at DESC, and walks the first 100 entries — zero sort work, zero scan beyond what's returned.
The single-column warehouse_id index is subsumed by the composite (the leftmost prefix rule means
any query that used the old single-column index now uses the composite for free) — covered in
Scenario11. Total scan is bounded by the LIMIT, not by the warehouse size.

hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 101
What NOT to say: "The optimizer can index-merge" — it can, sometimes, but the merge step is
expensive (bitmap-OR or sort-merge of row IDs) and rarely faster than a properly-designed composite.
Real-world rule: prefer composites over relying on index-merge plans. Index-merge is a fallback the
optimizer uses when nothing better is available; don't design indexes assuming the planner will rescue
you with a merge.
Common follow-up: "What if users sort by amount sometimes?" — Then you need a second composite
on (warehouse_id, amount DESC). Two indexes for two sort patterns is normal; just monitor write cost
and drop one if it's not earning its keep. A third sort dimension (e.g., by sku name) usually starts the
conversation about whether you need a different read path entirely — a search engine or a materialized
denormalized view.
Scenario91 · Remove Redundant Index Subsumed by Composite
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: DBA roles, senior backend rounds · Dialect: ANSI / All
Scenario setup: After adding the composite index from Scenario10, an old single-column index on
warehouse_id still exists. A write-heavy ETL is now slower than expected. The DBA wants to know
whether the single-column index can safely go.
-- Existing:
CREATE INDEX idx_inv_movements_warehouse ON inventory_movements(warehouse_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_inv_movements_warehouse_created
  ON inventory_movements(warehouse_id, created_at DESC);
Current perf vs target: ETL is 20% slower than before composite was added; target restoration to
baseline.
Thinking out loud: 1. A composite index on (A, B) can satisfy any query that a single-column index on A
could satisfy — leftmost-prefix rule applies to the read side too. The optimizer treats the composite as if
its leftmost slice were a standalone index, so a lookup like WHERE warehouse_id = 17 descends
the composite tree just as efficiently as the standalone index. 2. So the single-column index on
warehouse_id is duplicating work — every INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE maintains both indexes, but the
composite handles every read query the single-column index could. It's become pure overhead: paying
write cost and cache pages without ever being picked for a read plan. 3. Confirm no query specifically
benefits from the smaller key size of the single-column index — usually not a concern unless the second
column is very wide (multi-KB strings). For normal-sized columns like a timestamp, the savings are
imperceptible and the duplicate is genuinely pure waste. 4. Drop the redundant one; ETL latency should
drop back to baseline within minutes. Watch pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan for the composite
before and after to confirm the optimizer still picks it for the warehouse-only queries that previously used
the dropped index.
The diagnosis: Two indexes overlap — the composite subsumes the single-column index via leftmost-
prefix. Both must be maintained on every write, doubling index-write cost for no read benefit. On a write-
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 101 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 102
heavy ETL ingesting tens of thousands of rows per second, that wasted work compounds quickly and
shows up as p99 insert latency.
The fix:
DROP INDEX idx_inv_movements_warehouse;
-- Postgres: use CONCURRENTLY to avoid locking the table during drop
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_inv_movements_warehouse;
Why this works: Every write now updates one index instead of two — roughly 50% less index-
maintenance work for this table. The composite still satisfies every query that used the dropped index,
because (warehouse_id) is the leftmost prefix of (warehouse_id, created_at). ETL throughput bounces
back to baseline within minutes; cache pressure on the buffer pool also drops because there's one less
hot index competing for pages, which indirectly speeds up unrelated queries and reduces replication lag
on standbys.
What NOT to say: "It's fine to keep redundant indexes for safety" — it's not, because every redundant
index costs write throughput, storage, and cache budget without ever serving a read. Audit and prune.
Also avoid "we'll re-add it if needed" without first checking that the composite truly covers every existing
query — drop a real index only after a week of monitoring confirms no plan regressions, captured via 
pg_stat_statements before/after.
Common follow-up: "How do I find redundant indexes?" — Tools like pg_qualstats, MySQL's 
sys.schema_redundant_indexes view, or SHOW INDEX cross-referenced manually with grep.
Most DBAs run this audit quarterly and treat it like a code-review pass. Postgres extensions like 
pg_stat_statements show which indexes are actually used, so you can identify both redundant
and unused indexes in one pass. A strong answer mentions audit cadence and rollback plan, not just the
detection tool.
Scenario92 · Drop Unused Index — Consuming Write Budget
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: DBA / SRE rounds · Dialect: Postgres / MySQL
Scenario setup: A noisy table has 12 indexes accumulated over years. Writes are slowing down on the
events table — 50k inserts/second peak. An audit reveals 4 of the 12 indexes have zero scans recorded
in the last 30 days.
-- Postgres: check pg_stat_user_indexes
SELECT indexrelname, idx_scan
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
WHERE schemaname = 'public' AND relname = 'events'
ORDER BY idx_scan;
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 102 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 103
Current perf vs target: 12 indexes, 4 unused, p99 insert latency 30ms; target sub-15ms.
Thinking out loud: 1. Every index has a write cost — the engine maintains B-tree balance, updates leaf
pages, sometimes splits pages on insert. Twelve indexes means twelve maintenance operations per row
insert, each a small but real synchronous write to the WAL/redo log before the transaction can commit. 2.
Indexes with zero scans in 30 days are either genuinely unused, or used by a quarterly batch job that
hasn't run inside the window — check the application code, cron schedule, and BI tool's saved queries
before dropping. A common gotcha: month-end reconciliation that runs on the 30th when the audit
happened on the 28th. 3. Postgres exposes pg_stat_user_indexes with idx_scan and 
idx_tup_read counters that accumulate since stats reset; MySQL exposes 
sys.schema_unused_indexes from 5.7+ via performance_schema. Always check when stats were
last reset — a freshly-reset counter looks unused but might just be young. 4. Drop one at a time and
monitor — never in bulk in case the audit missed a quarterly job that runs tomorrow. Keep a one-line
rollback CREATE INDEX command in your runbook so you can restore in 30 seconds if a slow-query alert
fires post-drop.
The diagnosis: Unused indexes are still maintained on every write, adding latency without serving any
read query. Drop after confirming zero usage across a window long enough to catch your slowest-
cadence batch job. On a 50k-inserts/second table, even four unused indexes can swing p99 by 5-15ms
because every insert pays the maintenance tax synchronously.
The fix:
-- Postgres: stage the drop with INVALIDATE first (Postgres 12+)
-- Then DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY to avoid locks
DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_events_unused_thing;
-- Keep the CREATE statement in a runbook for instant rollback if needed
Why this works: Removing 4 of 12 indexes from a hot insert path reduces per-row maintenance work by
~33%. p99 latency drops proportionally — usually visible within minutes once WAL volume per
transaction shrinks. Freed cache and disk space help the remaining indexes stay hot, and you'll often
see secondary wins like faster VACUUM cycles and lower replication lag on standbys because there's
less index data to ship downstream.
What NOT to say: "Drop unused indexes immediately" — without a 30-day-plus monitoring window,
you'll catch the quarterly compliance report on the wrong week and break a CFO's month-end
dashboard. Always wait, then drop. Also avoid "if it's not used, it's safe to drop" without confirming 
pg_stat_user_indexes counters haven't been reset recently — a server restart or manual 
pg_stat_reset() zeroes them and makes everything look unused.
Common follow-up: "What about indexes used once a year?" — Keep them, but document why so the
next audit doesn't accidentally drop them. The audit threshold is "zero scans in 90 days" for most teams;
an annual job will show up in a full-year window. A strong answer says "I'd check idx_scan over 90
days plus grep the codebase plus ask the analytics team before dropping anything."

Scenario93 · Replace B-tree with GIN for JSON Path Query (Postgres)
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Postgres-first startups, Cred, Razorpay platform · Dialect: Postgres only
Scenario setup: An events table stores semi-structured payloads in a jsonb column. A new query filters
events where payload->>'event_type' = 'checkout_completed'. There's a B-tree
expression index on that exact path, but a follow-up query needs payload @> '{"source":
"android"}' containment — and the B-tree can't help.
SELECT id, user_id, created_at
FROM events
WHERE payload @> '{"source": "android"}'::jsonb;
Current perf vs target: 18s scan of 100M-row events; target sub-2s.
Thinking out loud: 1. B-tree is for exact-match or range queries on a single value — JSON containment
is neither, so the existing expression index is useless for @>. The expression index on payload-
>>'event_type' only helps when the query uses exactly that path with equality or range. 2. GIN
(Generalized Inverted Index) is built for "key/value exists in this document" queries — exactly what @>
does on jsonb. Internally GIN maps every indexable token (each key, value, or hashed path) to a posting
list of row IDs, so containment becomes a posting-list intersection rather than a per-row JSON walk. 3.
Postgres has two GIN flavors for jsonb: default (indexes every key + value, supports ?, ?|, ?&, 
@>, <@) and jsonb_path_ops (indexes only the hashed path, smaller and faster for @> but no
existence operators). Choice depends on whether you ever need ? outside containment. 4. For a
containment-only workload, jsonb_path_ops is the right choice — typically 30% the size of default GIN
and faster for @> because the posting list is keyed on hashed full paths. Smaller index means more of
it fits in cache.
The diagnosis: B-tree can't index unstructured JSON containment. Need a GIN index purpose-built for
jsonb operators, with the operator class chosen based on which jsonb operators the application actually
uses.
The fix:
-- For ?, ?|, ?&, @>, <@ — use default jsonb GIN
CREATE INDEX idx_events_payload_gin ON events USING gin (payload);
-- For @> only — smaller, faster
CREATE INDEX idx_events_payload_pathops
  ON events USING gin (payload jsonb_path_ops);
Why this works: GIN inverts the document — it stores a mapping from each key/value (or path) back to
the row IDs containing it. The containment query payload @> '{"source": "android"}'
becomes a fast inverted-index lookup: find the posting list for that key/value, return row IDs, then
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 104 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 105
recheck the jsonb document against the full predicate. Goes from a 100M-row sequential scan that
parses jsonb per row to a posting-list lookup returning candidates in milliseconds.
What NOT to say: "GIN works on any column" — it doesn't; it's built for composite values (jsonb, arrays,
tsvector) where each row contributes multiple indexable tokens. Don't suggest GIN for a plain integer
column where B-tree is dramatically better. Also avoid "GIN is always slower to write" without qualifying
— with fastupdate = on the cost moves to a pending list that flushes when full, so write latency
stays low for bursty inserts.
Common follow-up: "What's the write cost of GIN?" — Significantly higher than B-tree because every
key/value pair is indexed, and each insert may touch many posting lists. Use fastupdate to batch
updates into a pending list that flushes asynchronously; tune gin_pending_list_limit if writes
become a bottleneck. A senior answer mentions monitoring pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_blks_*
and watching VACUUM logs to ensure the pending list isn't growing unbounded.
Scenario94 · Replace B-tree with BRIN for Append-Only Large Table (Postgres)
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Data engineering, analytics platforms · Dialect: Postgres only
Scenario setup: A telemetry table holds 2 billion rows of sensor readings, ordered by recorded_at
because data only ever appends in time order. A B-tree index on recorded_at is 80GB — bigger than the
working set fits in cache. Range queries on recorded_at are slow because the index itself doesn't fit in
RAM.
SELECT device_id, AVG(temperature)
FROM telemetry
WHERE recorded_at BETWEEN '2026-05-01' AND '2026-05-07'
GROUP BY device_id;
Current perf vs target: 45s with cold B-tree; target sub-5s and tiny index.
Thinking out loud: 1. B-tree is overkill for a column naturally correlated with physical row order — every
row inserted goes to the end in time order. Maintaining an 80GB tree to map timestamps to row IDs when
those row IDs are already essentially in timestamp order is paying full tree-maintenance cost for a non-
problem. 2. BRIN (Block Range Index) stores a min/max per block range (default 128 pages = 1MB). For
a column where physical order matches logical order, BRIN narrows the scan to just the relevant block
ranges — instead of indexing every row, it indexes every chunk, which is wildly cheaper. 3. BRIN size:
roughly 1KB per 1GB of table at default pages_per_range. For a 200GB table, the BRIN index is
200KB vs 80GB for a B-tree. That's not a typo; the ratio is that extreme because BRIN only records
summary statistics, not individual row pointers. 4. The trade-off: BRIN is useless if the column is not
physically correlated (e.g., random uuid timestamps, or tables you frequently UPDATE in random places).
Always check pg_stats.correlation first; correlation near 1.0 or -1.0 means BRIN will work,
anything close to 0 means BRIN will scan most of the table.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 105 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 106
The diagnosis: B-tree on append-only time-series column is unnecessarily large because the data is
already physically ordered. BRIN exploits the correlation for a 1000x smaller index that lives entirely in
cache and serves range scans by jumping directly to the relevant heap chunks.
The fix:
DROP INDEX idx_telemetry_recorded_at;
CREATE INDEX idx_telemetry_recorded_at_brin
  ON telemetry USING brin (recorded_at)
  WITH (pages_per_range = 32);
Why this works: BRIN stores one min/max pair per 32-page chunk. The range query for May 1-7 finds
the chunks whose min/max overlap that window, then scans just those chunks sequentially from the
heap. For an append-only table this might be 0.1% of the total — dramatic I/O reduction with a
microscopic index. Smaller pages_per_range gives finer-grained pruning at the cost of slightly larger
BRIN; 32 is a reasonable starting point you can tune based on workload shape.
What NOT to say: "BRIN is always smaller, use it everywhere" — it's only useful when physical order
correlates with the indexed column, which is a strong precondition. On a randomly-distributed column,
BRIN scans most of the table because min/max ranges overlap too much. Also avoid "BRIN is just a B-
tree alternative" — it's a fundamentally different structure (lossy summary vs precise pointers) with a
different cost model.
Common follow-up: "How do I keep correlation high?" — On append-only tables it stays high naturally
because every new row lands at the physical tail. If you bulk-update old rows (e.g., backfilling a new
column), correlation degrades and you'll need CLUSTER or pg_repack to restore physical order. For
high-churn tables, BRIN is a poor choice — every UPDATE that changes the indexed column scrambles
the min/max boundaries and summarisation drifts from reality.
Scenario95 · Trigram Index for LIKE '%suffix' Search
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Search-heavy products, Postgres startups · Dialect: Postgres
(pg_trgm) / Some MySQL via plugins
Scenario setup: A product-search bar runs WHERE name ILIKE '%shirt%'. There's a B-tree on
name. The query takes 3 seconds on 5M products because the leading % makes the B-tree useless —
no index can seek to a prefix that starts with a wildcard.
SELECT id, name, price
FROM products
WHERE name ILIKE '%shirt%';
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 106 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 107
Current perf vs target: 3s scan; target sub-200ms.
Thinking out loud: 1. B-tree indexes are prefix-sortable, so LIKE 'shirt%' works (the engine seeks
to 'shirt' and walks the leaf pages) but LIKE '%shirt%' does not — the leading wildcard prevents
prefix matching because the tree has no way to know which leaf contains 'shirt' as a substring versus a
prefix. 2. The pg_trgm extension breaks strings into 3-character chunks (trigrams) and indexes them via
GIN or GiST. Any substring search becomes "find rows whose trigrams overlap with the query's trigrams"
— a posting-list intersection, not a tree descent. The word 'shirt' becomes the trigrams _sh, shi, 
hir, irt, rt_ after pg_trgm's standard padding. 3. For full-text search there's also tsvector with 
to_tsvector and to_tsquery, but trigram is the right pick for LIKE-style substring matching
where you don't want stemming, stopword filtering, or language-specific tokenisation. Trigram matches
the exact byte sequence; full-text matches lexemes. 4. Trigram indexes also accelerate fuzzy match via
the % similarity operator and the <-> distance operator, which is a free bonus for "did you mean"
features and typo-tolerant search. The same index serves substring LIKE, ILIKE, and similarity queries.
The diagnosis: Leading-wildcard LIKE can't use a B-tree because the tree depends on prefix order.
Trigram indexes break strings into 3-char chunks and use GIN/GiST for fast substring lookup — turning
containment into an inverted-index lookup over the trigram tokens.
The fix:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;
CREATE INDEX idx_products_name_trgm
  ON products USING gin (name gin_trgm_ops);
Why this works: The query name ILIKE '%shirt%' is converted to a trigram lookup for 'shi', 'hir',
'irt' — the GIN index returns row IDs that contain all three trigrams, then the engine confirms each
candidate with a final ILIKE check (the "recheck" step). Goes from a 5M-row scan to a few thousand
candidate rows in milliseconds. The recheck is necessary because the trigram set can produce false
positives (e.g., 'shir' + 't' as separate words), but the candidate set is small enough that the final filter is
essentially free.
What NOT to say: "Use full-text search instead" — for short single-word substring matches like product
names, trigram is faster and simpler. Full-text shines for natural-language queries (multi-word, ranking,
stemming, multi-language), not raw substring containment in a product catalogue. Also avoid "trigrams
are always faster than B-tree" — for a pure prefix match like LIKE 'shirt%', a regular B-tree still
wins because trigram has extra recheck cost.
Common follow-up: "What about MySQL?" — MySQL doesn't have trigrams natively, so the standard
answer is full-text indexes (FULLTEXT INDEX with the MATCH ... AGAINST operator) for word-
boundary search, or a third-party search engine like Elasticsearch / Meilisearch for non-trivial workloads.
A senior answer also mentions that for an Indian e-commerce stack on MySQL 8, many teams just push
search to OpenSearch or Typesense rather than fight the in-database tooling, because LIKE-with-
leading-wildcard at scale really is a search engine's job.

Scenario96 · Index on Generated Column for Case-Insensitive Search
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: MySQL shops, e-commerce GCCs · Dialect: MySQL 8 / Postgres
Scenario setup: A vendor lookup uses WHERE LOWER(vendor_code) = 'in-blr-001'. A plain
index on vendor_code doesn't help because of the function call. The team is on MySQL 8 and prefers
generated columns over expression indexes for readability.
SELECT id, vendor_name, address
FROM vendors
WHERE LOWER(vendor_code) = 'in-blr-001';
Current perf vs target: 700ms scan of 500k vendors; target sub-20ms.
Thinking out loud: 1. Same root problem as Scenario6 — function-wrapped column disables the plain
index, because the optimizer can't translate LOWER(vendor_code) = 'X' into a B-tree seek against
the raw column. Without proof that LOWER is monotonic and deterministic, the planner scans every row.
2. MySQL 8 supports expression indexes via ((expr)) syntax, but many teams prefer a generated
stored column that's plainly visible in the schema, then a normal B-tree on it. The generated column
shows up in DESCRIBE output; an expression index is invisible unless someone runs SHOW INDEX.
3. The trade-off: generated stored column doubles storage for the column (original plus lowercased
copy), but is clearer to future maintainers than an expression index. For a 500k-row table the storage
cost is trivial — maybe 25MB — and worth the clarity. 4. Generated virtual columns also work and don't
take storage, but the index on them is essentially an expression index under the hood. For lookup-heavy
workloads, stored is preferred because the value is materialised and read paths are simpler.
The diagnosis: Function call in WHERE disables the plain index. Use a generated column (or expression
index) to give the optimizer something to seek on — the index stores the pre-computed function result
and the optimizer matches the predicate directly.
The fix:
-- MySQL 8
ALTER TABLE vendors
  ADD COLUMN vendor_code_lower VARCHAR(50)
    GENERATED ALWAYS AS (LOWER(vendor_code)) STORED;
CREATE INDEX idx_vendors_code_lower ON vendors(vendor_code_lower);
-- Then either rewrite the query or trust the optimizer to use the generated column
Why this works: The generated column holds the lowercased version, kept in sync automatically on
every INSERT and UPDATE of vendor_code — no application change needed. The B-tree on it
serves direct equality queries on LOWER(vendor_code) — most MySQL 8 versions recognize the
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 108 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 109
function-on-source-column expression and use the index automatically. If the optimizer is stubborn,
rewrite the WHERE to filter on the generated column directly and the pick becomes unambiguous.
What NOT to say: "Just rewrite the application to store lowercase" — sometimes you can't, because
multi-team data ownership or legacy callers prevent a coordinated release, and the generated column
gives the same outcome without that coordination. Also avoid "indexes always understand function
calls" — they don't, and pretending otherwise is the kind of confident-but-wrong claim that costs you a
senior interview.
Common follow-up: "Stored vs virtual generated column?" — Stored consumes disk but is fast to read
because the value is materialised at write time; virtual is computed on the fly every read. For indexed
lookups, stored is usually right because the index needs the value materialised anyway, and storing once
in the table avoids re-computing on every related UPDATE. A strong answer also mentions that stored
columns participate in row-format limits (innodb_default_row_format and the 65,535-byte row limit) while
virtual columns don't.
Scenario97 · Hash Index for Equality-Only Column (Postgres 10+)
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Postgres-deep teams, infra-leaning roles · Dialect: Postgres 10+ only
Scenario setup: A session-token lookup happens on every API call — WHERE session_id =
'abc123...'. The session_id is a 64-char hex string, lookups are equality-only (never range, never
sort). A B-tree on session_id is being maintained, but the team wonders if hash would be faster.
SELECT user_id, expires_at
FROM sessions
WHERE session_id = 'a8f3e2c4b1...';
Current perf vs target: 0.6ms p50 with B-tree; want lower variance under high concurrency.
Thinking out loud: 1. Postgres hash indexes were unreliable pre-10 (no WAL logging, couldn't survive
crash, not replicable). Post-10 they're crash-safe and replicable — finally usable in production. The
internet still has stale 9.x-era advice saying "never use hash indexes," which trips up candidates who
haven't tracked the change. 2. Hash indexes are smaller than B-tree for long keys (constant-size hash
buckets vs full sortable keys) and have O(1) lookup vs O(log N). For a 64-char hex string, B-tree stores
~64 bytes per entry while the hash bucket is just the hash plus row pointer — dramatically smaller index
and shorter traversal. 3. The catch: hash supports only =, never <, >, BETWEEN, ORDER BY. If
any query needs those, you need a B-tree anyway, and dropping to hash makes you re-add B-tree later
— losing the benefit. Confirm the access pattern is genuinely equality-only before switching. 4. For a
strict equality lookup on a long opaque string, hash wins on size and lookup cost. Postgres 14+
benchmarks show ~30% smaller index and ~10-15% faster lookups under contention, with the gap
widening as keys get longer because B-tree key comparisons get more expensive while hash
comparisons stay constant.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 109 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 110
The diagnosis: B-tree is overkill for equality-only lookups on long opaque strings. Hash indexes are
smaller and have O(1) lookup — ideal for session tokens, API keys, or any opaque identifier never sorted
or range-queried.
The fix:
DROP INDEX idx_sessions_session_id;
CREATE INDEX idx_sessions_session_id_hash
  ON sessions USING hash (session_id);
Why this works: Hash buckets give constant-time lookup regardless of table size — no tree descent.
The index is smaller because it stores buckets keyed by a 4-byte hash instead of full sortable keys. For a
session-lookup hot path running millions of times per second, the savings add up — both in p99 latency
(less variance under contention because no tree depth) and in cache pressure (smaller index means more
stays resident).
What NOT to say: "Hash indexes are deprecated" — they were unreliable pre-Postgres 10, but are fully
supported now and recommended for the right workload. If the interviewer says "I heard they're unsafe,"
correct politely with the version history; it's a chance to demonstrate you read release notes. Also avoid
"hash is always faster than B-tree" — for short integer keys the gap is negligible and B-tree's range
support outweighs any micro-benefit.
Common follow-up: "What about MySQL hash indexes?" — MySQL has them only on MEMORY tables
and some NDB cluster configs. For InnoDB you're stuck with B-tree, although InnoDB maintains an
"adaptive hash index" automatically for hot keys behind the scenes — different mechanism but similar
lookup-speed benefit for equality. Calling out the dialect difference signals depth, especially since most
candidates assume MySQL has parity with Postgres on index types.
Scenario98 · Partial Index for is_active = true Hot Path
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: SaaS startups, multi-tenant platforms · Dialect: Postgres / SQL
Server
Scenario setup: A multi-tenant SaaS has a tenants table with 80k rows, of which only 12k are 
is_active = true — paying customers. Almost every query filters by is_active = true AND
tenant_id = X. A composite index on (is_active, tenant_id) works but is bloated with inactive rows.
SELECT id, plan_tier, billing_email
FROM tenants
WHERE is_active = TRUE
  AND tenant_id = 99284;
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 110 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 111
Current perf vs target: 8ms p95 with composite; want smaller index and lower cache footprint.
Thinking out loud: 1. The is_active = true rows are a small minority (12k of 80k, roughly 15%) but
account for ~99% of query volume because inactive tenants don't generate dashboard traffic. The other
85% is dead weight in the index — pages in the B-tree that never match at read time but still cost write-
maintenance work and cache space. 2. A partial index WHERE is_active = TRUE shrinks the index
to 12k entries — fits comfortably in cache, often in a single megabyte of RAM. Once it's cache-resident,
every lookup becomes a memory-only operation with no disk I/O. 3. Bonus: the index doesn't need
is_active as a column, because that constraint is implicit in the WHERE-clause predicate. So the partial
index is just on tenant_id, making the B-tree key as narrow as possible and maximising fanout. 4. The
optimizer matches the query WHERE against the index WHERE — both must be identical or the query
predicate must be a provable subset, or the index is skipped. So WHERE is_active = TRUE AND
tenant_id = X matches; WHERE is_active = TRUE OR tenant_id = X does not.
The diagnosis: Composite index includes inactive rows that are never queried. A partial index covering
only active rows is smaller, hotter, and serves the same queries — with zero loss of correctness because
the predicate excluding inactive rows is encoded into the index definition itself.
The fix:
DROP INDEX idx_tenants_active_tenant;
CREATE INDEX idx_tenants_active_partial
  ON tenants(tenant_id)
  WHERE is_active = TRUE;
Why this works: The partial index is ~1/7 the size of the full composite. It lives entirely in
shared_buffers / buffer pool, often comfortably under a megabyte. Lookups become memory-resident
hash-like operations because the tree is small enough that every level is hot. The is_active filter is implicit
in the index definition, so no extra check at read time and no extra column in the B-tree key. Write cost
also drops because rows in the inactive 85% never touch the index — only active-row INSERTs and
UPDATEs trigger maintenance.
What NOT to say: "Partial indexes are too restrictive" — they're the right tool when the hot subset is
small and stable. For dynamic predicates (like WHERE created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '7
days'), partial indexes are a bad fit because the predicate window slides over time and yesterday's
matching rows become today's non-matching rows without any UPDATE happening. Use partial only for
stable predicates that don't drift.
Common follow-up: "What if a tenant is reactivated?" — Row enters the partial index automatically on
the UPDATE that flips is_active to TRUE; deactivation removes it. Maintenance is transparent. A strong
answer also notes the partial index works hand-in-hand with the leftmost-prefix rule from Scenario11 —
if other queries filter by tenant_id without the is_active predicate, you may need a separate full index and
accept the duplication.
