Scenario99 · Index for ORDER BY with NULLS LAST
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Postgres-leaning teams, reporting platforms · Dialect: Postgres /
Oracle / MySQL 8
Scenario setup: A "users who haven't logged in" report sorts users by last_login_at ascending
with NULLS LAST so never-logged-in users appear at the bottom. There's a plain index on last_login_at
ASC. The query plan shows an explicit sort step despite the index, because the default NULLS ordering
differs from what the query requests.
SELECT id, email, last_login_at
FROM users
ORDER BY last_login_at ASC NULLS LAST
LIMIT 100;
Current perf vs target: 4s with sort step on 30M users; target sub-100ms.
Thinking out loud: 1. Postgres defaults: ASC → NULLS LAST, DESC → NULLS FIRST. Oracle defaults:
ASC → NULLS LAST, DESC → NULLS LAST. They differ — and the index must match the query's
request, otherwise the engine has to physically re-order the result. This is exactly the kind of dialect detail
that catches teams porting reports between databases. 2. If the index was built without an explicit
NULLS clause, Postgres uses NULLS LAST for ASC — which matches in this case. But if the index was
built DESC, NULLS would default FIRST, mismatching ORDER BY ... DESC NULLS LAST and
forcing a sort. Many production schemas have indexes that "look right" but mismatch on NULLS
ordering. 3. The fix is to declare NULLS ordering explicitly in both index and query, so they match and
the sort step disappears. Explicit beats implicit here — defaults differ across versions and dialects, but
explicit syntax is always portable. 4. MySQL 8 finally supports NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST syntax;
before 8, NULL ordering was fixed (NULLs sort low, so ASC puts NULLs first, DESC puts NULLs last)
and you had to use IS NULL tricks like ORDER BY field IS NULL, field. The trick worked but
disabled the index for ordering, costing a sort.
The diagnosis: Index NULLS ordering differs from query NULLS ordering; the engine adds a sort step to
physically rearrange the result. Align them explicitly so the index leaves are already in the exact order the
query wants — no sort needed.
The fix:
CREATE INDEX idx_users_last_login_nullslast
  ON users(last_login_at ASC NULLS LAST);
Why this works: The leaf pages are physically ordered with NULLs at the end — exactly the order the
query wants. The LIMIT 100 walks the first 100 non-NULL entries and stops; no sort, no scan beyond the
LIMIT. On a 30M-row users table where most have a last_login_at value and only a fraction are
NULL, the index serves the query as an ordered stream and the planner short-circuits after the LIMIT.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 112 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 113
What NOT to say: "Just rewrite the query to push NULLs out" — you can hack it with 
COALESCE(last_login_at, '9999-12-31') and ORDER BY that expression, but it's fragile (what
if a real timestamp ever exceeds your sentinel?) and the expression sort still disables the index. The
declarative NULLS LAST is cleaner, portable, and obvious to the next reader. Sentinel-value hacks are a
credibility hit in senior interviews — they show willingness to encode assumptions in data.
Common follow-up: "What about MySQL 5.7?" — No native NULLS LAST. Common workaround: 
ORDER BY (last_login_at IS NULL), last_login_at — but it disables index ordering for the
second clause, costing a sort over the whole result set. A strong answer adds "we'd push the team
toward MySQL 8 specifically for this kind of ORDER BY semantics, because the cost of working around
it adds up across many reports."
Scenario100 · Index Leading Column with Wrong Cardinality
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Senior backend, query-tuning rounds · Dialect: ANSI / All
Scenario setup: A composite index on (status, country_code, created_at) was built years ago. status
has 4 values; country_code has 200; created_at is a timestamp. Almost every query hits status =
'completed' AND country_code = 'IN' — and is slow because the leading column has terrible cardinality.
SELECT id, amount, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'completed'
  AND country_code = 'IN'
  AND created_at >= '2026-01-01';
Current perf vs target: 6s with poor index selectivity; target sub-500ms.
Thinking out loud: 1. The composite leads with status (4 values), so the first index descent only narrows
to 1/4 of the table — still 50M rows on a 200M-row table. That's not a useful narrowing; the index has to
walk an enormous slice before any secondary filter can engage, and the planner often gives up and falls
back to a sequential scan. 2. Then within that subset, country_code narrows to 1/200 — but the index
has to walk a large chunk before it can use country_code, because country_code is the second column
and the engine can only seek to it after fixing the leading status value. The 50M-row first-level scan is the
bottleneck. 3. Better leading column: country_code (200 values) or even created_at (effectively unique) —
but range columns can't lead a composite well for equality+range workloads, so country_code wins. The
classic recipe is: lead with the equality column that has the highest cardinality, follow with other equality
columns by descending cardinality, end with the range column. 4. Rebuild with country_code first, then
status (still useful for filtering after the country narrows), then created_at last for the range walk. This
matches the standard composite-index recipe and gives each level of the descent maximum selectivity.
The diagnosis: Leading column has poor cardinality, so the initial seek doesn't narrow the search space
enough. Reorder columns so the most-selective equality leads — selectivity-first composite design is the
rule of thumb for any equality+equality+range workload.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 113 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 114
The fix:
DROP INDEX idx_orders_status_country_created;
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_country_status_created
  ON orders(country_code, status, created_at);
Why this works: The descent narrows by 1/200 immediately (country = IN), then by 1/4 (status =
completed), then walks created_at as a sorted range. Each step is dramatically more selective than
before — the search space shrinks from 200M rows to 1M after the first descent, then to 250k after the
second, then narrowed further by the date range. Engine reads far fewer index pages and far fewer heap
rows, and the optimizer's cost estimate makes index-scan obviously cheaper than sequential-scan so
the plan choice is stable.
What NOT to say: "Selectivity doesn't matter for composites" — it absolutely does, because the
leftmost column determines how big a slice the index has to scan before secondary filters kick in. A
composite led by a 4-value column is essentially a sequential-scan-with-extra-steps for most queries.
Also avoid "always lead with the column most queries filter on" without the selectivity check — if the
most-common filter is on a low-cardinality column, you need either a partial index or a different
composite shape.
Common follow-up: "What if status is sometimes queried alone?" — Then you need an additional index
leading with status, or you accept the slower plan for that less-frequent query. Trade-offs are explicit and
worth measuring: count how often each query shape runs, multiply by its current latency, and compare
against the write cost of a second index. A senior answer talks numbers, not just "it depends."
Scenario101 · Index on Date Column for Range Filter
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Every analytics-touching role · Dialect: ANSI / All
Scenario setup: A monthly revenue report sums payments for a date range. The payments table has
200M rows. There's no index on captured_at. The report takes 90 seconds.
SELECT SUM(amount) AS monthly_total
FROM payments
WHERE captured_at >= '2026-05-01'
  AND captured_at <  '2026-06-01';
Current perf vs target: 90s full scan; target sub-10s.
Thinking out loud: 1. Range filter on a column with no index = full table scan, regardless of how small
the range is. A query targeting one day out of three years still reads all 200M rows, because without an
index the engine can't skip ahead — it has to inspect every row's captured_at value. 2. B-tree on
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 114 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 115
captured_at lets the engine seek to May 1 and walk sequentially until June 1 — pages read proportional
to the range, not the table. Tree descent finds the starting leaf in log time, then leaf-page traversal is a
contiguous walk in the index's physical order. 3. For a month of payments out of years of history, that's
maybe 5% of the table — 20x less work in pages touched, and even less CPU because there's no per-
row predicate evaluation. Just walk and emit. 4. Bonus: if SUM is the only aggregation and the column
set is small, consider a covering index (Scenario4) to skip heap reads entirely — INCLUDE (amount)
makes index leaves carry the sum input and the query becomes index-only. For aggregation-heavy
reports on a single numeric column, often a 5-10x further speed-up.
The diagnosis: No index on the range column forces a full scan of the entire 200M-row table to find
rows in a one-month window. A simple B-tree on captured_at narrows the scan to the requested date
range — index seek to find the start, then sequential leaf-page walk to the end.
The fix:
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_captured_at ON payments(captured_at);
-- For an aggregation hot path, consider INCLUDE (amount) for index-only scan
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_captured_at_amt ON payments(captured_at) INCLUDE (amount);
Why this works: B-tree finds May 1 in O(log N), then walks leaves sequentially until June 1 — pages
proportional to (range / total). 90 seconds becomes 4-5 seconds with the basic index, mostly heap I/O
for matching rows; with the covering variant the heap visit disappears and you're looking at maybe 1-2
seconds because leaves carry the amount values directly. The range walk is also a sequential disk
pattern, dramatically faster than the random access B-tree typically requires.
What NOT to say: "Add an index on every date column just in case" — only if queried with range filters
or order-by; an index on a never-read date column is pure write tax. Date columns only written and never
queried (like soft-delete timestamps checked only by a nightly cleanup) often don't need indexes. Also
avoid "B-tree always beats sequential scan" — for queries selecting more than ~10-20% of the table,
sequential scan wins because random I/O for heap lookups loses.
Common follow-up: "Why not partition by date?" — Partitioning helps at 1B+ row scale where even
indexed scans touch too much data, or where you need cheap retention drops (drop partition =
millisecond DDL, delete = hours). For 200M rows, an index is enough; partitioning adds operational
complexity. The right answer is usually "index now, partition when the table outgrows the buffer pool or
when retention deletes become painful."
Scenario102 · Index on date_trunc Expression for Daily Aggregation
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Postgres analytics teams · Dialect: Postgres (date_trunc) / Most
engines via expression index
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 115 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 116
Scenario setup: A daily metrics dashboard groups events by day with date_trunc('day',
created_at). There's an index on created_at, but the GROUP BY runs a sort step over millions of
rows. The dashboard takes 22 seconds to render.
SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at) AS day,
       COUNT(*) AS event_count
FROM events
WHERE created_at >= '2026-05-01'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
Current perf vs target: 22s with sort; target sub-3s.
Thinking out loud: 1. The index on created_at supports the range filter (find rows where created_at >=
May 1), but the GROUP BY on date_trunc requires a separate sort step to bucket the trimmed
timestamps. The raw index is sorted by full timestamp, not by day boundary, so the engine materialises
the full filtered set and sorts or hashes it for the GROUP BY. 2. An expression index on date_trunc('day',
created_at) physically stores the day-bucketed values, so the GROUP BY can walk the sorted index
without a sort step. The leaves are already ordered by day, which is exactly the grouping key. 3. Trade-
off: the expression index doesn't help the original range filter on raw created_at, so you may end up
wanting both — or restructure the query to filter and group on the same expression. The cleanest fix is to
push date_trunc into the WHERE as well, so the index serves both filter and group. 4. For really hot daily
aggregates, the better long-term move is a materialized view refreshed nightly — the dashboard then
queries a 30-row summary table instead of aggregating millions of rows per page load. But the
expression index is the first quick win that doesn't require refresh-schedule operational changes.
The diagnosis: GROUP BY on an expression requires sort because the underlying index sorts raw
values, not bucketed ones. An expression index on the bucketed value eliminates the sort and turns the
aggregation into a streaming walk.
The fix:
CREATE INDEX idx_events_created_day
  ON events (date_trunc('day', created_at));
-- And rewrite the WHERE to use the same expression for clarity
SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at) AS day, COUNT(*)
FROM events
WHERE date_trunc('day', created_at) >= '2026-05-01'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
Why this works: Index leaves are already sorted by day, so GROUP BY 1 streams through buckets in
order — no sort, no hash aggregation, no temp file spill. COUNT(*) increments per bucket as the engine
walks the leaves, emitting one row per day as soon as the bucket boundary is crossed. For 31 days of
data over millions of events, the output is at most 31 rows produced from a contiguous index walk —
wall-clock time is dominated by index leaf I/O, not aggregation.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 116 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 117
What NOT to say: "Just cache the result in the application" — sometimes right, but the question is
about the query and caching is a separate layer that shouldn't excuse a quadratic database query.
Application caching complements query tuning, not substitutes for it. Also avoid "expression indexes are
always better than B-tree" — for queries filtering on raw timestamps (not bucketed), the raw B-tree wins;
the expression index is workload-specific.
Common follow-up: "What about partitioning by day?" — At scale (multi-billion rows), partition pruning
beats expression indexes because the planner skips entire partitions without touching their data. At
hundreds of millions, the expression index wins on simplicity — no partition maintenance, no schema-
change coordination, just a single CREATE INDEX. A senior answer notes the right move evolves: index
now, partition when the table hits buffer-pool ceiling or when retention drops become the cheap way to
delete old data.
Scenario103 · Foreign Key Without Index → Slow Cascade DELETE
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Senior backend, data-platform roles · Dialect: Postgres / MySQL
InnoDB
Scenario setup: A GDPR-style "delete user" request takes 8 minutes per user. The users table cascades
to orders, payments, sessions, events, addresses, devices, refunds — seven child tables. Five of the
seven have no index on user_id.
DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 99284;
-- ON DELETE CASCADE fires on 7 child tables
Current perf vs target: 8 minutes per user delete; target sub-5 seconds.
Thinking out loud: 1. Postgres doesn't auto-index FK columns; the developer has to add the index
explicitly. Same for SQL Server. MySQL InnoDB does auto-create one, but only for the constraint's
referencing column — and many teams assume the universal default is MySQL's behaviour, which
causes silent slow-delete bugs on Postgres for years. 2. Without the index, every cascade-delete on a
child table is a full table scan to find matching child rows. The constraint enforcement adds a "find rows
where user_id = X" query for each child, executed inside the delete transaction, and without an index
that's a full scan. 3. For seven child tables, that's seven full scans of potentially huge tables — easily 8
minutes of wall time even at 100MB/s scan speed, plus extra lock contention because the delete holds
row-level locks on every parent and child row it touches. GDPR / data-protection workflows specifically
hit this pattern hard. 4. The fix is one index per child FK column. Add them concurrently to avoid
downtime — CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in Postgres takes longer wall time but doesn't block
writes on the table, which matters when the child tables are receiving live traffic.
The diagnosis: Multiple child tables have FK columns with no index, so cascade deletes scan each child
table fully. Adding FK indexes is the standard fix and should be treated as a schema-completeness
requirement, not an optimisation.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 117 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 118
The fix:
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_user_id    ON orders(user_id);
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_payments_user_id  ON payments(user_id);
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_sessions_user_id  ON sessions(user_id);
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_events_user_id    ON events(user_id);
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_addresses_user_id ON addresses(user_id);
-- repeat for every cascading FK
Why this works: Each cascade now uses an index seek into the child table to find dependent rows —
O(log N) per child instead of O(N). For seven child tables, total delete time drops from 8 minutes to a few
seconds because the constraint check becomes a quick seek-and-walk rather than a full table read.
Lock contention also drops dramatically because the engine holds locks only on actual referenced rows,
not on every row it had to scan to find them.
What NOT to say: "Just disable cascade and delete manually" — pushes the problem to the application
layer, risks orphan rows when the application crashes mid-cascade, and breaks the database's ability to
enforce referential integrity. The constraint is correct; the missing indexes are the bug. Also avoid
"cascades are slow, avoid them" — properly indexed cascades are fast and the alternative (manual
deletes) is error-prone in production code.
Common follow-up: "How do I audit this across the schema?" — Run a query joining 
pg_constraint against pg_index to find FK columns without matching indexes. Most teams
keep a saved query for this and run it before any compliance review or major schema migration. A strong
answer also mentions automating the check in CI — a schema-lint job that fails the build if any new FK is
added without a covering index — so the bug class doesn't recur.
Scenario104 · Multi-Column Index for IN + Range Filter Combo
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Marketplace platforms, reporting tools · Dialect: ANSI / All
Scenario setup: A merchant dashboard shows orders across a list of warehouses for a date range — 
warehouse_id IN (...) AND created_at BETWEEN .... There's an index on warehouse_id
alone. The plan does an index lookup for each warehouse, then sorts the union by created_at — slow
when the IN list has 50+ values.
SELECT id, amount, warehouse_id, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE warehouse_id IN (17, 18, 19, /* ... 50 warehouses ... */)
  AND created_at BETWEEN '2026-05-01' AND '2026-05-31'
ORDER BY created_at;
Current perf vs target: 3s with multiple lookups + sort; target sub-300ms.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 118 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 119
Thinking out loud: 1. IN with N values is essentially N separate equality lookups OR'd together. Each
lookup uses the warehouse_id index, returning a slice for that warehouse — then the engine UNIONs
them all and applies remaining filters and sorts. For a 50-warehouse IN list, that's 50 separate index
seeks plus a merge. 2. The created_at range filter has to be applied per row from the unioned set, and
the final ORDER BY adds a sort over the merged-and-filtered result. Each step is independent work the
engine can't fuse with the lookup when the index doesn't carry created_at. 3. A composite on
(warehouse_id, created_at) lets each per-warehouse lookup land in an already-sorted slice for that date
range — narrower scan per warehouse, and the union can be merge-sorted by created_at without a
separate sort step. The plan becomes "for each warehouse, walk the May 1 - May 31 slice in order,
merge the streams." 4. The optimizer may still need help — sometimes a UNION ALL of explicit per-
warehouse queries with explicit ORDER BY clauses is faster than IN because the planner has clearer
signal about each branch's row estimates. Worth A/B testing on production-sized data.
The diagnosis: IN + range + sort is three workloads stacked on one index. A composite covering filter +
sort gives each per-value lookup a pre-sorted slice, so the engine stream-merges results in the desired
order instead of materialising and sorting them.
The fix:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_warehouse_created
  ON orders(warehouse_id, created_at);
Why this works: For each warehouse in the IN list, the engine seeks to (warehouse_id, '2026-05-01')
and walks sequentially to '2026-05-31'. The N per-warehouse slices are already sorted by created_at, so
merging them is a streaming merge — no full sort, no temp file spill. Often 10x faster than two single-
column indexes because each per-value lookup pays log-N cost once and then walks a contiguous slice
already in the desired output order.
What NOT to say: "Indexes don't help with IN clauses" — they absolutely do; the engine runs one
lookup per value and the optimizer chooses between index-scan-per-value and a bitmap-OR plan that
intersects per-value posting lists. If the IN list is small (<100), per-value lookups work fine; if huge (>10k),
consider a temp table join because per-value descent overhead dominates. Avoid blanket "always use
IN" or "never use IN" — it's a sizing question.
Common follow-up: "What if IN list has 10,000 values?" — Switch to a JOIN against a values list (FROM
(VALUES (17), (18), ...)) or a temp table. The optimizer often picks a hash join, which beats N
lookups at high N because per-warehouse fixed cost is amortised across the hash build. A senior answer
notes that for truly large IN lists, parameter-binding limits in client libraries (libpq's 65k cap) force the join-
against-temp-table approach anyway.
Scenario105 · Filtered Index (SQL Server) for Sparse Hot Subset
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: SQL Server / .NET shops, GCC enterprise teams · Dialect: SQL Server
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 119 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 120
Scenario setup: A SQL Server claims-processing system has a Claims table with 200M rows. The
processing queue is WHERE status = 'pending_review' AND assigned_to IS NULL —
typically 5,000 rows. A regular index on status is too coarse and includes hundreds of millions of
irrelevant rows.
SELECT TOP 100 claim_id, claimant_name, filed_at
FROM Claims
WHERE status = 'pending_review' AND assigned_to IS NULL
ORDER BY filed_at;
Current perf vs target: 1.4s with regular composite; target sub-50ms with smaller cache footprint.
Thinking out loud: 1. SQL Server's filtered index is the equivalent of Postgres's partial index — same
idea (an index containing only rows matching a predicate), different syntax (WHERE on CREATE INDEX).
The mental model is identical; only the keyword and a few restrictions differ. 2. The hot subset is tiny (5k
rows out of 200M), so a filtered index covering only those rows is a 5k-entry mini-index — fits in cache,
served entirely from RAM. The cache-benefit-to-write-overhead ratio is overwhelmingly positive when the
hot subset is this small. 3. Bonus: include filed_at as the index key so the ORDER BY is satisfied by
index order — no explicit sort. The TOP 100 becomes a head-of-tree walk that stops after 100 rows
regardless of underlying queue size. 4. Filtered indexes must use SARGable predicates (no functions, no
implicit conversions, no OR across unrelated columns); IS NULL is allowed and is a common queue-
style predicate. SQL Server's restrictions here are slightly tighter than Postgres's, but cover most real-
world queue patterns.
The diagnosis: Regular index on status includes hundreds of millions of non-pending rows that the
queue query never touches. A filtered index restricted to the queue subset is dramatically smaller and
hotter, and the optimizer matches the query predicate against the filter predicate so the index is picked
automatically.
The fix:
CREATE INDEX ix_claims_pending_unassigned
  ON Claims (filed_at)
  WHERE status = 'pending_review' AND assigned_to IS NULL;
Why this works: The index has ~5k entries, sized at perhaps 200KB total — small enough to live entirely
in buffer pool RAM. The query becomes a tiny B-tree walk against a fully-cached index, returning the first
100 rows by filed_at without ever touching the heap (if SELECT columns are included) or with one heap
fetch per row otherwise. Plan goes from Index Seek + Filter + Sort to Index Seek + Top
— measurably visible in the execution plan.
What NOT to say: "SQL Server doesn't support partial indexes" — it does, under the name "filtered
index," and knowing the dialect name matters when working with a SQL Server team that's been hearing
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 120 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 121
about Postgres partial indexes from blog posts. Also avoid "filtered indexes are exactly the same as
partial indexes" without the caveat that SQL Server has SARGability restrictions Postgres doesn't.
Common follow-up: "What if the WHERE predicate changes?" — Filtered indexes are static; if the
queue definition evolves (e.g., adds a priority column), you must drop and recreate — there's no in-place
modification. Versioning the index name (e.g., ix_claims_pending_v2) helps coordinate the rebuild
across environments and lets you keep both around briefly during transition. A strong answer mentions
monitoring sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats to confirm the new version gets picked up.
Scenario106 · Avoid Wide Index — Large Key Length Hurts Cache
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Performance-focused senior rounds · Dialect: ANSI / All
Scenario setup: A naive index on (email, name, address, phone, gst_number) was added because a
developer thought "more columns = more covering." The index is enormous — 12GB on a 4GB-RAM
box. Index lookups are now slow because the index itself doesn't fit in cache, and B-tree fanout is low.
-- The bad index:
CREATE INDEX idx_vendors_everything
  ON vendors(email, name, address, phone, gst_number);
Current perf vs target: 200ms p95 lookups (cache misses); target sub-10ms.
Thinking out loud: 1. B-tree page size is fixed (8KB Postgres, 16KB InnoDB). Wider keys = fewer keys
per page = lower fanout = deeper tree = more I/O per lookup. Fanout drop compounds because every
level pays the same penalty, so even a single-level depth increase means meaningfully more page reads
per lookup. 2. The wide index also evicts other useful pages from buffer pool — cache pressure spreads
to unrelated queries because the big index hogs slots that could serve narrower indexes. You'll see
cache hit rate drop across the board, not just on this table, after a fat index lands. 3. The fix: narrow the
index key to what actually filters (usually 1-3 columns), and use INCLUDE for additional output columns if
covering is the goal. INCLUDE columns live in leaf pages only — they don't bloat the key, so upper levels
stay narrow and fanout stays high while leaves still carry everything the query needs. 4. The original
wasn't covering anything useful; nobody queries by (email, name, address, phone,
gst_number) as a tuple, so the wide composite key bloated the tree without enabling any real query.
Wide indexes are usually cargo-cult "more columns = more coverage" thinking rather than analysing
actual query shapes.
The diagnosis: Wide composite key reduces B-tree fanout, increases tree depth, and bloats cache. Slim
the key to what actually filters; use INCLUDE for output-only columns when covering is genuinely
needed. The result is a small key + rich leaves design that gives both fast lookup and index-only scan
capability.
The fix:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 121 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 122
DROP INDEX idx_vendors_everything;
-- Postgres 11+ / SQL Server
CREATE INDEX idx_vendors_email
  ON vendors(email)
  INCLUDE (name, phone);
Why this works: B-tree key is now ~50 bytes instead of 600 bytes. Fanout goes from ~25 keys/page to
~150 keys/page — roughly 6x more keys per page, which translates to one fewer tree level for the same
row count. Every lookup does one less page read. Index size shrinks to ~1.5GB, fits in cache, lookup p95
drops to single digits. INCLUDE columns ride along in the leaves so the query still gets name and 
phone without a heap fetch, preserving the index-only scan benefit.
What NOT to say: "Bigger indexes always cover more queries" — they cover more queries badly, and
"cover" in the index-design sense doesn't mean "include more columns just in case." Targeted slim
indexes beat one giant fat index almost always because the planner picks best-fit per query rather than
always paying the widest cost. Also avoid "INCLUDE columns are free" — they consume cache space
and write maintenance, just not at the same rate as key columns.
Common follow-up: "What's the max width before it becomes a problem?" — Rule of thumb: index key
over ~200 bytes starts hurting fanout noticeably; over 1KB you're definitely doing it wrong and probably
violating Postgres's 2712-byte hard limit anyway. Use INCLUDE for everything that doesn't need to be in
the key. A senior answer says "measure don't guess" — pull leaf fanout from pgstattuple or 
sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats and compare against page size.
Scenario107 · Index for Self-Join Lookup (Parent-Child)
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Org-hierarchy / CRM platforms · Dialect: ANSI / All
Scenario setup: An employees table self-joins to show every employee with their manager's name. The
PK on id is fine for the left side; the join m.id = e.manager_id uses the PK on id for the right side.
But there's no index on manager_id — and a downstream query "find all reports of manager X" scans the
table.
-- Slow query: who reports to manager 4587?
SELECT id, name, designation
FROM employees
WHERE manager_id = 4587;
Current perf vs target: 1.8s scan of 800k employees; target sub-50ms.
Thinking out loud: 1. The self-join in one direction (employee → their manager) uses the PK and is fast
— every employee has at most one manager_id and the PK on id resolves it in O(log N). The reverse
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 122 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 123
direction (manager → their reports) needs an index on manager_id, because finding every row where
manager_id = some_id without an index is a full scan. 2. This is a special case of Scenario7 (FK without
index), but specifically about self-referential FKs which people forget more often because the parent and
child are the same table — the visual reminder "child table needs FK index" doesn't trigger when there's
only one table. 3. Bonus: the same index helps recursive CTEs walking down the hierarchy from a root
manager — each WITH RECURSIVE iteration does a manager_id = current_level lookup, and
without the index every level is a full scan, turning a 5-level walk into 5 full table scans. 4. If org-chart
queries are super hot, consider a closure table (pre-materialized ancestor-descendant pairs) — but the
missing index is the first fix and the closure table is the long-term optimisation. Don't jump to the
complex solution before the simple one is in place.
The diagnosis: Self-referential FK column has no index. Queries walking down the hierarchy (manager
→ reports) full-scan the entire employees table, and recursive CTE traversals multiply that cost by
hierarchy depth.
The fix:
CREATE INDEX idx_employees_manager_id ON employees(manager_id);
Why this works: The lookup manager_id = 4587 now uses an index seek to find all direct reports in
O(log N) — for an 800k-row table that's roughly 20 page reads instead of a full scan. Recursive CTEs
walking down N levels do N seeks instead of N full scans, so a 10-level org-chart traversal becomes 10
quick seeks. Org-chart queries scale to enterprise-sized hierarchies with millions of employees and still
return in tens of milliseconds.
What NOT to say: "Self-joins are inherently slow" — they're not; missing indexes make them slow, and
with both PK (on id) and FK (on manager_id) indexed, self-joins are no different in cost from any other
equi-join. Also avoid "recursive CTEs are always slow" — they're slow when underlying lookups are slow,
and adding the FK index fixes both flat-join and recursive-CTE cases simultaneously.
Common follow-up: "What about indexing rarely-changing dimension tables?" — Dimension tables
(countries, cities, plan tiers) are read-mostly and tiny; usually indexes on the join and lookup columns are
enough, and the table often fits entirely in cache so even a full scan is microseconds. Over-indexing a
200-row dimension table is pointless — full scan is already memory-resident and index lookup overhead
can be slower. A strong answer separates "self-referential FK indexes are mandatory" from "dimension-
table indexes are optional and workload-dependent."

Scenario108 · IN With Subquery That Should Be EXISTS
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Flipkart · Topic: Query rewrite
The scenario: A reporting team complains that the "users who placed an order this week" query takes
seven seconds on a 40 million row users table. The query uses IN with a subquery.
SELECT id, email
FROM users
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT user_id FROM orders WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - 7
);
Current performance: 7.1 seconds, full sequential scan on users, materialised subquery of 1.8
million user_id rows held in memory.
Target performance: Under 400 ms by letting the planner switch to a semi-join on the orders index.
Thinking out loud: 1. " IN (subquery) looks innocent, but older planners (MySQL 5.7, Postgres
pre-12 in some shapes) materialise the entire inner result before deciding the join order. With 1.8 million 
user_id values, that materialisation alone costs seconds." 2. " EXISTS is a row-by-row probe that
stops at the first match — semantically identical for non-NULL columns, and the planner is far more likely
to pick a nested-loop semi-join using the orders(user_id, created_at) composite index." 3. "I
would also confirm the index on orders(created_at, user_id) exists — without it, no rewrite
saves us." 4. "Postgres 12+ usually folds IN into a semi-join automatically — so the rewrite matters
most on MySQL, older Postgres, and SQL Server with stale statistics."
Diagnosis: The planner is materialising the subquery instead of pushing it as a semi-join. The EXISTS
form makes the semi-join intent explicit and the planner has a tighter contract to fulfil.
Fix SQL:
SELECT u.id, u.email
FROM users u
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o
  WHERE o.user_id = u.id
    AND o.created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - 7
);
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 124 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 125
Why it speeds up: EXISTS is a short-circuit boolean — the planner picks a semi-join, walks the small 
orders index range (one week of data), and probes users.id (primary key). No materialisation, no
1.8M-row hash table, no full scan of users.
What NOT to say: - "IN and EXISTS are identical, just style." — They are semantically identical for
non-NULL data, but the planner often executes them very differently. - "I would add a hint to force a hash
join." — Hints are a last resort; an EXISTS rewrite is cleaner and portable.
Common follow-up: "What changes if the user_id column in orders is nullable?" — Then NOT IN
becomes dangerous (next scenario), but IN and EXISTS are still equivalent because NULL on the
inner side simply does not match.
Scenario109 · NOT IN Trap — Rewrite to NOT EXISTS
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Cred, Zerodha, PhonePe · Topic: Query rewrite, NULL safety
The scenario: The marketing team wants users who have never placed an order. Their query uses NOT
IN and silently returns zero rows after a recent data migration that introduced NULLs in 
orders.user_id.
SELECT id, email
FROM users
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders);
Current performance: Returns zero rows (wrong answer) — and was already slow at 12 seconds before
that.
Target performance: Correct result in under 600 ms.
Thinking out loud: 1. " NOT IN has a three-valued-logic landmine — if even one inner row has a NULL 
user_id, the entire result becomes empty because x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) evaluates to 
UNKNOWN for every x." 2. "This is not a perf bug first, it is a correctness bug. The migration
introduced NULLs, and now the query lies. I would fix correctness before performance." 3. " NOT
EXISTS does not suffer this — it explicitly checks for the absence of a matching row using equality, and
NULL on the inner side simply does not produce a match." 4. " NOT EXISTS also tends to plan as an
anti-join, which is index-driven and far faster than the hash-anti-join NOT IN typically gets."
Diagnosis: Two problems stacked — NOT IN is NULL-unsafe, and it is also slower because the
planner cannot guarantee anti-join semantics in the presence of NULLs.
Fix SQL:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 125 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 126
SELECT u.id, u.email
FROM users u
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id
);
Why it speeds up: The planner picks an anti-join using the orders(user_id) index, walks each user
once, and uses index lookups to confirm absence — no materialisation, no NULL-induced wrong
answers, and roughly 20x faster on a 40M-user table.
What NOT to say: - "Just add WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL to the inner query and keep 
NOT IN." — It works, but it leaks implementation detail; future schema changes can re-break it. -
"NULL is the same as zero." — Wrong on every database; reveals a deep gap.
Common follow-up: "What is the SQL standard's reasoning for NOT IN behaving this way?" — Three-
valued logic: NULL means "unknown", and you cannot prove a value is not in a set that contains an
unknown.
Scenario110 · Correlated Subquery Rewritten as JOIN
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Meesho, Walmart Labs · Topic: Query rewrite
The scenario: A finance dashboard query attaches each user's latest order amount with a correlated
scalar subquery and runs in 18 seconds for 500k users.
SELECT u.id, u.email,
  (SELECT amount FROM orders o
   WHERE o.user_id = u.id
   ORDER BY o.created_at DESC LIMIT 1) AS last_order_amount
FROM users u;
Current performance: 18 seconds — the subquery fires once per outer row, so 500k subquery
executions.
Target performance: Under 1.2 seconds via a single grouped join.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Per-row scalar subqueries are the classic N+1 inside a single SQL statement —
500k executions of even a fast 0.03 ms lookup is 15 seconds of cumulative overhead." 2. "I can rewrite it
as a single JOIN to a derived table that pre-computes the latest order per user, then read the amount
from that join." 3. "On Postgres, DISTINCT ON is the cleanest expression. On MySQL or older
Postgres, ROW_NUMBER with a WHERE rn = 1 works everywhere." 4. "The planner can now use the 
orders(user_id, created_at DESC) index once, hash-aggregate or sort-merge with users — a
single pass instead of half a million."
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 126 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 127
Diagnosis: The correlated subquery forces a nested-loop pattern where each outer user row triggers a
fresh inner execution. Aggregating the inner query once and joining flips this to a single pass.
Fix SQL:
WITH latest AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (user_id) user_id, amount
  FROM orders
  ORDER BY user_id, created_at DESC
)
SELECT u.id, u.email, l.amount AS last_order_amount
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN latest l ON l.user_id = u.id;
Why it speeds up: One pass over orders produces the latest row per user using the (user_id,
created_at DESC) index. The outer JOIN is hash- or merge-driven — 500k correlated lookups
collapse into a single scan plus a merge.
What NOT to say: - "Correlated subqueries are always bad." — Sometimes they win, especially with
very small outer row sets. - "I would add an index on users.id." — It is the primary key; it already
exists.
Common follow-up: "What if the planner already rewrote this internally — would it still help?" —
Postgres 12+ may decorrelate simple cases, but the DISTINCT ON form forces the optimal plan and is
more readable.
Scenario111 · De-Duping JOIN With a Semi-Join via EXISTS
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, BookMyShow · Topic: Query rewrite, de-
duplication
The scenario: A query for "users who have at least one paid transaction" uses an INNER JOIN plus 
DISTINCT, runs in 9 seconds, and produces 2 million duplicate rows that get collapsed at the end.
SELECT DISTINCT u.id, u.email
FROM users u
INNER JOIN transactions t ON t.user_id = u.id AND t.status = 'paid';
Current performance: 9.2 seconds — INNER JOIN explodes the user row to one row per matching
transaction, then DISTINCT collapses them.
Target performance: Under 800 ms with a semi-join.
Thinking out loud: 1. " DISTINCT over a JOIN is the classic smell — we generated rows we did not
want and then paid CPU to remove them." 2. "What we actually want is a semi-join: for each user, does at
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 127 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 128
least one matching transaction exist? Stop at one." 3. " EXISTS expresses semi-join intent. The planner
can short-circuit at the first matching transaction per user instead of fetching all of them." 4. "This also
removes the DISTINCT sort/hash, which on 2M rows is the second-biggest cost in the original plan."
Diagnosis: The query is using an INNER JOIN as a back-door semi-join, then patching the cardinality
with DISTINCT. The planner cannot tell that we only want one match per user, so it fetches them all.
Fix SQL:
SELECT u.id, u.email
FROM users u
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM transactions t
  WHERE t.user_id = u.id AND t.status = 'paid'
);
Why it speeds up: Semi-join short-circuits at the first matching transaction per user, the index on 
transactions(user_id, status) is walked once per user with an early-exit, and the 
DISTINCT step is eliminated entirely. CPU and memory both drop sharply.
What NOT to say: - "DISTINCT is free." — It is a sort or a hash, both O(n log n) or O(n) with memory
cost. - "GROUP BY would also work." — True, but it still forces all rows to be produced before grouping;
semi-join is strictly better.
Common follow-up: "What if we also want to count transactions per user?" — Then a GROUP BY is
correct because the count requires every row; the semi-join trick only applies to existence checks.
Scenario112 · SELECT * Replaced With Column Enumeration
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Cognizant · Topic: Query rewrite, column pruning
The scenario: A list endpoint that returns user IDs and names for a dropdown is fetching 220 KB per row
because the users table has a profile_jsonb column with 200 KB of analytics blob per user, and
the query uses SELECT *.
SELECT * FROM users WHERE city = 'Mumbai';
Current performance: 4.5 seconds for 12k Mumbai users — 2.6 GB of data over the wire.
Target performance: Under 200 ms; under 5 MB on the wire.
Thinking out loud: 1. "The endpoint needs only id and name, but SELECT * is fetching the wide 
profile_jsonb blob for every row — that is the entire cost of the query." 2. "This is also a covering-
index opportunity — if I enumerate just id and name, and there is a (city, name) INCLUDE
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 128 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 129
(id) index, the heap is never touched." 3. "Beyond raw bandwidth, the JSONB column may be TOAST-
ed in Postgres — decompressing it for every row adds CPU on top of bandwidth." 4. "Column-pruning is
a free win for the API layer too — serialisation, network, garbage collection on the app server all drop."
Diagnosis: SELECT * pulls every column including a large JSONB blob the API does not need. The
cost is dominated by reading and shipping the blob, not by row filtering.
Fix SQL:
SELECT id, name
FROM users
WHERE city = 'Mumbai';
Why it speeds up: The TOAST/LOB column is never read or de-compressed; the row size shrinks from
~220 KB to ~120 bytes; the network is no longer the bottleneck; and if a covering index exists, the heap
is skipped entirely. Two orders of magnitude faster.
What NOT to say: - "SELECT * is fine in dev." — It corrodes habits and breaks the moment a wide
column is added. - "The ORM does this for me." — Most ORMs default to selecting all columns; you
have to teach them otherwise.
Common follow-up: "How would you enforce this across a team?" — Code review checklists, a lint rule
banning SELECT * in repository layer code, and a CI check on slow-query logs.
Scenario113 · Scalar Subquery in SELECT Rewritten as JOIN
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Flipkart · Topic: Query rewrite
The scenario: An admin order report shows user_name, payment_status and last_login
per order using three scalar subqueries in the SELECT list. The query runs in 22 seconds for 80k orders.
SELECT o.id,
  (SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = o.user_id) AS user_name,
  (SELECT status FROM payments WHERE order_id = o.id ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1) AS payment_status,
  (SELECT MAX(created_at) FROM sessions WHERE user_id = o.user_id) AS last_login
FROM orders o
WHERE o.created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - 30;
Current performance: 22 seconds — 80k × 3 subqueries = 240k subquery executions.
Target performance: Under 1.5 seconds via three joins.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Three scalar subqueries in SELECT means 3N subquery executions where N is
outer rows. At 80k orders, that is a quarter-million round-trips inside the planner." 2. "Two of these are
simple lookups — user_name is a direct users.id join, and last_login is a grouped MAX
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 129 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 130
from sessions. Both can become joins." 3. " payment_status (latest payment per order) needs the 
DISTINCT ON or ROW_NUMBER pattern — same as Scenario 3." 4. "After rewriting, the planner can
hash-join users (small), aggregate sessions once, and merge-join the pre-computed latest payment per
order. Three passes instead of 240k."
Diagnosis: SELECT-list scalar subqueries are per-row executions. Each one is an N+1 problem
disguised as a single query.
Fix SQL:
WITH latest_payment AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (order_id) order_id, status
  FROM payments
  ORDER BY order_id, created_at DESC
),
last_session AS (
  SELECT user_id, MAX(created_at) AS last_login
  FROM sessions
  GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT o.id, u.name AS user_name,
       lp.status AS payment_status,
       ls.last_login
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN users u ON u.id = o.user_id
LEFT JOIN latest_payment lp ON lp.order_id = o.id
LEFT JOIN last_session ls ON ls.user_id = o.user_id
WHERE o.created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - 30;
Why it speeds up: Each derived table is materialised exactly once. The joins are hash- or merge-based.
We have replaced 240k correlated calls with three single passes — typically 15-20x faster on this row
volume.
What NOT to say: - "Scalar subqueries in SELECT are sometimes faster." — They are faster only when
the outer row count is tiny (under a few hundred); on 80k rows they are catastrophic. - "Just add more
indexes." — Indexes do not save you from 240k separate executions; the per-call overhead itself
dominates.
Common follow-up: "What if one of the scalar subqueries returns a value used by another?" — Then
chain CTEs; CTEs run top-down and the planner can fold them.
Scenario114 · UNION Replaced by UNION ALL When Duplicates Are Impossible
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, Cognizant, HCL · Topic: Query rewrite
The scenario: A monthly revenue report unions the current month and previous month from two
partitioned tables. The query takes 11 seconds and the engineer who wrote it used UNION.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 130 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 131
SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders_2026_04
UNION
SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders_2026_05;
Current performance: 11 seconds — the planner runs a full deduplication step on the combined 24
million rows.
Target performance: Under 2 seconds.
Thinking out loud: 1. " UNION always deduplicates — it runs a sort or hash over every column in the
combined result. On 24M rows that is the entire query cost." 2. " UNION ALL skips deduplication and
just appends. We need to ask: can a duplicate occur? If the two source tables are partitioned by month,
no order_id can appear in both — duplication is impossible by design." 3. "This is the most common
preventable perf mistake in monthly partitioned reports — UNION is the SQL default many people type
without thinking." 4. "Cost saving scales linearly with row count and number of unioned tables — on 12
months of partitions, the savings are dramatic."
Diagnosis: UNION is doing an expensive deduplication that the schema design has already ruled out.
Fix SQL:
SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders_2026_04
UNION ALL
SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders_2026_05;
Why it speeds up: No sort/hash for deduplication; rows stream straight through. The planner can also
parallelise the two scans independently. Memory pressure drops because the dedup hash table is gone.
What NOT to say: - "UNION and UNION ALL are interchangeable." — Semantically very different; 
UNION removes duplicates, UNION ALL does not. - "Always use UNION ALL." — Only when
duplicates are impossible or acceptable; otherwise you change the answer.
Common follow-up: "How would you verify the no-duplicates assumption?" — A one-off SELECT
order_id, COUNT(*) FROM (... UNION ALL ...) GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*)
> 1 LIMIT 1. If empty, you are safe.
Scenario115 · OR Conditions Split Into UNION ALL for Index Use
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Swiggy, Zomato, BookMyShow · Topic: Query rewrite
The scenario: A customer-support query searches orders by either phone or email, both
individually indexed. The query uses OR and runs in 6 seconds because the planner falls back to a
sequential scan.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 131 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 132
SELECT id, status FROM orders
WHERE phone = '+919876543210' OR email = 'rahul@example.com';
Current performance: 6.3 seconds — full scan because the planner cannot combine two separate
indexes through an OR.
Target performance: Under 50 ms.
Thinking out loud: 1. "With OR across two columns, many planners cannot use both indexes — they
pick the cheaper full scan instead. Postgres can do a BitmapOr but only when statistics convince it."
2. "Splitting into two queries unioned together forces each branch to use its own index — the planner
now has two clearly-indexed paths to combine." 3. " UNION ALL is correct here only if duplicates are
impossible or acceptable. Since a single order could plausibly match both predicates, I would consider
whether the user wants dedup; for a support lookup, UNION ALL followed by a manual eyeball is fine."
4. "If true dedup is required, UNION (not ALL) is still faster than the full-scan original because each
branch is index-driven."
Diagnosis: OR across independently-indexed columns disables single-index plans. The planner often
picks a sequential scan as a safer-cost choice.
Fix SQL:
SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE phone = '+919876543210'
UNION ALL
SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE email = 'rahul@example.com'
  AND phone IS DISTINCT FROM '+919876543210';
Why it speeds up: Each branch is a fast index lookup (one row each). The IS DISTINCT FROM guard
in the second branch removes the rare double-match. Total cost is roughly two B-tree lookups instead of
a 12M-row scan.
What NOT to say: - "Just create a composite index on (phone, email)." — A composite is only useful
when both columns are filtered together, not in an OR. - "Modern planners handle this." — They
sometimes do; the rewrite is portable and guarantees the plan.
Common follow-up: "What if the OR has three or four branches?" — Same pattern, three or four unions,
each with progressively longer IS DISTINCT FROM guards if you want strict dedup.
Scenario116 · Long IN List Rewritten as VALUES or Temp Table
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Meesho, Walmart Labs · Topic: Query rewrite
The scenario: A bulk export job filters orders by 14,000 specific user_ids. The query has a 14k-
element IN list, takes 9 seconds to parse, and then 28 seconds to plan.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 132 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 133
SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE user_id IN (12, 47, 89, ..., 9_998_402);
Current performance: 37 seconds — most of it spent in parsing and planning a giant IN list.
Target performance: Under 3 seconds.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Long IN lists are parsed as flat array literals — the parser and planner both
struggle past a few thousand elements. Many databases impose hard limits (Oracle 1000, SQL Server
32k)." 2. "Rewriting as a VALUES constructor or a temp table lets the planner treat the list as a real
relation — it can hash-join, use statistics, and plan a normal nested-loop or hash-join." 3. " VALUES is
in-line, no DDL needed, and on Postgres it gives the planner a row-count estimate via VALUES's known
cardinality." 4. "For repeated use across queries, a temporary table with an index on user_id is faster
still."
Diagnosis: The planner is choking on the literal list, not on the actual data fetch. Converting the list into a
relational input lets the planner reason about it normally.
Fix SQL:
SELECT o.id, o.amount
FROM orders o
JOIN (VALUES (12), (47), (89), ..., (9998402)) AS ids(user_id)
  ON o.user_id = ids.user_id;
Why it speeds up: Parsing is faster (the VALUES form is a single relation, not 14k separate expressions),
and the planner picks a hash-join between ids (small) and orders (large via the user_id index).
Parse + plan time drops from 37 seconds to about 200 ms.
What NOT to say: - "Just keep adding to the IN list." — It will eventually exceed parser or driver buffer
limits. - "Use a temporary table for everything." — DDL has its own cost; VALUES is enough for one-
shot queries.
Common follow-up: "What if the list itself comes from another query?" — Then it is already a subquery;
rewrite as EXISTS or a JOIN, never as IN.
Scenario117 · LATERAL Join for Per-Row Top-N
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, PhonePe · Topic: Query rewrite, LATERAL
The scenario: A merchant dashboard needs the three most recent transactions for each of 50k
merchants. The current query uses a window function over the full 80M-row transactions table and
runs in 47 seconds.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 133 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 134
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT t.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY merchant_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM transactions t
) ranked
WHERE rn <= 3;
Current performance: 47 seconds — window function partitions across all 80M rows before filtering.
Target performance: Under 4 seconds via LATERAL.
Thinking out loud: 1. "The window function processes every transaction row even though we only want
three per merchant — that is 80M rows of useless ranking work." 2. "A LATERAL subquery fires once per
merchant, with each invocation returning just the top three rows using the 
transactions(merchant_id, created_at DESC) index. Cost is proportional to merchants × 3,
not to transactions." 3. "LATERAL is the cleanest expression of 'for each row in the outer table, run this
correlated query'. The optimiser will use the index and stop at LIMIT 3." 4. "50k × 3 = 150k rows fetched,
versus 80M rows scanned and ranked in the original — roughly 500x less work."
Diagnosis: Window functions process the whole partition before the filter is applied. For top-N per
group, a LATERAL join lets the planner use the index and stop early.
Fix SQL:
SELECT m.id, t.*
FROM merchants m
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT * FROM transactions
  WHERE merchant_id = m.id
  ORDER BY created_at DESC
  LIMIT 3
) t ON true;
Why it speeds up: One index scan per merchant, stopping at 3 rows. The composite index on 
(merchant_id, created_at DESC) is walked from the top of each merchant's range. Total work
scales with merchants × N, not with table size.
What NOT to say: - "Window functions are always optimal for top-N." — They are convenient but rarely
the fastest for small N per group. - "LATERAL is only for Postgres." — Standard SQL since 1999; MySQL
8 and SQL Server support it; only ancient versions miss it.
Common follow-up: "What if N is 1?" — Then DISTINCT ON (Postgres) or a correlated subquery is
even simpler; LATERAL shines from N=2 upward.

Scenario118 · DISTINCT ON for Latest Row Per Group (Postgres)
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Postman · Topic: Postgres-specific rewrite
The scenario: Build a "current price per product" report from a price-history table on Postgres. The
current query joins the table to itself to find the max effective_date per product and runs in 14
seconds.
SELECT p1.product_id, p1.price, p1.effective_date
FROM price_history p1
INNER JOIN (
  SELECT product_id, MAX(effective_date) AS max_date
  FROM price_history GROUP BY product_id
) p2 ON p1.product_id = p2.product_id AND p1.effective_date = p2.max_date;
Current performance: 14 seconds — two passes over the 25M-row table plus a hash-join.
Target performance: Under 1.5 seconds with DISTINCT ON.
Thinking out loud: 1. "The self-join to find the latest row per group is the canonical pattern, but Postgres
has a clean operator: DISTINCT ON (product_id) ... ORDER BY product_id,
effective_date DESC." 2. "With the right index (product_id, effective_date DESC), 
DISTINCT ON walks the index and picks the first row per product_id group — a single pass." 3. 
"The self-join version reads the table twice and pays for a hash-join; DISTINCT ON reads it once and
uses no join at all." 4. "Caveat: DISTINCT ON is Postgres-only. For cross-database code, use 
ROW_NUMBER with WHERE rn = 1 (next scenario)."
Diagnosis: The self-join pattern is a generic answer; Postgres provides a faster, native operator.
Fix SQL:
SELECT DISTINCT ON (product_id) product_id, price, effective_date
FROM price_history
ORDER BY product_id, effective_date DESC;
Why it speeds up: A single index-ordered scan picks one row per product_id group. No join, no two
passes, no hash table. The index on (product_id, effective_date DESC) is walked in order,
and the planner skips to the next product_id after taking one row.
What NOT to say: - "DISTINCT ON is the same as DISTINCT." — Wrong; DISTINCT ON keeps
the first row per group based on ORDER BY, while DISTINCT deduplicates whole rows. - "It is non-
standard, so I avoid it." — It is Postgres-only but blazingly fast; for Postgres-only systems it is the right
tool.
Common follow-up: "What if I want the second-latest row?" — Switch to ROW_NUMBER with WHERE
rn = 2, or LATERAL with LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1.

Scenario119 · ROW_NUMBER With rn = 1 for Latest Per Group (Portable)
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Flipkart, Zomato · Topic: Query rewrite
The scenario: Same "latest order per customer" report, but the team runs on MySQL 8 (no DISTINCT
ON). Current query uses a correlated subquery and takes 31 seconds for 2 million customers.
SELECT o.* FROM orders o
WHERE o.created_at = (
  SELECT MAX(created_at) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = o.customer_id
);
Current performance: 31 seconds — correlated MAX subquery per customer.
Target performance: Under 3 seconds with ROW_NUMBER.
Thinking out loud: 1. "The correlated subquery is a per-row execution; for 2M customers that is 2M MAX
calls. Even if each is fast, the overhead is fatal." 2. " ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY
customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) ranks each customer's orders in one pass; filtering 
WHERE rn = 1 keeps the latest." 3. "Window functions are a single sort over the input, ideally
streamed using the index on (customer_id, created_at DESC)." 4. "This is the portable rewrite
— works on Postgres, MySQL 8, SQL Server, Snowflake, BigQuery. DISTINCT ON is Postgres-only; 
ROW_NUMBER is universal."
Diagnosis: Correlated subqueries scale linearly with outer rows; window functions are a single ranking
pass.
Fix SQL:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT o.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM orders o
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;
Why it speeds up: One pass with a single sort over (customer_id, created_at DESC) ranks all
rows. If the index supports the ordering, the sort is free. 2M correlated subquery calls collapse into one
streamed scan.
What NOT to say: - "ROW_NUMBER is slow." — On large data with the right index, it is much faster than
correlated subqueries. - "Just GROUP BY." — GROUP BY customer_id would lose the row identity;
you need the entire row, not just the max date.

Scenario120 · Moving Filter Into JOIN ON for Outer Joins
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Swiggy, Flipkart, Walmart Labs · Topic: Query rewrite, semantics
The scenario: A LEFT JOIN of users to orders with WHERE orders.status = 'paid'
accidentally turns the outer join into an inner join, dropping 8 million users who have no paid orders. The
query also misses the index on orders(user_id, status).
SELECT u.id, u.email, o.id AS order_id
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid';
Current performance: 5 seconds and wrong answer (acts as INNER JOIN).
Target performance: Correct LEFT JOIN behaviour, under 1.5 seconds.
Thinking out loud: 1. " WHERE o.status = 'paid' filters out all NULL rows from the LEFT JOIN —
and those NULLs are exactly the users without paid orders. The outer-join semantics are silently broken."
2. "To preserve outer-join semantics, the filter must move into the ON clause — that way, unmatched
users are still returned with NULL order_id." 3. "As a bonus, moving the filter into ON often lets the
planner use the composite index (user_id, status) for the join lookup itself, rather than fetching
all matches then filtering." 4. "This is the most common LEFT-JOIN bug I have ever seen in code review
— it usually shows up only when reported numbers do not match expectations."
Diagnosis: A WHERE on the right side of a LEFT JOIN converts it to an INNER JOIN. The fix is to push
the filter into ON.
Fix SQL:
SELECT u.id, u.email, o.id AS order_id
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON o.user_id = u.id AND o.status = 'paid';
Why it speeds up: Correctness aside, the planner can now use the composite index (user_id,
status) directly during the join probe — no post-join filter pass. Outer rows are preserved as NULLs.
What NOT to say: - "The query was wrong but at least it was fast." — Wrong answers are not fast, they
are wrong. - "I would add OR o.status IS NULL to the WHERE." — Works but is fragile and
obscures intent; the ON-clause fix is the standard idiom.

Common follow-up: "What if I want only users who do not have any paid order?" — That is the anti-join
pattern: LEFT JOIN ... ON ... AND status = 'paid' WHERE o.id IS NULL.
Scenario121 · WHERE Pushed Past OUTER JOIN
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Postman · Topic: Query rewrite, predicate
pushdown
The scenario: A reporting query LEFT JOINs three tables and filters on the outer table at the end. The
optimiser does not push the predicate down past the outer joins, scans every row, and takes 18
seconds.
SELECT u.id, u.email, o.id, p.id
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id
WHERE u.country = 'IN' AND u.created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - 30;
Current performance: 18 seconds — predicate on users is applied late because the planner is
uncertain it is safe to push past the LEFT JOINs.
Target performance: Under 1.2 seconds.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Predicate pushdown lets the planner apply the most selective filter as early as
possible — in this case, filter users first, then join only the filtered set." 2. "The planner is conservative
with LEFT JOINs; it often will not push WHERE predicates that reference the outer side because of NULL
semantics. Hoisting the filter into a derived table forces the issue." 3. "By wrapping the filtered users
in a derived table or CTE, I make the row count explicit before the joins — the planner now joins 50k
IN+30-day users to orders, not 40M total users." 4. "This rewrite is also more readable; intent is obvious."
Diagnosis: WHERE clauses on outer-join inputs are sometimes not pushed down due to NULL handling
concerns. Manually pre-filtering removes ambiguity.
Fix SQL:
WITH recent_in_users AS (
  SELECT id, email FROM users
  WHERE country = 'IN' AND created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - 30
)
SELECT u.id, u.email, o.id, p.id
FROM recent_in_users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id;
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 138 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 139
Why it speeds up: The CTE produces a tiny 50k-row driving set; joins are now driven by a small relation
with index lookups on orders.user_id and payments.order_id. The planner no longer scans
40M users.
What NOT to say: - "Pushdown happens automatically." — Sometimes it does; for LEFT JOINs with
multi-table predicates, it often does not. - "CTEs are always slower." — Postgres 12+ inlines them by
default; even when materialised, a small result is cheap.
Common follow-up: "How would you confirm pushdown happened?" — Read EXPLAIN and check that
the filter is applied on the users scan node, not on the join output node.
Scenario122 · Rewriting OR as IN
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, TCS, Wipro, Capgemini · Topic: Query rewrite
The scenario: A status-filter query lists orders in one of six statuses using OR and runs in 4.5 seconds.
The planner picks a sequential scan.
SELECT id, amount FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid' OR status = 'shipped' OR status = 'delivered'
   OR status = 'returned' OR status = 'refunded' OR status = 'cancelled';
Current performance: 4.5 seconds — OR chain confuses the planner.
Target performance: Under 200 ms.
Thinking out loud: 1. " OR on the same column with multiple constants is exactly what IN was
designed for. The planner is better at recognising index-friendly access patterns from IN than from
chained ORs." 2. "With IN, the planner sees a known small set and picks an index range scan (or
multiple index seeks) on orders(status)." 3. "With chained OR, some planners still figure it out,
but it is fragile and version-dependent." 4. "The readability win is also real — IN is the universal idiom
for membership."
Diagnosis: Multi-OR on the same column is a syntactic disguise of an IN predicate. The planner is
more reliable with the explicit form.
Fix SQL:
SELECT id, amount FROM orders
WHERE status IN ('paid', 'shipped', 'delivered', 'returned', 'refunded', 'cancelled');
Why it speeds up: The planner now plans an index scan that walks the six status buckets directly (or, for
low-cardinality columns, picks a single sequential scan with the filter applied during the scan). Either way,
it is faster and more predictable than the OR chain.

What NOT to say: - "OR and IN are identical." — Logically they are; physically the planner often
handles them differently. - "Always use IN." — IN is for one column; cross-column conditions still
need OR.
Common follow-up: "What if status only has 6 distinct values and 90% of rows are in this set?" —
Then a seq scan with predicate evaluation is actually optimal; the index would not help. Always check

Scenario123 · Avoid Function on Indexed Column
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Flipkart · Topic: Query rewrite, sargability
The scenario: A query searches for users by email, but wraps the column in LOWER(). The B-tree
index on email is bypassed and the query does a full scan in 6 seconds.
SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE LOWER(email) = 'rahul@example.com';
Current performance: 6.1 seconds — function wraps the indexed column, index is unusable.
Target performance: Under 30 ms.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Once you wrap an indexed column in a function, the index is dead — the planner
cannot use it because the indexed values are email, not LOWER(email)." 2. "Two fixes: store the
column already-normalised (best long-term), or create a functional/expression index on 
LOWER(email), or rewrite the query to push the function to the right side of the equality." 3. "If the
column is always stored lowercase (validated on insert), the LOWER() is redundant and can simply be
removed." 4. "A functional index CREATE INDEX ON users (LOWER(email)) is the second-best
option — works without changing the query."
Diagnosis: The function on the left side of = makes the predicate non-sargable. Move the function to
the right side (which is a constant), or remove it, or build a functional index.
Fix SQL:
-- Best: if column is normalised at write time
SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE email = 'rahul@example.com';
-- Otherwise, expression index:
CREATE INDEX users_email_lower_idx ON users (LOWER(email));
-- Original query then uses the new index.
Why it speeds up: With the predicate email = 'constant', the planner does a B-tree seek — one
or two page reads. The expression index alternative builds a separate B-tree on LOWER(email) that
the planner can use when the query keeps the LOWER() wrapping.

What NOT to say: - "Indexes always work." — They only work for sargable predicates. - "Just scan the
table; it is fast." — On 40M rows it is not.
Common follow-up: "What if email matching needs to be case-insensitive but the column is stored with
original case?" — Functional index is the cleanest portable fix; CITEXT (Postgres) is even cleaner if you

Scenario124 · Avoid Implicit Cast in WHERE
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Swiggy, Zomato, Cred · Topic: Query rewrite, sargability
The scenario: A query filters phone (stored as VARCHAR) using an integer literal. The implicit cast
forces every row to be cast to integer, the index on phone is unused, and the query takes 5 seconds.
SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE phone = 9876543210;
Current performance: 5.2 seconds — every row's phone is cast to integer for the comparison.
Target performance: Under 30 ms.
Thinking out loud: 1. "The column is VARCHAR; the literal is an integer. The database has to cast one
side or the other to make the comparison legal. Many databases cast the column (the wrong side), which
kills the index." 2. "Wrapping the literal in quotes makes the comparison string-to-string — the index on 
phone is usable directly." 3. "This bug often hides because the query returns the right answer (slowly)
— it is only flagged when a perf review notices the sequential scan." 4. "Lesson: match the literal type to
the column type explicitly; do not rely on implicit coercion."
Diagnosis: Implicit casts on the indexed-column side make the predicate non-sargable. Match types
explicitly.
Fix SQL:
SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE phone = '9876543210';
Why it speeds up: The literal is now the same type as the column, the index is used for a direct B-tree
seek, and no per-row cast is performed. Six orders of magnitude less work for a unique-index lookup.
What NOT to say: - "It works, who cares?" — Senior interviewers grade you down for this answer. -
"Add an index on CAST(phone AS BIGINT)." — Works, but you are papering over a type-design
issue.
Common follow-up: "What if the column should be numeric?" — Then the migration is to change the
column type, not patch the query. Until then, keep types matched.

Scenario125 · Nested Subquery Refactored Into a CTE for Clarity
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro · Topic: Readability, query rewrite
The scenario: A nested-subquery query is correct but unreadable; future maintainers fear it. A CTE
rewrite keeps the same plan but makes intent obvious.
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT u.id, u.email, (
    SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id
  ) AS order_count
  FROM users u
) t WHERE t.order_count > 0;
Current performance: 6 seconds — correlated COUNT per user (we will address that in Scenario 24).
Target performance: Same correctness, dramatically better readability; plan parity.
Thinking out loud: 1. "This is primarily a readability rewrite, not a perf one — but readability is a real
interview signal, and modern Postgres 12+ usually plans CTEs identically to inlined subqueries." 2. "A
CTE names each intermediate step, which makes the query easier to debug, easier to add columns to,
and easier to test in isolation." 3. "Older Postgres (pre-12) treated CTEs as optimisation fences — a real
perf consideration we will revisit in Scenarios 19 and 20." 4. "For MySQL 8+, SQL Server, and BigQuery,
CTEs are inlined and behave like derived tables."
Diagnosis: Nested subqueries hurt human readability without helping performance on modern planners.
Fix SQL:
WITH user_order_counts AS (
  SELECT u.id, u.email,
         (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id) AS order_count
  FROM users u
)
SELECT * FROM user_order_counts WHERE order_count > 0;
Why it speeds up: It does not, materially — the win is intent. (To actually speed this up, see Scenario 24
— convert the correlated COUNT to a GROUP BY join.)
What NOT to say: - "CTEs are always faster." — They are usually plan-equivalent; on older Postgres
they were slower due to materialisation. - "Nested subqueries are fine; CTEs are noise." — Try
maintaining a five-level nested subquery in six months; you will change your mind.
Common follow-up: "Now make this fast — the correlated COUNT is the real bottleneck." — See
Scenario 24.
