Scenario126 · MATERIALIZED Hint to Force CTE Reuse (Postgres 12+)
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Postman · Topic: Postgres-specific, CTE behaviour
The scenario: A Postgres 14 query references the same expensive CTE three times. The planner inlines
it (Postgres 12+ default), causing the expensive query to run three times. Total time: 24 seconds.
WITH expensive_aggregation AS (
  SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM transactions GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT u.id, e.total
FROM users u
JOIN expensive_aggregation e ON e.user_id = u.id
WHERE e.total > 1000
   OR e.total IN (SELECT total FROM expensive_aggregation WHERE total > 100000)
   OR u.id IN (SELECT user_id FROM expensive_aggregation WHERE total < 50);
Current performance: 24 seconds — the aggregation runs three times.
Target performance: Under 10 seconds with MATERIALIZED.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Postgres 12 changed the default — CTEs are now inlined like derived tables.
Usually faster, but if the same CTE is referenced N times, inlining causes N evaluations." 2. 
" MATERIALIZED is the explicit override — Postgres will compute the CTE once, store the result, and
reuse it for every reference." 3. "This is exactly the inverse of the older perf complaint where CTEs were
always materialised even when reuse did not justify it." 4. "Pre-12 Postgres, all CTEs were materialised by
default; we did not need the hint."
Diagnosis: Multiple references to the same expensive CTE are being inlined and re-evaluated. Force
materialisation.
Fix SQL:
WITH expensive_aggregation AS MATERIALIZED (
  SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM transactions GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT u.id, e.total
FROM users u
JOIN expensive_aggregation e ON e.user_id = u.id
WHERE e.total > 1000
   OR e.total IN (SELECT total FROM expensive_aggregation WHERE total > 100000)
   OR u.id IN (SELECT user_id FROM expensive_aggregation WHERE total < 50);
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 143 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 144
Why it speeds up: The aggregation runs exactly once; results are stored in a temporary structure and
reused for the three references. Total CPU drops to roughly 1/3 of the inlined plan.
What NOT to say: - "Inlining is always better." — Not when the CTE is referenced multiple times and is
expensive. - "Just paste the subquery three times." — Defeats the purpose of named composition.
Common follow-up: "What if I want the opposite — force inlining?" — See the next scenario, NOT
MATERIALIZED.
Scenario127 · NOT MATERIALIZED Hint to Let Planner Inline
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Postman, Cred · Topic: Postgres-specific, CTE behaviour
The scenario: A Postgres 11 query (or a Postgres 14 query the team upgraded from 11) has a CTE that
filters a large table, then joins. The CTE materialises 50M rows in memory and runs in 33 seconds.
WITH recent_transactions AS (
  SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - 365
)
SELECT u.id, u.email, COUNT(*) AS txn_count
FROM users u
JOIN recent_transactions r ON r.user_id = u.id
WHERE u.country = 'IN'
GROUP BY u.id, u.email;
Current performance: 33 seconds on Postgres 11 (forced materialisation), or in Postgres 12+ if 
MATERIALIZED was added by an over-eager engineer.
Target performance: Under 3 seconds via inlining.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Materialising the entire recent_transactions set means storing 50M rows in
a temp structure before doing any filtering by user country — wasteful." 2. "If the CTE is inlined, the
planner can push the users.country = 'IN' filter down past the join and pre-filter the transactions
scan." 3. "On Postgres 12+, the default is inlining and we do not need a hint. On Postgres 11, the only
way to inline is to remove the CTE — or upgrade. The team should upgrade." 4. "If we are on 12+ and
someone added MATERIALIZED, we want to either remove it or switch to NOT MATERIALIZED to
make the inline behaviour explicit."
Diagnosis: A CTE that is referenced once and would benefit from predicate pushdown should be inlined,
not materialised.
Fix SQL:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 144 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 145
WITH recent_transactions AS NOT MATERIALIZED (
  SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - 365
)
SELECT u.id, u.email, COUNT(*) AS txn_count
FROM users u
JOIN recent_transactions r ON r.user_id = u.id
WHERE u.country = 'IN'
GROUP BY u.id, u.email;
Why it speeds up: Inlined CTEs let the planner push predicates and combine filters; only Indian users'
recent transactions are scanned, not all 50M rows. The materialised temp structure is gone.
What NOT to say: - "Use MATERIALIZED for everything to be safe." — Disables the planner's best
trick. - "CTEs are always inlined." — Only on Postgres 12+ and only without MATERIALIZED.
Common follow-up: "When is MATERIALIZED actually the right call?" — Multi-reference CTEs
(Scenario 19), recursive CTEs (always materialised), and CTEs whose result is statistically much smaller
than the planner believes.
Scenario128 · Window Function in CTE vs Subquery — Planner Behaviour
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Flipkart, Walmart Labs, Postman · Topic: Window functions, query
rewrite
The scenario: A query computes a running total per user using a window function in a CTE, then filters
to the top day. The CTE materialises 80M rows; the filter is applied at the end. Query takes 41 seconds.
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT user_id, day, amount,
         SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day) AS running_total
  FROM daily_spend
)
SELECT * FROM daily WHERE day = CURRENT_DATE - 1;
Current performance: 41 seconds — window function processes all rows; filter applied after.
Target performance: Under 3 seconds.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Window functions are computed before WHERE filters that reference other
columns — predicates cannot push past a window function partition." 2. "Materialising the CTE forces
the entire 80M-row window computation before the WHERE on day is applied." 3. "Restructuring as a
subquery with the filter inside lets the planner first reduce the input (one day's worth of data), then
compute the window on the reduced set." 4. "Be careful: if the window function needs the full history to
compute (e.g., a cumulative total), restructuring changes the answer. In that case, pre-aggregate the
running total in a daily materialised view."
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 145 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 146
Diagnosis: Window functions block predicate pushdown across partitions. The CTE materialises an
enormous intermediate that the final filter discards.
Fix SQL:
-- If "running total as of yesterday" is the goal, pre-aggregate:
WITH cumulative AS (
  SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) AS total_so_far
  FROM daily_spend
  WHERE day <= CURRENT_DATE - 1
  GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT user_id, total_so_far FROM cumulative;
Why it speeds up: GROUP BY does the aggregation directly without a per-row window pass; only
relevant days are scanned; no 80M-row intermediate.
What NOT to say: - "Always materialise CTEs with window functions." — Materialisation is exactly what
makes this slow. - "Window functions and GROUP BY are interchangeable." — They are not; window
keeps row-level detail, GROUP BY collapses it. Pick the one your output requires.
Common follow-up: "What if I genuinely need the per-row running total preserved for an audit trail?" —
Build a daily materialised view; serve the audit from it. Do not compute it at query time.
Scenario129 · Temp Table Replaced With CTE When Reuse Is Limited
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant · Topic: Query rewrite
The scenario: A stored procedure CREATEs a temp table, INSERTs filtered data, then SELECTs from it
once. The DDL and cross-statement overhead costs 4 seconds before the actual query starts.
CREATE TEMP TABLE recent_orders AS
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - 7;
SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) FROM recent_orders GROUP BY user_id;
Current performance: 4.7 seconds total — 4 seconds is DDL and write overhead.
Target performance: Under 700 ms with a CTE.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Temp tables have setup cost — CREATE TABLE, INSERT, sometimes statistics
collection, and on commit DROP. If the data is referenced only once, all this overhead pays for nothing."
2. "A CTE (or even an inlined subquery) achieves the same isolation without the DDL — the optimiser
sees both halves and may even push filters." 3. "Temp tables make sense when (a) the result is reused 3+
times in subsequent statements, (b) you need an index on the intermediate result, or (c) the planner
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 146 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 147
statistics on the live table mislead the optimiser." 4. "For single-use, a CTE is universally faster on every
modern database I have measured."
Diagnosis: Temp tables carry DDL overhead that single-use queries never recover.
Fix SQL:
WITH recent_orders AS (
  SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - 7
)
SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) FROM recent_orders GROUP BY user_id;
Why it speeds up: No DDL, no INSERT, no temp-table tracking. The CTE is inlined (Postgres 12+,
MySQL 8, BigQuery) or treated as a derived table; the planner picks an index range scan on 
orders(created_at) and aggregates in one pass.
What NOT to say: - "Temp tables are always slower." — They are faster for multi-use intermediates; only
single-use is wasteful. - "Temp tables persist across sessions." — They do not; they are session-scoped
by default.
Common follow-up: "When would you still pick a temp table?" — Re-use across many follow-up
statements, the need for an index on the intermediate, or when the planner makes bad cardinality
estimates on the inlined form.
Scenario130 · Aggregate Pushdown — Pre-Aggregate Before Join
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Flipkart · Topic: Query rewrite, aggregate pushdown
The scenario: A query joins orders (50M rows) to users (40M rows), aggregates orders by user,
and returns total spend per user. Joining first then aggregating moves 50M rows through the join; the
query takes 26 seconds.
SELECT u.id, u.email, SUM(o.amount) AS total_spend
FROM users u
JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
GROUP BY u.id, u.email;
Current performance: 26 seconds — join produces 50M rows, then aggregates down to 40M users.
Target performance: Under 4 seconds.
Thinking out loud: 1. "The join is moving 50M rows through the planner before aggregation. If I pre-
aggregate orders per user first (40M result), then join, the join input is much smaller." 2. "This is 
aggregate pushdown — manually performing what some planners do automatically but many do
not." 3. "After pre-aggregation, the join is 40M users against 40M user-totals — a balanced hash- or
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 147 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 148
merge-join, much cheaper than the 40M × 50M shape." 4. "This rewrite shines when the aggregation
reduces row count significantly — multiple orders per user collapsed to one total per user."
Diagnosis: Joining before aggregating moves more rows than necessary. Pre-aggregate to shrink the
join input.
Fix SQL:
WITH spend_per_user AS (
  SELECT user_id, SUM(amount) AS total_spend
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT u.id, u.email, s.total_spend
FROM users u
JOIN spend_per_user s ON s.user_id = u.id;
Why it speeds up: The aggregation is one pass over orders using the (user_id) index; the join is
then balanced and small. We avoid moving 50M rows through the join machinery.
What NOT to say: - "The planner does this for me." — Sometimes; never count on it for large data. -
"Pre-aggregation is always faster." — Only when the aggregation actually reduces row count.
Common follow-up: "What if some users have no orders?" — Switch to LEFT JOIN and COALESCE the
total to 0.
Scenario131 · Correlated COUNT Converted to GROUP BY JOIN
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Meesho, Cred · Topic: Query rewrite
The scenario: A dashboard query counts orders per user using a correlated subquery in SELECT. For
500k users, the correlated count runs 500k times and takes 39 seconds.
SELECT u.id, u.email,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id) AS order_count
FROM users u;
Current performance: 39 seconds.
Target performance: Under 2 seconds.
Thinking out loud: 1. "This is the same N+1 pattern from Scenarios 3 and 6, specialised to COUNT. 500k
correlated COUNTs is 500k separate index scans." 2. "A single GROUP BY user_id over orders
produces all counts in one pass; left-join back to users to include zero-count users." 3. " LEFT JOIN
plus COALESCE(count, 0) preserves users with zero orders — the correlated subquery returned 0
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 148 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 149
for those automatically, and the rewrite must match that behaviour." 4. "Same shape applies to SUM,
AVG, MIN, MAX — any correlated aggregate is a candidate for this rewrite."
Diagnosis: Correlated aggregates in SELECT are N+1 query patterns. Aggregate once and join.
Fix SQL:
WITH counts AS (
  SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
  FROM orders GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT u.id, u.email, COALESCE(c.order_count, 0) AS order_count
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN counts c ON c.user_id = u.id;
Why it speeds up: One pass over orders aggregates everything; one hash-join applies counts to users.
500k correlated scans collapse into two streamed operations. 20x or better is typical.
What NOT to say: - "Correlated subqueries are sometimes faster." — For tiny outer sets, occasionally;
for 500k rows, never. - "Just drop users with zero orders." — Changes the result; the LEFT JOIN
preserves them.
Common follow-up: "What if I need three different aggregates — count, sum, max — per user?" —
Compute all three in the same GROUP BY in the CTE; the cost is shared.
Scenario132 · UNION ALL of Indexed Paths Instead of OR
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Swiggy, Zomato, BookMyShow · Topic: Query rewrite
The scenario: A query searches messages where the user is either the sender or the recipient. Both
columns are indexed individually. The OR query falls back to a sequential scan and takes 12 seconds.
SELECT id, subject, body
FROM messages
WHERE sender_id = 42 OR recipient_id = 42;
Current performance: 12 seconds — neither single-column index can be used cleanly with OR.
Target performance: Under 80 ms.
Thinking out loud: 1. "This is the same shape as Scenario 8, but with the role of dedup mattering more
— a message could have the same user as both sender and recipient (a draft to self) and we may or may
not want to dedup." 2. "Splitting into two UNIONed queries lets each branch use its index — 
messages(sender_id) for one, messages(recipient_id) for the other." 3. " UNION ALL is
correct if duplicates are impossible (no self-messages) or acceptable. UNION deduplicates at extra cost
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 149 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 150
— usually negligible for the output volume here." 4. "On Postgres, BitmapOr can sometimes combine the
two indexes automatically — but only when statistics align. Manual UNION is more reliable."
Diagnosis: OR across independently-indexed columns blocks single-index plans on most planners.
Manual UNION forces each branch to use its index.
Fix SQL:
SELECT id, subject, body FROM messages WHERE sender_id = 42
UNION
SELECT id, subject, body FROM messages WHERE recipient_id = 42;
Why it speeds up: Each branch is a fast indexed lookup, typically returning a few dozen rows; the
UNION dedup is over a tiny combined set. 12-second seq scan becomes two B-tree probes.
What NOT to say: - "Create a composite index (sender_id, recipient_id)." — Composite is
only useful when both are filtered together, not in an OR. - "Modern planners handle this." — They
sometimes do; manual UNION is portable and guarantees the plan.
Common follow-up: "What if I want messages where the user is either sender OR recipient, but ordered
by timestamp?" — UNION the two paths, then wrap in an outer ORDER BY with LIMIT; or use a UNION
ALL + dedup + sort, depending on data volume.
Scenario133 · LIMIT Pushdown for Early Termination
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Flipkart · Topic: Query rewrite, LIMIT semantics
The scenario: A query fetches the 10 most recent orders for each of 1000 VIP users. The current query
joins, sorts the full join result, then LIMITs — 38 seconds for 80M total orders scanned.
SELECT o.* FROM orders o
JOIN vip_users v ON v.user_id = o.user_id
ORDER BY o.created_at DESC LIMIT 10;
Current performance: 38 seconds — full join, then global sort, then limit.
Target performance: Under 1 second.
Thinking out loud: 1. "The current shape forces the planner to sort 1000 × 80k = 80M rows globally to
find the top 10. The LIMIT only saves output, not work." 2. "If the goal is genuinely just the top 10 across
all VIP users, push the LIMIT into a per-user subquery — top 10 per user — then take the top 10 overall.
The per-user index range scan can terminate early." 3. "Better yet, use LATERAL (Scenario 10) for per-
user top-N; then take top 10 of the unioned result." 4. "The general lesson: LIMIT only helps when the
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 150 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 151
planner can stop work early — that usually requires the data to arrive in the sort order, ideally via an
index."
Diagnosis: A global LIMIT after a join with no per-user reduction wastes work. Push the LIMIT down to a
per-key subquery.
Fix SQL:
WITH top_per_vip AS (
  SELECT o.*
  FROM vip_users v
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = v.user_id
    ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10
  ) o
)
SELECT * FROM top_per_vip
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10;
Why it speeds up: Each VIP user contributes at most 10 rows via an index-driven early-exit; the outer
LIMIT then sorts at most 10,000 rows. 80M-row sort becomes a 10k-row sort plus 1000 small index
lookups.
What NOT to say: - "LIMIT always saves work." — Only when it can terminate the underlying scan early.
- "Just add LIMIT 10 and hope." — The planner cannot help if the data is not pre-sorted.
Common follow-up: "What if I want top 10 per VIP user, not top 10 overall?" — Drop the outer LIMIT; the
LATERAL already produces top 10 per user.
Scenario134 · OFFSET Pagination Replaced With Keyset (Cursor) Pagination
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Flipkart, Zomato · Topic: Query rewrite, pagination
The scenario: An admin panel shows orders, 25 per page, with 
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 25 OFFSET 9975 for page 400. On a 40M-row table the
page load takes 14 seconds and gets slower with every page.
SELECT id, user_id, amount, created_at
FROM orders
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 25 OFFSET 9975;
Current performance: 14 seconds on page 400; page 4000 would be effectively unusable.
Target performance: Under 100 ms regardless of page depth.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 151 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 152
Thinking out loud: 1. "OFFSET makes the database fetch and discard the first N rows. On page 400 of
25, that is 9,975 rows fetched, sorted, and thrown away before delivering 25." 2. "The cost grows linearly
with page depth — page 4,000 means discarding 99,975 rows. OFFSET pagination is unscalable for large
datasets." 3. "Keyset pagination uses the last-seen value as the next page's starting point. WHERE
(created_at, id) < (last_created_at, last_id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id
DESC LIMIT 25 is a single index range scan — constant cost regardless of page." 4. "Tradeoff: keyset
cannot jump to an arbitrary page number; it only supports next and previous. For admin tools
where most users go page by page, that is fine. For ones with a 'jump to page 400' input, hybrid solutions
exist."
Diagnosis: OFFSET pagination is O(offset) per page. Keyset (cursor) pagination is O(1) per page when an
index supports the ordering.
Fix SQL:
-- Page 1
SELECT id, user_id, amount, created_at
FROM orders
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 25;
-- Page 2 onward — pass last row's (created_at, id) from previous page
SELECT id, user_id, amount, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-04-12 10:33:00', 871334)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 25;
Why it speeds up: The (created_at, id) < (...) predicate is sargable against an index on 
(created_at DESC, id DESC) — a single B-tree seek to the cursor position, then read 25 rows.
No rows are fetched and discarded. Page 1 and page 4,000 cost identically.
What NOT to say: - "OFFSET is fine if you do not have many pages." — A polite way to say it does not
scale; senior interviewers will press on what "many" means. - "Add a covering index and OFFSET will be
fast." — A covering index helps the per-row cost but does not change the O(offset) shape.
Common follow-up: "How would you support 'jump to page 400'?" — Either accept the OFFSET cost
for direct navigation (rare), or precompute a (page_number, first_id) map periodically, or design
the UX around continuous scroll. Most modern systems pick the third.
