Scenario135 · Stale Statistics Forcing the Wrong Plan
Asked at: Razorpay · Walmart Labs · ThoughtSpot · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Statistics · Dialect:
Postgres · SQL Server (vendor-agnostic principle)
The interviewer's prompt: "Your nightly batch job loads 8 crore rows into orders every day. The
morning report query that ran in 12 seconds yesterday is now taking 9 minutes. Same SQL, same data
shape. What's the first thing you check?"
Thinking out loud (the diagnosis path): 1. "Same SQL, same indexes, same data volume — but a wildly
different runtime means the planner picked a different plan. The most common reason for a plan flip after
a bulk load is stale statistics. The planner saw row counts from before the load and made a join-order
choice that no longer fits." 2. "I'd pull the plan first — EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) in Postgres or
the Actual Execution Plan in SQL Server — and compare estimated rows vs actual rows on each
operator. If estimated says 12,000 and actual says 80,00,000, statistics are stale." 3. "For a bulk-loaded
table, autovacuum or auto-update-stats may not have fired yet. After 8 crore rows of churn the sample is
meaningless."
The likely root cause: The planner used row estimates from before the nightly load and chose a nested-
loop join on what it thought was a small driving table. After the load, that "small" table is now huge, and
the nested loop is doing crores of inner-side lookups.
The fix (and the verification step): - Postgres: run ANALYZE orders; immediately after the load
completes. For a permanent fix, add ANALYZE as the last step of the ETL job, not as a background
task. - SQL Server: UPDATE STATISTICS dbo.orders WITH FULLSCAN; for critical tables; WITH
SAMPLE 30 PERCENT if FULLSCAN is too slow. - MySQL 8: ANALYZE TABLE orders; — same
intent. - Verify by re-running the query and confirming the estimated row counts in EXPLAIN now match
actual within an order of magnitude.
What NOT to say: - "Just rebuild the indexes — that updates stats too." — Rebuilding indexes only
updates index stats in some engines, and it is a far heavier operation than ANALYZE. Wrong tool. - "Stats
update automatically, so this can't be the issue." — Autovacuum thresholds are percentage-based; after
a fresh load on an empty table they may not trigger until the next day.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 153 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 154
Common follow-up: "How would you set up monitoring to catch stale stats before they cause a slow
query in production?" — Postgres: pg_stat_user_tables.last_analyze vs 
n_mod_since_analyze; SQL Server: sys.dm_db_stats_properties; alert when modification
count crosses 10% of row count.
-- Postgres: after the nightly load, always
ANALYZE orders;
-- SQL Server: critical-table refresh
UPDATE STATISTICS dbo.orders WITH FULLSCAN;
-- Diagnostic: which tables have stale stats?
SELECT schemaname, relname, n_live_tup, n_mod_since_analyze, last_analyze
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE n_mod_since_analyze > n_live_tup * 0.1
ORDER BY n_mod_since_analyze DESC;
Scenario136 · Extended Statistics for Correlated Columns
Asked at: PhonePe · Zomato · Atlassian GCC · Difficulty: Hard · Topic: Statistics · Dialect: Postgres
(10+) primary · SQL Server has filtered statistics analogue
The interviewer's prompt: "You have a customers table with state and pincode. You filter 
WHERE state = 'Maharashtra' AND pincode LIKE '400%'. The planner estimates 30 rows;
actual is 3 lakh. Index is not used, query is slow. Why is the estimate so wrong?"
Thinking out loud (the diagnosis path): 1. "Classic correlated-column problem. The planner multiplies
selectivities assuming independence — Maharashtra times pincodes starting 400. But pincodes starting
400 are almost entirely in Maharashtra, so the columns are heavily correlated. The independence
assumption breaks." 2. "This underestimate makes the planner think it has 30 rows, so it picks a nested
loop or skips the bitmap index in favour of a sequential scan. It actually finds 3 lakh rows and does 3 lakh
inner-side lookups — the slow path we see." 3. "The fix is to tell the planner about the correlation.
Postgres has extended statistics since version 10 for exactly this case." 4. "I would also confirm the same
misestimate is not corrupting downstream join cardinality — a wrong number at the bottom of the plan
tree cascades upward into wrong join algorithm choices."
The likely root cause: Per-column statistics assume independence. state is roughly 1/30 selective, 
pincode LIKE '400%' is roughly 1/600 selective. Multiplied, that gives ~1/18,000 — hence the 30-
row estimate. Reality: pincode and state are functionally dependent because Indian PIN codes
are state-prefixed by design — 4xxxxx is Maharashtra, 5xxxxx is Karnataka/Andhra/Telangana, 7xxxxx is
West Bengal, and so on.
The fix (and the verification step): - Postgres 10+: create extended statistics. sql CREATE
STATISTICS customers_state_pin (dependencies, ndistinct) ON state, pincode
FROM customers; ANALYZE customers; The dependencies kind tells the planner about
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 154 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 155
functional dependencies; ndistinct improves group-by estimates across the combined columns. -
SQL Server: there is no direct equivalent, but filtered statistics on common state values can help — 
CREATE STATISTICS s_pin_mh ON customers(pincode) WHERE state =
'Maharashtra';. - MySQL: no extended-stats mechanism; either rewrite the query to expose only the
more selective predicate, denormalise into a precomputed region column, or accept the bad plan and
force an index hint. - Verify with EXPLAIN that the estimated row count is now within ~2x of actual,
and that the planner switches from a sequential scan to a bitmap index scan or index range scan.
What NOT to say: - "Increase the statistics target so the histogram is finer." — Helps for single-column
skew, not for cross-column correlation. The histogram is per column. - "Rewrite as pincode LIKE
'400%' only since it implies state." — You lose the semantic check, and it does not fix the underlying
planner problem for other correlated pairs (date and quarter, city and state, brand and category). - "Just
disable the index — sequential scan with the right filter is fine at this size." — 3 lakh rows out of millions is
exactly where a bitmap index scan wins; abandoning the index is wasteful.
Common follow-up: "What kinds of extended statistics does Postgres support and when do you use
each?" — ndistinct for GROUP BY estimates over multiple columns, dependencies for
functional dependency between columns (this scenario), mcv (Postgres 12+) for most-common-value
lists across multiple columns when the data is skewed toward a handful of combinations.
Scenario137 · Sort Spilling to Disk — Raise work_mem
Asked at: Razorpay · Cred · Postman · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Memory tuning · Dialect: Postgres
The interviewer's prompt: "A report query that sorts 50 lakh rows is taking 3 minutes. EXPLAIN
ANALYZE shows Sort Method: external merge Disk: 480MB. The box has 64 GB of RAM.
What's happening and how do you fix it?"
Thinking out loud (the diagnosis path): 1. " external merge Disk means the sort did not fit in 
work_mem and spilled to a temp file. Disk sorts are 10 to 50 times slower than in-memory sorts,
depending on the storage. So the cure is to let the sort live in memory." 2. " work_mem is per sort or
hash operation, per backend — not per query, not per server. Default is 4 MB. The box has 64 GB so we
have plenty of headroom on the machine itself." 3. "I would not raise it globally to 1 GB — that multiplies
across every concurrent operation. A query with three sorts and two hash joins uses five times
work_mem. With 200 connections each doing five operations, the math gets scary fast." 4. "The right
pattern is to raise it for this session, this role, or this query class only — keep the global modest."
The likely root cause: Default work_mem = 4MB is far too small for an analytics workload sorting 480
MB of data — the sort cannot possibly fit, so Postgres spills batches to temp files and merges them,
paying disk I/O cost for what should be a CPU-only operation.
The fix (and the verification step): - Per-session for the report: SET work_mem = '512MB';
SELECT ... ORDER BY ...; - Per-role for the BI user: ALTER ROLE bi_user SET work_mem =
'512MB'; — applies to every session that user opens. - Per-statement scope inside a transaction: 
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 155 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 156
BEGIN; SET LOCAL work_mem = '512MB'; SELECT ...; COMMIT; - Globally only after
capacity math: work_mem × max_connections × ~2 (sort + hash per query) must fit in
available RAM with headroom for OS cache and shared_buffers. On a 64 GB box with 200 connections,
that caps global work_mem at around 30 MB if you want safety. - Verify with EXPLAIN ANALYZE —
the sort line should now read Sort Method: quicksort Memory: 480MB and the query should
drop from 3 minutes to under 10 seconds. If it still spills, double the setting.
What NOT to say: - "Set work_mem to 4GB globally so this never happens again." — Will blow up the
box the moment 50 BI users connect simultaneously and each runs a multi-sort query. - "Disk sorts are
fine on SSDs." — Even on NVMe, in-memory sort wins by an order of magnitude; the syscall and copy
overhead dominates over raw read latency. - "Use a temp table to break up the sort." — Does not help;
the temp table itself needs a sort to populate, and you still spill.
Common follow-up: "How do you decide per-role vs per-statement vs global for work_mem?" — Per-
statement when the query is one-off and you want isolation; per-role for a known workload class (analyst
user, BI tool service account); global only when the workload mix is genuinely uniform — rare in practice.
Scenario138 · Plan Regression After a Postgres Minor Upgrade
Asked at: Swiggy · Flipkart · Atlassian GCC · Difficulty: Hard · Topic: Plan diagnosis · Dialect: Postgres
(pg_stat_statements) · SQL Server (Query Store)
The interviewer's prompt: "You bumped Postgres from 15.4 to 15.6 on Saturday. By Monday, two
queries that used to take 200 ms are taking 8 seconds. Same data, same indexes. Walk me through the
diagnosis."
Thinking out loud (the diagnosis path): 1. "A minor version bump should not change plans in theory, but
in practice it sometimes does — planner bug fixes, costing-model tweaks, or a stats refresh during the
upgrade can flip a plan sitting at the cost threshold." 2. "I would lean on pg_stat_statements to
find offending queries by mean_exec_time jump, then capture the current plan with EXPLAIN
(ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and compare to a known-good plan from staging or a pre-upgrade snapshot."
3. "On SQL Server I would do the same with Query Store — it stores plan history per query and you can
force the old plan with one click. Postgres makes you work harder; SQL Server gives you a button." 4. 
"Before changing anything, I want both plans side by side and an explicit understanding of which
operator changed. Otherwise you are guessing."
The likely root cause: A statistics refresh during the upgrade re-sampled histograms; or a small costing
change tipped the planner from a nested loop to a merge join (or the other way) for a query sitting right at
the cost threshold; or a partial index that the new planner version now costs slightly differently and
refuses to pick.
The fix (and the verification step): - First identify: SELECT queryid, mean_exec_time, calls
FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY mean_exec_time * calls DESC LIMIT 20; (reset
stats first with pg_stat_statements_reset() after the upgrade to compare clean windows). -
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 156 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 157
Postgres: there is no first-class "force this plan" — but you can shape it. Try ANALYZE the affected
tables first; a stats refresh often realigns the planner. If that does not fix it, install the pg_hint_plan
extension and pin a join order or operator. Last resort: rewrite the query slightly to nudge the planner —
adding a redundant OFFSET 0 in a subquery, for instance, disables some optimisations. - SQL Server:
open Query Store, find the regression, click "Force Plan" on the old one. This is a genuine emergency
button — use it during the incident and remove the forcing once the root cause is fixed. - Verify by re-
running and capturing the plan; mean execution time should drop back to baseline within a few minutes.
What NOT to say: - "Roll back the minor version." — Drastic and rarely necessary; minor versions ship
security patches you want and the regression usually has a per-query fix. - "Just restart Postgres." —
Does not change the plan choice; only clears caches that may briefly help and then re-degrade. - 
"Disable autovacuum so stats stop changing." — Catastrophic for table bloat; addresses a symptom by
causing a much worse problem.
Common follow-up: "Why does SQL Server let you force a plan but Postgres does not?" — Different
philosophy. SQL Server bets on operator stability for OLTP and gives DBAs explicit plan-pinning tooling;
Postgres bets that the planner with current stats is usually right and gives you pg_hint_plan only as
an out-of-tree escape hatch. Neither view is wrong.
Scenario139 · Forcing a Plan via Hint — When It Is Justified
Asked at: Walmart Labs · Goldman Sachs GCC · Difficulty: Hard · Topic: Hints · Dialect: SQL Server
(OPTION) · MySQL (USE/FORCE INDEX) · Postgres (pg_hint_plan extension)
The interviewer's prompt: "You are debugging a slow query. The planner picks a hash join, but a nested
loop is 10x faster on this data. Should you force the plan with a hint? When is it justified and when is it a
code smell?"
Thinking out loud (the diagnosis path): 1. "Hints are escape hatches, not first-line tools. If a hint is the
only thing between production and an outage, use it — but log a follow-up ticket the same day, because
the underlying planner mismatch will bite again on a different query." 2. "Legitimate cases are narrow: a
known-stable plan for a hot OLTP query where data shape is predictable for years, or a documented
workaround for a planner bug the vendor has not patched." 3. "Illegitimate cases are far more common in
production codebases: hiding a stats problem, hiding a missing index, papering over a correlated-column
misestimate, or 'we always did it this way' tribal knowledge nobody dares touch." 4. "My default in an
interview — investigate root cause first, hint as last resort, always with a comment explaining when to re-
evaluate."
The likely root cause (of the wrong plan, not of the question): A row-count misestimate driving the cost
model toward the wrong join algorithm — usually either stale stats or correlated columns that defeat the
independence assumption.
The fix (and the verification step): - Step 1: try to fix the root cause first. ANALYZE, create extended
statistics, add the missing index, rewrite a correlated predicate. Hints are step 5, not step 1. - Step 2: if a
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 157 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 158
hint is truly needed in the moment: - SQL Server: OPTION (LOOP JOIN) or OPTION (FORCE
ORDER, USE PLAN N'...') for full plan-forcing. - MySQL: SELECT /*+ JOIN_ORDER(a, b)
*/ ... or USE INDEX (idx_x) / FORCE INDEX (idx_x). - Postgres: install pg_hint_plan
extension, then /*+ HashJoin(a b) */ or /*+ NestLoop(a b) Leading((a b)) */. - Step
3: leave a comment in the SQL explaining why the hint is needed and what would let you remove it —
"Stats correlation between region and pincode; remove when extended stats added in #JIRA-1234."
Future-you will thank present-you. - Verify post-hint latency matches expectation, and add a monitor that
alerts if the same query slows again — that is your signal that the hint has become wrong.
What NOT to say: - "Add a hint everywhere — predictable plans are good." — Hints freeze the plan
against data growth; what was right at 1 lakh rows is wrong at 10 crore. The planner adapts; a hint does
not. - "Hints are always bad." — Sometimes they are the right tool, and a senior interviewer wants to hear
nuance. Black-and-white answers signal lack of production experience. - "Force the plan in Query Store
and forget about it." — Forcing without fixing the underlying problem is technical debt with compound
interest.
Common follow-up: "How would you know to revisit and remove a hint?" — Track query latency post-
hint; when underlying stats or schema changes (column added, partitioning introduced, data grows 10x,
new index added), re-test without the hint and confirm the planner now picks well. Some teams put a
"remove by" date in the hint comment as a forcing function.
Scenario140 · Parallel Query Enablement
Asked at: Razorpay · PhonePe · Walmart Labs · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Parallelism · Dialect:
Postgres · SQL Server (MAXDOP) · MySQL 8 (limited)
The interviewer's prompt: "Your analytical query scans 5 crore rows and runs serially in 4 minutes. The
box has 16 cores. How do you get the planner to use them?"
Thinking out loud (the diagnosis path): 1. "Parallel query is on by default in Postgres 10+ and SQL
Server, but the planner only picks it if estimated cost crosses a threshold and a handful of setup
parameters are configured to allow it. On managed services like AWS RDS and DigitalOcean, the defaults
are sometimes conservative." 2. "In Postgres, the relevant knobs are 
max_parallel_workers_per_gather (how many workers per Gather node), 
max_parallel_workers (total system-wide), min_parallel_table_scan_size (when
scanning is worth parallelising), and the cost factors parallel_setup_cost / 
parallel_tuple_cost that the planner weighs." 3. "I would check EXPLAIN first — if there is no 
Gather or Gather Merge node, the planner did not even consider parallelism. That points to either
a setting blocking it or a query construct that disables it (function safety, locking, CTE materialisation)." 4. 
"After enabling, I would also watch CPU utilisation during the query — if I see one core pegged and
others idle, parallelism is configured but not actually engaging at execution time."
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 158 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 159
The likely root cause: max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0 (default in some managed
services), or the table is too small to clear min_parallel_table_scan_size = 8MB, or the query
uses a parallel-unsafe function — covered in detail in the next scenario.
The fix (and the verification step): - Postgres: 
SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 4; SET max_parallel_workers = 8; then re-
EXPLAIN. Lower parallel_setup_cost (default 1000) if the planner still rejects parallel. For a 16-
core box, the typical sizing is max_parallel_workers = 8 and max_worker_processes =
16. - SQL Server: OPTION (MAXDOP 8) on the query, or set instance-level max degree of
parallelism. Watch the cost threshold for parallelism (default 5 — way too low for
modern hardware; most DBAs raise it to ~50 so OLTP queries do not get parallelised). - MySQL 8: limited
— parallel only for read scans of partitioned tables and InnoDB cluster index reads. For real analytical
parallelism you usually need a different engine (Snowflake, BigQuery, ClickHouse). - Verify with EXPLAIN
— you should see Gather over Parallel Seq Scan or Parallel Index Scan in Postgres;
query time should drop roughly N-fold where N is worker count, until I/O bandwidth becomes the
bottleneck (usually around 4-6 workers on a single disk).
What NOT to say: - "Just set workers to 32 — more is always better." — Each worker has setup
overhead and competes for I/O bandwidth; sweet spot is usually 4-8 for I/O-bound, more for CPU-bound
aggregations. - "Parallel query speeds up OLTP." — It speeds up scans on large data; OLTP point
lookups gain nothing and may pay the parallel-setup cost for no benefit. - "Increase
max_parallel_workers to 64 across the board." — Causes context-switching storms when many users run
analytical queries concurrently; the server thrashes.
Common follow-up: "What kinds of queries cannot go parallel in Postgres?" — Queries calling parallel-
unsafe functions, queries inside a CTE that the planner materialises non-parallel, queries acquiring row
locks (SELECT FOR UPDATE), and write paths (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE — parallel writes only landed
in Postgres 14 for the apply phase).
Scenario141 · Parallel-Safe vs Parallel-Restricted Functions
Asked at: Atlassian GCC · ThoughtSpot · Difficulty: Hard · Topic: Parallelism · Dialect: Postgres primary
The interviewer's prompt: "You added parallel workers but the planner still runs the query serially. The
only oddity is that the query calls a custom function format_invoice_number(id). Why might that
disable parallelism?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "In Postgres, every function has a parallel safety marker — parallel safe, 
parallel restricted, or parallel unsafe. The default for user-defined functions is 
parallel unsafe, the most conservative, because Postgres cannot introspect the body and prove
safety — it assumes the worst." 2. "If the planner sees even one parallel unsafe function
anywhere in the query, it disables parallelism for the whole plan. A single innocuous helper poisons the
whole query." 3. "The fix is to mark the function correctly — if it is safe in parallel workers, declare it so.
The marker is a promise from the developer to the planner; declare carefully." 4. "I would also audit
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 159 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 160
nearby UDFs in the same query class — formatters, currency converters, geo-coders. They tend to live
together in a utils schema and were created with the same wrong default."
The likely root cause: The custom function was created without the PARALLEL SAFE clause, so
Postgres assumes it might call something that does not work in parallel workers — sequence touches,
temp tables, advisory locks, prepared statement state, listen/notify. A formatter that just does string
concatenation is almost certainly safe, but you have to say so explicitly.
The fix: - If the function is genuinely pure: ALTER FUNCTION format_invoice_number(int)
PARALLEL SAFE; — and ideally also mark it IMMUTABLE if its output depends only on inputs, which
unlocks further planner optimisations like expression-result caching. - If it touches sequences or temp
objects but is otherwise read-only: PARALLEL RESTRICTED — the function can run in the leader
process but not in worker processes, which still lets the planner parallelise scans even if the leader does
the formatting at the top. - Re-run EXPLAIN — Parallel Seq Scan should now appear under a 
Gather node, and elapsed time should drop to roughly serial-time / worker-count.
What NOT to say: - "Mark every function as PARALLEL SAFE to be safe." — That hides bugs; an unsafe
function called from a worker can produce wrong results because workers do not share session state
with the leader (advisory locks, temp tables, sequence nextval order). - "This only affects Postgres." —
True that other engines do not use this exact mechanism, but SQL Server has similar restrictions around
scalar UDFs that prevent parallelism (the inline scalar UDFs feature in 2019+ helps), and Oracle has its
own pragma for this. - "Recreate the function — defaults will be right now." — The default is still
PARALLEL UNSAFE in current Postgres; recreating with the same DDL changes nothing.
Common follow-up: "What makes a function genuinely parallel-unsafe?" — Writes (INSERT/UPDATE/
DELETE inside the function body), advisory locks (pg_advisory_lock), sequence nextval, temp
table creation, listen/notify, anything that mutates non-transactional state. A good rule of thumb: if the
function would behave differently when called twice in the same transaction from different processes, it is
unsafe.
Scenario142 · Partition Pruning — Make Sure the Planner Can Prune
Asked at: Flipkart · Razorpay · Walmart Labs · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Partitioning · Dialect:
Postgres · SQL Server · vendor-agnostic principle
The interviewer's prompt: "You partitioned orders by month. The query WHERE created_at =
'2026-04-15' is still scanning every partition. Why?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Partition pruning works only when the planner can prove at plan time which
partitions are relevant. If the predicate uses a function on the partition key, or compares against a
parameter from a non-pruned source, pruning is disabled and every partition is scanned — defeating the
whole point." 2. "Common pruning killers: WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2026-04-15' (function
destroys the constraint-exclusion match), WHERE created_at = $1 in a prepared statement that
planned generically, or a join condition where the partition key is on the inner side of a nested loop." 3. "I
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 160 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 161
would EXPLAIN and check the number of partitions touched — if it shows all 36 monthly partitions in an 
Append node instead of one, pruning is off. The plan literally enumerates each partition, very visual." 4. 
"Also check whether timezone semantics hide a function — WHERE created_at AT TIME ZONE
'IST' = '...' is sneaky because the conversion is a function on the partition key."
The likely root cause: Either a wrapping function (DATE(), CAST(), AT TIME ZONE) on the
partition key that prevents Postgres from matching the predicate against the partition boundary
expression, or a prepared statement that planned generically before the parameter value was known.
The fix: - Rewrite to expose the raw partition key: WHERE created_at >= '2026-04-15' AND
created_at < '2026-04-16' instead of WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2026-04-15'. The
half-open range matches the partition boundary, so constraint exclusion fires. - For prepared statements,
Postgres has run-time partition pruning since v11 — confirm enable_partition_pruning = on
and look for Subplans Removed: N in EXPLAIN ANALYZE. - For joins, ensure the partition key is on
the outer side or partition-wise join is enabled (next scenario). - Verify EXPLAIN — only one partition
should show in the plan tree.
What NOT to say: - "Partitioning automatically makes queries fast." — Only if predicates align with the
partition key; otherwise it adds overhead without read benefit. - "Pruning happens at the storage layer."
— It happens at planner (plan-time) or executor (run-time); storage just stores per-partition files. - "Use a
global non-partitioned index to fix this." — Postgres does not support global indexes across partitions;
even where vendors offer it, maintenance cost during partition swap usually outweighs the gain.
Common follow-up: "Plan-time vs run-time pruning?" — Plan-time happens before execution and is
visible in EXPLAIN as fewer partitions; run-time happens during execution for parameterised plans and
shows up as Subplans Removed: N. Pre-v11 Postgres only did plan-time, which made prepared
statements painful — run-time pruning was a major fix.
Scenario143 · Partition-Wise Join in Postgres
Asked at: PhonePe · Swiggy · ThoughtSpot · Difficulty: Hard · Topic: Partitioning · Dialect: Postgres
(11+)
The interviewer's prompt: "You have orders and order_items, both partitioned by 
order_month with matching boundaries. Joining them takes forever because Postgres joins the whole
tables instead of partition-by-partition. How do you fix this?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "This is exactly what partition-wise join is for — if two tables have matching
partition schemes, the planner can join partition-1 with partition-1, partition-2 with partition-2. Without it,
the planner unions all partitions of both tables, then joins the two giant unions — losing the partitioning
benefit and forcing a hash join over the full data size." 2. "Partition-wise join is off by default in Postgres
because it can explode plan time on tables with hundreds of partitions. The planner evaluates join
strategies per partition pair, so planning time grows with partition count." 3. "Enable it when the workload
benefits — typically BI and reporting workloads joining two large partitioned fact tables along the same
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 161 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 162
axis." 4. "Confirm partition keys match exactly in name, type, and boundary expressions — Postgres
requires structural equivalence. A partition by order_date and one by order_month will not co-
partition even if semantically aligned."
The likely root cause: enable_partitionwise_join = off (the default for new clusters), so the
planner unions partitions before joining instead of joining partition-by-partition.
The fix: - SET enable_partitionwise_join = on; (session or per-role for the BI workload).
Setting it cluster-wide is fine if your workload is dominated by partitioned analytical queries and few
partitioned tables have hundreds of partitions. - For aggregates over the same partition key: SET
enable_partitionwise_aggregate = on;. This lets the planner aggregate per-partition before
combining, which is a huge win for GROUP BY over the partition key. - Confirm partition schemes
match exactly — same column, same boundaries, same partitioning strategy (range vs list). A mismatch
silently falls back to the un-partitioned join, with no warning. - Verify with EXPLAIN — you should see one
Append containing multiple per-partition Hash Join (or Nested Loop) nodes, instead of one big
Hash Join over two Append nodes. Per-partition working sets are smaller, so each join fits in 
work_mem and avoids spilling.
What NOT to say: - "Enable globally — it is free." — It can blow up planning time on tables with many
partitions; turn on per workload and verify planning time stays acceptable. - "Works in MySQL and SQL
Server the same way." — SQL Server has partition-wise via colocation but the planner heuristics and
required matching are different; MySQL does not have true partition-wise join in InnoDB, only partition
pruning. - "Just write per-partition queries and UNION them manually." — Defeats the abstraction and
creates maintenance nightmare when you add or drop partitions; the planner's job is to do exactly this
for you.
Common follow-up: "Why is partition-wise join off by default in Postgres?" — Planning cost grows
roughly linearly with partition count because the planner has to consider join algorithms per partition pair,
and for short OLTP queries the planning overhead outweighs the execution benefit. A good follow-on is
to mention that for analytical workloads with daily or monthly partitions (12-36 of them), the planning cost
is trivial relative to query time, so enabling it pays off; for tables with thousands of partitions, you re-
evaluate.
Scenario144 · Materialised View for Repeated Heavy Query
Asked at: Razorpay · Cred · Flipkart · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Materialisation · Dialect: Postgres
(MATERIALIZED VIEW) · SQL Server (indexed view) · MySQL (manual table)
The interviewer's prompt: "Your dashboard runs the same 12-second aggregation every page load — 
SUM(amount) per merchant per day over 6 months of orders. 200 dashboard users. How do
you stop re-running this every time?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Textbook materialised view case. The aggregation is expensive (a full 6-month
scan of crores of orders), the result is small (a few lakh merchant-day rows), data changes slowly for
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 162 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 163
historical days, and many readers want the same answer. Compute once, read cheap — at 200
concurrent users you save 200 × 12 = 40 minutes of CPU per page-load cycle." 2. "In Postgres I would
create a MATERIALIZED VIEW and refresh nightly or hourly depending on staleness tolerance. SQL
Server has indexed views that refresh on every write — different tradeoff, much heavier on the write path
but always fresh. MySQL has no native equivalent; people roll their own with a scheduled INSERT INTO a
summary table." 3. "I would also index the view for the dashboard filter — typically (merchant_id,
day). Without the index, even though the view is small, dashboards re-scan it on every page hit." 4. 
"Dashboard code should query the view directly, not be told to choose between view and base table at
runtime — keeps the abstraction clean."
The likely root cause: The same expensive aggregate runs on every page load instead of once per
refresh window; the database does 200x the work it needs to do.
The fix: - Postgres: ```sql CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_merchant_daily_revenue AS SELECT
merchant_id, DATE(created_at) AS day, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE created_at >=
CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '6 months' GROUP BY merchant_id, DATE(created_at);
CREATE INDEX idx_mv_merchant_day ON mv_merchant_daily_revenue(merchant_id, day); `` -
Refresh on a schedule via cron (concurrent variant in next scenario). For a 6-
month rolling window, also schedule a daily "trim" so the view does not grow
forever. - SQL Server:CREATE VIEW ... WITH SCHEMABINDINGthen aUNIQUE
CLUSTERED INDEX` makes it indexed; auto-maintained on writes — watch OLTP throughput as every
order INSERT now also updates the indexed view. - Verify dashboard query drops from 12 seconds to
under 100 ms; peak DB CPU falls dramatically.
What NOT to say: - "A view would solve this." — A regular view is a saved query; runs every time, no
caching. The interviewer is testing whether you know the difference. - "Cache it in Redis." — Valid for
some shapes but moves truth out of the database, complicates invalidation, and makes joins back to live
data harder. - "Add more indexes to the orders table." — Indexes help filter and lookup; they do not
eliminate the aggregation cost. The 12 seconds is the GROUP BY scan and sum, not the seek.
Common follow-up: "How do you decide refresh frequency?" — Driven by business tolerance for
staleness — financial reports nightly is fine; live operational dashboards may need hourly. You can also
layer — hourly view for the last 7 days, daily for the older 6 months — to balance freshness with refresh
cost.
Scenario145 · CONCURRENTLY Refresh of a Materialised View
Asked at: Cred · Atlassian GCC · PhonePe · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Materialisation · Dialect:
Postgres
The interviewer's prompt: "Your materialised view refresh takes 4 minutes and the dashboard goes
blank during the refresh because the view is exclusively locked. How do you fix it?"
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 163 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 164
Thinking out loud: 1. "By default, REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE
lock on the view — no reads, no writes, until the refresh completes. That is why the dashboard goes
blank: every dashboard query against the view hangs waiting for the lock, then either times out or returns
the moment refresh finishes." 2. "Postgres has REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY for
exactly this — it computes the new version in a side table and then merges deltas (INSERT for new keys,
DELETE for missing keys, UPDATE for changed values) into the original storage without blocking readers.
Readers continue to see the old version until commit, then atomically see the new version." 3. "The catch
is that CONCURRENTLY requires a unique index on the view (so Postgres can match old and new rows),
and it is slower than the standard refresh — it does a row-by-row diff against the old version instead of a
clean truncate-and-insert." 4. "For high-availability dashboards this trade is almost always worth it. The
refresh time goes up maybe 50%, but the user-visible blank window goes to zero."
The likely root cause: Standard REFRESH takes a long ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the entire 4-
minute compute window; every reader of the view blocks behind that lock, and dashboards show empty
results or time out.
The fix: - Add a unique index on the view first — this is the prerequisite, Postgres will reject
CONCURRENTLY without it: sql CREATE UNIQUE INDEX mv_merchant_daily_pk ON
mv_merchant_daily_revenue (merchant_id, day); - Then refresh concurrently: sql
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY mv_merchant_daily_revenue; - Readers see
the old data until the refresh commits, then see the new data atomically — no blank dashboard, no
flicker, no error toast. - Verify with SELECT * FROM pg_locks WHERE relation =
'mv_merchant_daily_revenue'::regclass; during the refresh — you should see only a SHARE
UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock, not the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock that the standard refresh takes.
What NOT to say: - "Just refresh during off-peak hours." — Fine for daily refresh on a domestic-only
product, but does not scale to hourly or live workloads, and even "off-peak" in a 24x7 India product is
just less peak. - "Drop and recreate the view." — Same lock-up problem during the recreate, plus you
lose downstream grants, dependent views, and any indexes you carefully built — a multi-hour clean-up
exercise to recover from. - "Use a regular index instead of unique." — Postgres specifically requires a
unique index because the diff algorithm needs to identify rows; a non-unique index will not satisfy
CONCURRENTLY and the command errors out.
Common follow-up: "Why is CONCURRENTLY slower than the standard refresh?" — It does a diff
against the old version row-by-row to compute inserts, deletes, and updates, instead of a clean truncate-
and-insert. It also has to write WAL for the deltas. A good answer adds that for very high-churn views
(most rows change every refresh), the diff overhead can be significant — at that point you might rethink
the materialisation strategy or refresh more frequently with smaller deltas.
Scenario146 · VACUUM ANALYZE on Hot Tables
Asked at: Razorpay · Swiggy · Flipkart · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Maintenance · Dialect: Postgres
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 164 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 165
The interviewer's prompt: "You have a payment_attempts table with 50 lakh inserts and 30 lakh
updates per day. Queries on it have slowed steadily over the past month. EXPLAIN shows the table
reading way more pages than its row count would suggest. What is happening?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "In Postgres MVCC, an UPDATE does not modify the row in place — it writes a
new row version and marks the old one dead. VACUUM scans for dead tuples and marks the space
reusable. If autovacuum cannot keep up with churn — common on heavily-updated tables — dead tuples
pile up and reads scan extra pages full of garbage to find live rows." 2. "This is table bloat. ANALYZE is
the stats-refresh half; VACUUM is the space-reclaim half. VACUUM ANALYZE does both in one pass." 3. 
"Autovacuum's default trigger is 20% of the table changing (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor =
0.2). On a hot table with 80 lakh changes per day, 20% is reached in hours, and one pass cannot finish
before the next 20% accumulates — permanent bloat." 4. "I would check pg_stat_user_tables for 
n_dead_tup vs n_live_tup — anything above 20-30% dead is suspicious; above 50% is
screaming."
The likely root cause: Autovacuum falling behind on a high-churn table; dead tuples accumulate; reads
touch many pages of dead tuples for the same logical row count, blowing up buffer cache miss rates.
The fix: - Tune autovacuum per table — defaults assume modest churn: sql ALTER TABLE
payment_attempts SET ( autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.05, -- trigger at 5%
churn autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.02, -- analyze at 2%
autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit = 2000 -- more I/O budget ); - One-off manual cleanup:
VACUUM (ANALYZE, VERBOSE) payment_attempts; — verbose output tells you how many dead
tuples were removed. - For severe bloat where in-place VACUUM cannot reclaim disk, use pg_repack
(next scenario). - Verify n_dead_tup drops close to zero post-vacuum and the steady-state dead ratio
sits under 10%.
What NOT to say: - "Run VACUUM FULL nightly." — Takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, rewrites the
entire table — kills the app, and payment_attempts has no nightly window. - "Autovacuum handles
everything." — On hot tables it cannot keep up at defaults; saying "it handles itself" misses the
diagnosis. - "Disable autovacuum and run VACUUM from cron." — Loses adaptive triggering; a forgotten
cron job leads to runaway bloat. Tune autovacuum aggressively instead.
Common follow-up: "VACUUM vs VACUUM FULL vs pg_repack?" — VACUUM reclaims space within
the table (marks tuples reusable) without exclusive lock, does not return space to OS; VACUUM FULL
rewrites the whole table into a new file with ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, releasing space to the filesystem;
pg_repack achieves the same end-state as VACUUM FULL but uses a trigger-based shadow table to do
almost all the work online, with only a brief swap lock at the end.
Scenario147 · pg_repack for Severe Bloat
Asked at: ThoughtSpot · Atlassian GCC · Cred · Difficulty: Hard · Topic: Maintenance · Dialect:
Postgres
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 165 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 166
The interviewer's prompt: "Your events table is 200 GB on disk but only contains 40 GB of live rows.
VACUUM has run but disk usage has not dropped. The table is heavily read 24x7 — no downtime
window. How do you reclaim the space?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "VACUUM marks space reusable but does not return it to the OS. The 160 GB of
dead-tuple space is reused by future inserts within the existing file, but disk footprint stays — Postgres
only truncates if dead space happens to be at the very end. To shrink the file you need VACUUM FULL or
pg_repack." 2. "VACUUM FULL takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for the entire rewrite — hours on a 200 GB
table, during which no SELECT, no INSERT, nothing works. Not acceptable for a 24x7 service." 3. 
"pg_repack is the right tool — builds a fresh compacted copy in the background, captures concurrent
changes via triggers into a log table, replays them onto the new copy, then swaps with only a brief
ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock at the very end (seconds, not hours)." 4. "I would also identify what caused the
bloat — long-running transactions blocking VACUUM cleanup are the usual culprit; if I do not fix that,
bloat returns in weeks."
The likely root cause: Long-running transactions (forgotten BI query, stuck replication slot) held an old
xmin horizon, which prevented VACUUM from reclaiming dead tuples; once vacuum fell behind, heavy
load means VACUUM cannot catch up enough to truncate the file from the end and release space to OS.
The fix: - Install the extension: CREATE EXTENSION pg_repack; (superuser; needs to create
temporary triggers). - Run from the shell: pg_repack -d mydb -t events --jobs 4 — 
--jobs parallelises index rebuild. - Mechanism: builds new heap in a side table, copies live rows in
batches, replays trigger-captured changes, then swaps. Brief ACCESS EXCLUSIVE at the swap
(seconds). - Verify \dt+ events — drops from 200 GB to ~40 GB plus index overhead. - Investigate
the root: 
SELECT pid, xact_start, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'idle in
transaction' AND xact_start < now() - interval '1 hour'; and kill or fix the source
app.
What NOT to say: - "Just take downtime and run VACUUM FULL." — Not acceptable for the workload;
a 200 GB rewrite is 30 minutes to several hours of full lockout. - "DELETE all the bloat." — Bloat IS dead
tuples; DELETE creates more dead tuples, making it worse. - "Run CLUSTER on the table." — CLUSTER
also rewrites with ACCESS EXCLUSIVE; same blocking problem.
Common follow-up: "What can go wrong with pg_repack?" — Long-running transactions block the final
swap (it queues behind any concurrent transaction); triggers add overhead during the repack window;
index bloat needs --only-indexes or REINDEX CONCURRENTLY; and pg_repack needs 1-2x the
live table size as free disk space during operation.
Scenario148 · Forcing Hash Join on Big × Big
Asked at: Walmart Labs · Razorpay · PhonePe · Difficulty: Hard · Topic: Join algorithms · Dialect:
Postgres · SQL Server (similar) · MySQL 8 (hash join 8.0.18+)
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 166 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 167
The interviewer's prompt: "You are joining orders (10 crore rows) with payments (8 crore rows)
on order_id. The planner picks a nested loop and the query runs for an hour. What is wrong and how
do you fix it?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Nested loop on big × big is almost always a planner mistake. Nested loop is right
when the outer side is tiny and the inner side has a great index — you do outer-size lookups. With both
sides at the crore scale, you are doing crores of inner-side lookups, and even at one millisecond each that
is hours." 2. "Hash join is the right operator here — build a hash on the smaller side, probe with the larger.
O(N + M) instead of O(N × M). The cost is work_mem to hold the hash; if it does not fit, hash join spills
to disk in batches but is still vastly faster than nested loop." 3. "The planner picked nested loop because
it misestimated one side as tiny — a filter selectivity miscalculation, stale stats, or correlated columns. Fix
the estimate first; force the hash join as a backup if the misestimate is structural." 4. "I would also confirm
there is no LIMIT near the top of the plan tricking the planner into thinking it can stop early — one of
the few cases nested loop is genuinely better on large inputs."
The likely root cause: A stats error or filter the planner over-estimated as highly selective made one side
look like a few hundred rows when it is actually crores. The planner then picked nested loop — right
algorithm for the row counts it believed, wrong for reality.
The fix: - Step 1 — fix the stats: ANALYZE orders; ANALYZE payments;. The gap between
estimated and actual rows in EXPLAIN ANALYZE tells you which operator was fooled. - Step 2 — if stats
are correct, increase the planner's search: SET join_collapse_limit = 12; so it explores more
orderings. - Step 3 — last resort, force the operator: - Postgres (pg_hint_plan): /*+ HashJoin(o p)
*/. Add a comment explaining why. - SQL Server: INNER HASH JOIN o, p ON o.order_id =
p.order_id. - MySQL 8.0.18+: hash join is automatic for equi-joins where no index is usable. - Verify
EXPLAIN shows Hash Join over two Seq Scan or Index Scan nodes; runtime drops from
hours to single-digit minutes. Check Hash Batches: 1 — if it spills, raise work_mem.
What NOT to say: - "Add an index on payments.order_id — it will help the nested loop." — Wrong
operator; the index makes nested loop less terrible but still vastly slower than hash join because you still
do 10 crore lookups. - "Increase work_mem and let it figure itself out." — Only helps if hash join is
chosen; if planner sticks with nested loop, memory is wasted. - "Just disable nested loops: SET
enable_nestloop = off." — Heavy-handed; kicks even OLTP queries to hash or merge join.
Common follow-up: "When is merge join better than hash join?" — When both inputs are already sorted
on the join key (from the same index), merge join wins on memory because it streams in O(1) memory —
useful over very large inputs or when the next step is sort-aware like a window function.
Scenario149 · Increase shared_buffers / buffer_pool_size
Asked at: Razorpay · Cred · Atlassian GCC · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Memory tuning · Dialect:
Postgres (shared_buffers) · MySQL (innodb_buffer_pool_size) · SQL Server (max server memory)
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 167 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 168
The interviewer's prompt: "Your active working set is 25 GB. The box has 64 GB of RAM. Postgres
shared_buffers is at the default 128 MB. Queries are I/O-bound — every read hits disk. What is the right
tuning?"
Thinking out loud: 1. " shared_buffers is Postgres's own page cache, sitting on top of (and
separate from) the OS page cache. At the default 128 MB the database cannot hold any meaningful
working set — every query reads from disk or relies on the kernel page cache to bail it out, which is far
less efficient than holding pages in the database's own cache." 2. "Postgres conventional wisdom is 25%
of RAM for shared_buffers — 16 GB on a 64 GB box — leaving room for OS cache, work_mem
allocations per connection, WAL buffers, and other backend memory. Going higher than 40% rarely helps
and often hurts." 3. "MySQL InnoDB is different — the InnoDB buffer pool is the only meaningful cache
layer (largely bypasses OS cache via O_DIRECT), so the standard is 50-70% of RAM." 4. "Before
bumping shared_buffers I would confirm the workload is genuinely cache-cold — check 
pg_stat_database.blks_hit vs blks_read for the hit ratio."
The likely root cause: shared_buffers at default 128 MB; the hot working set of 25 GB has no
room in the database's cache, so every read hits OS cache (slower than shared_buffers due to syscall
and copy) or disk.
The fix: - Postgres: edit postgresql.conf — shared_buffers = 16GB. Restart required (fixed
allocation at process start). Also bump effective_cache_size = 48GB so the planner knows how
much data is likely cached. - MySQL: innodb_buffer_pool_size = 48G (75% of RAM). Dynamic
since MySQL 5.7. - SQL Server: EXEC sp_configure 'max server memory (MB)', 56000; —
leaves ~8 GB for OS and non-buffer-pool consumers. - Verify with pg_buffercache what is actually
resident; cache hit ratio (blks_hit / (blks_hit + blks_read)) should climb toward 99%.
What NOT to say: - "Set shared_buffers to 90% of RAM." — Starves the OS cache, work_mem,
connection memory, and the kernel; performance gets worse, and the box risks OOM under load. - 
"More RAM is always better." — Diminishing returns once the working set fits; beyond that, money is
better spent on CPU, faster disks, or replicas. - "Restart Postgres nightly so the cache is fresh." —
Catastrophically backwards; a warm cache is what makes Postgres fast. Cold cache causes sustained
latency until pages re-warm.
Common follow-up: "shared_buffers vs OS page cache?" — shared_buffers is process-shared inside
Postgres with its own clock-sweep eviction; OS cache is unified across all processes with strict LRU.
Pages can be in both — a small inefficiency called double buffering, but in practice the two layers
diverge enough that having both is a net win for hot pages.
Scenario150 · Connection Pooling with PgBouncer
Asked at: Razorpay · Swiggy · PhonePe · Cred · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Infrastructure · Dialect:
Postgres (PgBouncer) · MySQL (ProxySQL)
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 168 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 169
The interviewer's prompt: "During peak hours, your service throws FATAL: sorry, too many
clients already. Postgres is set to max_connections = 200, you have 50 app pods each with
a connection pool of 20. The math obviously does not work. How do you fix this without raising 
max_connections to 1000?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Postgres connections are expensive — each forks a backend process with ~10
MB of base memory plus per-connection work_mem. 1000 connections is 10 GB of overhead before the
database has done any work, plus a lot of context-switching as the scheduler shuffles between them." 2. 
"The right answer is a transaction-pooling broker between app pods and Postgres. PgBouncer in 
transaction mode lets 1000 client connections share say 50 server connections, because most
clients are idle at any moment — they only need a backend for the duration of a transaction." 3. "App
pods talk to PgBouncer; PgBouncer multiplexes onto the actual database. Each Postgres backend
handles many client transactions, one at a time, returned to the pool the instant the transaction commits."
4. "Size the pool right — too small and clients wait; too big and you defeat the purpose. Rule of thumb: 
default_pool_size slightly less than Postgres max_connections divided by distinct (user,
database) pairs."
The likely root cause: 50 pods × 20 connections = 1000 client connection demand against a 200-
connection database limit. App pools are sized for per-pod peak; the database is not sized for the sum.
The moment ten pods peak simultaneously, the server refuses connections.
The fix: - Deploy PgBouncer in pool_mode = transaction. Config: default_pool_size = 25
max_client_conn = 2000 pool_mode = transaction reserve_pool_size = 5 - App pods
connect to PgBouncer on port 6432 instead of Postgres on 5432; Postgres stays at 200 connections,
PgBouncer holds ~50 of those. - MySQL: ProxySQL plays the same role with connection multiplexing. -
Verify with SHOW POOLS; — cl_active high, sv_active much lower, few cl_waiting. If 
cl_waiting is persistent, raise default_pool_size modestly.
What NOT to say: - "Raise max_connections to 2000." — Each connection is a process; more memory
on idle backends than on data, and the scheduler thrashes under load. Exactly the wrong direction. - 
"Use session pooling mode." — Defeats the purpose; one session equals one server connection until
disconnect, so 1000 client connections still need 1000 server connections. - "Add more app replicas with
smaller pools." — Same total demand distributed differently; the database does not care which pod sent
the connection.
Common follow-up: "What features break under transaction pooling?" — Named prepared statements
(next transaction may land on a different backend), SET without LOCAL outside a transaction,
advisory locks across transactions, temp tables across transactions, listen/notify. PgBouncer 1.21+
added protocol-level prepared statement support which fixes the most common breakage.
Scenario151 · Read Replicas for Read-Heavy Workloads
Asked at: Razorpay · Flipkart · Cred · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Replication · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
principle · Postgres (streaming replication) · MySQL (async replication) · SQL Server (Always On)
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 169 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 170
The interviewer's prompt: "Your primary database is at 90% CPU. 80% of queries are reads — product
browsing, search, dashboards. Writes are only 20%. How do you scale this without re-architecting the
application?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Read-heavy workload with a single primary is the textbook case for read replicas.
Reads route to one or more replicas; writes still go to the primary. Primary CPU drops because it only
handles the 20% write workload; total read capacity scales roughly linearly with replica count up to a few
replicas." 2. "The catch is replication lag — replicas are eventually consistent. With Postgres streaming or
MySQL async, a replica lags by a few milliseconds healthy, seconds under load. You cannot do read-
after-write from a replica without risk of staleness — the row you just inserted may not be visible yet." 3. 
"The application or a smart proxy needs to route appropriately — read-after-write queries to primary,
eventually-consistent reads to replicas. This is the 'application change' part of 'no re-architecture'." 4. "I
would also want session-stickiness for flows where a user's own writes must be immediately visible —
easiest implementation is a 'last write timestamp' per user, and route reads to primary if within the lag
window."
The likely root cause: Single primary serving the entire read load when most reads do not need primary-
fresh data; read CPU dominates with nowhere else to go.
The fix: - Spin up streaming replicas (Postgres async streaming via primary_conninfo; MySQL 
CHANGE MASTER TO; SQL Server Always On with read-intent routing). - Route reads at the app layer
(master/replica DataSource in Hibernate/Spring Data) or via a proxy (PgPool-II, ProxySQL, RDS Proxy). -
Tag queries that need primary-fresh — "just placed an order, show detail" or "check balance after
deposit" — and pin them to primary. Everything else (catalog, search, dashboards, reports) goes to a
replica. - Verify primary CPU drops to under 30%; replica lag stays under 1 second via 
pg_stat_replication.replay_lag; alert if lag exceeds 5 seconds.
What NOT to say: - "Replicas are perfect copies, route everything to them." — They lag; reading a just-
written row may return pre-write state. Worse, the staleness is invisible — the query succeeds with old
data. - "Just upgrade the primary's CPU." — Vertical scaling hits a ceiling fast, is expensive (5x cost for
2x compute), and does not help when you eventually need horizontal scaling anyway. - "Replicas are
free, add 10." — Each replica adds streaming bandwidth load on the primary's WAL plus operational
complexity. 2-3 typically saturate the benefit.
Common follow-up: "How do you decide which reads tolerate replica lag?" — Reports and dashboards:
yes. List of products: usually yes. Reading the row you just inserted: no — route to primary or wait for
replication using a "monotonic read" pattern. Some teams use a feature flag per query class to rebalance
during incidents.
Scenario152 · Sharding When Vertical Scaling Is Not Enough
Asked at: Flipkart · Swiggy · Cred · PhonePe · Difficulty: Hard · Topic: Horizontal scaling · Dialect:
vendor-agnostic principle
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 170 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 171
The interviewer's prompt: "Your orders table is at 50 crore rows, the largest box you can buy is
already running it, and writes are saturating the primary. What is the next step?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Vertical scaling is out — you're on the largest instance. Read replicas do not help
because writes are the bottleneck and replicas only scale reads. The honest answer is sharding — split
data horizontally across multiple primaries by a shard key, so each shard handles a fraction of total
writes." 2. "The killer question is the shard key, answered by workload not convenience. For an e-
commerce orders table, customer_id is usually right — keeps a customer's data on one shard, lets
you do customer-centric queries (order history, returns, refunds) without cross-shard joins. order_id
itself is wrong because it scatters one customer's orders across all shards." 3. "Sharding is a major lift —
application changes, routing layer, rebalancing for hot shards, distributed transactions for cross-shard
writes. Make sure simpler options (caching, archival, columnar offload for analytics) are genuinely
exhausted first." 4. "I would also push back gently — 'is the entire 50 crore rows hot, or is the last 6
months getting all the writes?' Time-based archival is often more pragmatic than sharding."
The likely root cause: Single primary write bottleneck on a workload that cannot fit vertically — even
SSD-backed writes have a ceiling defined by WAL throughput per primary.
The fix: - Pick a shard key driven by query patterns (customer_id for customer-centric workloads,
merchant_id for merchant dashboards, geographic region for residency). The choice is permanent in
practice — get it wrong and re-sharding is far worse than choosing well upfront. - Add a routing layer —
Citus for Postgres (transparent), Vitess for MySQL (proven at YouTube scale), or app-level sharding with a
lookup service. - Migrate in waves — dual-write during cutover (read from old, write to both), backfill, cut
reads one query class at a time, then cut writes. - Hardest part is cross-shard queries — analytics, "top
100 customers by revenue" — typically need a separate analytical store (warehouse, ClickHouse,
BigQuery) populated by CDC.
What NOT to say: - "Just shard by hash of primary key." — Loses locality; every customer query
becomes scatter-gather across all shards, making latency unpredictable. - "NoSQL solves all this." —
Different tradeoffs; you trade joins and ACID for partition tolerance, and end up rebuilding joins in the
application. - "Start with 256 shards so we never re-shard." — Operational complexity scales with shard
count; start with 4-16 and split when needed.
Common follow-up: "Sharding vs partitioning?" — Partitioning splits a table within one database server
(same RAM, CPU, disk); sharding splits across multiple servers, each with its own storage and CPU.
Partitioning helps with pruning and maintenance; sharding scales beyond a single machine's limits.
Scenario153 · Sequential Scan of Huge Cold Table — Partition or Pre-Aggregate
Asked at: Walmart Labs · ThoughtSpot · Atlassian GCC · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Cold storage · 
Dialect: vendor-agnostic
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 171 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 172
The interviewer's prompt: "You have an events table with 5 years of data, 80 crore rows, that gets
queried only for monthly reports. Each report sequentially scans the whole table. How do you make this
not painful?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Two angles, often layered. One — partition by month and the planner only scans
the relevant partition; that alone cuts an 80-crore scan down to 1-2 crore for a monthly report. Two — for
reports that aggregate the same dimensions repeatedly, store pre-aggregated rollups in a separate table."
2. "For 5 years of cold data, a third lever is moving older partitions to cheaper storage — tablespaces on
slow disk, or archive to S3 and query via a foreign data wrapper. The 2025 partition lives on NVMe; the
2021 partition on cold HDD or S3." 3. "The right choice depends on query shape. 'Last month' style with
raw access — partitioning alone works. 'YTD aggregate by region' — pre-aggregation wins because the
output is tiny regardless of input size." 4. "I would also ask the business: do reports need row-level
access or just summaries? If summaries, pre-aggregation suffices and cold partitions become audit-only."
The likely root cause: Single monolithic table on hot storage, scanned in full for queries that need only
summaries or only a recent slice; the database does crores of pointless reads per report.
The fix: - Partition by month: PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at); old partitions can live on a
slower tablespace via CREATE TABLESPACE cold_storage LOCATION '/mnt/hdd' and ALTER
TABLE events_2021_01 SET TABLESPACE cold_storage;. The planner's partition pruning
makes the cold partitions invisible to "last month" queries. - Pre-aggregate via a daily/weekly summary
table maintained by the ETL or a materialised view: 
SELECT region, DATE(created_at) AS day, COUNT(*), SUM(amount) FROM events
GROUP BY 1, 2; populated incrementally on append. - Archive truly cold data — older than 2 years
— to columnar storage (Parquet on S3) or external object store; access via Postgres parquet_fdw or 
s3_fdw if rarely needed. This pushes the inactive 60-70% of data off your primary's expensive SSD. -
Verify reports run in seconds against summaries, not minutes against raw events; primary's disk footprint
drops dramatically once cold partitions move off.
What NOT to say: - "Add more indexes to the events table." — A 5-year sequential scan does not
benefit from indexes when the query touches all rows; indexes help filter to a subset, but if the report
aggregates the entire history, the planner correctly chooses a sequential scan. - "Cache the results in the
app." — Caching helps for repeated identical queries; analytical queries vary by date range, filter, and
grouping, so cache hit ratio will be low. - "Just rebuild the table to compress old rows." — Postgres has
TOAST for large values but no native row-level compression for analytical workloads; columnar storage is
the right tool, not a clever rewrite.
Common follow-up: "How would you keep the pre-aggregation up to date efficiently?" — Append-only
rollup — for each new day, INSERT that day's aggregate into the summary table; never re-aggregate
history because history does not change. For corrections (rare), reprocess only the affected day's slice
rather than full rebuild.

Scenario154 · Hash Aggregate Spilling — Same Fix Family
Asked at: PhonePe · Cred · ThoughtSpot · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Aggregation · Dialect: Postgres
primary
The interviewer's prompt: "Your GROUP BY user_id over a billion-row events table is slow.
EXPLAIN shows HashAggregate with Batches: 32 Memory: 4 MB Disk: 800MB. What is
happening?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "HashAggregate builds an in-memory hash of group keys to running aggregates. If 
work_mem cannot hold all distinct groups, Postgres spills to disk in batches — Batches: 32 means
32 disk passes, each reading and writing partial hashes to temp files. Disk I/O dominates the runtime." 2. 
"The fix mirrors the sort-spill fix — raise work_mem for this query so the aggregate fits in memory.
Same caveats: per-query or per-role, not global, because work_mem multiplies across operations and
connections." 3. "Alternatively, if GROUP BY columns match an existing index order (user_id
indexed), the planner can do a sorted GroupAggregate, which streams in O(1) memory regardless of how
many distinct groups exist — a completely different algorithm." 4. "I would also confirm group cardinality
with SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id); — if there are 50 crore distinct users, no amount of
work_mem will fit; you must use sort-based GroupAggregate or pre-aggregate."
The likely root cause: work_mem too small for the cardinality of user_id — many crore distinct
users with per-group state does not fit in 4 MB; 32 batches is Postgres doing the right thing within its
memory budget.
The fix: - Per-query: SET work_mem = '1GB'; SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) ... GROUP BY
user_id; - If GroupAggregate over an index is feasible, ensure stats are fresh and the planner picks it
— check EXPLAIN for GroupAggregate over Index Scan. May need SET enable_hashagg =
off; to force the planner. - Pre-aggregate via a materialised view if the query is repeated; at billion-row
scale, an incremental rollup pays for itself in a single report cycle. - Verify EXPLAIN now reads Memory:
800MB instead of Disk: 800MB, Batches: 1; runtime drops from minutes to single-digit
seconds.
What NOT to say: - "Use DISTINCT instead." — Same spill problem (implemented as hash or sort), often
slower than GROUP BY because GROUP BY can compute the aggregate in the same pass. - "Drop the
index — it must be misleading the planner." — Wrong; the index helps the streaming GroupAggregate
path. Dropping it forces hash, which is the spill case. - "Add LIMIT 10 to make it small." — Does not
help; HashAggregate must process all input before knowing which 10 groups make the cut; LIMIT only
saves work at the end.
Common follow-up: "HashAggregate vs GroupAggregate?" — Hash builds a hash table of group keys;
works on unsorted input but needs memory proportional to group count. Group needs sorted input and
streams in O(1) memory regardless of group count, because it only holds the current group's running
aggregate. Choose based on group count and whether a sorted input is available.

Scenario155 · Hot Row Contention — Sharded Counter Pattern
Asked at: Razorpay · Swiggy · Flipkart · Difficulty: Hard · Topic: Contention · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
principle
The interviewer's prompt: "You maintain a single row total_orders_today that every order
increments. During a flash sale, the database starts deadlocking and throughput tanks. What is happening
and how do you fix it?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "That single row is a serialisation point. Every order transaction takes a row-level
lock on it via the UPDATE, so concurrent orders queue behind whoever holds it. Throughput caps at 1 /
lock_hold_time — at a typical 5 ms transaction, that is ~200 increments per second regardless of
hardware. Deadlocks happen when transactions touch the counter and other rows in inconsistent orders."
2. "The classic fix is the sharded counter — instead of one row, keep N rows (say 64) and each
transaction increments a random shard. Total is SUM(count) across shards. Writes spread across 64
lock targets, contention drops 64x; reads pay a tiny aggregation cost." 3. "Trade-off: writes scale roughly
linearly with shard count; reads pay a microsecond SUM on 64 rows. Acceptable for almost all real
workloads — counters, vote tallies, view counts." 4. "I would also push back on whether you really need
real-time accuracy — for a 'today's order count' display, a 30-second-stale value via periodic batch often
works and avoids contention entirely."
The likely root cause: Row-level lock on the single counter row is the per-transaction bottleneck; under
flash-sale concurrency the lock queue grows faster than transactions finish, and deadlocks happen when
transactions update the counter alongside other rows in inconsistent orders.
The fix: - Create a sharded counter table: 
sql CREATE TABLE counter_shards( name TEXT NOT NULL, shard INT NOT NULL, count
BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, PRIMARY KEY(name, shard) ); INSERT INTO
counter_shards SELECT 'orders', s, 0 FROM generate_series(0, 63) s; - On write:
pick a random shard (e.g., shard = pg_backend_pid() % 64) and UPDATE counter_shards
SET count = count + 1 WHERE name = 'orders' AND shard = ?. - On read: SELECT
SUM(count) FROM counter_shards WHERE name = 'orders'; - Verify write QPS scales
roughly N-fold; deadlock rate drops close to zero.
What NOT to say: - "Use SELECT FOR UPDATE to serialise cleanly." — Removes deadlock noise but
does not solve the throughput cap; transactions still queue. - "Disable transactions for that statement."
— Loses durability; rarely acceptable for a payment-adjacent counter, and Postgres autocommit is still a
transaction. - "Use Redis INCR instead." — Valid for many cases but moves truth out of the database
and introduces consistency gaps with the orders table.
Common follow-up: "How do you avoid drift if a shard gets deleted or a server fails mid-increment?" —
Idempotent operations (UPSERT with ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE), tolerate eventual consistency on the
SUM, and reconcile against the authoritative source (the orders table itself) hourly or daily.

Scenario156 · Batch vs Row-by-Row Processing
Asked at: Cred · Walmart Labs · Razorpay · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Throughput · Dialect: vendor-
agnostic
The interviewer's prompt: "Your ETL script processes 50 lakh rows by looping in Python and issuing one
UPDATE per row. It takes 6 hours. How do you make it not take 6 hours?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Row-by-row processing means 50 lakh round-trips between Python and the
database. Each round-trip is at least a few hundred microseconds on a local socket, often a millisecond
across a VPC. At 50 lakh × 1 ms that is over an hour just in network latency, plus per-statement parse,
plan, and lock overhead." 2. "The fix is batched processing — write the update in SQL itself, joining
against a temp table or a multi-row VALUES list, so the database does the loop natively in one
statement." 3. "Even within the round-trip model, batching N rows per statement and using prepared
statements (parse-plan happens once) cuts wall time an order of magnitude — useful intermediate if you
cannot restructure." 4. "I would also confirm we are not committing per row — if the loop does 
execute; commit per row, every commit is an fsync. Batching commits every 1000 rows alone is a
large win."
The likely root cause: Network round-trip overhead times 50 lakh rows, plus per-statement parse/plan,
plus per-row commit fsync if commits are not batched. Each UPDATE is microscopic in the database
itself, but the wrapper costs dominate.
The fix: - Option A — load the deltas into a temp table, then one UPDATE: sql CREATE TEMP TABLE
updates(id BIGINT, new_status TEXT); COPY updates FROM '/tmp/updates.csv';
UPDATE orders SET status = u.new_status FROM updates u WHERE orders.id =
u.id; The COPY is the fastest path to load the deltas; the join-based UPDATE is one statement, one
parse, one plan, one transaction. - Option B — multi-row VALUES in chunks of 1000: UPDATE orders
SET status = v.s FROM (VALUES (1,'paid'),(2,'paid')...) v(id,s) WHERE
orders.id = v.id; Useful when CSV staging is not convenient. - Verify by timing — 6 hours
typically drops to under 5 minutes; the UPDATE itself is then bound by index maintenance and WAL
throughput, which are the only legitimate costs.
What NOT to say: - "Add an index — it will speed up the per-row UPDATE." — Per-row UPDATE is
already O(log N) with the primary-key index; the bottleneck is round-trips, not lookup time, so the index
does not help. - "Parallelise the Python loop with 16 threads." — Adds connection pressure on the
database and still pays round-trip per row; you might shave 2-3x off the wall time but you are still hours
away from the right answer, which is set-based SQL. - "Use a stored procedure to loop inside the
database." — Better than Python looping, but still a row-at-a-time loop; the right pattern is set-based
SQL, which is what the database is built for.
Common follow-up: "What about for inserts — does the same advice apply?" — Yes, but for inserts
COPY is even better than VALUES (next scenario). The general principle is: any time you find yourself
looping in application code to do per-row data modification, look for a way to express the same logic as
one SQL statement against a staged dataset.

Scenario157 · COPY / Bulk Load Instead of Multi-Row INSERT
Asked at: PhonePe · Razorpay · ThoughtSpot · Difficulty: Medium · Topic: Ingestion · Dialect: Postgres
(COPY) · MySQL (LOAD DATA INFILE) · SQL Server (BULK INSERT / bcp)
The interviewer's prompt: "Your daily ingest is loading a 2 GB CSV via batched INSERT INTO ...
VALUES statements and takes 90 minutes. How do you speed it up?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Multi-row INSERT is faster than per-row INSERT (one parse per batch instead of
one parse per row), but every dialect has a dedicated bulk-load path that bypasses statement parsing,
WAL overhead, and a lot of constraint-checking machinery. That is the right tool for bulk ingestion." 2. 
"Postgres: COPY ... FROM — typically 5-10x faster than equivalent INSERT for the same data
because it uses a streaming protocol that avoids per-row parse and pipelines WAL writes. MySQL: LOAD
DATA INFILE is the same idea — extremely fast bulk load with minimal per-row overhead. SQL Server: 
BULK INSERT or the bcp utility, with TABLOCK hint for full-batch optimisation." 3. "For maximum
throughput, drop secondary indexes before the load, COPY in, then rebuild indexes in one shot — this is
faster than incremental index maintenance for large loads because each rebuild can use the bulk sorting
path." 4. "I would also consider whether the source CSV can be sorted by primary key before loading,
because Postgres physically inserts in CSV order and a sorted-by-PK load gives you a clustered heap,
which speeds up subsequent range scans without needing a separate CLUSTER step."
The likely root cause: INSERT statement overhead (parse, plan, execute, per-row WAL record, per-row
constraint check) dominates; the actual write of bytes is a small fraction of total time, so the wrapper
costs eat almost all the wall clock.
The fix: - Postgres: sql COPY orders (order_id, customer_id, amount, created_at)
FROM '/var/data/orders_2026-04-15.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true); - Pre-
load: DROP INDEX idx_orders_user; and other secondary indexes (optional, do this only if the
table will be loaded in one shot — for incremental loads keep indexes live). - Post-load: rebuild indexes
( CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY if the table must stay readable), then run ANALYZE orders; so
the planner has fresh stats. - Verify: 2 GB load drops from 90 minutes to under 10 minutes; CPU during
load is dominated by parse-and-tuple-form rather than statement overhead.
What NOT to say: - "Use an ORM bulk_insert method." — Most ORM bulk methods still issue multi-row
INSERTs under the hood; they do not switch to COPY unless explicitly configured (psycopg 
copy_expert, SQLAlchemy bulk_insert_mappings does NOT use COPY). Many ORM users
discover this the hard way. - "Just turn off transactions." — Postgres still uses WAL inside an implicit
transaction; the gain from "no transaction" is mostly imaginary, and you lose atomicity if the load fails
partway. - "Pre-compute the SQL in Python and execute one giant INSERT." — Parser memory pressure
becomes the bottleneck; very long SQL strings hit pathological behaviour in the parser. COPY avoids this
entirely.
Common follow-up: "Why is COPY so much faster than INSERT?" — Single statement parse, batched
WAL records (one WAL flush per few thousand rows instead of per row), batched constraint checks, a
streamlined wire protocol that skips per-row planning, and the absence of per-statement command tag
round-trips. Combined, these compound to the 5-10x speedup.
