Scenario158 · Async Commit for Non-Critical Writes
Asked at: Cred · ThoughtSpot · Atlassian GCC · Difficulty: Hard · Topic: Durability · Dialect: Postgres
(synchronous_commit) · MySQL (innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit)
The interviewer's prompt: "You have a high-throughput logging table — user_activity — that
receives 50,000 inserts per second. Disk I/O on the WAL is saturated. The data is useful but losing a few
seconds is acceptable. How do you trade durability for throughput?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Default Postgres behaviour is synchronous commit — the WAL record is fsync'd
to disk before COMMIT returns success. That fsync is expensive (microseconds to milliseconds even on
NVMe) and serialises commits because each waits for disk acknowledgement before the next can
proceed." 2. "For workloads not financially critical — analytics events, app logs, traces — 
synchronous_commit = off lets COMMIT return immediately and WAL flush happens later. You
gain throughput at the cost of losing up to roughly 3 × wal_writer_delay of data if the server
crashes between WAL write to OS and flush to disk." 3. "Same idea in MySQL — 
innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 2 flushes to OS page cache but not disk on commit; 
= 0 flushes once per second." 4. "Critically, the database remains consistent after crash — async
commit only loses recent transactions, does not corrupt anything. Very different from fsync = off,
which can corrupt the database on crash."
The likely root cause: fsync per commit is the I/O bottleneck for high-throughput log ingestion; 50,000
inserts/sec means 50,000 fsyncs/sec, well beyond what a single disk can do.
The fix: - Postgres per-session: SET synchronous_commit = off; then run the bulk-insert path. -
Per-role: ALTER ROLE logger SET synchronous_commit = off; — applies to every session
that role opens, no application code change. - Per-statement: SET LOCAL synchronous_commit =
off; inside the transaction. - MySQL: SET GLOBAL innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 2;
(or = 0 for more throughput at slightly more risk). - Verify throughput goes up 5-10x for fsync-bound
workloads; understand the recovery contract — a few hundred ms of recent log writes may be lost on
power cut.
What NOT to say: - "Turn synchronous_commit off everywhere for speed." — Catastrophic for financial
data; must scope per workload (per role/session/statement) so orders and payments still get full
durability. - "This is the same as fsync=off." — Critically different. synchronous_commit = off
keeps the database consistent on crash, only loses last few hundred ms. fsync = off may corrupt
the database because WAL records may be missing or out of order. Never use fsync = off in production. -
"Use a non-transactional table type." — Postgres has no such thing; MyISAM in MySQL loses ACID
entirely.
Common follow-up: "What is the data loss window when synchronous_commit is off?" — At most 3 ×
wal_writer_delay (default 200 ms, so under a second) on a crash. The database remains
consistent; only the most recent unflushed transactions are missing. For systems-level durability you can
also use Postgres remote_apply / remote_write modes for sync replication.

Scenario159 · TEMP Table with Index for Multi-Statement Reuse
Asked at: Walmart Labs · ThoughtSpot · Goldman Sachs GCC · Difficulty: Medium · Topic:
Materialisation · Dialect: Postgres · SQL Server · MySQL
The interviewer's prompt: "Your report runs five queries in sequence, each one filtering and aggregating
the same 50 lakh-row derived set. Each query re-derives it. How do you compute it once and reuse it?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "CTEs are scoped to one statement; the derived set is not reusable across
separate statements. The right tool is a TEMP table — create it, fill it once, index it for the downstream
access patterns, then run all five queries against it. Derivation cost paid once, not five times." 2. "TEMP
tables in Postgres live for the session and are dropped on disconnect; with ON COMMIT DROP they
survive only until the transaction commits. They have their own statistics (after ANALYZE) and can be
indexed like a regular table." 3. "For five queries hitting the same derived set, this is a clear win — 5x
derivation collapses to 1x derivation plus 5x cheap lookups." 4. "TEMP tables in Postgres do NOT use
shared_buffers — they use per-session temp_buffers. For large temp tables, raising 
temp_buffers keeps them hot in memory."
The likely root cause: Repeated derivation of the same intermediate result across five separate
statements, each time paying the full filter + aggregate computation. The database has no way to know it
could cache the result.
The fix:
BEGIN;
CREATE TEMP TABLE tmp_active_users ON COMMIT DROP AS
SELECT user_id, MAX(last_login) AS last_seen, COUNT(*) AS sessions
FROM sessions
WHERE last_login >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'
GROUP BY user_id;
CREATE INDEX ON tmp_active_users(user_id);
ANALYZE tmp_active_users;  -- so the planner has stats for downstream joins
-- Run the five reports against tmp_active_users
SELECT ...;
SELECT ...;
COMMIT;
Verify report time drops from 5x derivation cost to 1x plus 5x cheap lookups; for a 50 lakh-row set,
typically minutes to under a minute total.
What NOT to say: - "Use a CTE and reference it five times." — CTEs do not persist across statements;
you would need one massive statement, and pre-v12 Postgres materialised CTEs unconditionally (now
inlines by default) — reuse semantics changed across versions. - "Use a materialised view." — Persistent
• 
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 178 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 179
and global; overkill for session-scoped intermediate data, incurs refresh cost, leaves a stale artifact in the
schema. - "Run the five queries in parallel — they share buffer cache." — Buffer cache helps with raw
page reads but not with re-running GROUP BY; aggregate work is still done five times.
Common follow-up: "Lifetime of a TEMP table?" — Until end of session (default), or end of transaction
with ON COMMIT DROP, or with ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS (table persists, contents wiped on
commit). Other sessions cannot see it — each session has its own private namespace, which is exactly
why TEMP tables scale: no cross-session contention.
Scenario160 · Diagnosing Plan Regression Across Releases — End-to-End
Asked at: Razorpay · Cred · Goldman Sachs GCC · Atlassian GCC · Difficulty: Hard · Topic: Plan-driven
diagnosis · Dialect: Postgres (pg_stat_statements + auto_explain) · SQL Server (Query Store)
The interviewer's prompt: "After a feature release on Saturday, three queries that used to run in under a
second are now taking 30 seconds intermittently. Same SQL, same schema. Walk me through your
diagnosis end-to-end."
Thinking out loud: 1. "Intermittent slowness with the same SQL strongly suggests plan flips — the
planner is picking a bad plan some of the time, driven by parameter values or stats freshness. The SQL
text is identical, so the variable is what the planner does with it at any given moment." 2. "Capture data
first. In Postgres: enable auto_explain with auto_explain.log_min_duration = 1000 and 
log_analyze = on to log full actual-row plans for slow runs. Compare with a fast plan from staging."
3. "In SQL Server: open Query Store and look at the regressed-queries report — it lists queries whose
plan has changed and shows old vs new plans side by side, with wait-stats breakdown so you can see
whether it is CPU, I/O, or lock-wait dominated." 4. "Common causes: parameter sniffing (planner cached
a plan for one parameter set, now reused with a very different one), stale stats after a release-time backfill,
a new index the planner is now considering badly because cost estimates shifted."
The likely root cause: The release brought a stats-invalidating data shift (backfill, new tenant
onboarded, big import) and the planner now misjudges selectivity for some parameter values; combined
with cached plans reused across different parameter combinations, you get intermittent slowness.
The fix: - Step 1 — capture: enable auto_explain, gather plans for fast and slow runs of the same
query. - Step 2 — compare plans: identify the operator that flipped (nested loop vs hash, index choice,
join order, a new Sort or Filter). - Step 3 — fix the root cause: ANALYZE the affected tables; in SQL
Server use OPTION (RECOMPILE) for worst-case queries or OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN; in
Postgres, consider plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan so prepared statements re-plan
each time with fresh parameter values. - Step 4 — verify with both fast and slow parameter values;
confirm both pick the right plan. - Step 5 — guardrail: add a latency alert on p99 so the next regression
is caught in hours, not days.
What NOT to say: - "Roll back the release." — May not be possible; the release may not even be the
cause (correlation with release time can be coincidental with a stats event), and you waste the diagnostic
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 179 / 586

opportunity. - "Hint the plan and move on." — Hides the root cause; the same shape will appear
elsewhere on other queries with the same misestimate or sniffing pattern. - "Restart Postgres — it will fix
itself." — Clears the plan cache so queries re-plan with current stats, but only treats the symptom — the
regression returns next time stats drift.
Common follow-up: "How would you set up a plan regression monitor going forward?" — Postgres: 
pg_stat_statements + a daily diff on mean_exec_time per queryid, alerting on more than

Category 3, Part A — Design This Schema: OLTP Patterns
Design problems are open-ended — the interviewer says "design tables for X" and you walk them
through entities, relationships, indexes, and edge cases. There is rarely one correct answer; what matters
is the structure of your thinking. Part A is OLTP (transactional) schemas — payments, ledgers, multi-
tenant data, audit trails, booking flows, messaging — the kind of write-heavy, concurrency-sensitive
systems that power real Indian product companies. Part B (covered separately) shifts to analytics and
warehousing. For each scenario below, you get the prompt, what to verbalize, a working schema, the
rationale, edge cases, and the follow-up the interviewer is most likely to ask next.
Scenario161 · Double-Entry Payment Ledger
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Jupiter, Slice · Domain: Payments
The prompt:
"Design tables for a payments ledger that tracks money moving between user wallets, merchants,
and our internal accounts. Walk me through your tables, relationships, indexes, and how you'd
handle a failed partial settlement."
Thinking out loud (what to verbalize): 1. "First, what are the entities and access patterns — accounts
hold balances, transactions group entries, entries are the atomic debit and credit lines. Reads are mostly
statements per account and reconciliation jobs." 2. "Next, the relationships — one transaction has at least
two entries that must net to zero. Accounts and entries are many-to-one." 3. "For indexes I'd consider —
entries by account_id and posted_at for statements, transactions by external_ref for idempotency." 4. 
"Edge cases to flag — partial failures, reversals, currency mismatch, and ensuring sum of entries per txn
is zero via a constraint or trigger."
The schema:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 180 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 181
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    account_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    owner_type VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL CHECK (owner_type IN ('user','merchant','internal')),
    owner_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    currency CHAR(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'INR',
    account_kind VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    UNIQUE (owner_type, owner_id, account_kind, currency)
);
CREATE TABLE transactions (
    txn_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    external_ref VARCHAR(80) UNIQUE,
    txn_type VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    posted_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    metadata JSONB
);
CREATE TABLE ledger_entries (
    entry_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    txn_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES transactions(txn_id),
    account_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(account_id),
    direction CHAR(1) NOT NULL CHECK (direction IN ('D','C')),
    amount_paise BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (amount_paise > 0),
    posted_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX idx_entries_account_time ON ledger_entries (account_id, posted_at DESC);
Why each choice: - Amounts stored as BIGINT paise — no floating-point drift, and INR easily fits. - 
external_ref UNIQUE makes retries idempotent — same upstream reference cannot post twice. -
Entries are append-only — reversals create new compensating entries instead of mutating history.
Edge cases handled: - Partial settlement failure — transaction stays in pending status with no
entries, retried as a fresh txn id, original external_ref blocks duplicates. - Currency mismatch —
accounts carry currency; entries inherit via account, FX is its own transaction with FX accounts.
Alternatives considered + rejected: - Storing balance directly on the account row — rejected because
it hides discrepancies; balance is derived SUM(direction-signed amount), cached in a snapshot
table for performance.
What NOT to say: - "I'll just update the wallet balance directly in a single UPDATE." That works for toys,
not for any audit-grade system.
Common follow-up: "How would you reconcile this ledger against the bank statement at end of day, and
where would mismatches surface?"

Scenario162 · Order Management with Line Items
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Meesho, Myntra, Nykaa · Domain: Commerce
The prompt:
"Design tables for an e-commerce order — header, line items, status transitions. Walk me through
relationships, indexes, and how price changes mid-checkout get handled."
Thinking out loud (what to verbalize): 1. "First, what are the entities — orders are the header, order_items
are the lines, and status_history captures every transition. Customers and products live elsewhere; I'll just
reference them." 2. "Next, the relationships — order to items is one-to-many, items reference a product
snapshot, not the live product, so a later price edit doesn't rewrite history." 3. "For indexes I'd consider —
orders by customer_id and created_at, items by order_id, and a partial index on orders where status =
'pending' for the operations dashboard." 4. "Edge cases — price changes mid-checkout, partial
cancellations of one line, and refunds that touch only some items."
The schema:
CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    order_number VARCHAR(20) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
    subtotal_paise BIGINT NOT NULL,
    tax_paise BIGINT NOT NULL,
    shipping_paise BIGINT NOT NULL,
    total_paise BIGINT NOT NULL,
    placed_at TIMESTAMP,
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
CREATE TABLE order_items (
    order_item_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    order_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(order_id),
    product_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    sku VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL,
    product_name_snapshot VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    unit_price_paise BIGINT NOT NULL,
    quantity INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
    line_total_paise BIGINT NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending'
);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_recent ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_pending ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending';
CREATE INDEX idx_order_items_order ON order_items (order_id);

Why each choice: - Snapshot fields on order_items ( product_name_snapshot, 
unit_price_paise) freeze the contract at order time. - order_number separate from 
order_id so the customer-facing identifier is shareable without exposing surrogate keys. - Per-item
status enables partial cancel and partial fulfilment without splitting orders.
Edge cases handled: - Price change mid-checkout — checkout compares the customer's confirmed

Alternatives considered + rejected: - Single denormalised orders table with a JSON of items —

Scenario163 · Order Status State Machine
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Swiggy, Zomato, Dunzo · Domain: Workflow
The prompt:
"Design tables to enforce a strict order state machine — only certain status transitions are legal.
Walk me through how you'd prevent an illegal jump like 'delivered' to 'pending'."
Thinking out loud (what to verbalize): 1. "First, the entities — the order itself, the legal-transitions
catalogue, and the immutable status_history audit." 2. "Next, the access pattern — most reads are
'current status'; writes are 'attempt transition' and must validate atomically." 3. "For indexes —
order_status_history by order_id and changed_at, and the legal-transitions table is tiny so a primary key
on (from, to) is enough." 4. "Edge cases — concurrent transition attempts, system-initiated vs user-
initiated transitions, and replaying history for support."
The schema:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 183 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 184
CREATE TABLE order_status_transitions (
    from_status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    to_status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    requires_role VARCHAR(20),
    PRIMARY KEY (from_status, to_status)
);
CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    current_status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'created',
    status_version INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    updated_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
CREATE TABLE order_status_history (
    history_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    order_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(order_id),
    from_status VARCHAR(20),
    to_status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    changed_by BIGINT,
    change_reason VARCHAR(255),
    changed_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
CREATE INDEX idx_status_history_order ON order_status_history (order_id, changed_at);
Why each choice: - Transitions live in a table, not code, so the rules can be edited and audited like data.
- status_version on orders supports optimistic locking — concurrent transitions detect each other.
- History is append-only; the current status on orders is just a denormalised cache of "latest row".
Edge cases handled: - Concurrent transitions — UPDATE orders SET status = ...,
status_version = status_version + 1 WHERE order_id = ? AND status_version = ?
— one of two wins, the other retries. - System vs user transitions — requires_role column blocks
customer-initiated delivered directly.
Alternatives considered + rejected: - Enforcing the state machine purely in application code — rejected
because two services bypassing the check would corrupt state; the DB-level catalogue plus a transition
stored procedure is harder to bypass.
What NOT to say: - "We'll just trust the application layer to validate." That falls apart with multiple
services or background workers.
Common follow-up: "How would you support a soft 'on hold' state that any role can enter from any
other state but only an admin can leave?"

Scenario164 · User Authentication with Sessions and Roles
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Freshworks, Zoho, Postman, BrowserStack · Domain: Identity
The prompt:
"Design auth tables — users, password credentials, sessions, roles, permissions. Walk me

Scenario168 · Soft Delete Pattern
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Freshworks, Zoho, Razorpay, Postman · Domain: General OLTP
The prompt:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 192 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 193
"Add soft-delete semantics across the schema — users can be 'deleted' but recoverable for 30
days. Walk me through the column design, query implications, and unique-constraint pitfalls."
Thinking out loud (what to verbalize): 1. "First, the marker — a nullable deleted_at timestamp on
every business table, indexed via a partial index." 2. "Next, query hygiene — every read needs WHERE
deleted_at IS NULL; we either centralise this in a view or in the data-access layer." 3. "For indexes
— partial indexes on WHERE deleted_at IS NULL keep them small and fast." 4. "Edge cases —
unique constraints that should ignore deleted rows, foreign keys to deleted parents, and hard-delete after
30 days."
The schema:
CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    name VARCHAR(150) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    deleted_at TIMESTAMP,
    deleted_by BIGINT,
    deletion_reason VARCHAR(255)
);
-- Email must be unique among live customers, but reusable after soft delete
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_customers_email_active 
    ON customers (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
CREATE INDEX idx_customers_active ON customers (created_at DESC) 
    WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
CREATE INDEX idx_customers_purge_due ON customers (deleted_at) 
    WHERE deleted_at IS NOT NULL;
CREATE VIEW v_customers AS 
    SELECT * FROM customers WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
Why each choice: - Partial unique index lets the same email re-register after the previous account is
soft-deleted. - v_customers view gives accidental-safety — joining to the view never accidentally
pulls deleted rows. - idx_customers_purge_due makes the nightly purge job a fast bounded scan.
Edge cases handled: - Deleted parent, live child — child FK has ON DELETE RESTRICT, so soft-
deleting the parent does not orphan; deletion job must cascade soft-deletes. - Audit visibility — admin/
support views read the base table directly; only customer-facing queries use the view.
Alternatives considered + rejected: - Moving deleted rows to a customers_archive table —
rejected because reverting takes a re-insert with a new id; soft delete preserves identity.

hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 194
What NOT to say: - "I'll just add is_deleted BOOLEAN." A boolean loses the timestamp; without
"when" you cannot drive the 30-day purge.
Common follow-up: "A user wants to be permanently deleted today, not in 30 days. What changes?"

The prompt:
"Design an append-only event log for an event-sourced order service. Walk me through the table,

Thinking out loud (what to verbalize): 1. "First, the entities — events keyed by aggregate (order_id),
versioned per aggregate, with a global monotonically-increasing sequence." 2. "Next, immutability — only
INSERT is permitted; the application role does not have UPDATE/DELETE." 3. "For indexes — primary

writes to the same aggregate, projection backfills, and snapshotting old aggregates."
The schema:

CREATE TABLE events (
    event_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    aggregate_type VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    aggregate_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    aggregate_version INTEGER NOT NULL,
    event_type VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,
    payload JSONB NOT NULL,
    metadata JSONB,
    occurred_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    UNIQUE (aggregate_type, aggregate_id, aggregate_version)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_events_aggregate ON events 
    (aggregate_type, aggregate_id, aggregate_version);
CREATE INDEX idx_events_global ON events (event_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_events_type ON events (event_type, occurred_at);
CREATE TABLE snapshots (
    aggregate_type VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    aggregate_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    aggregate_version INTEGER NOT NULL,
    state JSONB NOT NULL,
    taken_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    PRIMARY KEY (aggregate_type, aggregate_id, aggregate_version)
);
Why each choice: - UNIQUE (aggregate_type, aggregate_id, aggregate_version) is the
optimistic concurrency lock — two parallel writers cannot both insert version 7. - event_id
BIGSERIAL gives a global ordering that downstream projections can checkpoint against. - Snapshots
make replay bounded — rebuild reads "snapshot version N" then events after N.
Edge cases handled: - Concurrent writes — second writer fails the unique constraint, retries with re-
read latest version. - Projection backfill — a new projection starts at event_id = 0, processes in order,
checkpoints regularly.
Alternatives considered + rejected: - Mutable state table with an events audit on the side —
rejected because it stops being the source of truth; events-as-the-truth makes rebuilds and time-travel
trivial.
What NOT to say: - "I'll allow updates to old events to fix typos." That breaks every downstream
consumer that already saw the old data.
Common follow-up: "How would you garbage-collect events for an aggregate that the user has the right
to be forgotten from?"

Scenario170 · Outbox Pattern
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Postman, Chargebee · Domain: Reliable messaging
The prompt:
"Design an outbox table for reliably publishing events to a message queue from the same
transaction as the business write. Walk me through how the relay works."
Thinking out loud (what to verbalize): 1. "First, the problem — we cannot atomically write to the DB and
publish to Kafka. The outbox solves it by making the publish a DB write." 2. "Next, the relay — a separate
process polls (or tails the WAL) and ships outbox rows to the queue, marking them dispatched." 3. "For
indexes — partial index on undispatched rows so the relay scan is cheap." 4. "Edge cases — at-least-
once delivery, ordering within an aggregate, and outbox table bloat."
The schema:
CREATE TABLE outbox (
    outbox_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    aggregate_type VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    aggregate_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    event_type VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,
    payload JSONB NOT NULL,
    target_topic VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    dispatched_at TIMESTAMP,
    dispatch_attempts INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    next_attempt_at TIMESTAMP
);
CREATE INDEX idx_outbox_pending ON outbox (created_at) 
    WHERE dispatched_at IS NULL;
CREATE INDEX idx_outbox_retry ON outbox (next_attempt_at) 
    WHERE dispatched_at IS NULL AND dispatch_attempts > 0;
Why each choice: - Same transaction as the business write — atomicity is free. - next_attempt_at
plus dispatch_attempts give exponential backoff. - Partial index keeps the relay query
O(undispatched), not O(total).
Edge cases handled: - At-least-once — consumers must be idempotent; we send a stable 
outbox_id as the message key. - Ordering — relay processes rows in created_at order per
aggregate, partitioning the queue by aggregate_id.
Alternatives considered + rejected: - Distributed transactions (XA) between DB and broker — rejected
because they are operationally fragile and most modern brokers don't support them well.

hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 197
What NOT to say: - "After publishing, the application calls UPDATE outbox." If the app crashes after
publish but before update, you'll re-publish — fine for at-least-once, but design the consumer for it.
Common follow-up: "The outbox has 50 million rows because the cleanup job stopped. How do you
recover without locking the table?"

    is_critical BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE

The prompt:

"Edge cases — global usage cap race conditions, per-user cap, stacking rules, expiry, and fraud."

CREATE TABLE coupons (
    coupon_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    coupon_code VARCHAR(40) UNIQUE NOT NULL,

    discount_value_paise BIGINT,
    discount_percent NUMERIC(5,2),
    max_discount_paise BIGINT,
    min_cart_paise BIGINT,
    starts_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    expires_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    total_usage_cap INTEGER,
    per_user_cap INTEGER,

    is_stackable BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE,
    is_active BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE

    coupon_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES coupons(coupon_id),
    rule_type VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,

CREATE TABLE coupon_redemptions (
    redemption_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    coupon_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES coupons(coupon_id),
    user_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    order_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    discount_applied_paise BIGINT NOT NULL,

Why each choice: - redemption_count on coupons cached via atomic UPDATE ... WHERE

cap exhausted. - Per-user cap — SELECT COUNT(*) FROM coupon_redemptions WHERE
coupon_id = ? AND user_id = ? inside the same transaction as the order.

Scenario175 · Shopping Cart with Anonymous-to-Logged-In Merge
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Myntra, Nykaa, Meesho · Domain: Commerce
The prompt:
"Design a shopping cart that supports anonymous browsing and merges with the user's cart on
login. Walk me through the schema and the merge algorithm."
Thinking out loud (what to verbalize): 1. "First, the entities — carts keyed by either user_id or
anonymous_token, and cart_items as lines." 2. "Next, the merge — on login, take the anonymous cart's
items, dedupe by SKU into the user cart, sum quantities, delete the anonymous cart." 3. "For indexes —
cart by user_id (unique) and by anonymous_token (unique), items by cart_id." 4. "Edge cases — both
carts have the same SKU, stock validation at merge, price changes since add."
The schema:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 204 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 205
CREATE TABLE carts (
    cart_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id BIGINT UNIQUE,
    anonymous_token CHAR(36) UNIQUE,
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    last_active_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    CHECK ((user_id IS NOT NULL)::int + (anonymous_token IS NOT NULL)::int = 1)
);
CREATE TABLE cart_items (
    cart_item_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    cart_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES carts(cart_id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    sku VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL,
    product_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    quantity INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
    added_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    UNIQUE (cart_id, sku)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_carts_anonymous_stale ON carts (last_active_at) 
    WHERE user_id IS NULL;
Why each choice: - CHECK constraint enforces "either anonymous or logged in, never both, never
neither". - UNIQUE (cart_id, sku) makes "add again" a single UPSERT. - Cascade delete on cart
cleanup means anonymous-cart purge is a single DELETE.
Edge cases handled: - Both carts have same SKU — UPSERT with quantity = anonymous.qty +
user.qty, capped at per-customer max if any. - Stock validation — done at view time and again at
checkout; cart row doesn't enforce stock.
Alternatives considered + rejected: - Keeping the anonymous cart in cookies/localStorage only —
rejected because cross-device continuity and basket-abandonment campaigns need server-side state.
What NOT to say: - "On login, just delete the old cart and use the anonymous one." The user lost their
saved-for-later items; merge, don't replace.
Common follow-up: "How long do you keep anonymous carts before purging, and what's the storage
trade-off?"

Scenario177 · Inventory + Reservation (Prevent Overselling)
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Flipkart, BigBasket, BookMyShow, Swiggy Instamart · Domain:
Inventory
The prompt:
"Design inventory tables that prevent overselling — multiple customers try to buy the last unit at
the same instant. Walk me through reservation, expiry, and confirmation."
Thinking out loud (what to verbalize): 1. "First, the entities — inventory (per SKU per warehouse with
available and reserved counts), reservations (held units with TTL)." 2. "Next, the flow — add-to-cart
reserves, expiry releases, order-confirm converts reservation to a stock movement." 3. "For indexes —
inventory by (sku, warehouse) for the hot update; reservations by expires_at for the sweeper." 4. "Edge
cases — concurrent reservations, partial reservation, expiry race with confirmation, warehouse failure."
The schema:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 207 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 208
CREATE TABLE inventory (
    sku VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL,
    warehouse_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
    available_qty INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (available_qty >= 0),
    reserved_qty INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (reserved_qty >= 0),
    version INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    updated_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    PRIMARY KEY (sku, warehouse_id)
);
CREATE TABLE reservations (
    reservation_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    sku VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL,
    warehouse_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
    quantity INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
    user_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    cart_id BIGINT,
    expires_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'held',
    FOREIGN KEY (sku, warehouse_id) REFERENCES inventory(sku, warehouse_id)
);
CREATE TABLE stock_movements (
    movement_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    sku VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL,
    warehouse_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
    movement_type VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    quantity_delta INTEGER NOT NULL,
    reference_id BIGINT,
    occurred_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
CREATE INDEX idx_reservations_expiry ON reservations (expires_at) 
    WHERE status = 'held';
CREATE INDEX idx_movements_sku ON stock_movements (sku, warehouse_id, occurred_at);
Why each choice: - Reserve via UPDATE inventory SET available_qty = available_qty
- ?, reserved_qty = reserved_qty + ? WHERE ... AND available_qty >= ? — atomic;
zero rows means insufficient. - Stock movements are the immutable truth; inventory row is a cached
aggregate, reconcilable. - Reservations have TTL so abandoned carts don't lock inventory.
Edge cases handled: - Concurrent reservations — DB-level conditional UPDATE is the lock; no separate
SELECT FOR UPDATE needed. - Expiry race — sweeper does UPDATE reservations SET
status = 'expired' WHERE expires_at < NOW() AND status = 'held' and reverses the
inventory update; confirmation does the opposite, checking status = 'held' first.
Alternatives considered + rejected: - Holding inventory only in Redis — fast but durability is uncertain;
DB-backed with optional Redis cache is the standard.

What NOT to say: - "We'll fetch available, check it's >= requested, then update." Race condition; you'll
oversell.

alone?"

The prompt:
"Design a booking system where customers book resources (a doctor, a meeting room, a salon

Thinking out loud (what to verbalize): 1. "First, the entities — resources, availability rules (recurring),
bookings (the actual reservation), and optionally pre-generated slots." 2. "Next, the conflict model —
exclude-style constraint on overlapping ranges, or generated discrete slots with a unique key." 3. "For
indexes — bookings by (resource_id, start_at, end_at); availability by resource_id." 4. "Edge cases —
timezones, overlapping reschedule, recurring bookings, blackout dates."
The schema:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 209 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 210
CREATE TABLE resources (
    resource_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    resource_type VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    name VARCHAR(150) NOT NULL,
    timezone VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Asia/Kolkata',
    is_active BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE
);
CREATE TABLE availability_rules (
    rule_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    resource_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES resources(resource_id),
    day_of_week SMALLINT NOT NULL CHECK (day_of_week BETWEEN 0 AND 6),
    start_time TIME NOT NULL,
    end_time TIME NOT NULL,
    slot_minutes INTEGER NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE blackouts (
    blackout_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    resource_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES resources(resource_id),
    starts_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    ends_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    reason VARCHAR(255)
);
CREATE TABLE bookings (
    booking_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    resource_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES resources(resource_id),
    customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    starts_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    ends_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'confirmed',
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    EXCLUDE USING GIST (
        resource_id WITH =,
        tstzrange(starts_at, ends_at) WITH &&
    ) WHERE (status = 'confirmed')
);
CREATE INDEX idx_bookings_resource_time ON bookings (resource_id, starts_at);
Why each choice: - GIST exclude constraint physically prevents two confirmed bookings from
overlapping on the same resource — the DB rejects the second insert. - Timestamps stored in UTC
(TIMESTAMPTZ); resource carries its display timezone. - Availability rules and blackouts are checked in
the application before insert, but the exclusion constraint is the safety net.
Edge cases handled: - Concurrent double-booking — exclusion constraint causes the second
transaction to fail; the app retries or shows "slot taken". - Reschedule — UPDATE bookings SET
starts_at = ?, ends_at = ? re-evaluates the exclude; new conflict raises.

hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 211
Alternatives considered + rejected: - Pre-generating one row per slot per day — works for fixed-grid
scheduling like cinemas but doesn't fit flexible-duration bookings.
What NOT to say: - "We'll just check WHERE NOT EXISTS overlapping booking then insert."
Race condition without the exclude constraint.
Common follow-up: "How would you support a booking that requires two resources simultaneously, like
a doctor plus a room?"
Scenario179 · Friend / Connection Graph (Mutual)
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Hike, ShareChat, Josh, Koo · Domain: Social
The prompt:
"Design a mutual friendship graph — connection is symmetric, requires both sides to accept.
Walk me through how you'd model it without storing each pair twice."
Thinking out loud (what to verbalize): 1. "First, the entities — friend_requests (directional, pending state)
and friendships (mutual, confirmed)." 2. "Next, the trick — store the pair with LEAST(a, b) and 
GREATEST(a, b) to avoid duplicate (1,2) and (2,1) rows." 3. "For indexes — friendships need lookups
from either side, so we add both (user_low, user_high) PK and a redundant index on 
(user_high)." 4. "Edge cases — block, unfriend, simultaneous requests, and mutual-friend queries
at scale."
The schema:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 211 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 212
CREATE TABLE friend_requests (
    request_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    requester_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    recipient_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    responded_at TIMESTAMP,
    UNIQUE (requester_id, recipient_id),
    CHECK (requester_id <> recipient_id)
);
CREATE TABLE friendships (
    user_low BIGINT NOT NULL,
    user_high BIGINT NOT NULL,
    became_friends_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    PRIMARY KEY (user_low, user_high),
    CHECK (user_low < user_high)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_friendships_high ON friendships (user_high, user_low);
CREATE TABLE blocks (
    blocker_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    blocked_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    blocked_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    PRIMARY KEY (blocker_id, blocked_id)
);
Why each choice: - Canonical ordering user_low < user_high halves storage and dedupes the
relationship. - Index on (user_high, user_low) lets us look up friends from either direction with
the same plan. - Block is directional and separate — A blocks B doesn't imply B blocks A.
Edge cases handled: - Simultaneous requests — the unique constraint catches the duplicate; the
second one converts the first to accepted at the application layer. - Unfriend — single DELETE on
friendships; friend_requests history stays for analytics.
Alternatives considered + rejected: - Storing both (A, B) and (B, A) rows — symmetric but 2× storage
and update hazard if one row gets missed.
What NOT to say: - "We can ignore the ordering trick because storage is cheap." It's not just storage —
it's the dedup invariant; without it you can have inconsistent state.
Common follow-up: "How would you compute 'mutual friends with X' for a user with 5000 friends?"

    WHERE left_at IS NULL;
Why each choice: - Same model for 1-1 and group — fewer joins, no special cases. - 
last_read_message_id on participants gives O(1) unread = count of messages with id > last_read.
- deleted_for_everyone_at is soft — the tombstone is needed to suppress on every reader's
device.
Edge cases handled: - Leave and rejoin — left_at set, new participant row not created; on rejoin,
clear left_at, history visibility decided by group policy. - Very large groups — separate read-receipt
table is optional; for 10000-member groups you don't track per-user-per-message reads.

Scenario182 · Read-Receipt Tracking

The prompt:
"Design read receipts for a group chat — show 'seen by N' under a message. Walk me through

Scenario184 · Wallet / Loyalty Points with Balance

The prompt:
"Design a loyalty-points wallet — users earn points on orders, redeem on future orders, points

partial redemption against multiple credit lots (FIFO), expiry mid-redemption, and balance drift."
The schema:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 220 / 586

CREATE TABLE wallets (
    wallet_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id BIGINT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    wallet_type VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'loyalty',
    current_balance INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    last_recomputed_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
CREATE TABLE wallet_transactions (
    txn_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    wallet_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES wallets(wallet_id),
    txn_type VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    points INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (points > 0),
    reference_type VARCHAR(30),
    reference_id BIGINT,
    expires_at TIMESTAMP,
    posted_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
CREATE TABLE wallet_redemption_lots (
    redemption_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES wallet_transactions(txn_id),
    credit_txn_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES wallet_transactions(txn_id),
    points_consumed INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (points_consumed > 0),
    PRIMARY KEY (redemption_id, credit_txn_id)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_wt_wallet_time ON wallet_transactions (wallet_id, posted_at DESC);

    WHERE txn_type = 'credit' AND expires_at IS NOT NULL;
Why each choice: - Redemption lots table records which credits a debit consumed (FIFO) — auditable
and supports partial reversals. - current_balance is a cache; a nightly job recomputes from
transactions to catch drift. - Credits and debits are positive numbers with a txn_type discriminator —
easier to read than signed math.
Edge cases handled: - Expiry — scheduled job inserts compensating expiry debit for unredeemed
remainder of each expired credit; balance decreases atomically. - FIFO redemption — application picks
oldest unexpired credits first; redemption_lots table records the allocation.
Alternatives considered + rejected: - Single balance column with no transaction history — fast but
uncountable and unauditable.
What NOT to say: - "We'll keep the balance correct via a trigger on transactions." Triggers are easy to
drift; explicit recompute job is more honest.

    dead_lettered_at TIMESTAMP

CREATE TABLE webhook_deliveries (
    delivery_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    event_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES webhook_events(event_id),

Edge cases handled: - Endpoint disabled mid-retry — dispatcher checks endpoints.is_active

simple, with edge-burst risk) and sliding window (more accurate, more storage)." 2. "Next, the entities —
rate_limit_policies (rules), rate_limit_counters (the bucket state)." 3. "For indexes — counters keyed by
(api_key, endpoint, window_start) with TTL via partial scan; policies looked up by (api_key, endpoint)." 4. 
"Edge cases — clock skew across servers, distributed counters, burst allowance, and counter reset."
The schema:

CREATE TABLE rate_limit_policies (
    policy_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    api_key_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    endpoint_pattern VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    limit_count INTEGER NOT NULL,
    window_seconds INTEGER NOT NULL,
    burst_allowance INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    is_active BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE,
    UNIQUE (api_key_id, endpoint_pattern)
);
CREATE TABLE rate_limit_counters (
    api_key_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    endpoint_pattern VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    window_start TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    count INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    last_request_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    PRIMARY KEY (api_key_id, endpoint_pattern, window_start)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_rl_counters_cleanup ON rate_limit_counters (window_start);
CREATE TABLE rate_limit_violations (
    violation_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    api_key_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    endpoint_pattern VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    request_count INTEGER NOT NULL,
    occurred_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
Why each choice: - Fixed window keyed by truncated window_start ( date_trunc('minute',
NOW())) — single UPSERT per request. - UPSERT with count = count + 1 RETURNING count
checks the limit and increments in one round-trip. - Old window rows cleaned by a periodic DELETE; not
held forever.
Edge cases handled: - Edge burst (twice the limit straddling the boundary) — to tame this, use a sliding-
window of two adjacent fixed buckets, weight by overlap. - Distributed counters — DB row is the single
source; for very high QPS, move to a per-shard counter and aggregate, or use Redis with the DB as
fallback.
Alternatives considered + rejected: - Per-request audit row, counting on read — works at small scale;
at high QPS the count query becomes a bottleneck.
What NOT to say: - "We'll just block when the count exceeds the limit by writing a log row." Logs aren't
enforcement; the counter row is.
Common follow-up: "At 50000 requests per second across keys, the rate_limit_counters table is the
hottest table in your DB. How do you scale it?"

Category 3, Part B — Design This Schema: Analytics &
Warehousing Patterns
Part B covers the analytics half of the design round — star schema, slowly-changing dimensions, event
tables, time-series, columnar warehouses, attribution models, and the layered modelling pattern (staging
→ intermediate → mart) that every modern data team uses. These show up heavily at product
companies (Razorpay, Swiggy, Cred, Meesho, Flipkart, PhonePe), at data-role GCC panels (Walmart
Labs, Target, Wells Fargo, Goldman, AmEx) and at every Snowflake / BigQuery / dbt-shaped opening.
The interviewer is testing whether you can think in facts and dimensions, reason about late-arriving data,
and pick the right grain — not whether you can recite Kimball verbatim. Each scenario below gives the
prompt, the thinking, the schema sketch, the choices defended, the edge cases, the alternatives, the
things to avoid saying, and the follow-up that usually lands.
Scenario191 · Star schema for sales
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Target, Flipkart, Meesho · Topic: Dimensional
modelling
The interviewer's prompt: "Design a star schema for an e-commerce sales reporting workload. Daily
revenue by product, by city, by category — that kind of slicing."
Thinking out loud: 1. "First clarification — what's the grain of the fact? Per order line, or per order? I'll go
per order line because that's the lowest grain we'll need to roll up from." 2. "Then dimensions: date,
product, customer, store/channel, payment method. Keep dim keys as surrogate integers, never natural
keys." 3. "Measures live in the fact — quantity, unit price, discount, tax, line total. Anything additive goes
in the fact; anything descriptive goes in a dim."
Schema sketch:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 233 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 234
CREATE TABLE dim_date (
  date_key      INT PRIMARY KEY,           -- YYYYMMDD
  date_actual   DATE NOT NULL,
  day_of_week   SMALLINT, month SMALLINT, quarter SMALLINT, year SMALLINT,
  is_weekend    BOOLEAN, is_holiday BOOLEAN
);
CREATE TABLE dim_product (
  product_key   BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  product_id    VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,      -- natural key from source
  product_name  VARCHAR(255), category VARCHAR(100), brand VARCHAR(100)
);
CREATE TABLE dim_customer (
  customer_key  BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id   VARCHAR(50), city VARCHAR(100), state VARCHAR(100), tier VARCHAR(20)
);
CREATE TABLE fact_sales (
  sale_key       BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  date_key       INT REFERENCES dim_date(date_key),
  product_key    BIGINT REFERENCES dim_product(product_key),
  customer_key   BIGINT REFERENCES dim_customer(customer_key),
  order_id       VARCHAR(50),               -- degenerate dimension
  quantity       INT,
  unit_price     NUMERIC(12,2),
  discount_amt   NUMERIC(12,2),
  line_total     NUMERIC(12,2)
);
CREATE INDEX ON fact_sales(date_key);
CREATE INDEX ON fact_sales(product_key, date_key);
Why each choice: - Surrogate date_key as YYYYMMDD INT because BI tools and partition pruning
both love it; cheaper to join than a date string. - Dims hold the natural key (product_id) so we can re-
link if source IDs change. - Order ID stays in the fact as a degenerate dim — we will need it to count
distinct orders, but it has no other attributes worth a table. - Measures are pre-computed at line grain so
any roll-up is a SUM — no row-level math at query time.
Edge cases: - Refunds and cancellations — add a transaction_type or store negative line totals
so net revenue stays a simple SUM. - Currency — if multi-country, store a currency_code and a 
local_amount, plus a converted inr_amount against dim_date FX rates. - Returns arriving
days later — these are late-arriving facts (see Scenario20).
Alternatives: - Snowflake schema (next scenario) — normalised dims save space at the cost of more
joins. - OBT — one big table denormalised, easier to query but storage-heavy.
What NOT to say: - "Just use the OLTP orders table for reporting" — kills production load, mixes
write and read patterns, no historical preservation. - "Skip the date dimension, use the timestamp
directly" — you lose easy holiday/weekend flags and partition keys.
Common follow-up: "How would you handle a product changing category — do you overwrite, version,
or both?" (Leads into SCD discussion.)

Scenario192 · Snowflake schema — when normalised dims help
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan India, Wells Fargo · Topic: Dimensional
modelling
The interviewer's prompt: "You designed a star schema. When would you normalise a dimension into a
snowflake? Show me where."
Thinking out loud: 1. "Snowflaking means splitting a dim into multiple normalised tables — 
dim_product → dim_product + dim_brand + dim_category." 2. "Worth it when a dim has
very wide attribute branches, or when the same sub-dim is reused across many parent dims." 3. "Cost:
more joins per query, harder for BI tools. Win: fewer updates if a brand attribute changes, smaller storage
on huge dims."
Schema sketch:
CREATE TABLE dim_category (
  category_key   INT PRIMARY KEY,
  category_name  VARCHAR(100), parent_category VARCHAR(100)
);
CREATE TABLE dim_brand (
  brand_key      INT PRIMARY KEY,
  brand_name     VARCHAR(100), brand_owner_country VARCHAR(50)
);
CREATE TABLE dim_product (
  product_key    BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  product_id     VARCHAR(50),
  product_name   VARCHAR(255),
  category_key   INT REFERENCES dim_category(category_key),
  brand_key      INT REFERENCES dim_brand(brand_key)
);
Why each choice: - Category and brand are reused across dim_product and potentially 
dim_supplier — normalising avoids duplicating brand details on every product row. - Brand
attributes (owner country, holding company) update independently of products. One row to update in 
dim_brand versus thousands in dim_product. - Category hierarchy is recursive and stored once.
Edge cases: - Modern columnar warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift) compress repeated strings
extremely well, so the storage saving is often tiny. Snowflaking can hurt query perf there. - BI tools that
auto-generate joins (Tableau, Looker) may not pick up snowflake hops cleanly.
Alternatives: - Keep star schema; let column compression handle redundancy. - Hybrid — snowflake the
genuinely shared sub-dims (geography, time-of-day) but star-flatten the rest.
What NOT to say: - "Always snowflake to follow third normal form" — modern analytics warehouses do
not reward 3NF; they reward join elimination. - "Snowflake is always faster because tables are smaller"
— opposite; extra joins are usually the bottleneck.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 235 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 236
Common follow-up: "Same question, but the warehouse is BigQuery — does your answer change?"
(Yes — flatter is better on columnar; consider nested STRUCT for the sub-dim attributes.)
Scenario193 · SCD Type 1 — overwrite in place
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Wipro · Topic: Slowly changing dimensions
The interviewer's prompt: "A customer changes their phone number. The business does not care about
the old number. How do you store this in the dimension?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "This is the classic SCD Type 1 — overwrite. We lose history, but we save storage
and queries stay simple." 2. "Use Type 1 when the attribute is corrective (typo fix, phone update) or
business-irrelevant for historical reporting." 3. "I will still record an updated_at so debugging is
possible, even though we do not version the row."
Schema sketch:
CREATE TABLE dim_customer (
  customer_key   BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id    VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  full_name      VARCHAR(200),
  email          VARCHAR(255),
  phone_number   VARCHAR(20),         -- Type 1 column — overwrite
  city           VARCHAR(100),         -- Type 1 column — overwrite
  signup_date    DATE,
  updated_at     TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
-- ETL pattern
UPDATE dim_customer
SET phone_number = :new_phone, updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
WHERE customer_id = :cust_id
  AND phone_number IS DISTINCT FROM :new_phone;
Why each choice: - One row per customer — joins stay cheap, fact tables do not multiply. - IS
DISTINCT FROM avoids no-op updates (matters for change-data-capture pipelines). - updated_at
is a forensic field, not a historical one — you cannot answer "what was the phone number on
2024-03-15" with Type 1.
Edge cases: - If downstream models cache the old value (BI extracts, ML features) you need to
invalidate them on overwrite. - Auditing — Type 1 leaves no audit trail; pair with a CDC log if compliance
demands it.
Alternatives: - Type 2 (next scenario) if any future report might need history. - Type 3 if you only ever
need the most recent previous value.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 236 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 237
What NOT to say: - "Type 1 means just INSERT over the old row" — UPDATE, not INSERT. -
"Type 1 is always wrong because we lose data" — for corrective fields it is the right answer; do not over-
engineer.
Common follow-up: "Marketing now wants to know which city the customer was in when they placed a
particular order — does your schema still work?" (No, because we overwrote city. Pivot to Type 2.)
Scenario194 · SCD Type 2 — full history rows
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Target, Wells Fargo, AmEx GCC · Topic: Slowly
changing dimensions
The interviewer's prompt: "Same customer table, but now any change must be queryable historically.
Design the schema and the ETL pattern."
Thinking out loud: 1. "Type 2 keeps history by versioning rows — every change inserts a new row, the
old row is closed out." 2. "Need valid_from, valid_to, is_current. Surrogate key per
version, natural key shared across versions." 3. "Facts must join on the surrogate key, not the natural key,
so each fact row picks up the dim version that was active when the fact happened."
Schema sketch:
CREATE TABLE dim_customer (
  customer_key    BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,    -- changes with every version
  customer_id     VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,      -- stable natural key
  full_name       VARCHAR(200),
  city            VARCHAR(100),
  tier            VARCHAR(20),
  valid_from      TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  valid_to        TIMESTAMP,                 -- NULL when current
  is_current      BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE,
  UNIQUE (customer_id, valid_from)
);
CREATE INDEX ON dim_customer (customer_id, is_current) WHERE is_current;
Why each choice: - Surrogate customer_key lets each fact row pin to the exact dim version at the
time of the event. - valid_to NULL on the current row is the SQL idiom most warehouses recognise;
pair with is_current for fast lookup. - Partial index on is_current keeps the "give me the live
row" query cheap even on millions of versions.
Edge cases: - Concurrent updates — wrap the close-out and insert in a transaction so a customer never
has two current rows. - Same-day multiple changes — decide whether you collapse them into one
version (last-write-wins per day) or version each. - Storage explosion — bound by change frequency; for
very hot dims, mix Type 1 (overwrite) for cheap fields with Type 2 (version) for important ones.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 237 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 238
Alternatives: - Type 6 (Scenario6) — combine Type 2 history with a Type 1 "current value" column for
convenience. - Bitemporal modelling — track effective and recorded timestamps separately.
What NOT to say: - "Just store the timestamp on the fact and look up the dim with BETWEEN" —
works but kills join performance at scale. - "Use the natural key as the join column" — defeats the entire
point of versioning.
Common follow-up: "How would you bulk-load a year of historical changes into this table from a system
that never tracked them?" (Reconstruct from CDC log, or accept a single Type 2 row per year.)
Scenario195 · SCD Type 3 — limited-history columns
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, Cognizant, Capgemini · Topic: Slowly changing dimensions
The interviewer's prompt: "We only ever need to compare the customer's current tier with their previous
one. Full history is overkill. Design for this."
Thinking out loud: 1. "SCD Type 3 — keep the current value and one previous value in the same row." 2. 
"One row per entity, two columns per tracked attribute: current_value, previous_value, 
previous_changed_at." 3. "Useful when business explicitly says 'I just want before/after' — for
example, plan upgrades, tier changes."
Schema sketch:
CREATE TABLE dim_customer (
  customer_id            VARCHAR(50) PRIMARY KEY,
  full_name              VARCHAR(200),
  city                   VARCHAR(100),
  current_tier           VARCHAR(20),
  previous_tier          VARCHAR(20),
  tier_changed_at        TIMESTAMP,
  updated_at             TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
-- ETL pattern when tier changes
UPDATE dim_customer
SET previous_tier   = current_tier,
    current_tier    = :new_tier,
    tier_changed_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    updated_at      = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
WHERE customer_id = :cust_id
  AND current_tier IS DISTINCT FROM :new_tier;
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 238 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 239
Why each choice: - One row per customer — joins remain trivial. - Only one prior value preserved —
second-previous is lost forever, which is acceptable given the brief. - tier_changed_at lets reports
filter by "tier changes this month".
Edge cases: - If two attributes (tier and city) both follow Type 3, you double the columns — pair with
..._changed_at for each. - Reverting to the previous tier is silently lossy if you do not detect it
before the UPDATE.
Alternatives: - Type 2 if depth of history matters. - Type 4 — mini-dimensions in a separate table for fast-
changing attributes.
What NOT to say: - "Type 3 stores all history in one row" — it stores exactly one previous value. - "Type
3 is older and not used today" — still used heavily when business cares only about deltas.
Common follow-up: "What happens if a customer changes tier four times in a week and the report runs
at the end of the week?" (Only the last change is recoverable; pivot to Type 2 if all four matter.)
Scenario196 · SCD Type 6 — hybrid 1+2+3
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan India, Target, Walmart Labs · Topic: Slowly
changing dimensions
The interviewer's prompt: "You want full Type 2 history plus easy current-value lookups without joining
the latest row every time. How would you model it?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Type 6 = Type 1 (overwrite current value) + Type 2 (insert new version) + Type 3
(carry current alongside historical), all in one table." 2. "Each row has both tier (the value as of that
version) and current_tier (overwritten on every change, same across all versions of the same
customer)." 3. "Facts can either join on the version-specific column or the current column depending on
the question."
Schema sketch:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 239 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 240
CREATE TABLE dim_customer (
  customer_key      BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id       VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  tier              VARCHAR(20),               -- Type 2: as-of-version value
  current_tier      VARCHAR(20),               -- Type 1: overwritten on all versions
  city              VARCHAR(100),
  current_city      VARCHAR(100),
  valid_from        TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  valid_to          TIMESTAMP,
  is_current        BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE
);
-- ETL: when tier changes
BEGIN;
UPDATE dim_customer SET valid_to = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, is_current = FALSE
  WHERE customer_id = :cust_id AND is_current;
INSERT INTO dim_customer (customer_id, tier, current_tier, valid_from, is_current)
  VALUES (:cust_id, :new_tier, :new_tier, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, TRUE);
UPDATE dim_customer SET current_tier = :new_tier WHERE customer_id = :cust_id;
COMMIT;
Why each choice: - tier answers "what was their tier on 12 March" — Type 2 behaviour. - 
current_tier answers "what is their tier today" without joining the latest row — Type 1 behaviour,
repeated across all versions. - Single table — no maintenance overhead of a separate "current" view.
Edge cases: - The bulk UPDATE of current_tier across all versions can be expensive on hot
dims; alternative is a materialised view that joins to a is_current row. - The redundancy means
writes touch more rows; queries gain from it.
Alternatives: - Type 2 only, plus a dim_customer_current view filtered to is_current. - Pure
Type 2 with downstream models exposing both perspectives.
What NOT to say: - "Type 6 is just Type 2 with extra steps" — the convenience of current-value access
without a self-join is the whole point at scale. - "Storage is the same as Type 2" — no, it costs more on
writes; you trade write cost for read simplicity.
Common follow-up: "In your fact table, which column would you join to — tier or current_tier
— and why?" (Depends on the report; "revenue by tier" historically means tier; "current MRR by tier"
means current_tier.)
Scenario197 · Event tracking table — clickstream
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Meesho, PhonePe, Cred · Topic: Event modelling
The interviewer's prompt: "Design a table that captures every front-end event from our app — page
views, button clicks, form submits — at scale of 100 million events a day."
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 240 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 241
Thinking out loud: 1. "This is a fact-like table but with high cardinality and schemaless properties. Wide
rows are common." 2. "Core columns: event_id, event_name, user_id, session_id, timestamp, plus a
JSON properties blob for variable payload." 3. "On a warehouse like Snowflake or BigQuery I would
partition by event date and cluster by event_name, user_id."
Schema sketch:
CREATE TABLE events (
  event_id        UUID,
  event_name      VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,       -- "page_view", "add_to_cart"
  event_ts        TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  event_date      DATE NOT NULL,               -- partition key
  user_id         VARCHAR(50),
  anonymous_id    VARCHAR(50),                 -- pre-login tracker
  session_id      VARCHAR(50),
  device_type     VARCHAR(20),
  app_version     VARCHAR(20),
  properties      JSONB,                       -- variable payload
  context         JSONB                        -- IP, UA, referrer,
  PRIMARY KEY (event_id, event_date)
)
PARTITION BY RANGE (event_date);
-- Snowflake: CLUSTER BY (event_date, event_name, user_id)
-- BigQuery: PARTITION BY event_date CLUSTER BY event_name, user_id
Why each choice: - event_date partition prunes 99% of scans for the typical "last 7 days" query. - 
properties JSONB absorbs event-specific fields without a schema migration on every new event. -
Both user_id and anonymous_id cover pre-login and post-login funnels.
Edge cases: - Schema drift in properties — invest in a contract / event registry early or analytics
queries become a graveyard. - PII inside properties — strip or hash on ingestion; do not store raw
phone or email here. - Out-of-order events from mobile clients with offline mode — server-receive time vs
client-emit time matter; keep both.
Alternatives: - Per-event-type table (one table per event_name) — fewer JSON unpacks but a
schema explosion. - Columnar format on a data lake (Parquet on S3) queried via Trino/Athena.
What NOT to say: - "Just dump it all in one massive table and add indexes" — indexes do not help
columnar warehouses; partitioning and clustering do. - "Use TEXT instead of JSONB" — JSONB allows
operator-level extraction (properties->>'item_id') without parsing every row.
Common follow-up: "How would you make funnel queries — view → add-to-cart → purchase — fast on
this schema?" (Add session_id and order by event_ts; consider a pre-aggregated funnel mart —
see Scenario9.)

Scenario198 · Sessionisation-ready event schema
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Meesho, Swiggy, Walmart Labs · Topic: Sessionisation
The interviewer's prompt: "Your events have a user_id and a timestamp. Reporting wants 'sessions' —
groups of activity separated by 30 minutes of inactivity. Design the schema so downstream queries are
easy."
Thinking out loud: 1. "Two layers — raw events with no session, and a derived session_id assigned by a
batch or stream job." 2. "Session boundary: gap of > 30 minutes between consecutive events for the
same user." 3. "Store session_id back on the raw event row and also a sessions table for session-
level aggregates."
Schema sketch:
CREATE TABLE events_with_session (
  event_id        UUID,
  user_id         VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  event_ts        TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  event_date      DATE NOT NULL,
  event_name      VARCHAR(100),
  session_id      UUID NOT NULL,             -- assigned by sessioniser
  session_seq     INT NOT NULL,              -- 1-indexed within session
  properties      JSONB
)
PARTITION BY RANGE (event_date);
CREATE TABLE sessions (
  session_id      UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id         VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  session_start   TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  session_end     TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  event_count     INT,
  page_view_count INT,
  device_type     VARCHAR(20),
  utm_source      VARCHAR(100),
  utm_campaign    VARCHAR(100)
);
-- Sessioniser query pattern (window function)
WITH gaps AS (
  SELECT *,
    LAG(event_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts) AS prev_ts,
    CASE WHEN event_ts - LAG(event_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts)
         > INTERVAL '30 minutes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_new_session
  FROM events_raw
)
SELECT *, SUM(is_new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts) AS session_num
FROM gaps;
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 242 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 243
Why each choice: - session_id on the event row eliminates expensive sessionisation at query time.
- session_seq lets you ask "first event in session" without another window function. - Separate 
sessions table pre-aggregates the per-session metrics most dashboards need.
Edge cases: - Anonymous → logged-in stitching mid-session — keep an anonymous_id column and
stitch in the sessioniser. - Late-arriving events from mobile offline buffers can re-open closed sessions;
decide a cut-off (e.g. ignore events older than 24h for sessionisation). - Cross-device sessions —
typically not modelled at the session level; handled at the journey level.
Alternatives: - Compute sessions on the fly in every query — works for small data, dies at scale. -
Streaming sessioniser (Flink / Kafka Streams) for near-real-time session tables.
What NOT to say: - "Just use a different table per session" — sessions are entities, not partitions. - "Use
IP address as session_id" — fails with NAT, mobile networks, IP rotation.
Common follow-up: "What changes if the inactivity threshold becomes configurable per product line?"
(Move it to a config table; sessioniser reads at run time.)
Scenario199 · Funnel analysis schema
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Meesho, Flipkart · Topic: Funnel modelling
The interviewer's prompt: "Design a schema that lets PMs build any funnel — view → add-to-cart →
checkout → payment — without rewriting the SQL each time."
Thinking out loud: 1. "Two components — a generic event stream (Scenario7) plus a funnel-config table
that defines step order and event matching." 2. "Either compute funnels on demand from events using
window functions, or pre-compute a funnel_progressions mart for the top 5 funnels." 3. 
"Property-based matching matters — 'add_to_cart' is one event, but the PM may want to funnel only
Electronics adds."
Schema sketch:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 243 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 244
CREATE TABLE funnel_definitions (
  funnel_id       UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  funnel_name     VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  step_seq        INT NOT NULL,
  event_name      VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  match_filter    JSONB,                -- e.g. {"category":"Electronics"}
  step_window_min INT,                  -- max minutes from previous step
  UNIQUE (funnel_id, step_seq)
);
CREATE TABLE funnel_progressions (
  user_id         VARCHAR(50),
  funnel_id       UUID,
  entered_at      TIMESTAMP,
  step_1_at       TIMESTAMP,
  step_2_at       TIMESTAMP,
  step_3_at       TIMESTAMP,
  step_4_at       TIMESTAMP,
  completed       BOOLEAN,
  dropped_at_step INT,
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, funnel_id, entered_at)
);
Why each choice: - A definitions table decouples PM-driven funnel changes from engineering changes.
- A pre-aggregated funnel_progressions table answers "conversion by step" in milliseconds;
nightly job rebuilds it. - match_filter as JSONB lets PMs add filters without schema changes.
Edge cases: - Window between steps — strict (must be in same session) vs loose (within 7 days). Both
are valid; surface as config. - Cohort skew — funnel for users acquired in March vs April will differ; mart
should include a cohort_date slice. - Repeat funnels — a user can enter the same funnel twice; the
PK reflects this.
Alternatives: - Compute every funnel ad hoc with MATCH_RECOGNIZE (Snowflake) or row-pattern
recognition. - Use a third-party tool (Mixpanel-style) and skip the mart.
What NOT to say: - "Hard-code one funnel table per funnel" — defeats configurability. - "Use a single
event sequence column with comma-separated values" — analytics death; lose all filterability.
Common follow-up: "How would you answer 'what is the median time from step 2 to step 3'?"
( PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) on step_3_at - step_2_at for completed users.)
Scenario200 · A/B test exposure table
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Meesho, Cred, Swiggy · Topic: Experimentation
The interviewer's prompt: "Design a table that records which users saw which A/B test variant. We will
join this to metrics later."
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 244 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 245
Thinking out loud: 1. "Exposures are immutable — once a user is assigned to a variant, that assignment
is locked for the duration of the test." 2. "Need experiment_id, variant_id, user_id, first-exposure
timestamp; PK should prevent multiple variants per user per experiment." 3. "Hash-based assignment so
the same user always gets the same variant on retries."
Schema sketch:
CREATE TABLE experiments (
  experiment_id       UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  experiment_name     VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
  started_at          TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  ended_at            TIMESTAMP,
  hypothesis          TEXT,
  primary_metric      VARCHAR(100)
);
CREATE TABLE experiment_variants (
  experiment_id       UUID REFERENCES experiments(experiment_id),
  variant_id          VARCHAR(50),
  variant_name        VARCHAR(100),
  allocation_pct      NUMERIC(5,2),
  PRIMARY KEY (experiment_id, variant_id)
);
CREATE TABLE experiment_exposures (
  exposure_id         UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  experiment_id       UUID NOT NULL,
  variant_id          VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  user_id             VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  exposed_at          TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  exposed_date        DATE NOT NULL,
  device_type         VARCHAR(20),
  app_version         VARCHAR(20),
  UNIQUE (experiment_id, user_id)        -- one variant per user per test
)
PARTITION BY RANGE (exposed_date);
Why each choice: - UNIQUE (experiment_id, user_id) enforces single-variant-per-user — the
most common data integrity bug in experimentation platforms. - Separate experiments and 
variants allows multi-arm tests cleanly. - exposed_at is the first exposure, not every exposure —
analytics only needs the first.
Edge cases: - Reassignment mid-test — should be impossible; if it happens, treat as a contamination
metric, not data. - Anonymous users — store anonymous_id and stitch on login. - Forced variants for
QA — flag with a is_qa column so they are excluded from analysis.
Alternatives: - Emit an exposure event into the events table — works but harder to enforce
uniqueness. - Store exposures in the experimentation tool only; ETL into warehouse for analysis.

What NOT to say: - "Just look at the events table to figure out who saw the variant" — flaky; you need

Scenario201 · A/B test conversion tracking
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Meesho, Swiggy, Razorpay · Topic: Experimentation
The interviewer's prompt: "We have exposures. Now design the conversion metrics table so the
experimentation dashboard renders in under a second."
Thinking out loud: 1. "Conversions per user per experiment per metric — pre-aggregated, refreshed
daily or hourly." 2. "Wide-table approach: one row per user per experiment with all metric values as
columns; works at small scale." 3. "Long-table approach: one row per user per metric, scales better and
supports unbounded metric list."
Schema sketch:
CREATE TABLE experiment_metrics_long (
  experiment_id       UUID NOT NULL,
  variant_id          VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  user_id             VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  metric_name         VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  metric_value        NUMERIC(18,4),
  window_start        DATE NOT NULL,
  window_end          DATE NOT NULL,
  computed_at         TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (experiment_id, user_id, metric_name, window_end)
);
-- Dashboard query pattern
SELECT variant_id, metric_name,
       AVG(metric_value)      AS mean,
       STDDEV(metric_value)   AS sd,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS n
FROM experiment_metrics_long
WHERE experiment_id = :exp_id AND window_end = CURRENT_DATE
GROUP BY variant_id, metric_name;
Why each choice: - Long format absorbs new metrics without DDL. - window_end lets you compute
trailing-7-day, trailing-14-day metrics from the same table. - Pre-aggregation per user means the
dashboard scans tens of thousands of rows, not billions.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 246 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 247
Edge cases: - Users with zero conversions still need a row (with value 0) for correct denominators. -
Metric drift — definitions change; track metric_definition_version to avoid mixing apples and
oranges. - Late-arriving conversions — re-compute the trailing window on a schedule (Scenario20).
Alternatives: - Wide table with one column per metric — simpler queries but every new metric is an
ALTER. - Compute on demand from raw events — accurate but slow; only viable for small experiments.
What NOT to say: - "Use the raw events table for the dashboard" — kills the warehouse at peak. -
"Recompute everything every page load" — pre-aggregate; recompute on a schedule.
Common follow-up: "A metric definition changes mid-experiment. How do you avoid mixing the old and
new metric values?" (Version the metric; freeze in-flight experiments to the version they started on.)
Scenario202 · Time-series schema for sensor readings
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Target, Goldman, IoT GCCs · Topic: Time-series
The interviewer's prompt: "Design a schema for sensor readings — 10,000 sensors emitting one
reading per second. Queries are mostly 'last hour for sensor X' and 'aggregate per minute over last day'."
Thinking out loud: 1. "This is high-frequency append-only data. Partition by time, cluster by sensor." 2. 
"Pre-aggregate at minute, hour, and day grains because asking '7-day chart at second resolution' will
melt the warehouse." 3. "On Postgres I would reach for TimescaleDB or partitioned tables; on BigQuery I
would partition by hour and cluster by sensor_id."
Schema sketch:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 247 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 248
CREATE TABLE sensor_readings (
  sensor_id       INT NOT NULL,
  reading_ts      TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  reading_date    DATE NOT NULL,
  reading_value   NUMERIC(10,4),
  quality_flag    SMALLINT,
  PRIMARY KEY (sensor_id, reading_ts)
)
PARTITION BY RANGE (reading_date);
CREATE TABLE sensor_readings_1min (
  sensor_id       INT NOT NULL,
  bucket_ts       TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,         -- floor to minute
  avg_value       NUMERIC(10,4),
  min_value       NUMERIC(10,4),
  max_value       NUMERIC(10,4),
  sample_count    INT,
  PRIMARY KEY (sensor_id, bucket_ts)

CREATE TABLE sensor_readings_1hour (

  bucket_ts       TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,

);
