Scenario203 · Retention cohort schema
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Meesho, Flipkart, Cred · Topic: Cohort analysis
The interviewer's prompt: "Design a schema that powers a retention curve — 'of users who signed up
in March, what % were active in week 1, week 2, week 4, week 8'."
Thinking out loud: 1. "Need a cohort definition table (anchor date), a user-cohort table (which cohort
each user belongs to), and an activity-per-period table." 2. "Pre-aggregate weekly because daily retention
curves are noisy and rarely useful at this grain." 3. "Output table is a cohort_retention_pct mart
that the dashboard pivots."
Schema sketch:
CREATE TABLE user_cohorts (
  user_id         VARCHAR(50) PRIMARY KEY,
  signup_date     DATE NOT NULL,
  cohort_week     DATE NOT NULL,             -- Monday of signup week
  cohort_month    DATE NOT NULL,             -- 1st of signup month
  acquisition_src VARCHAR(50)
);
CREATE TABLE user_activity_weekly (
  user_id         VARCHAR(50),
  week_start      DATE,
  was_active      BOOLEAN,
  events_count    INT,
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, week_start)
);
CREATE TABLE cohort_retention (
  cohort_week     DATE NOT NULL,
  weeks_since     INT NOT NULL,
  active_users    INT,
  cohort_size     INT,
  retention_pct   NUMERIC(5,2),
  PRIMARY KEY (cohort_week, weeks_since)
);
Why each choice: - cohort_week and cohort_month precomputed so dashboards do not re-

Alternatives: - Compute the entire curve from raw events on demand (slow at scale). - Cohort matrix

Scenario204 · DAU / MAU precomputed table
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Flipkart, Meesho, Cred, PhonePe, Swiggy · Topic: Activity metrics
The interviewer's prompt: "Design the table that backs the 'Daily Active Users' and 'Monthly Active
Users' chart on the exec dashboard."
Thinking out loud: 1. "DAU is a COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) for a given day — expensive on raw
events at scale." 2. "Pre-aggregate by day; MAU is then computed via a 30-day rolling distinct count or
via HyperLogLog sketches if the warehouse supports them." 3. "Snowflake HLL, BigQuery 
HLL_COUNT.MERGE, DuckDB approx_count_distinct — all give MAU at constant cost."
Schema sketch:
CREATE TABLE dau_daily (
  activity_date   DATE PRIMARY KEY,
  dau             INT NOT NULL,
  new_users       INT,
  returning_users INT,
  hll_sketch      BYTEA            -- serialized HyperLogLog of distinct users
);
-- BigQuery example
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dau_daily AS
SELECT
  DATE(event_ts)              AS activity_date,
  COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)     AS dau,
  HLL_COUNT.INIT(user_id)     AS hll_sketch
FROM events
WHERE event_ts >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL 1 DAY
GROUP BY activity_date;
-- 30-day MAU from sketches (BigQuery)
SELECT HLL_COUNT.MERGE(hll_sketch) AS mau_30d
FROM dau_daily
WHERE activity_date BETWEEN CURRENT_DATE - 29 AND CURRENT_DATE;
Why each choice: - HLL sketches let MAU be computed in O(days) work, not O(events). - new_users
vs returning_users precomputed because the dashboard always shows both. - Daily grain table is
small (one row per day) — trivial to query.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 250 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 251
Edge cases: - DAU spikes from bots — filter at the events layer, not the mart. - Timezone — "day" in IST
vs UTC matters for an Indian product; document and apply consistently. - Sketches are approximate
(~2% error); fine for DAU/MAU, not for billing.
Alternatives: - Exact distinct counts on raw events — accurate but slow. - Materialised view auto-
refreshed by the warehouse.
What NOT to say: - "Just query raw events with COUNT(DISTINCT)" — kills the warehouse on a 10B
row table. - "MAU is just 30x DAU" — wrong; distinct count is not additive.
Common follow-up: "What changes if we want WAU (weekly) as well — can we reuse the sketches?"
(Yes, merge sketches over a 7-day window.)

Scenario206 · Revenue by product × month rollup
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Target, Flipkart, Meesho · Topic: Aggregate marts
The interviewer's prompt: "The CFO opens the dashboard and wants revenue per product per month in
1 second. Design the mart."
Thinking out loud: 1. "Fact already exists at line grain (Scenario1). Build a monthly roll-up keyed by
product and month." 2. "Include gross, returns, net, units, distinct customers. Cover the common slices."
3. "Materialised view or scheduled mart, refresh nightly."
Schema sketch:
CREATE TABLE mart_product_monthly (
  product_key       BIGINT NOT NULL,
  month_start       DATE NOT NULL,
  gross_revenue     NUMERIC(18,2),
  refund_amount     NUMERIC(18,2),
  net_revenue       NUMERIC(18,2),
  units_sold        INT,
  unique_customers  INT,
  refreshed_at      TIMESTAMP,
  PRIMARY KEY (product_key, month_start)
);
CREATE INDEX ON mart_product_monthly (month_start);
-- Refresh job (idempotent)
DELETE FROM mart_product_monthly WHERE month_start = :target_month;
INSERT INTO mart_product_monthly
SELECT
  product_key,
  DATE_TRUNC('month', date_actual)                  AS month_start,
  SUM(line_total)                                   AS gross_revenue,
  SUM(CASE WHEN transaction_type='refund' THEN line_total ELSE 0 END) AS refund_amount,
  SUM(CASE WHEN transaction_type='sale'   THEN line_total ELSE -line_total END) AS net_revenue,
  SUM(quantity)                                     AS units_sold,
  COUNT(DISTINCT customer_key)                      AS unique_customers,
  CURRENT_TIMESTAMP                                 AS refreshed_at
FROM fact_sales f JOIN dim_date d ON f.date_key = d.date_key
WHERE d.month_start = :target_month
GROUP BY product_key, month_start;
Why each choice: - Idempotent DELETE+INSERT per month makes back-fills safe. - 
unique_customers precomputed; otherwise dashboard does its own distinct count. - Refresh per
month gives clean recompute windows.
Edge cases: - Late-arriving refunds — refresh the last 3 months on every run. - Currency conversion —
apply with monthly average FX from a dim. - Time-zone — pin to financial close calendar, not naive UTC.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 253 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 254
Alternatives: - Snowflake / BigQuery materialised view with auto-refresh. - Cube.dev or dbt incremental
model.
What NOT to say: - "Just SELECT from fact_sales with GROUP BY" — works at small scale only.
- "INSERT-only mart, never delete" — back-fills become impossible without dedup logic.
Common follow-up: "How would you let the CFO drill down to a single product's daily revenue from this
mart?" (Mart is monthly; click-through hits a daily mart or the fact directly, scoped by product key.)

  created_at        TIMESTAMP,
  packed_at         TIMESTAMP,
  shipped_at        TIMESTAMP,
  delivered_at      TIMESTAMP,
  returned_at       TIMESTAMP,
  pack_duration_h   NUMERIC(8,2),            -- packed_at - created_at
  ship_duration_h   NUMERIC(8,2),
  deliver_duration_h NUMERIC(8,2),
  is_returned       BOOLEAN,
  current_status    VARCHAR(30),
  refreshed_at      TIMESTAMP
);
Why each choice: - Accumulating snapshot is UPDATE-heavy as new milestones land — fine for one
row per order. - Durations precomputed because every dashboard asks for them. - History table
preserves the audit trail and supports re-derivation.
Edge cases: - Out-of-order events — the snapshot updater must check timestamps before overwriting. -
Skipped milestones — packed_at NULL means it was never packed; treat as still-in-progress, not
zero. - Returns reopen the lifecycle — model carefully (separate returned_at rather than a new row).
Alternatives: - Pure event-source via order_status_history; compute lifecycle on the fly. -
Stream-processed snapshot via Flink / Kafka.
What NOT to say: - "Just one row per order, no history" — first time the business asks 'what changed
when', you are stuck. - "Use a single timestamp column with current status only" — loses every previous
state.
Common follow-up: "How would you alert when an order has been in 'packed' for more than 24 hours?"
(Query the snapshot for packed_at < NOW() - 24h AND shipped_at IS NULL.)

Scenario210 · Late-arriving facts
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Goldman, JP Morgan India, Target · Topic: Data quality
The interviewer's prompt: "Sales for 1 May arrived in your warehouse on 5 May because the source
system was down. Your daily mart already ran for 1 May. How do you handle it?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Late-arriving facts are normal. Design assuming they will happen rather than
treating them as exceptions." 2. "Either (a) refresh a window of past days every run, or (b) use append-
only fact with an arrival_date separate from event_date." 3. "For dashboards, the natural
answer is option (a) — refresh the last 7 days nightly so anything that lagged catches up."
Schema sketch:
CREATE TABLE fact_sales (
  sale_id           BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  event_date        DATE NOT NULL,            -- business day
  arrival_date      DATE NOT NULL,            -- when we received it
  product_key       BIGINT, customer_key BIGINT,
  line_total        NUMERIC(12,2)
)
PARTITION BY RANGE (event_date);
CREATE TABLE mart_sales_daily (
  event_date        DATE PRIMARY KEY,
  gross_revenue     NUMERIC(18,2),
  order_count       INT,
  refreshed_at      TIMESTAMP,
  is_finalised      BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE      -- true after 7d lookback closes
);
-- Refresh window pattern
DELETE FROM mart_sales_daily WHERE event_date BETWEEN :start AND :end;
INSERT INTO mart_sales_daily ...
WHERE event_date BETWEEN :start AND :end;
Why each choice: - arrival_date separate from event_date lets data engineering compute
"arrival lag" SLAs. - 7-day rolling refresh absorbs most lateness automatically. - is_finalised flag
tells downstream BI tools when numbers stop moving.
Edge cases: - Very late facts (months out) — finance often locks numbers; corrections go into a 
prior_period_adjustments table rather than mutating history. - Schema changes between old
and new facts — store schema_version per row. - Reconciliation alerts — compute "arrival lag > 3
days" as a quality metric.
Alternatives: - Append-only corrections table layered over the original mart. - Snowflake 
STREAM + TASK for incremental, continuous catch-up.

What NOT to say: - "Pretend late data does not exist" — silently understates revenue. - "Re-run the

Scenario211 · Late-arriving dimensions
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Goldman, Target, Wells Fargo · Topic: Dimensional
modelling
The interviewer's prompt: "A fact references customer_id 12345, but the customer dimension does not
have that row yet — it shows up an hour later. What does your ETL do?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "This is a late-arriving dimension. Three strategies — reject, defer, or insert a
placeholder." 2. "Best practice in modern warehouses — insert a placeholder dim row with a known
surrogate, fill in attributes when they arrive." 3. "Track these explicitly so they do not silently corrupt
cohorts and segmentation."
Schema sketch:
CREATE TABLE dim_customer (
  customer_key      BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id       VARCHAR(50) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  full_name         VARCHAR(200),
  city              VARCHAR(100),
  tier              VARCHAR(20),
  is_inferred       BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE,    -- TRUE when placeholder
  inferred_at       TIMESTAMP,
  attributes_arrived_at TIMESTAMP,
  updated_at        TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
-- ETL pseudo-flow
-- 1. Fact references customer_id X
-- 2. Lookup dim_customer; if missing, INSERT placeholder
--    (customer_id, is_inferred=TRUE, inferred_at=NOW())
-- 3. When customer dim batch arrives, UPDATE attributes,
--    SET is_inferred=FALSE, attributes_arrived_at=NOW().
Why each choice: - Fact-table writes never block on dim arrival — keeps ingestion flowing. -
Placeholder rows are visible in audits, not silently merged. - is_inferred lets analysts exclude these
rows when working on customer segmentation if needed.
Edge cases: - Some attributes (like city) drive partitioning of downstream marts; recomputing marts after
dim back-fill matters. - The customer may never arrive — treat ghosts as a data quality alert. - Duplicates
— natural-key uniqueness must hold even for placeholders.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 260 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 261
Alternatives: - Quarantine table — defer facts until the dim row arrives; sometimes required when fact
joins must produce correct labels. - Backfill-and-replay — wait, then process the whole batch.
What NOT to say: - "Drop the fact row if the dim is missing" — silent data loss. - "Insert a random new
customer row each time" — duplicates the customer dim and breaks reporting.
Common follow-up: "What if 5% of facts trigger placeholders consistently — what does that suggest?"
(Source system has a different cadence than the customer feed; widen ingestion windows or fix the
upstream contract.)
Scenario212 · Conformed dimensions across multiple facts
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Target, Goldman, JP Morgan India · Topic:
Dimensional modelling
The interviewer's prompt: "We have fact_sales, fact_returns, fact_marketing. All three
reference dim_customer and dim_date. How do you guarantee they all use the same dim
definitions?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Conformed dims — exactly one canonical dim table per business entity, used by
every fact." 2. "This is what makes 'drill across' work: a single chart can blend sales, returns, and
marketing per customer." 3. "Govern via dbt models / governed datasets; never let a fact reach into a
custom local dim."
Schema sketch:
-- Shared dims
CREATE TABLE dim_customer (...);          -- one customer record per row
CREATE TABLE dim_date (...);
CREATE TABLE dim_product (...);
-- Multiple facts referencing them
CREATE TABLE fact_sales       (date_key, customer_key, product_key, ...);
CREATE TABLE fact_returns     (date_key, customer_key, product_key, ...);
CREATE TABLE fact_marketing   (date_key, customer_key, campaign_key, ...);
-- A "drill across" SQL pattern
SELECT c.tier,
       SUM(s.line_total) AS revenue,
       SUM(r.refund_amount) AS refunds,
       SUM(m.cost) AS marketing_cost
FROM dim_customer c
LEFT JOIN fact_sales      s ON s.customer_key = c.customer_key
LEFT JOIN fact_returns    r ON r.customer_key = c.customer_key
LEFT JOIN fact_marketing  m ON m.customer_key = c.customer_key
GROUP BY c.tier;
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 261 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 262
Why each choice: - Shared dims mean a single chart can blend three facts without a hand-rolled key
map. - Surrogate customer_key is stable across facts because it points at the same dim version. -
The dim becomes the contract — all facts conform to it, not the other way.
Edge cases: - Different facts at different grains — a sale is per order line, a marketing touch is per click;
conformation works at the dim level, not the grain. - A fact-specific attribute (e.g. seller_id only
meaningful for sales) belongs in the fact, not the customer dim. - Schema drift in the dim — version dim
updates; downstream models test on the dim contract.
Alternatives: - Per-domain dims with bridge tables — heavier, only when business definitions truly
diverge. - Federated query approach if dims live in different systems.
What NOT to say: - "Let each fact carry its own copy of customer attributes" — guarantees
inconsistency. - "Conformation is a Kimball relic" — still the default in dbt-style marts today.
Common follow-up: "What is the test you would write to ensure conformation does not break?" (Assert
that every customer_key in every fact exists in dim_customer; dbt's relationships test
does exactly this.)
Scenario213 · Junk dimension for low-cardinality booleans
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan India, Walmart Labs · Topic: Dimensional
modelling
The interviewer's prompt: "My fact has 6 boolean flags — is_gift, is_prepaid, is_first_order, is_promo,
is_cod_eligible, is_express. Where do they go?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Six booleans means 64 possible combinations — too small to be its own dim per
flag, too inelegant to dump on the fact." 2. "Junk dimension — one row per combination, single key on
the fact." 3. "Trades a tiny dim table for narrower facts and clean group-by semantics."
Schema sketch:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 262 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 263
CREATE TABLE dim_order_flags (
  order_flags_key   SMALLINT PRIMARY KEY,
  is_gift           BOOLEAN, is_prepaid BOOLEAN, is_first_order BOOLEAN,
  is_promo          BOOLEAN, is_cod_eligible BOOLEAN, is_express BOOLEAN,
  description       VARCHAR(255)              -- human-readable
);
CREATE TABLE fact_sales (
  sale_id           BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  date_key          INT,
  customer_key      BIGINT,
  product_key       BIGINT,
  order_flags_key   SMALLINT REFERENCES dim_order_flags(order_flags_key),
  line_total        NUMERIC(12,2)
);
Why each choice: - Single small INT on the fact replaces 6 BOOLEANs — narrower row, better
compression. - Dim is up to 64 rows; queries can group by combinations and slice with WHERE
is_gift = TRUE. - Reports needing names (description) get them from the dim, not hard-
coded.
Edge cases: - If flag set explodes (12 booleans → 4096 rows), revisit — junk dim is for small sets. - New
flag added — backfill the junk dim and update flag combinations. - Sparse combinations — only create
dim rows for combinations that actually appear.
Alternatives: - Store flags directly on the fact — fine at small scale; ugly when flags multiply. - Bitfield
INT — compact but unreadable.
What NOT to say: - "One dim per boolean" — explosion of pointless dims. - "Just use a JSONB column
for flags" — kills filter pushdown.
Common follow-up: "What if you have a non-boolean low-cardinality flag like 'priority' = HIGH/MED/
LOW?" (Same junk dim, just more values per row.)
Scenario214 · Degenerate dimension
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Goldman, AmEx GCC · Topic: Dimensional modelling
The interviewer's prompt: "Where should order_id live in your star schema? It is unique per order,
but the order has no real attributes worth a dim."
Thinking out loud: 1. "Classic degenerate dimension — an ID with no attributes of its own. Lives on the
fact, no dim table needed." 2. "You still query by it ('distinct count of orders this month') so it has to be on
the fact." 3. "Same pattern for invoice_number, ticket_id, anything ID-shaped with no
descriptive attributes."
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 263 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 264
Schema sketch:
CREATE TABLE fact_sales (
  sale_id           BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,    -- surrogate
  date_key          INT,
  customer_key      BIGINT,
  product_key       BIGINT,
  order_id          VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,     -- degenerate dim
  invoice_number    VARCHAR(50),               -- degenerate dim
  line_total        NUMERIC(12,2)
);
CREATE INDEX ON fact_sales (order_id);
-- Distinct order count
SELECT date_key, COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS orders
FROM fact_sales
GROUP BY date_key;
Why each choice: - No table for order_id means no join cost to count orders. - Indexed so distinct
counts are fast. - Same row holds the customer dim key — easy customer-per-order analytics.
Edge cases: - If order_id later acquires attributes (channel, source), promote to a real dim and
remove from fact. - Be wary of treating a degenerate as a join key to other systems — it is meant for self-
contained aggregations.
Alternatives: - Build an order_dim even if attributes are sparse — overhead without payoff. - Store
both order_id and a surrogate order_key — redundant unless joining to an order-detail fact.
What NOT to say: - "Order ID belongs in a customer dim" — different grain, breaks the customer-per-
row rule. - "Use order_id as the surrogate sale_key" — couples your warehouse to the source
system's ID format.
Common follow-up: "When does a degenerate dim graduate into a full dim?" (When it acquires its own
attributes — channel, source, fulfilment SLA — that need slicing.)
Scenario215 · Bridge table for many-to-many in star schema
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Target, JP Morgan India · Topic: Dimensional modelling
The interviewer's prompt: "A product can belong to multiple categories — Electronics and Gifts, say.
How do you model this in a star schema?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Many-to-many between fact and dim needs a bridge table. Bridge sits between
the fact (or product dim) and the multi-valued dim (category)." 2. "Bridge carries a weight column so SUM
aggregations are not double-counted." 3. "Same pattern for product-tag, customer-segment, account-
owner."
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 264 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 265
Schema sketch:
CREATE TABLE dim_category (
  category_key      INT PRIMARY KEY,
  category_name     VARCHAR(100)
);
CREATE TABLE bridge_product_category (
  product_key       BIGINT REFERENCES dim_product(product_key),
  category_key      INT REFERENCES dim_category(category_key),
  weight            NUMERIC(5,4),             -- e.g. 0.5 if equal split
  PRIMARY KEY (product_key, category_key)
);
-- "Revenue by category" without double counting
SELECT cat.category_name,
       SUM(f.line_total * b.weight) AS attributed_revenue
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN bridge_product_category b ON f.product_key = b.product_key
JOIN dim_category cat ON cat.category_key = b.category_key
GROUP BY cat.category_name;
Why each choice: - Bridge encodes the many-to-many relationship without duplicating fact rows. - 
weight lets users choose between summed-across (full credit each side) and apportioned (weights
sum to 1.0). - PK ensures no duplicate product-category pairs.
Edge cases: - Weights summing to less than 1 means unassigned credit — decide if that is OK. -
Categories changing over time — bridge becomes Type 2 with valid_from/ valid_to. - "Primary
category" — add an is_primary flag for the case where you must pick one.
Alternatives: - Pre-join into a fact_category table that duplicates the fact row per category (simpler
queries, larger storage). - Use ARRAY/STRUCT in BigQuery instead of a bridge table.
What NOT to say: - "Just denormalise: store categories as a comma-separated string" — kills filter and
join. - "Pick the first category and ignore the rest" — destroys analytic completeness.
Common follow-up: "What if the same product can move from one category to another over time?"
(Bridge becomes time-aware with valid_from/ valid_to; join requires temporal predicate.)
Scenario216 · Star schema vs One Big Table (OBT) tradeoff
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Meesho, Cred, Flipkart, modern data GCCs · Topic:
Modelling tradeoffs
The interviewer's prompt: "Modern thinking on Snowflake / BigQuery says 'just build one big table'.
Why would you still use a star schema?"
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 265 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 266
Thinking out loud: 1. "OBT denormalises everything into one wide table — no joins at query time." 2. 
"Star schema keeps facts narrow and joins to dims — less storage churn on dim updates, easier
governance." 3. "In 2026 most modern teams use a hybrid — star at the warehouse layer, OBT at the BI
consumption layer."
Schema sketch:
-- OBT shape
CREATE TABLE obt_sales (
  sale_id           BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  event_date        DATE,
  event_year        INT, event_month INT, event_quarter INT,    -- date fields inlined
  product_id        VARCHAR(50), product_name VARCHAR(255),
  product_category  VARCHAR(100), brand_name VARCHAR(100),
  customer_id       VARCHAR(50), customer_city VARCHAR(100),
  customer_tier     VARCHAR(20),
  line_total        NUMERIC(12,2)
);
-- Snowflake: CLUSTER BY (event_date, product_category)
-- BigQuery: PARTITION BY event_date CLUSTER BY product_category
Why each choice for OBT: - Zero joins for the most common queries — fast on columnar storage. - BI
tools love flat tables — fewer wrong-join bugs. - Compression handles the redundancy well.
Why star is still a thing: - Updating a dim (e.g. category rename) updates one row, not millions. -
Governance — dim ownership and lineage are clear. - Reuse — dim_customer powers sales, returns,
marketing, churn marts.
Edge cases: - OBT on hot dims (SCD Type 2 every day) — storage and refresh cost explodes. - Star with
too many small dims — endless joins; OBT-flatten the small ones into the fact. - Hybrid: star at the
warehouse layer, OBT views or marts on top.
Alternatives: - Data vault — agnostic intermediate layer. - Activity schema — single events-shaped table
for all activities.
What NOT to say: - "OBT is always the modern answer" — depends on dim volatility and dataset size. -
"Star is always the modern answer" — modern columnar warehouses subvert old tradeoffs.
Common follow-up: "At what data scale or query pattern would you reverse this choice?" (When dims
change daily, star wins; when BI users are non-technical, OBT wins.)
Scenario217 · Snowflake clustering key for an analytics fact
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Snowflake-shape GCCs · Topic: Snowflake
performance
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 266 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 267
The interviewer's prompt: "You have a 5-billion-row fact table on Snowflake. Queries filter on 
event_date and customer_id. How would you cluster it?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Snowflake stores data in micro-partitions; clustering keys colocate rows so
partition pruning is effective." 2. "Most common predicate first — event_date because almost every
query filters by time." 3. "Then customer_id for the secondary pattern. Avoid high-cardinality
clustering on its own — Snowflake prefers ranges."
Schema sketch:
CREATE TABLE fact_events (
  event_id          STRING,
  event_date        DATE NOT NULL,
  event_ts          TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  customer_id       STRING NOT NULL,
  product_id        STRING,
  event_name        STRING,
  properties        VARIANT
)
CLUSTER BY (event_date, customer_id);
-- Inspect clustering health
SELECT SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION('fact_events',
       '(event_date, customer_id)');
Why each choice: - event_date first — the universal range predicate. - customer_id second —
narrows within a day for per-customer queries. - Snowflake auto-reclusters in the background; you pay
credits for the reclustering work.
Edge cases: - High clustering depth = bad — large delta between min/max micro-partition values for the
cluster key. - Wide updates re-cluster everything; large batch deletes can fragment. - Sorting on load
(ORDER BY in COPY INTO) reduces reclustering cost.
Alternatives: - Materialised views with their own clustering for sub-query patterns. - Search optimisation
service on high-cardinality predicates.
What NOT to say: - "Add an index" — Snowflake has no traditional indexes; clustering is the
mechanism. - "Cluster on everything" — diminishing returns; pick 2-3 columns at most.
Common follow-up: "How do you know your clustering is helping?"
( SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION; look at depth and overlap; compare query elapsed before/
after.)

Scenario218 · BigQuery partitioning + clustering for facts
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Meesho, Swiggy, BigQuery-shape GCCs · Topic: BigQuery
performance
The interviewer's prompt: "Same problem on BigQuery — 5 billion rows, time and customer filters. How
do you design the table?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "BigQuery has explicit partitioning (one date-shaped column) plus clustering (up to
4 columns)." 2. "Partition by ingestion date or event date — both prune scans massively." 3. "Cluster by 
customer_id, product_id — top filter columns."
Schema sketch:
CREATE TABLE analytics.fact_events (
  event_id          STRING,
  event_ts          TIMESTAMP,
  event_date        DATE,
  customer_id       STRING,
  product_id        STRING,
  event_name        STRING,
  properties        JSON
)
PARTITION BY event_date
CLUSTER BY customer_id, product_id
OPTIONS (
  partition_expiration_days = 730,    -- two-year retention
  require_partition_filter = TRUE     -- forces queries to scope by partition
);
Why each choice: - PARTITION BY event_date — partition pruning means a 1-day query scans
1/1000 of data. - require_partition_filter = TRUE — saves the team from accidental full-
table scans (which BigQuery bills by bytes scanned). - Clustering by customer_id, product_id
because both appear in most predicates.
Edge cases: - Daily partitions are the default; hourly partitions exist (BigQuery has time-unit partitioning)
but cost more in metadata. - Number of partitions per table is capped (currently 4000) — design for
retention vs grain. - Updates and merges within a partition are fine; cross-partition operations cost more.
Alternatives: - Integer-range partitioning if event_date is not natural. - Sharded tables
(table_YYYYMMDD pattern) — older approach, partitioning is now preferred.
What NOT to say: - "Partition by both date and customer_id" — partition is one column only. - "Don't
bother clustering if you partition" — clustering still meaningfully reduces bytes scanned within a partition.
Common follow-up: "What is the difference between _PARTITIONTIME and a column-based
partition?" ( _PARTITIONTIME is ingestion-time; column-based is event-time. Event-time matches
business semantics for late-arriving data.)

Scenario219 · dbt-style staging → intermediate → mart layering
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Flipkart, Meesho, modern data GCCs · Topic:
Modern data stack
The interviewer's prompt: "Walk me through the layered schema design we would use in dbt — staging,
intermediate, mart. Why three layers?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Staging — one-to-one with source tables; rename columns, cast types, no joins."
2. "Intermediate — business logic, joins between cleaned-up sources; reusable building blocks." 3. "Mart
— dashboard-ready; star schemas, wide tables, exposed to BI."
Schema sketch:
-- 1. STAGING (stg_orders.sql)
WITH source AS (SELECT * FROM raw.shopify.orders)
SELECT
  id              AS order_id,
  customer_id,
  CAST(total_price AS NUMERIC(12,2)) AS total_amount,
  status,
  TIMESTAMP(created_at)              AS created_at,
  CURRENT_TIMESTAMP                  AS dbt_loaded_at
FROM source;
-- 2. INTERMEDIATE (int_orders_with_customer.sql)
SELECT
  o.order_id, o.total_amount, o.created_at,
  c.tier, c.city
FROM {{ ref('stg_orders') }}    o
LEFT JOIN {{ ref('stg_customers') }} c USING (customer_id);
-- 3. MART (mart_sales_daily.sql)
SELECT
  DATE(created_at)              AS order_date,
  city, tier,
  COUNT(*)                      AS orders,
  SUM(total_amount)             AS revenue
FROM {{ ref('int_orders_with_customer') }}
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3;
Why each layer: - Staging isolates source changes — one rename here, no breakage downstream. -
Intermediate prevents reimplementing the same joins in multiple marts. - Mart is the contract with the
business — change only with explicit communication.
Edge cases: - Skipping intermediate is fine for tiny projects; mandatory for 100+ models. - Tests live at
every layer — staging tests source quality, mart tests business invariants. - Snapshots (dbt's SCD Type 2
tool) live alongside staging.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 269 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 270
Alternatives: - Data Vault layering — raw vault, business vault, marts. - Single mart layer for very small
teams.
What NOT to say: - "Layers are overhead" — at 50+ models, no layering means unmaintainable. -
"Marts can read from staging directly" — couples marts to source changes; defeats the layering.
Common follow-up: "Where would you put a custom UDF or macro?" (Macros in macros/; reusable
transforms applied across staging or intermediate.)
Scenario220 · Data lake + warehouse hybrid (Iceberg / Hudi pattern)
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Flipkart, Walmart Labs, Meesho, JP Morgan India, Goldman · Topic:
Lakehouse architecture
The interviewer's prompt: "We have terabytes of raw events landing in S3 daily. We want SQL on it via
the warehouse but also keep the raw lake for ML. Design the layering."
Thinking out loud: 1. "Lakehouse pattern — Iceberg or Hudi tables on object storage, queried by
Snowflake / BigQuery / Trino / Spark." 2. "Raw zone (immutable JSON/Avro), curated zone (Iceberg with
schema), serving zone (warehouse marts)." 3. "Iceberg gives ACID, schema evolution, time travel —
without leaving open storage."
Schema sketch:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 270 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 271
s3://datalake/
  raw/events/dt=2026-05-26/...avro
  curated/events_iceberg/                           -- Iceberg table
    metadata/
    data/dt=2026-05-26/part-00001.parquet
  serving/                                          -- mart layer
    mart_user_sessions/
-- Iceberg DDL (Spark / Trino syntax)
CREATE TABLE curated.events (
  event_id   STRING,
  event_ts   TIMESTAMP,
  user_id    STRING,
  event_name STRING,
  properties MAP<STRING, STRING>
)
USING iceberg
PARTITIONED BY (days(event_ts))
TBLPROPERTIES ('format-version' = '2');
-- Warehouse external table (Snowflake reads Iceberg)
CREATE OR REPLACE ICEBERG TABLE serving.events_iceberg
  EXTERNAL_VOLUME = 'datalake_vol'
  CATALOG = 'glue_catalog'
  CATALOG_TABLE_NAME = 'curated.events';
Why each choice: - Raw zone preserves source-of-truth bytes — required for replay and ML feature
regeneration. - Iceberg in curated zone adds ACID and schema evolution while staying open-format. -
Warehouse reads the same Iceberg files — no double-copy of data.
Edge cases: - Small files problem — frequent micro-batches create thousands of tiny Parquet files;
periodic compaction is mandatory. - Schema evolution — additive only (add columns); breaking changes
need versioned tables. - Cross-engine compatibility — confirm your engine's Iceberg version
compatibility (V1 vs V2 manifests).
Alternatives: - Hudi for upsert-heavy workloads; Iceberg for analytic appends. - Delta Lake on
Databricks ecosystem. - Direct warehouse-native ingestion (Snowpipe, BigQuery batch load) — simpler if
open-format is not required.
What NOT to say: - "Just dump CSVs in S3 and query with Athena" — works at small scale; chokes on
schema drift and updates. - "Lake and warehouse are obsolete; pick one" — the hybrid is the modern
default for any team with both ML and BI needs.
Common follow-up: "How would you handle a GDPR-style right-to-erasure request on Iceberg?"
(Iceberg row-level delete; Hudi delete API; or rewrite affected files and create a new snapshot.)

Category 4, Part A — What Will This Return: NULL, Type &
Ordering
The classic SQL interview format goes like this — the interviewer slides a query across the table and
asks, "What does this return? Walk me through your reasoning." They are not testing if you can run it in
your head. They are testing whether you understand the silent rules the engine applies before producing
output. Part A of this category focuses on the three areas that trip up the largest number of candidates:
NULL semantics (the three-valued logic that breaks naive boolean thinking), implicit type coercion (where
the engine quietly converts between integer, string and date and changes the answer), and result
ordering (where two reasonable-looking queries return rows in different orders on different engines). Walk
through each one out loud — even when the answer feels obvious, narrate the steps so the interviewer
can follow your thinking.
Scenario221 · The NULL = NULL Trap
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Flipkart, Razorpay, Swiggy, Zoho · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The setup:
-- Table data
CREATE TABLE customers (id INT, phone VARCHAR(15));
INSERT INTO customers VALUES
  (1, '9876543210'),
  (2, NULL),
  (3, NULL),
  (4, '9123456789');
-- The query
SELECT id FROM customers WHERE phone = NULL;
The question: "What does this query return? Walk me through your reasoning."
Thinking out loud: 1. "At first glance you might think rows 2 and 3 match because their phone is NULL."
2. "But SQL uses three-valued logic — NULL is not a value, it represents 'unknown'." 3. "Any comparison
with NULL using = returns NULL, not TRUE. The WHERE clause keeps only rows where the predicate
is TRUE." 4. "So even NULL = NULL evaluates to NULL, which is filtered out. The result is zero rows."
The answer (with output):
id
----
(0 rows)
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 272 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 273
Why this output: The expression phone = NULL evaluates to NULL for every row, and WHERE
discards rows where the predicate is not TRUE. The correct form is WHERE phone IS NULL.
The trap: Candidates assume NULL behaves like a normal value and that equality works the same way
as on integers or strings.
What NOT to say: - "It returns rows 2 and 3 because their phone column is NULL." - "It will throw an
error because you cannot compare to NULL."
Common follow-up: "How would you rewrite this to actually return the rows with missing phone
numbers?"
Scenario222 · The NULL Inequality
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Paytm, Zomato, Freshworks · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The setup:
-- Table data
CREATE TABLE orders (id INT, status VARCHAR(20));
INSERT INTO orders VALUES
  (101, 'shipped'),
  (102, 'cancelled'),
  (103, NULL),
  (104, 'shipped');
-- The query
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status <> 'cancelled';
The question: "What does this query return? Walk me through your reasoning."
Thinking out loud: 1. "Looks straightforward — give me every order that is not cancelled." 2. "Row 101
has status 'shipped', which is not equal to 'cancelled', so the predicate is TRUE." 3. "Row 102 is
excluded. Row 104 is included by the same logic as 101." 4. "Now row 103 — status is NULL. NULL <>
'cancelled' evaluates to NULL, not TRUE, so it is filtered out."
The answer (with output):
id
----
101
104
Why this output: NULL is excluded from inequality predicates just as it is from equality predicates —
both evaluate to NULL, which is not TRUE.

PAGE 274
The trap: Candidates expect "not cancelled" to mean "everything except cancelled" and include the
NULL row.
What NOT to say: - "It returns 101, 103, 104 because all three are not cancelled."
Common follow-up: "What if the requirement is to include rows where status is missing — how would
you write that?"
Scenario223 · IS NULL vs Equals NULL
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, TCS, Wipro, Cognizant · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The setup:
-- Table data
CREATE TABLE employees (emp_id INT, manager_id INT);
INSERT INTO employees VALUES
  (1, NULL),
  (2, 1),
  (3, 1),
  (4, NULL);
-- The query
SELECT emp_id FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL;
The question: "What does this query return, and how does it differ from 
WHERE manager_id = NULL?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "This uses IS NULL, which is the proper way to test for NULL — it returns TRUE
or FALSE, never NULL." 2. "Rows 1 and 4 have NULL manager_id, so IS NULL returns TRUE for
them." 3. "Rows 2 and 3 have a manager, so IS NULL returns FALSE — they are filtered out." 4. "The
result is emp_id 1 and 4. With = NULL instead, the result would be zero rows."
The answer (with output):
emp_id
------
1
4
Why this output: IS NULL is a special operator built for NULL detection — it always evaluates to a
boolean. = NULL always evaluates to NULL.
The trap: Some candidates know IS NULL is right but cannot articulate why = NULL is wrong.
What NOT to say: - "Both forms work, but IS NULL is just the preferred style."

Scenario224 · COALESCE Walks the Chain
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Cred · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The setup:
-- Table data
CREATE TABLE contact (user_id INT, work_phone VARCHAR(15), home_phone VARCHAR(15), mobile VARCHAR(15));
INSERT INTO contact VALUES
  (1, NULL, NULL, '9876500001'),
  (2, '02212345678', NULL, '9876500002'),
  (3, NULL, '04412345678', NULL),
  (4, NULL, NULL, NULL);
-- The query
SELECT user_id, COALESCE(work_phone, home_phone, mobile, 'No contact') AS reach_at
FROM contact;
The question: "What does this query return for each row?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument from left to right." 2. "User 1:
work is NULL, home is NULL, mobile is '9876500001' — that wins." 3. "User 2: work is '02212345678' —
first non-NULL, that wins, the rest are not even checked." 4. "User 3: work NULL, home '04412345678'
wins. User 4: all NULL, falls back to literal 'No contact'."
The answer (with output):
user_id | reach_at
--------+-------------
1       | 9876500001
2       | 02212345678
3       | 04412345678
4       | No contact
Why this output: COALESCE evaluates its arguments left to right and short-circuits at the first non-
NULL value. A literal at the end provides a safe default.
The trap: Candidates sometimes think COALESCE returns the last non-NULL value, or returns NULL if
any argument is NULL.
What NOT to say: - "It returns the last non-NULL value in the list."
Common follow-up: "What is the difference between COALESCE and ISNULL in SQL Server?"

Scenario225 · NULLIF Flips the Script
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Zoho, Freshworks, Postman · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The setup:
-- Table data
CREATE TABLE survey (resp_id INT, rating INT);
INSERT INTO survey VALUES
  (1, 5),
  (2, 0),
  (3, 3),
  (4, 0),
  (5, 4);
-- The query
SELECT resp_id, NULLIF(rating, 0) AS valid_rating
FROM survey;
The question: "What does NULLIF do here, and what does the result look like?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL when a = b, otherwise it returns a." 2. "It is the inverse
of COALESCE in a sense — used to convert sentinel values like 0 or '' into proper NULLs." 3. "Row 1:
rating 5, not equal to 0, returns 5. Rows 2 and 4: rating 0 equals 0, returns NULL." 4. "Rows 3 and 5:
ratings 3 and 4, returned as-is."
The answer (with output):
resp_id | valid_rating
--------+-------------
1       | 5
2       | NULL
3       | 3
4       | NULL
5       | 4
Why this output: NULLIF is the standard way to convert sentinel placeholders (0, -1, '') into proper
NULLs so that downstream aggregations like AVG ignore them.
The trap: Candidates confuse NULLIF with COALESCE or think NULLIF returns 0 when the values
match.
What NOT to say: - "NULLIF replaces NULLs with the second argument."
Common follow-up: "If you AVG over the valid_rating column above, what does the engine return?"

Scenario226 · IS DISTINCT FROM Saves the Day
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Setu · Dialect: Postgres
The setup:
-- Table data
CREATE TABLE audit_log (record_id INT, old_status VARCHAR(20), new_status VARCHAR(20));
INSERT INTO audit_log VALUES
  (1, 'pending', 'shipped'),
  (2, 'pending', 'pending'),
  (3, NULL, 'shipped'),
  (4, 'shipped', NULL),
  (5, NULL, NULL);
-- The query
SELECT record_id FROM audit_log WHERE old_status IS DISTINCT FROM new_status;
The question: "What does IS DISTINCT FROM return, and how is it different from <>?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "IS DISTINCT FROM treats two NULLs as equal — it returns FALSE if both sides
are NULL." 2. "It returns TRUE if the values differ, including the case where one side is NULL and the
other is not." 3. "Row 1: pending vs shipped — distinct, included. Row 2: pending vs pending — not
distinct, excluded." 4. "Row 3: NULL vs shipped — distinct, included. Row 4: shipped vs NULL —
distinct, included. Row 5: NULL vs NULL — not distinct, excluded."
The answer (with output):
record_id
---------
1
3
4
Why this output: IS DISTINCT FROM is null-safe equality — it gives the answer people usually intend
when comparing two columns that may have NULLs.
The trap: With plain <>, rows 3, 4 and 5 would all be excluded because NULL comparisons yield
NULL.
What NOT to say: - "IS DISTINCT FROM is the same as <> but newer."
Common follow-up: "How do you express the same logic in MySQL, which does not support IS
DISTINCT FROM?"

Scenario227 · COUNT Star vs COUNT Column
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Flipkart, Myntra, Nykaa, Meesho · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The setup:
-- Table data
CREATE TABLE deliveries (id INT, delivered_at TIMESTAMP);
INSERT INTO deliveries VALUES
  (1, '2026-05-01 10:00'),
  (2, NULL),
  (3, '2026-05-02 14:00'),
  (4, NULL),
  (5, '2026-05-03 09:00');
-- The query
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total, COUNT(delivered_at) AS delivered FROM deliveries;
The question: "What is the difference between these two counts, and what do they return?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "COUNT() counts rows, regardless of whether any column is NULL." 2. 
"COUNT(column) counts only the rows where that specific column is non-NULL." 3. "Five rows total, so
COUNT() is 5." 4. "Three rows have a non-NULL delivered_at, so COUNT(delivered_at) is 3."
The answer (with output):
total | delivered
------+----------
5     | 3
Why this output: COUNT(*) operates on the row itself. COUNT(expr) operates on the expression and
ignores NULLs — that is the only aggregate that treats * differently from a column name.
The trap: Candidates assume both produce the same answer, especially on tables they have not
inspected for NULLs.
What NOT to say: - "They are the same — * is just shorthand."
Common follow-up: "What about COUNT(DISTINCT delivered_at) — what would that return here?"

80

Scenario230 · CASE Without ELSE
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, Accenture, Capgemini · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The setup:

-- Table data
CREATE TABLE products (id INT, price DECIMAL(10,2));
INSERT INTO products VALUES
  (1, 999),
  (2, 200),
  (3, 5000),
  (4, 50);
-- The query
SELECT id, price,
  CASE
    WHEN price >= 1000 THEN 'premium'
    WHEN price >= 500 THEN 'mid'
  END AS tier
FROM products;
The question: "What does the tier column show for each row?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "CASE evaluates branches top to bottom and returns the first one that matches."
2. "Row 1, price 999: not >= 1000, but >= 500, so 'mid'." 3. "Row 2, price 200: neither branch matches.
Without an ELSE, CASE returns NULL." 4. "Row 3 is 'premium', row 4 is NULL for the same reason as
row 2."
The answer (with output):
id | price | tier
---+-------+--------
1  | 999   | mid
2  | 200   | NULL
3  | 5000  | premium
4  | 50    | NULL
Why this output: A CASE expression with no ELSE clause returns NULL whenever no WHEN branch
matches — there is an implicit ELSE NULL.
The trap: Candidates miss the silent NULL and assume an empty string or 0 will appear instead.
What NOT to say: - "Rows 2 and 4 return an empty string because no branch matched."
Common follow-up: "How would you label everything below 500 as 'budget' instead of NULL?"
Scenario231 · CASE And Three-Valued Logic
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Cred, Setu, Razorpay · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The setup:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 281 / 586

-- Table data
CREATE TABLE accounts (id INT, balance DECIMAL(10,2));
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES
  (1, 5000),
  (2, NULL),
  (3, 0),
  (4, -100);
-- The query
SELECT id, balance,
  CASE
    WHEN balance > 0 THEN 'positive'
    WHEN balance < 0 THEN 'negative'
    WHEN balance = 0 THEN 'zero'
    ELSE 'unknown'
  END AS status
FROM accounts;
The question: "What status does each row get? Pay attention to row 2."
Thinking out loud: 1. "Row 1: balance 5000, first branch matches, 'positive'." 2. "Row 2: balance NULL. 
NULL > 0 is NULL, NULL < 0 is NULL, NULL = 0 is NULL — none are TRUE." 3. "Since no
WHEN branch is TRUE, control falls to ELSE, returning 'unknown'." 4. "Row 3: 'zero'. Row 4: 'negative'."
The answer (with output):
id | balance | status
---+---------+---------
1  | 5000    | positive
2  | NULL    | unknown
3  | 0       | zero
4  | -100    | negative
Why this output: All comparisons against NULL evaluate to NULL — never TRUE — so a NULL value
will fall through every WHEN branch and only the ELSE catches it.
The trap: Candidates assume balance = 0 would catch NULL because both are "missing or zero".
What NOT to say: - "Row 2 returns 'zero' because NULL behaves like 0 in arithmetic."
Common follow-up: "How would you write a branch that specifically catches the NULL case?"

-- Table data

INSERT INTO listings VALUES
  (1, '2026-05-01'),
  (2, NULL),
  (3, '2026-05-10'),
  (4, NULL),
  (5, '2026-05-05');
-- The query (Postgres)
SELECT id FROM listings ORDER BY sold_at ASC;
The question: "In what order do these rows come back in Postgres, and would MySQL behave the same
way?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "ORDER BY puts the smallest values first by default. NULLs are not really
comparable to dates, so the engine has to pick a position for them." 2. "Postgres default is NULLS
LAST for ASC, NULLS FIRST for DESC." 3. "MySQL default is the opposite — NULLS FIRST for
ASC, NULLS LAST for DESC." 4. "On Postgres, the order is row 1, 5, 3, then the two NULLs (2 and 4).

The answer (with output):
-- Postgres
id
----
1
5
3
2
4
Why this output: Each engine has a default position for NULLs in ORDER BY, and that default varies —
Postgres puts them last on ASC, MySQL puts them first.
The trap: Candidates assume ORDER BY is fully deterministic across engines and write portable code
that silently rearranges.
What NOT to say: - "NULLs always go to the bottom in every database."
Common follow-up: "How do you make ordering NULL-position explicit across engines?"

id

2

discards the rest. Other engines like SQL Server may throw a conversion error or use stricter parsing.

Scenario236 · CHAR vs VARCHAR Trailing Space
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Oracle India, Salesforce India, IBM India · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The setup:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 286 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in

-- Table data
CREATE TABLE products_char (id INT, code CHAR(5));
CREATE TABLE products_varchar (id INT, code VARCHAR(5));
INSERT INTO products_char VALUES (1, 'ABC');
INSERT INTO products_varchar VALUES (1, 'ABC');
-- The query (run against both)
SELECT id FROM products_char WHERE code = 'ABC  ';      -- trailing spaces
SELECT id FROM products_varchar WHERE code = 'ABC  ';   -- trailing spaces
The question: "Both stored values are 'ABC'. Which queries return the row?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "CHAR is fixed length — 'ABC' is stored as 'ABC ' with two trailing spaces." 2. 
"The ANSI rule for CHAR comparison: the shorter string is padded with spaces before comparison. So
'ABC' vs 'ABC ' is treated as equal." 3. "VARCHAR stores 'ABC' as 'ABC' — no padding. But the
comparison still pads the shorter side to match length in most engines." 4. "Different engines treat trailing
spaces in VARCHAR comparison differently — Postgres preserves them strictly for VARCHAR, MySQL
ignores them, SQL Server pads on comparison."
The answer (with output):
-- products_char (both engines):
id
----
1
-- products_varchar (Postgres):
id
----
(0 rows)
-- products_varchar (MySQL/SQL Server):
id
----
1
Why this output: CHAR is space-padded by storage and ANSI defines space-padded comparison.
VARCHAR behaviour diverges — Postgres treats trailing spaces as significant, while MySQL and SQL
Server typically pad on comparison.
The trap: Code that works on one engine silently breaks on migration, especially Postgres.
What NOT to say: - "All engines ignore trailing whitespace in string comparisons."
Common follow-up: "How do you defensively compare strings where trailing spaces should not matter,
across engines?"

Scenario237 · Date String Parsing Surprise

The setup:
-- Table data
CREATE TABLE bookings (id INT, booking_date DATE);
INSERT INTO bookings VALUES
  (1, '2026-05-10'),
  (2, '2026-05-11'),
  (3, '2026-05-12');
-- The query (SQL Server, default region en-US)
SELECT id FROM bookings WHERE booking_date = '10/05/2026';
The question: "This is an Indian developer expecting dd/mm/yyyy — 10 May 2026. What does SQL
Server actually return?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "In en-US default locale, SQL Server reads mm/dd/yyyy from a slash-separated
literal." 2. "So '10/05/2026' is parsed as October 5, 2026 — not May 10, 2026." 3. "None of our stored
dates are October 5, 2026, so the query returns zero rows." 4. "In MySQL, the engine is stricter —
typically requires yyyy-mm-dd and would error or return zero rows."
The answer (with output):
id
----
(0 rows)
Why this output: String-to-date parsing depends on the engine and session locale. The ANSI-safe form
is the ISO 8601 literal 'yyyy-mm-dd', which is unambiguous everywhere.
The trap: Indian developers default to dd/mm/yyyy mentally — many production bugs come from this
exact confusion.
What NOT to say: - "It returns the May 10 row because 10/05 is obviously day 10, month 5."
Common follow-up: "What is the safest date literal format to use across engines and locales?"
Scenario238 · DATE vs TIMESTAMP
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Setu, Cred · Dialect: Postgres
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 288 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 289
The setup:
-- Table data
CREATE TABLE events (id INT, ts TIMESTAMP);
INSERT INTO events VALUES
  (1, '2026-05-10 00:00:00'),
  (2, '2026-05-10 09:30:00'),
  (3, '2026-05-10 23:59:59');
-- The query
SELECT id FROM events WHERE ts = DATE '2026-05-10';
The question: "Which rows match?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "The literal DATE '2026-05-10' is a date — it has no time component." 2. 
"When compared to a TIMESTAMP, the engine promotes the date to a timestamp at midnight: 
2026-05-10 00:00:00." 3. "So only rows with exactly midnight match — row 1." 4. "Rows 2 and 3
are on the same calendar day, but their time portion is non-zero, so they do not equal midnight."
The answer (with output):
id
----
1
Why this output: A DATE compared to a TIMESTAMP coerces to midnight. To match a full day, use a
range predicate: ts >= DATE '2026-05-10' AND ts < DATE '2026-05-11'.
The trap: Candidates write WHERE ts = current_date and miss every row whose timestamp is
not exactly midnight.
What NOT to say: - "All three rows match because they are on May 10."
Common follow-up: "How do you efficiently query all events from a specific day on a TIMESTAMP
column that has an index?"

The question: "Which rows match?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends — equivalent to percentage >= 75 AND

Scenario241 · IN With NULL in the List
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Freshworks · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The setup:

-- Table data
CREATE TABLE orders (id INT, status VARCHAR(20));
INSERT INTO orders VALUES
  (1, 'shipped'),
  (2, 'pending'),
  (3, 'cancelled'),
  (4, NULL);
-- The query
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status IN ('shipped', 'pending', NULL);
The question: "Does row 4 (status NULL) match because NULL is in the list?"
Thinking out loud: 1. " x IN (a, b, c) is sugar for x = a OR x = b OR x = c." 2. "For row
4, status = NULL. That expands to 
NULL = 'shipped' OR NULL = 'pending' OR NULL = NULL — all three evaluate to NULL." 3. 
"NULL OR NULL OR NULL is NULL, not TRUE. The row is filtered out." 4. "Rows 1 and 2 match normally.
Row 3 status 'cancelled' is not in the list."
The answer (with output):
id
----
1
2
Why this output: Adding NULL to an IN list does nothing — every comparison involving NULL yields
NULL, never TRUE. Use IS NULL separately if you want to match NULL rows.
The trap: Candidates add NULL to the IN list expecting it to cover NULL rows.
What NOT to say: - "Row 4 matches because NULL is included in the list."
Common follow-up: "How would you correctly include NULL rows along with 'shipped' and 'pending'?"
Scenario242 · NOT IN With NULL
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Flipkart, Zomato, Swiggy, Paytm · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The setup:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 292 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 293
-- Table data
CREATE TABLE products (id INT);
INSERT INTO products VALUES (1), (2), (3), (4), (5);
CREATE TABLE blocked (product_id INT);
INSERT INTO blocked VALUES (2), (4), (NULL);
-- The query
SELECT id FROM products WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM blocked);
The question: "What does this return?"
Thinking out loud: 1. " id NOT IN (2, 4, NULL) expands to id <> 2 AND id <> 4 AND id
<> NULL." 2. "That last predicate, id <> NULL, evaluates to NULL for every row." 3. " TRUE AND
TRUE AND NULL evaluates to NULL, not TRUE." 4. "So no row produces a TRUE result — the query
returns zero rows."
The answer (with output):
id
----
(0 rows)
Why this output: NOT IN with a NULL in the right-hand side is a notorious trap — the moment one NULL
appears, the entire predicate becomes "not knowable" for every row.
The trap: This is the single most common SQL bug in production — a child table with a NULL silently
makes the parent NOT IN return nothing.
What NOT to say: - "It returns 1, 3, 5 because those are the products not blocked."
Common follow-up: "How do you rewrite this safely so a NULL in the blocked table does not nuke the
result?"

Scenario244 · DISTINCT Drops Ordering
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Myntra, Swiggy · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The setup:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 294 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in

-- Table data
CREATE TABLE orders (city VARCHAR(20), amount INT);
INSERT INTO orders VALUES
  ('Mumbai', 500),
  ('Delhi', 300),
  ('Mumbai', 700),
  ('Bengaluru', 200),
  ('Delhi', 900);
-- The query
SELECT DISTINCT city FROM orders;
The question: "In what order do the cities come back?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "DISTINCT removes duplicates — we get Mumbai, Delhi, Bengaluru once each." 2.
"But the order is not guaranteed. DISTINCT does not imply ORDER BY." 3. "In Postgres or SQL Server,
the order depends on the hash or sort plan the optimiser picks — could be anything." 4. "If a consistent
order matters, add an explicit ORDER BY clause."
The answer (with output):
city
---------
Bengaluru
Delhi
Mumbai
-- or any other order; engine-defined
Why this output: DISTINCT is a set operation, not an ordering operation. Many engines implement it via
hashing or sorting, which incidentally orders results — but you cannot rely on it.
The trap: Candidates assume DISTINCT returns rows in insertion order or alphabetic order.
What NOT to say: - "It always comes back sorted because DISTINCT sorts internally."
Common follow-up: "How do you guarantee an alphabetical order on a DISTINCT query?"

  (102, 700),
  (103, 200),
  (104, 900),
  (105, 100);
-- The query

The question: "Which three IDs come back?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "LIMIT 3 returns three rows — but which three?" 2. "Without ORDER BY, the
engine is free to return any three rows it likes — usually whichever ones it finds first based on storage
layout, indexes or parallel scan order." 3. "On the same data, the same query can return different rows
after a vacuum, an index rebuild, or a schema change." 4. "The honest answer: it returns three rows, but
the choice is non-deterministic."

id

-- depending on storage and execution plan
Why this output: SQL does not define a row order unless you specify ORDER BY. LIMIT slices an
unordered set, so it produces undefined-but-deterministic-for-this-run results.
The trap: Candidates assume insertion order, primary-key order, or visual order in their last SELECT.
What NOT to say: - "It returns 101, 102, 103 because those were inserted first."

-- vs

Lucknow, Jaipur. West has Mumbai, Jaipur, Pune. Six rows total." 3. "Jaipur is in both, so UNION

Lucknow
Jaipur
Mumbai

Pune
Why this output: UNION applies an implicit DISTINCT across the combined result set — more expensive

Scenario247 · INTERSECT With Duplicates
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Oracle India, Postman, Setu · Dialect: Postgres / SQL Server / Oracle
The setup:
-- Table data
CREATE TABLE list_a (val INT);
INSERT INTO list_a VALUES (1), (2), (2), (3);
CREATE TABLE list_b (val INT);
INSERT INTO list_b VALUES (2), (2), (2), (4);
-- The query
SELECT val FROM list_a INTERSECT SELECT val FROM list_b;
The question: "How many 2s does the result contain?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "INTERSECT returns rows present in both sets, with duplicates removed by
default." 2. "Both sides have the value 2 — so 2 is in the intersection." 3. "But INTERSECT dedupes, so
only one 2 comes back regardless of how many duplicates either side had." 4. "1 is only in A, 3 is only in
A, 4 is only in B — none survive. Result: one row, value 2."
The answer (with output):
val
----
2
Why this output: INTERSECT, like UNION, applies set semantics — duplicates are removed.
INTERSECT ALL (Postgres, Oracle) preserves duplicate counts and would return two 2s here (the
minimum of A's count and B's count).
The trap: Candidates expect duplicate preservation and are surprised that the multiplicity disappears.
What NOT to say: - "It returns three 2s because B has three 2s."
Common follow-up: "What does INTERSECT ALL return here, and which engines support it?"
Scenario248 · EXCEPT Semantics
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Freshworks · Dialect: Postgres / SQL Server
The setup:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 298 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 299
-- Table data
CREATE TABLE active_users (user_id INT);
INSERT INTO active_users VALUES (1), (2), (3), (4), (5);
CREATE TABLE blacklisted (user_id INT);
INSERT INTO blacklisted VALUES (2), (4), (4);
-- The query
SELECT user_id FROM active_users EXCEPT SELECT user_id FROM blacklisted;
The question: "What does EXCEPT return?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "EXCEPT returns rows in the first query that are not in the second." 2. "Active has
1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Blacklisted has 2 and 4." 3. "Remove 2 and 4 from active — left with 1, 3, 5." 4. "EXCEPT
also dedupes by default, so even if active had duplicates, the result would be a set."
The answer (with output):
user_id
-------
1
3
5
Why this output: EXCEPT is set difference — rows of the left set whose values do not appear in the right
set, deduplicated. MySQL did not support EXCEPT until version 8.0.31; many MySQL codebases
emulate it with LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right IS NULL.
The trap: Candidates conflate EXCEPT with MINUS (Oracle's keyword) or write NOT IN and hit the
NULL-in-list trap from Scenario 22.
What NOT to say: - "EXCEPT is exactly the same as NOT IN."
Common follow-up: "How would you write this with a LEFT JOIN, and why is that safer when the right
side may contain NULLs?"
Scenario249 · Integer Division Surprise

The question: "What is the ratio column?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Both columns are INT. In Postgres and SQL Server, integer divided by integer
returns integer — the fractional part is truncated." 2. "Row 1: 7 / 10 = 0 (the 0.7 is truncated). Row 2: 3 / 4

The trap: Candidates expect 0.7 and write reports that silently show zero for everyone.

Scenario250 · Mixed Arithmetic With NULL
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The setup:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 300 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 301
-- Table data
CREATE TABLE order_charges (order_id INT, subtotal INT, tax INT, discount INT);
INSERT INTO order_charges VALUES
  (1, 1000, 180, 100),
  (2, 500, NULL, 50),
  (3, 2000, 360, NULL);
-- The query
SELECT order_id, subtotal + tax - discount AS net_total FROM order_charges;
The question: "What is the net_total for each row?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Any arithmetic with NULL produces NULL — that is the propagation rule." 2. 
"Row 1: 1000 + 180 - 100 = 1080. Clean." 3. "Row 2: 500 + NULL - 50 — the first sub-expression is
NULL, the whole thing is NULL." 4. "Row 3: 2000 + 360 - NULL = NULL by the same rule."
The answer (with output):
order_id | net_total
---------+----------
1        | 1080
2        | NULL
3        | NULL
Why this output: Arithmetic operators propagate NULL — there is no "skip" behaviour like there is in
aggregates. Use COALESCE to substitute a default before the arithmetic: subtotal +
COALESCE(tax, 0) - COALESCE(discount, 0).
The trap: Candidates assume the engine treats NULL as zero in arithmetic, the same way it treats it in
COUNT or SUM.
What NOT to say: - "Row 2 is 450 because NULL acts like 0."
Common follow-up: "Rewrite this so a missing tax or discount is treated as zero, but a missing subtotal
still produces NULL."

Scenario251 · LEFT JOIN preserving outer rows
Tags: Difficulty: Easy-Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, Wipro · Topic: Outer joins, NULL
handling
Setup:
customers:
customer_id name city
1 Anita Rao Bengaluru
2 Rohit Singh Pune
3 Meera Iyer Chennai
orders:
order_id customer_id amount
101 1 4500
102 1 1200
103 2 3300
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, o.order_id, o.amount
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id, o.order_id;
Question: "What rows come out and what is the row count?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left side — customers — whether or not a
match exists on the right." 2. "Anita has two orders, so she will appear twice. Rohit has one order. Meera
has none." 3. "Meera will still appear once, but the order_id and amount columns will be NULL because
no matching row exists in orders." 4. "Final count is two for Anita plus one for Rohit plus one for Meera as
a NULL row — four rows total."
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 302 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 303
Answer:
customer_id | name        | order_id | amount
1           | Anita Rao   | 101      | 4500
1           | Anita Rao   | 102      | 1200
2           | Rohit Singh | 103      | 3300
3           | Meera Iyer  | NULL     | NULL
Why (the non-obvious thing): The whole point of LEFT JOIN is to preserve unmatched left rows by
padding the right-side columns with NULL. If you forget that, you would predict three rows and miss
Meera entirely.
The trap: Candidates count only the matched rows and answer three. That is the row count for INNER
JOIN, not LEFT.
What NOT to say: - "Meera is dropped because she has no order" — that is the INNER JOIN answer -
"Four rows but no NULLs anywhere" — the right side must be NULL for the unmatched outer row
Common follow-up: "How would you count customers who have never ordered?" — WHERE
o.order_id IS NULL after the LEFT JOIN, then COUNT(*).
Scenario252 · LEFT JOIN silently converted to INNER by WHERE clause
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Walmart Labs · Topic: Outer joins, predicate
placement
Setup:
customers:
customer_id name
1 Anita Rao
2 Rohit Singh
3 Meera Iyer
orders:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 303 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 304
order_id customer_id amount status
101 1 4500 paid
102 2 3300 cancelled
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, o.order_id, o.status
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'paid';
Question: "How many rows come back and why?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "LEFT JOIN would give three rows — Anita with order 101, Rohit with order 102,
Meera with NULLs." 2. "Then the WHERE clause filters on o.status = 'paid'. For Meera the status
column is NULL, and NULL = 'paid' evaluates to UNKNOWN, which the WHERE drops." 3. "Rohit's
order has status cancelled, so he is also dropped." 4. "Only Anita's row survives. The LEFT JOIN has
been silently converted into an INNER JOIN by the WHERE predicate."
Answer:
customer_id | name      | order_id | status
1           | Anita Rao | 101      | paid
Why (the non-obvious thing): Any non-null filter on a right-side column inside WHERE turns LEFT JOIN
into INNER JOIN. To preserve outer rows the predicate must move into the ON clause.
The trap: You wrote LEFT JOIN expecting all three customers, but you lose Meera the moment you filter
on a right-side column.
What NOT to say: - "Three rows because LEFT JOIN keeps everyone" — the WHERE collapses it - "It
throws because Meera has NULL status" — NULL comparisons return UNKNOWN, not an error
Common follow-up: "How would you preserve Meera in the output?" — Move the predicate into ON: 
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'paid'.
Scenario253 · Self-join with a.id < b.id avoiding duplicates
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Zomato, JP Morgan · Topic: Self-join, pair generation
Setup:
employees:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 304 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 305
emp_id name dept
1 Aditi Sales
2 Bhavesh Sales
3 Chitra Sales
4 Devansh Engg
SELECT a.name AS emp1, b.name AS emp2, a.dept
FROM employees a
JOIN employees b ON a.dept = b.dept AND a.emp_id < b.emp_id
ORDER BY a.dept, a.emp_id, b.emp_id;
Question: "How many pairs and what are they?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Self-join on same department gives us every cross-product within a department,
then the a.emp_id < b.emp_id predicate keeps only one ordering per pair." 2. "Sales has three
people. Without the predicate we would get nine rows including self-pairs and both orderings. With 
a.emp_id < b.emp_id, that drops to C(3,2) = 3 pairs." 3. "Engineering has only Devansh, so no pair
can be formed." 4. "Final answer is three rows, all from Sales — Aditi-Bhavesh, Aditi-Chitra, Bhavesh-
Chitra."
Answer:
emp1     | emp2     | dept
Aditi    | Bhavesh  | Sales
Aditi    | Chitra   | Sales
Bhavesh  | Chitra   | Sales
Why (the non-obvious thing): The < predicate is the canonical trick for generating unordered pairs from
a self-join. It eliminates both the self-match and the mirror duplicate in one stroke.
The trap: Forgetting that without the predicate you get N squared rows including N self-pairs and N(N-1)
directional duplicates.
What NOT to say: - "Six pairs because Sales has three people" — that is the directed count, not
unordered - "Engineering gives one row of Devansh with himself" — the < predicate explicitly excludes
self-matches
Common follow-up: "What changes if you use a.emp_id <> b.emp_id instead?" — You get
directional pairs both ways: six Sales rows instead of three.

Scenario254 · Self-join without the inequality — counting pairs twice
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Paytm, Cred, Goldman Sachs · Topic: Self-join cardinality
Setup:
employees:
emp_id name dept
1 Aditi Sales
2 Bhavesh Sales
3 Chitra Sales
SELECT a.name AS emp1, b.name AS emp2
FROM employees a
JOIN employees b ON a.dept = b.dept AND a.emp_id <> b.emp_id;
Question: "Row count?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Three people in Sales. The join condition matches anyone in the same department
who is not the same row." 2. "For each of the three rows on side a, two rows on side b qualify — anyone
in Sales except itself." 3. "So 3 × 2 = 6 rows. Each unordered pair is counted twice: Aditi-Bhavesh and
Bhavesh-Aditi are both present." 4. "Final answer is six rows."
Answer:
emp1     | emp2
Aditi    | Bhavesh
Aditi    | Chitra
Bhavesh  | Aditi
Bhavesh  | Chitra
Chitra   | Aditi
Chitra   | Bhavesh
Why (the non-obvious thing): <> excludes self-matches but not mirror duplicates. For N rows in a
group you get N(N-1) ordered pairs, not N(N-1)/2 unordered.
The trap: Reports built on this pattern double-count pair-based metrics like "how many co-worker pairs
exist" and exaggerate by a factor of two.
What NOT to say: - "Three rows because there are three people" — that ignores the cross-product -
"Nine rows because 3 times 3" — that includes self-pairs which <> excludes

Scenario255 · CROSS JOIN cardinality

FROM sizes s
CROSS JOIN colors c;
Question: "How many rows and what is the shape of the output?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "CROSS JOIN has no ON clause — it pairs every row on the left with every row on
the right." 2. "Three sizes times four colors equals twelve rows." 3. "Output is every size and every color
combination, useful for generating a complete SKU grid." 4. "Order is not guaranteed unless we add
ORDER BY, but typically engines stream left-then-right."
Answer:

L    | Green

Why (the non-obvious thing): CROSS JOIN row count is the product of the two side counts. With 1,000

Scenario257 · One-to-many JOIN inflating row count for aggregation
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, PhonePe, Cred · Topic: Aggregation pitfalls
Setup:
orders:
order_id amount
101 1000
102 500
order_items:
item_id order_id qty
9001 101 1
9002 101 2
9003 102 1
SELECT o.order_id, SUM(o.amount) AS total
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY o.order_id;
Question: "What does the total column say for each order?"
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 310 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 311
Thinking out loud: 1. "Join inflates order 101 to two rows because it has two items. Order 102 stays at
one row." 2. "After grouping by order_id, the SUM(o.amount) is summing the amount once for every
joined row." 3. "Order 101: amount 1000 summed twice equals 2000. Order 102: 500 summed once
equals 500." 4. "So the reported totals are inflated for any order with more than one item."
Answer:
order_id | total
101      | 2000
102      | 500
Why (the non-obvious thing): Aggregating a parent-side column after joining to a child table produces
inflated sums because the parent row is duplicated for every child row.
The trap: This is one of the most common analytics bugs in production. Revenue dashboards
mysteriously double or triple after a "harmless" join.
What NOT to say: - "1000 and 500 because amount is on the orders table" — the join still duplicates the
parent row - "It throws a duplicate key error" — GROUP BY collapses cleanly, the bug is silent
Common follow-up: "How would you avoid this?" — Aggregate items first in a subquery, then join. Or
use SELECT DISTINCT on (order_id, amount) before summing.

Scenario259 · Inequality range join
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Goldman Sachs, Walmart Labs · Topic: Range joins
Setup:
payments:
payment_id amount
1 250
2 800
3 1500
4 4500
fee_tiers:
min_amt max_amt fee_pct
0 999 2.0
1000 4999 1.5
5000 99999 1.0
SELECT p.payment_id, p.amount, f.fee_pct
FROM payments p
JOIN fee_tiers f ON p.amount BETWEEN f.min_amt AND f.max_amt;
Question: "What rows come out?"
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 313 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 314
Thinking out loud: 1. "BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends. We need to walk each payment and find its
tier." 2. "Payment 1 has amount 250 — falls into tier 1 (0-999), fee 2.0." 3. "Payment 2 has amount 800 —
also tier 1, fee 2.0." 4. "Payment 3 has amount 1500 — tier 2 (1000-4999), fee 1.5. Payment 4 has amount
4500 — also tier 2, fee 1.5. Nothing hits tier 3."
Answer:
payment_id | amount | fee_pct
1          | 250    | 2.0
2          | 800    | 2.0
3          | 1500   | 1.5
4          | 4500   | 1.5
Why (the non-obvious thing): Range joins use inequality predicates instead of equality. They are correct,
but the optimiser cannot use a normal hash join — it falls back to nested loop or merge join, which gets
expensive on large inputs.
The trap: If your tier ranges overlap by even one unit, a payment can land in two tiers and the row count
doubles for boundary values.
What NOT to say: - "It throws because BETWEEN needs equality" — BETWEEN works fine in joins -
"Four rows in tier 1 because that is the first row" — every payment is checked against every tier
Common follow-up: "What if amount is exactly 999?" — Lands in tier 1. If you change to >= AND <,
the boundary handling changes.
Scenario260 · FULL OUTER JOIN with two partially-overlapping tables
Tags: Difficulty: Medium-Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan · Topic: Outer joins
Setup:
payroll:
emp_id salary
1 50000
2 60000
3 70000
benefits:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 314 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 315
emp_id plan
2 Premium
3 Standard
4 Premium
SELECT p.emp_id AS payroll_id, b.emp_id AS benefits_id, p.salary, b.plan
FROM payroll p
FULL OUTER JOIN benefits b ON p.emp_id = b.emp_id
ORDER BY COALESCE(p.emp_id, b.emp_id);
Question: "What rows come out?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "FULL OUTER JOIN keeps every row from both sides. Matches join up; unmatched
rows on either side appear with NULLs on the other side." 2. "Emp 1 only in payroll — appears with
benefits_id and plan NULL." 3. "Emps 2 and 3 are in both — clean join." 4. "Emp 4 only in benefits —
appears with payroll_id and salary NULL. Total of four rows."
Answer:
payroll_id | benefits_id | salary | plan
1          | NULL        | 50000  | NULL
2          | 2           | 60000  | Premium
3          | 3           | 70000  | Standard
NULL       | 4           | NULL   | Premium
Why (the non-obvious thing): FULL OUTER JOIN is the union of LEFT and RIGHT outer joins. The
unmatched rows on each side carry NULLs in the other side's columns — including the join key.
The trap: Selecting p.emp_id alone loses emp 4. You must use COALESCE to get a unified employee
identifier.
What NOT to say: - "Three rows because there are three payroll entries" — that ignores emp 4 on the
benefits side - "MySQL handles this with no syntax change" — MySQL did not support FULL OUTER
JOIN natively for years; needs UNION emulation
Common follow-up: "How would you find rows that exist in only one table?" — WHERE p.emp_id IS
NULL OR b.emp_id IS NULL.
