Scenario313 · Leading Wildcard in LIKE
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Walmart Labs · Topic: Sargability · Engines: All
Setup:
CREATE TABLE products (
  sku           VARCHAR(40) PRIMARY KEY,
  product_name  VARCHAR(200),
  brand         VARCHAR(80)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_products_name ON products (product_name);
-- Customer searches "soap" anywhere in the name
SELECT sku, product_name FROM products WHERE product_name LIKE '%soap%';
Question: "This query does a full scan even though product_name is indexed. Why does LIKE
'soap%' use the index but LIKE '%soap%' doesn't?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "A B-tree is sorted lexicographically. LIKE 'soap%' is equivalent to the range 
product_name >= 'soap' AND product_name < 'soat' — a contiguous range the index can
satisfy." 2. " LIKE '%soap%' has no contiguous range — soap could appear at any position, so the
index entries are not co-located. The planner correctly chooses Seq Scan." 3. "For real substring search,
you need a different data structure. Postgres has pg_trgm GIN indexes; MySQL has FULLTEXT
indexes; SQL Server has Full-Text Search. These index n-grams or tokens, not the full string." 4. "If the
column is small enough and lookup happens often, a reverse(product_name) expression index can
also handle trailing-wildcard searches like LIKE '%abc'."
Diagnosis: Leading wildcard makes the predicate non-sargable against a B-tree.
Fix:
-- Postgres trigram index for substring search
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;
CREATE INDEX idx_products_name_trgm ON products USING gin (product_name gin_trgm_ops);
SELECT sku, product_name FROM products WHERE product_name ILIKE '%soap%';
-- MySQL fulltext
ALTER TABLE products ADD FULLTEXT INDEX ft_name (product_name);
SELECT sku, product_name FROM products WHERE MATCH(product_name) AGAINST('soap');
Why: B-trees support prefix ranges, not arbitrary substrings. Substring search needs token-based
indexing (trigrams, fulltext).
NOT to say: "LIKE never uses an index" — LIKE 'prefix%' does. "Just add more memory" — the
issue is algorithmic, not RAM.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 375 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 376
Follow-up: "Why does pg_trgm need GIN and not B-tree?" — Trigram indexes store many entries per
row (one per overlapping 3-gram), so GIN's posting-list structure is the right fit. B-tree assumes one key
per row.
Scenario314 · Low Cardinality — Planner Picks Seq Scan Anyway
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Cred, Flipkart, Goldman · Topic: Selectivity · Engines: All
Setup:
CREATE TABLE shipments (
  shipment_id   BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id      BIGINT,
  status        VARCHAR(20),  -- only 5 distinct values
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ
);
CREATE INDEX idx_shipments_status ON shipments (status);
-- 80 million rows, status='delivered' is 78 million of them
SELECT shipment_id FROM shipments WHERE status = 'delivered';
Question: "I created an index on status but Postgres still does a Seq Scan. Why is it ignoring my
index?"
Thinking out loud: 1. " status has 5 distinct values and delivered covers 97% of rows. Reading
the index, then doing 78 million heap fetches (random I/O), is dramatically more expensive than one
sequential read of the table." 2. "The planner is correct — it estimated rows to fetch ≈ 78M, multiplied by
random_page_cost, came out higher than seq_page_cost × total_pages. Seq Scan wins." 3. "Indexes
earn their keep on selective predicates — roughly < 5-10% of rows. Above that, the random I/O penalty
plus the index traversal cost makes a scan cheaper." 4. "Real fix depends on workload: if delivered is
genuinely most of the data and we rarely query it, drop the index for that value. If we frequently query the
rare values (returned, lost), use a partial index that only covers those."
Diagnosis: Predicate matches majority of rows; planner correctly prefers Seq Scan.
Fix:
-- Partial index: only the rare, queryable values
DROP INDEX idx_shipments_status;
CREATE INDEX idx_shipments_status_active
  ON shipments (status)
  WHERE status IN ('pending', 'in_transit', 'returned', 'lost');
Tiny index, fast lookups for the values that matter; no overhead on the dominant delivered writes.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 376 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 377
Why: Index access is only cheaper than Seq Scan when selectivity is high (few rows match). On low-
cardinality columns where one value dominates, the index is the wrong tool.
NOT to say: "The planner is broken — force it to use the index" — forcing usually makes it slower. "Just
add more indexes" — won't help; selectivity is the problem.
Follow-up: "What if I really need WHERE status = 'delivered' to be fast?" — That's a date-
range or pagination problem, not a status problem. Index on (created_at) or a composite 
(status, created_at) and add a time bound.
Scenario315 · Composite Index Column-Order Mismatch
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Walmart Labs · Topic: Composite indexes ·
Engines: All
Setup:
CREATE TABLE bookings (
  booking_id    BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  city_id       INT,
  movie_id      INT,
  show_time     TIMESTAMPTZ,
  total_paise   BIGINT
);
CREATE INDEX idx_bookings_city_movie ON bookings (city_id, movie_id);
-- Query only filters on movie_id
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM bookings WHERE movie_id = 4421;
Question: "I have a composite index on (city_id, movie_id) but my WHERE movie_id =
4421 query doesn't use it. Why?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "B-tree composite indexes are sorted left-to-right. (city_id, movie_id) is
sorted primarily by city_id, then by movie_id within each city_id. Without a city_id
predicate, the movie_id values are scattered across the whole index." 2. "This is the leftmost-prefix
rule. The planner can use the index for queries on (city_id), (city_id, movie_id), or with a
range like (city_id = ? AND movie_id > ?). It cannot efficiently use it for (movie_id)
alone." 3. "Postgres can sometimes do an Index Skip Scan (loose index scan, Postgres 17+) if 
city_id has very few distinct values, but the default planner avoids it. MySQL 8 added skip scan in
limited cases. SQL Server has Index Skip Scan in some plans." 4. "Two options: add a second single-
column index on movie_id, or flip the composite to (movie_id, city_id) if queries on 
movie_id alone are common and city_id-only queries are rare."
Diagnosis: Query violates leftmost-prefix rule on composite index.
Fix:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 377 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 378
-- Add the missing index
CREATE INDEX idx_bookings_movie ON bookings (movie_id);
-- Or, if movie-only is more common, reorder the composite
CREATE INDEX idx_bookings_movie_city ON bookings (movie_id, city_id);
DROP INDEX idx_bookings_city_movie;
Why: Composite index keys are concatenated; without a prefix predicate the index is sorted on the
wrong dimension for the lookup.
NOT to say: "The planner should use any column in the index" — only the leftmost prefix is efficient. 
"Column order doesn't matter" — it dictates which queries the index can serve.
Follow-up: "How do I decide column order in a composite?" — Equality columns first, then range
columns, then ORDER BY columns. Within equality, put the higher-cardinality column first if both are
equally common in WHERE.
Scenario316 · OR Across Different Columns
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Swiggy, Zomato, AmEx · Topic: Predicate fragmentation · Engines:
All
Setup:
CREATE TABLE users (
  user_id       BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  phone         VARCHAR(15),
  email         VARCHAR(120)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_phone ON users (phone);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users (email);
-- Login flow that accepts either
SELECT user_id FROM users WHERE phone = '9876543210' OR email = 'priya@foo.in';
Question: "Both columns have indexes but this OR query still does a Seq Scan. Why?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "With AND, the planner can pick the most selective index and filter the rest in
memory. With OR, every row matching either condition needs to be returned — there is no single index
that covers both columns." 2. "Postgres handles this with a BitmapOr — scan idx_users_phone for
matches, scan idx_users_email for matches, OR the bitmaps, then heap-fetch. MySQL has 
index_merge_union for the same idea. SQL Server may pick a similar plan." 3. "The reason it
sometimes still does Seq Scan: if either branch is non-selective, the bitmap union becomes huge and a
Seq Scan wins. Or if the planner's statistics are off, it underestimates and picks the wrong shape." 4. 
"Cleanest pattern in application code: rewrite as UNION of two single-predicate queries. Each can use
its own index cleanly; UNION ALL plus DISTINCT if duplicates are a concern."
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 378 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 379
Diagnosis: OR across columns needs a BitmapOr / index_merge_union plan, which the planner skips if
statistics suggest a Seq Scan is cheaper.
Fix:
-- Rewrite as UNION
SELECT user_id FROM users WHERE phone = '9876543210'
UNION
SELECT user_id FROM users WHERE email = 'priya@foo.in';
Each branch uses its own index; planner has no ambiguity.
Why: A single index cannot satisfy a disjunction over different columns; the planner either combines
bitmaps or scans. UNION decomposes into two clean index lookups.
NOT to say: "OR is always slow" — OR on the same column with a few values is fine. "Add a multi-
column index" — composite indexes do not help with OR across different columns.
Follow-up: "What if it's WHERE phone IN ('A','B') OR email IN ('C','D')?" — Same
pattern: rewrite as UNION of two IN predicates, each using its own index.
Scenario317 · NOT IN With NULLs
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Cred · Topic: NULL semantics · Engines: All
Setup:
CREATE TABLE invoices (
  invoice_id    BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id   BIGINT,
  refund_id     BIGINT  -- nullable
);
CREATE INDEX idx_invoices_refund ON invoices (refund_id);
CREATE TABLE refunds (
  refund_id     BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  reason        VARCHAR(80)
);
-- "Show invoices not in the refunds table"
SELECT invoice_id FROM invoices
WHERE refund_id NOT IN (SELECT refund_id FROM refunds);
Question: "This query is doing a full scan plus a hash anti-join and returning wrong rows when there's
even one NULL in refunds.refund_id. Walk me through both issues."
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 379 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 380
Thinking out loud: 1. " NOT IN with a subquery that can return NULL has SQL-standard three-valued
logic semantics: x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) is UNKNOWN, not TRUE — so no rows ever match if any
NULL appears. The planner cannot push down index lookups because it has to materialise the full
subquery to check for NULLs." 2. "This forces a hash anti-join with extra NULL-handling logic. The index
on refund_id is bypassed because the engine has to scan everything in refunds anyway." 3. "The
fix is to use NOT EXISTS instead, which has clean two-valued semantics — NULL in the subquery
does not contaminate the result. NOT EXISTS correlates row-by-row and the planner can use an anti-
semi-join with the index." 4. "Alternatively LEFT JOIN ... WHERE r.refund_id IS NULL is
equivalent. Either pattern uses the index cleanly and gives correct results."
Diagnosis: NOT IN against a nullable subquery has UNKNOWN semantics on NULL, blocking index
use and producing wrong results.
Fix:
SELECT i.invoice_id
FROM invoices i
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM refunds r WHERE r.refund_id = i.refund_id
);
Postgres, MySQL 8, and SQL Server all plan this as an Anti Semi Join using the index on 
refunds.refund_id.
Why: SQL's three-valued logic makes NOT IN with NULLs return UNKNOWN. The planner cannot
prove safety, so it scans. NOT EXISTS is safe and indexable.
NOT to say: "NOT IN and NOT EXISTS are the same" — they differ on NULL. "Just add an index on 
refunds.refund_id" — the index is bypassed by the NULL semantics.
Follow-up: "If I add WHERE refund_id IS NOT NULL to the subquery, does it help?" — Yes,
semantically it makes NOT IN safe and the planner can then use the index, but NOT EXISTS is the
cleaner idiom.
Scenario318 · Stale Statistics, Wrong Plan
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Walmart Labs, Target · Topic: Statistics · Engines: All
Setup:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 380 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 381
CREATE TABLE events (
  event_id      BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id       BIGINT,
  event_type    VARCHAR(40),
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ
);
CREATE INDEX idx_events_user ON events (user_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_events_created ON events (created_at);
-- Bulk-loaded 200M rows yesterday; stats still show table at 50M
SELECT event_id FROM events WHERE user_id = 88012;
Question: "Yesterday this query used the index and ran in 20ms. After last night's bulk load, it does a Seq
Scan and takes 6 seconds. No index was changed. What happened?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Bulk loads (COPY, LOAD DATA INFILE, INSERT ... SELECT) on Postgres don't
automatically trigger ANALYZE. The planner is still using statistics that say the table has 50M rows and 
user_id has 5M distinct values. Estimated rows per user_id ≈ 10." 2. "After the load, real table is
200M rows but user_id distinct count didn't grow proportionally — maybe only 8M distinct now.
Estimated 10 rows per user is fine, but the planner's view of total work is wrong and it picks Seq Scan
because it thinks the table is only 50M rows and the random I/O cost vs sequential changed." 3. "In
Postgres, autovacuum should ANALYZE after a threshold of changes, but bulk loads can outrun it. In
MySQL, innodb_stats_persistent and innodb_stats_auto_recalc govern this. SQL
Server has Auto Update Statistics." 4. "Fix: run ANALYZE events; manually right after the bulk load.
Long-term, make sure autovacuum/auto-update-stats is tuned for the largest tables. For very large
changes, increase default_statistics_target per column to get better histograms."
Diagnosis: Statistics not updated after bulk load; planner's cost model uses stale row counts and
distributions.
Fix:
-- Postgres
ANALYZE events;
-- Or in the bulk-load script
ANALYZE events (user_id, created_at);
-- MySQL
ANALYZE TABLE events;
-- SQL Server
UPDATE STATISTICS dbo.events WITH FULLSCAN;
Why: The optimiser is a cost-based planner; its cost estimates depend on row count, distinct values,
histograms, and correlation. Stale stats mean wrong costs mean wrong plans.
NOT to say: "Just rebuild the index" — REINDEX doesn't update planner stats. "The planner randomly
changed" — it deterministically followed the costs it was given.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 381 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 382
Follow-up: "How often should I run ANALYZE on a 1TB OLTP table?" — Let autovacuum/auto-update-
stats handle it, but tune thresholds (autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor to 0.02 or lower for large
tables). After every bulk load, run it explicitly.
Scenario319 · Index Too Small To Bother With
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Cred, Zerodha, Goldman · Topic: Cost model · Engines: All
Setup:
CREATE TABLE pin_codes (
  pin       INT PRIMARY KEY,
  city      VARCHAR(80),
  state     VARCHAR(80)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_pin_codes_state ON pin_codes (state);
-- Only 19,000 rows, fits entirely in 1 MB of buffer cache
SELECT pin FROM pin_codes WHERE state = 'Maharashtra';
Question: "I created an index on state and EXPLAIN still shows Seq Scan. Why won't a 19,000-row
table use the index?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "The whole table fits in maybe 2-3 buffer pages. A Seq Scan is one page read after
another sequentially — basically free once cached. An Index Scan would have to traverse the B-tree, then
random-fetch from the heap for each match." 2. "For tables this small, the planner often picks Seq Scan
because the total I/O cost is lower than even the index traversal startup cost. This is the correct decision."
3. "It only matters for very small tables, but candidates panic and try to force the index with hints. Don't
— EXPLAIN ANALYZE will show the Seq Scan is faster end to end." 4. "Real lesson: indexes have a
fixed startup cost (root + intermediate pages). On a table where the entire heap fits in cache and the scan
is sub-millisecond, that startup cost dominates."
Diagnosis: Table is small enough that Seq Scan beats Index Scan; planner is correct.
Fix: Drop the unnecessary index, or accept the Seq Scan.
-- If the index is never used and only adds write overhead, drop it
DROP INDEX idx_pin_codes_state;
Why: Index Scan has fixed traversal cost. Below a threshold table size, Seq Scan is cheaper even for
selective predicates.
NOT to say: "Force the index with a hint" — almost always slower in this scenario. "The planner is
wrong" — measure with EXPLAIN ANALYZE first.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 382 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 383
Follow-up: "How small is too small for an index to ever earn its keep?" — Rule of thumb: less than 1000
rows, indexes rarely help unique-lookup workloads. For lookup tables under 10,000 rows, only index
columns you actually filter on in mixed-join contexts.
Scenario320 · Index Bloat — REINDEX Required
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Cred, Razorpay, Walmart Labs · Topic: Bloat · Engines: Postgres
especially
Setup:
CREATE TABLE wallet_transactions (
  txn_id        BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  wallet_id     BIGINT,
  amount_paise  BIGINT,
  status        VARCHAR(20),
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ
);
CREATE INDEX idx_wallet_txn_wallet ON wallet_transactions (wallet_id);
-- Heavy update workload, status changes pending -> success -> reconciled
-- pgstattuple shows idx_wallet_txn_wallet is 8GB; table is 3GB
Question: "The index is more than twice the size of the table. Queries on wallet_id got 4x slower
over the last quarter. What's happening and how do you fix it without downtime?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "In Postgres MVCC, an UPDATE creates a new heap tuple and a new index entry
pointing to it. The old entries are not removed immediately; they become dead and are only cleaned up
by VACUUM. Heavy update workloads leave the index full of dead entries — bloat." 2. "Bloat in B-trees
inflates leaf pages, increases tree height, and slows lookups because more pages must be fetched. Auto
VACUUM marks dead tuples reusable in the heap but does not aggressively reclaim space inside index
pages." 3. " pgstattuple and pg_stat_user_indexes (or the pgstattuple_approx
extension) tell you how much of an index is dead. Anything over 30% bloat is worth attention." 4. "Fix is
REINDEX, but plain REINDEX takes an AccessExclusiveLock — bad for production. REINDEX INDEX
CONCURRENTLY (Postgres 12+) does it online: builds a fresh index alongside, swaps it in, drops the old.
Slightly slower build, no downtime."
Diagnosis: B-tree index bloat from heavy updates; dead index entries accumulate faster than VACUUM
reclaims them.
Fix:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 383 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 384
-- Online REINDEX (Postgres 12+), no AccessExclusiveLock
REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_wallet_txn_wallet;
-- For very bloated tables, REINDEX TABLE CONCURRENTLY does all indexes
REINDEX TABLE CONCURRENTLY wallet_transactions;
After, autovacuum cadence should be tuned to prevent recurrence.
Why: MVCC update workloads bloat B-tree leaf pages. VACUUM marks dead entries but doesn't
physically rebalance. REINDEX compacts.
NOT to say: "Just run VACUUM FULL" — it works but rewrites the whole table with
AccessExclusiveLock; far worse for uptime than CONCURRENT REINDEX. "Bloat is a Postgres myth" —
it is measurable and real.
Follow-up: "What's the difference between table bloat and index bloat?" — Table bloat is dead tuples in
the heap; reclaimed by autovacuum and (slowly) reused. Index bloat is dead entries in B-tree leaves;
never reclaimed in-place at scale, requires REINDEX.
Scenario321 · Wrong Join Algorithm Picked
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Flipkart · Topic: Join planning · Engines: All
Setup:
CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id      BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id   BIGINT,
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ
);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders (customer_id);
CREATE TABLE customers (
  customer_id   BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  tier          VARCHAR(20)
);
-- 200M orders, 5M customers, 50K of which are tier='platinum'
SELECT o.order_id
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.tier = 'platinum';
Question: "This used to be fast as a Nested Loop with index lookups. After last week's stats update it's
now a Hash Join scanning all 200M orders. P95 is 4x worse. What went wrong?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Nested Loop with index lookup costs roughly outer_rows *
index_lookup_cost. For 50K platinum customers and a B-tree index lookup ~ 4 page reads each,
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 384 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 385
that's manageable." 2. "Hash Join builds an in-memory hash on the smaller side then scans the larger.
Costs build + scan_larger. Here it's building a 50K-row hash and scanning 200M orders —
sequentially, no index lookups. If the cost model thinks index lookups are expensive or the row estimate
for platinum is too high, Hash Join may win on paper but lose in reality due to cache effects." 3. "Most
common trigger: random_page_cost set too high (default 4.0 was tuned for spinning disks; SSDs
warrant 1.1). With SSDs, random index fetches are nearly as cheap as sequential, so Nested Loop with
index lookups should win. Stale or off cost parameters tip the balance toward Hash." 4. "Other cause:
row estimate for tier='platinum' is wrong — if stats say 5M instead of 50K, planner correctly
avoids Nested Loop. Refresh stats with CREATE STATISTICS or higher 
default_statistics_target for the column."
Diagnosis: Cost parameters or stats steered the planner toward Hash Join when index-driven Nested
Loop is actually cheaper on SSD.
Fix:
-- Postgres: tune for SSDs
ALTER SYSTEM SET random_page_cost = 1.1;
SELECT pg_reload_conf();
-- Improve cardinality estimate
ANALYZE customers;
ALTER TABLE customers ALTER COLUMN tier SET STATISTICS 500;
ANALYZE customers;
Why: Join algorithm choice is cost-driven. If random_page_cost overstates SSD random I/O or row
estimates are off, the planner picks the wrong algorithm.
NOT to say: "Force the join with a hint" — fix the root cause first. "Hash Join is always slower" — for two
big tables with no selective predicate, Hash Join wins.
Follow-up: "When is Merge Join actually the best choice?" — When both inputs are already sorted on
the join key (an index already in that order, or a prior sort step). Common in OLAP and after a sorted
GROUP BY.
Scenario322 · Cross Join Forced by Non-Sargable Join Condition
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Target, Goldman · Topic: Join sargability · Engines: All
Setup:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 385 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 386
CREATE TABLE auctions (
  auction_id    BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  start_time    TIMESTAMPTZ,
  end_time      TIMESTAMPTZ
);
CREATE INDEX idx_auctions_start ON auctions (start_time);
CREATE INDEX idx_auctions_end   ON auctions (end_time);
CREATE TABLE bids (
  bid_id        BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  auction_id    BIGINT,
  placed_at     TIMESTAMPTZ
);
-- "Which bids landed inside their auction's window"
SELECT b.bid_id
FROM bids b JOIN auctions a
  ON b.placed_at BETWEEN a.start_time AND a.end_time;
Question: "This is doing a Nested Loop with a Seq Scan on auctions for every bid — effectively a cross
product check. Why isn't it using any index?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "The join condition is a BETWEEN range. Neither column on the inner side has a
single-value lookup — the planner cannot use idx_auctions_start to seek both sides of the range
simultaneously." 2. "For interval queries like this, B-tree indexes on start/end individually don't help. The
correct data structure is a range type with a GiST index in Postgres, or a spatial index in some engines."
3. "Postgres tstzrange with a GiST index lets the planner do an Index Scan on range @>
timestamp containment lookups, turning the cross-product into an indexed lookup per bid." 4. "In
engines without range types (MySQL pre-8, SQL Server), the pragmatic fix is to add auction_id as a
foreign key to bids and join on equality first, then filter on the range — the equality join uses the index, the
range filter happens on fetched rows."
Diagnosis: BETWEEN join is non-sargable on B-tree indexes; planner falls back to nested loop without
index seek.
Fix:
-- Postgres: range type plus GiST
ALTER TABLE auctions ADD COLUMN window tstzrange
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (tstzrange(start_time, end_time, '[]')) STORED;
CREATE INDEX idx_auctions_window ON auctions USING gist (window);
SELECT b.bid_id
FROM bids b JOIN auctions a ON a.window @> b.placed_at;
Why: Range-containment joins need range indexes (GiST/SP-GiST in Postgres, spatial in others) — B-
tree indexes a point, not an interval.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 386 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 387
NOT to say: "Add an index on placed_at" — doesn't help the join shape. "This is fundamentally
O(nm)"* — not with the right index.
Follow-up: "What if I just need 'most recent auction before this bid'?" — That's a lateral join: LATERAL
(SELECT ... FROM auctions WHERE start_time <= b.placed_at ORDER BY start_time
DESC LIMIT 1). Indexable.
Scenario323 · Parameter Sniffing in SQL Server
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: AmEx, Goldman, Walmart Labs · Topic: Plan cache · Engines: SQL
Server primarily
Setup:
CREATE TABLE rides (
  ride_id       BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  driver_id     INT,
  city_id       INT,
  created_at    DATETIME2
);
CREATE INDEX idx_rides_city_created ON rides (city_id, created_at);
-- The proc
CREATE PROCEDURE GetRidesByCity @city_id INT, @from DATETIME2 AS
  SELECT ride_id FROM rides
  WHERE city_id = @city_id AND created_at >= @from;
GO
Question: "This proc runs in 30ms most of the time but every Monday morning it takes 8 seconds for the
first caller, then it's fast again. What's the pattern?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "SQL Server caches a plan based on the parameter values from the first execution.
If the first caller on Monday passed @city_id = 1 (Mumbai, 80% of rows), the planner picked a Seq
Scan plan because the predicate is non-selective. That plan stays cached." 2. "Subsequent callers asking
for @city_id = 47 (Pune, 0.5% of rows) reuse the cached Seq Scan plan, which is catastrophic for
selective lookups." 3. "This is parameter sniffing. Postgres has the same issue with prepared statements
once plan_cache_mode allows generic plans. Oracle had bind variable peeking, fixed by adaptive
cursor sharing." 4. "Fixes: OPTION (RECOMPILE) per query (recompiles every time, no caching), 
OPTIMIZE FOR hint (always plan for a representative value), local variables (the planner uses average
density), or split into two procs for skewed values."
Diagnosis: Plan cache pinned to a plan that suits the first-seen parameter values, not the current ones.
Fix:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 387 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 388
-- Option A: recompile every time
CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE GetRidesByCity @city_id INT, @from DATETIME2 AS
  SELECT ride_id FROM rides
  WHERE city_id = @city_id AND created_at >= @from
  OPTION (RECOMPILE);
-- Option B: optimize for a representative value
... OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR (@city_id = UNKNOWN));
Why: Plan caching trades recompile cost for stable plans, but a stable plan is wrong when parameter
selectivity varies wildly.
NOT to say: "Disable plan caching globally" — kills throughput. "It's a one-off blip" — it'll recur every
plan eviction.
Follow-up: "What's the trade-off of OPTION (RECOMPILE)?" — Always-fresh plan, but compile cost
on every call. Fine for low-frequency procs; not for hot OLTP paths.
Scenario324 · Plan Cache Pollution
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, Walmart Labs, JP Morgan · Topic: Plan cache · Engines: SQL
Server, Oracle, Postgres
Setup:
-- Application string-concatenates the user_id rather than binding
SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE user_id = 7724901;
SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE user_id = 7724902;
SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE user_id = 7724903;
-- ... thousands of variants
Question: "After a deploy that switched from prepared statements to raw string SQL, the plan cache
grew to 8GB and our buffer cache hit ratio crashed. Explain the link."
Thinking out loud: 1. "Each unique query text gets its own plan cache entry. With bound parameters, all 
user_id = ? queries share one plan. With concatenation, each user_id = 7724901, user_id
= 7724902 is a different text, so each gets its own cached plan." 2. "On a busy service with millions of
distinct values, you flood the plan cache with single-use plans. Memory that should hold data pages is
consumed by plan metadata. Buffer cache shrinks; disk I/O rises; latency suffers." 3. "SQL Server has 
optimize for ad hoc workloads to stash a small stub on first execution and the full plan on
second use, which helps with truly one-off queries. Postgres uses plan_cache_mode and prepared
statement reuse. Oracle has cursor sharing modes." 4. "Root fix is at the application layer: use
parameterised queries (PreparedStatement, ? placeholders). Database-side workarounds (forced
parameterisation, optimize for ad hoc) are mitigation, not solution."
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 388 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 389
Diagnosis: Non-parameterised SQL fragments the plan cache into millions of single-use entries, evicting
data pages.
Fix:
// Application: bind, don't concatenate
PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement(
  "SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE user_id = ?");
ps.setLong(1, userId);
Plus enable optimize for ad hoc workloads (SQL Server) or FORCED cursor sharing (Oracle)
as defence in depth.
Why: Plan cache is keyed on query text. Unique text per call defeats caching and steals memory from
the buffer cache.
NOT to say: "More RAM fixes plan cache pollution" — only delays it. "The cache will self-evict" — yes,
but at the cost of constant recompiles and cache churn.
Follow-up: "Why is recompiling so expensive?" — Optimisation walks join orders, picks plans across
many indexes, may run statistics queries; can be 10-100x the actual execution cost for a short query.
Scenario325 · Histograms Missing or Stale (MySQL 8)
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Swiggy, Razorpay · Topic: Statistics · Engines: MySQL 8
Setup:
CREATE TABLE listings (
  listing_id    BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  category_id   INT,
  price_paise   BIGINT,
  created_at    DATETIME
);
CREATE INDEX idx_listings_category ON listings (category_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_listings_price    ON listings (price_paise);
-- Skewed: category 1 has 100K rows, category 2 has 8M, category 3 has 4K
SELECT listing_id FROM listings WHERE category_id = 3 AND price_paise < 50000;
Question: "On MySQL 8, this picks the wrong index — uses idx_listings_price when it should
use idx_listings_category. InnoDB index dives sample a few pages and get the skew wrong.
What's the modern fix?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "MySQL 8 introduced explicit histograms via ANALYZE TABLE ... UPDATE
HISTOGRAM. Without histograms, InnoDB's cardinality estimates come from index dives (sampling a
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 389 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 390
small number of pages per index), which is fine for uniform data but bad for skew." 2. "For 
category_id = 3 (4K rows), index dives might estimate 2M rows because they hit pages dominated
by category 2. The planner thinks idx_listings_category returns too many rows and picks 
idx_listings_price instead, then filters." 3. "Histograms record actual value distribution buckets.
With an equi-height histogram on category_id, the planner sees that value 3 is only 4K rows — and
picks the right index." 4. "Postgres has had this since forever via pg_statistic histograms; SQL
Server has step histograms; MySQL 8 is catching up. Per-column setting, refreshed by ANALYZE
TABLE ... UPDATE HISTOGRAM ON category_id WITH 100 BUCKETS."
Diagnosis: Skewed column without a histogram; planner uses index dives that miss the skew.
Fix:
-- MySQL 8 explicit histogram
ANALYZE TABLE listings UPDATE HISTOGRAM ON category_id WITH 100 BUCKETS;
-- Re-EXPLAIN; planner now sees true selectivity
Why: Index dives sample pages, not values. They cannot detect skew if the rare value sits on rarely-
sampled pages.
NOT to say: "MySQL doesn't support statistics" — it does as of 8.0. "InnoDB stats are always wrong" —
only on skewed columns without histograms.
Follow-up: "How many buckets should I use?" — Default 100 is fine; up to 1024 if you have many
distinct values and tight selectivity matters. More buckets = more storage, slower ANALYZE.
Scenario326 · Extended Statistics for Correlated Columns
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, Walmart Labs, Cred · Topic: Statistics · Engines: Postgres
Setup:
CREATE TABLE addresses (
  address_id    BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  city          VARCHAR(80),
  state         VARCHAR(80),
  pincode       INT
);
CREATE INDEX idx_addresses_city_state ON addresses (city, state);
-- Mumbai is in Maharashtra, Bengaluru in Karnataka, etc — perfect functional dependency
SELECT * FROM addresses WHERE city = 'Mumbai' AND state = 'Maharashtra';
Question: "Postgres estimates 200 rows for this; reality is 80,000. It picks a Nested Loop on the outer
side which blows up. Why is the estimate so wrong?"
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 390 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 391
Thinking out loud: 1. "Postgres assumes independence between columns by default: P(city = 'Mumbai'
AND state = 'Maharashtra') = P(city = 'Mumbai') * P(state = 'Maharashtra'). With 400 cities and 30 states,
that's roughly 1/400 * 1/30 ≈ 8 in 100,000 — but every Mumbai row IS Maharashtra, so the true joint
probability is just 1/400." 2. "The independence assumption fails for correlated columns (city implies
state). The estimate is 100-1000x too low, and downstream join orders get picked based on wrong
cardinalities." 3. " CREATE STATISTICS (Postgres 10+) lets you declare multi-column statistics: 
ndistinct for distinct-value counts, dependencies for functional dependencies, mcv for most-
common-value lists across columns." 4. "After creating and ANALYZE-ing the extended statistics, the
planner uses the joint distribution and gets the row estimate right. The plan flips to the right shape —
often Bitmap Heap Scan or Hash Join instead of Nested Loop."
Diagnosis: Postgres assumes column independence; correlated columns yield wildly wrong joint
estimates.
Fix:
CREATE STATISTICS stats_addr_city_state (dependencies, mcv)
  ON city, state FROM addresses;
ANALYZE addresses;
-- EXPLAIN now shows accurate joint row estimate
Why: Cost-based planners assume independence between predicates unless told otherwise. Functional
dependencies break that.
NOT to say: "Just rewrite the query" — won't fix the cardinality model. "Postgres can't handle correlated
columns" — it can, with extended statistics.
Follow-up: "What other engines have something equivalent?" — SQL Server has multi-column statistics
auto-created on indexed combinations. Oracle has extended statistics via 
DBMS_STATS.CREATE_EXTENDED_STATS.
Scenario327 · Leftmost-Prefix Misuse on a Wide Composite
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: PhonePe, Razorpay, Walmart Labs · Topic: Composite indexes ·
Engines: All
Setup:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 391 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 392
CREATE TABLE app_events (
  event_id      BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id       BIGINT,
  session_id    UUID,
  event_type    VARCHAR(40),
  ts            TIMESTAMPTZ
);
CREATE INDEX idx_app_events_uset ON app_events (user_id, session_id, event_type, ts);
-- Query filters on user_id and event_type, skips session_id
SELECT * FROM app_events
WHERE user_id = 7724901 AND event_type = 'click'
ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 50;
Question: "The composite index covers all the right columns but only the user_id part of the prefix
gets used; event_type filter happens after. Why?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Composite index prefix is (user_id, session_id, event_type, ts).
With user_id equality, the index seeks to that user's range. Within it, entries are sorted by 
session_id then event_type — but we have no session_id predicate." 2. "Without the
second column predicate, the planner can use the prefix on user_id only; then it must scan all entries
for that user and filter on event_type post-fetch. The ts ordering for ORDER BY can't be cleanly
used either, because entries are sorted by session_id first within the user." 3. "Reorder the index: 
(user_id, event_type, ts). Now equality on the first two, range/ordering on the third — classic
equality-equality-range pattern. Drop session_id from the index unless it's needed for other queries."
4. "If session_id is needed for a different query, create a separate index. Don't try to make one
super-wide index serve every shape — it ends up serving none well."
Diagnosis: Wide composite with the wrong column placed second blocks the leftmost-prefix path past 
user_id.
Fix:
CREATE INDEX idx_app_events_user_type_ts
  ON app_events (user_id, event_type, ts DESC);
DROP INDEX idx_app_events_uset;
Optionally INCLUDE (event_id) for an index-only scan covering the SELECT list.
Why: B-tree composite indexes serve queries only along the leftmost prefix. A "skipped" middle column
means everything past it is scan-and-filter.
NOT to say: "Just add all columns and the planner figures it out" — column order matters more than
column count. "More columns in the index is always better" — wider indexes are slower to maintain and
bigger to traverse.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 392 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 393
Follow-up: "Do I always want equality columns first?" — Yes, then range columns, then ORDER BY
columns. That's the standard equality-equality-range rule.
Scenario328 · Index-Only Scan Blocked by Missing INCLUDE
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Cred, Razorpay, Goldman · Topic: Covering indexes · Engines: Postgres
11+, SQL Server, MySQL 8
Setup:
CREATE TABLE invoice_lines (
  line_id       BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  invoice_id    BIGINT,
  sku           VARCHAR(40),
  qty           INT,
  price_paise   BIGINT
);
CREATE INDEX idx_invoice_lines_invoice ON invoice_lines (invoice_id);
SELECT sku, qty FROM invoice_lines WHERE invoice_id = 88012;
Question: "EXPLAIN shows Index Scan + Heap Fetch, not Index Only Scan. The index has 
invoice_id. Why isn't it index-only?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "An Index Only Scan requires every column referenced in the query to be in the
index — the predicate columns AND the SELECT list columns. Here sku and qty are not in the
index, so the engine has to go to the heap to read them." 2. "Postgres supports INCLUDE columns
since version 11 — they're stored in the leaf pages but not part of the B-tree key, so they don't slow
comparisons but make the index covering for that query." 3. "SQL Server has had INCLUDE since
2005; MySQL 8's secondary indexes always include the PK at the leaf, so wider secondary indexes
naturally cover more. Postgres INCLUDE is the right primitive." 4. "Add INCLUDE (sku, qty) and
re-EXPLAIN. Should flip to Index Only Scan with Heap Fetches: 0 (assuming visibility map is up
to date — see next scenario)."
Diagnosis: Index is not covering — SELECT list references columns not in the index leaves.
Fix:
CREATE INDEX idx_invoice_lines_invoice_cover
  ON invoice_lines (invoice_id) INCLUDE (sku, qty);
DROP INDEX idx_invoice_lines_invoice;
Why: Index Only Scan avoids the heap altogether, but only if all needed columns live in the index leaves.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 393 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 394
NOT to say: "Add the include columns as part of the key" — works, but slows down comparisons and
bloats the tree. INCLUDE is the cleaner primitive.
Follow-up: "What's the trade-off of a covering index?" — Bigger on disk, slower writes (every UPDATE to
an included column rewrites the index entry), but eliminates heap fetches on hot read paths.
Scenario329 · Visibility Map Stale, Index-Only Falls Back
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Walmart Labs · Topic: MVCC, Index-only scan ·
Engines: Postgres
Setup:
CREATE TABLE ledger_entries (
  entry_id      BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  account_id    BIGINT,
  amount_paise  BIGINT,
  posted_at     TIMESTAMPTZ
);
CREATE INDEX idx_ledger_account_cover
  ON ledger_entries (account_id) INCLUDE (amount_paise, posted_at);
-- Recently bulk-inserted 50M rows
SELECT amount_paise, posted_at FROM ledger_entries WHERE account_id = 88012;
Question: "My covering index just got built. The query has all columns covered. But EXPLAIN
ANALYZE shows Heap Fetches: 4982 — why is it still going to the heap?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Postgres Index Only Scan needs to confirm that each tuple version is visible to the
current transaction. It uses the visibility map (VM) — one bit per heap page saying 'all tuples on this page
are visible to all transactions.' If the VM bit is set, no heap fetch is needed." 2. "The VM is updated by
VACUUM, not by INSERT. Freshly-loaded heap pages have the VM bit unset. So even though the index
has the data, the planner can't trust the visibility info without going to the heap." 3. "Fix: run VACUUM
(not VACUUM FULL) on the table. That sets the all-visible bits on stable pages. After VACUUM, Index
Only Scan can return data without any heap fetches." 4. "Autovacuum eventually does this, but on a
freshly-loaded table you can force it. For appliance-style ETL pipelines, run VACUUM ANALYZE as the
final step of the load."
Diagnosis: Visibility map bits not set on newly-loaded heap pages; Index Only Scan falls back to heap
fetches.
Fix:
VACUUM ANALYZE ledger_entries;
-- Re-EXPLAIN ANALYZE; Heap Fetches should drop to 0
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 394 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 395
Why: Postgres MVCC needs per-page visibility info to skip heap fetches. The VM is maintained by
VACUUM, not by writes.
NOT to say: "Index Only Scan doesn't work in Postgres" — it does, just needs an up-to-date VM. 
"Rebuild the index" — index is fine; the heap visibility map is the issue.
Follow-up: "Why doesn't VACUUM run more aggressively?" — Cost-based throttling
( vacuum_cost_limit). On heavy-write tables, you tune autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor
lower (default 0.2 means 20% dead tuples before triggering).
Scenario330 · Index on Column With High NULL Ratio
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Swiggy, Zomato, Cred · Topic: Sparse data · Engines: All
Setup:
CREATE TABLE delivery_attempts (
  attempt_id    BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id      BIGINT,
  driver_id     BIGINT,
  failure_reason VARCHAR(120)  -- NULL for successful attempts (99% of rows)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_delivery_failure_reason ON delivery_attempts (failure_reason);
-- Only failed attempts have a reason; we query those
SELECT order_id FROM delivery_attempts WHERE failure_reason = 'address_not_found';
Question: "99% of rows have NULL in failure_reason and my B-tree index is huge. Should NULLs
even be in the index? Why is this slow?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "By default, Postgres B-tree indexes include NULL entries. With 99% NULL, the
index is mostly useless padding — most pages hold NULL entries that we never query." 2. "This bloats
the index, slows scans, and increases write cost (every INSERT writes an index entry even for NULLs we'll
never query)." 3. "Partial index on the predicate side is the clean fix: 
WHERE failure_reason IS NOT NULL. Index becomes 1% of original size, fits in cache, lookups
are fast." 4. "Oracle excludes NULLs from B-tree indexes by default (which is why composite indexes with
all-NULL rows aren't indexed there) — different default, same lesson. SQL Server lets you create filtered
indexes for the same purpose."
Diagnosis: Index dominated by NULL entries that the query never uses; mostly wasted space and write
cost.
Fix:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 395 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 396
-- Postgres partial index
DROP INDEX idx_delivery_failure_reason;
CREATE INDEX idx_delivery_failure_reason_nn
  ON delivery_attempts (failure_reason)
  WHERE failure_reason IS NOT NULL;
-- SQL Server filtered index
CREATE INDEX idx_delivery_failure_reason
  ON delivery_attempts (failure_reason)
  WHERE failure_reason IS NOT NULL;
Why: Sparse data benefits from a partial/filtered index that excludes the dominant NULL value.
NOT to say: "Just drop the index" — you still need it for failure lookups. "NULLs don't take space in
indexes" — they do, except in Oracle.
Follow-up: "What's the difference between a partial index and a filtered index?" — Naming only.
Postgres calls it partial, SQL Server calls it filtered, same idea.
Scenario331 · Index Unused After TRUNCATE
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, AmEx, Walmart Labs · Topic: Statistics reset · Engines: All
Setup:
-- Nightly ETL truncates and reloads
TRUNCATE TABLE staging_orders;
COPY staging_orders FROM '/data/orders_2026_05_25.csv' CSV;
-- 80M rows loaded
CREATE INDEX idx_staging_orders_cust ON staging_orders (customer_id);
SELECT order_id FROM staging_orders WHERE customer_id = 7724901;
Question: "After the nightly TRUNCATE + COPY, the index exists but queries do Seq Scans for the first
hour. Then magically start using the index. What's going on?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "TRUNCATE resets table statistics — Postgres considers the table empty (reltuples
= 0) until ANALYZE runs. COPY adds rows but doesn't update stats." 2. "For the first hour, autovacuum
hasn't analysed the table yet. Planner sees a 0-row table and figures Seq Scan is cheaper than even one
index lookup. So it scans the (now huge) heap." 3. "After autovacuum runs ANALYZE (triggered by 
autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor of changes — but on a 'zero-row' table, even one row is
infinite percent change, so it usually fires quickly), stats reflect reality and the planner switches to Index
Scan." 4. "Don't wait. Always run ANALYZE immediately after a TRUNCATE + reload. Or wrap the load
in a script that ends with ANALYZE staging_orders;."
Diagnosis: TRUNCATE reset stats to zero; planner uses stale 0-row estimate until ANALYZE catches up.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 396 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 397
Fix:
TRUNCATE TABLE staging_orders;
COPY staging_orders FROM '/data/orders_2026_05_25.csv' CSV;
ANALYZE staging_orders;  -- run explicitly
Why: TRUNCATE is metadata-only fast, but it nukes the row count and stats. Planner cannot make good
decisions on empty-table stats.
NOT to say: "TRUNCATE is the same as DELETE for stats" — DELETE keeps stats but marks rows dead;
TRUNCATE resets to zero. "Just rebuild the index" — index is fine; stats are stale.
Follow-up: "Why does autovacuum take an hour to catch up here?" — 
autovacuum_analyze_threshold (50 rows default) plus scale_factor; on tables with frequent
zero-to-huge cycles, lower the scale_factor or run ANALYZE explicitly.
Scenario332 · Partial Index Predicate Doesn't Match Query
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Cred, Razorpay, Flipkart · Topic: Partial indexes · Engines: Postgres,
SQL Server
Setup:
CREATE TABLE payouts (
  payout_id     BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  vendor_id     BIGINT,
  status        VARCHAR(20),
  amount_paise  BIGINT,
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ
);
CREATE INDEX idx_payouts_pending
  ON payouts (vendor_id, created_at)
  WHERE status = 'pending';
-- Query
SELECT payout_id FROM payouts
WHERE vendor_id = 88012 AND status IN ('pending', 'failed');
Question: "My partial index on status = 'pending' doesn't get used when the query asks for 
status IN ('pending', 'failed'). The index would still help for the pending portion. Why
doesn't the planner use it?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "For a partial index to be used, the planner must prove the query's predicate
implies the index's WHERE clause. status IN ('pending', 'failed') is a superset of status
= 'pending' — it does NOT imply status = 'pending', it could match failed too. So the
planner cannot use the partial index alone — it would miss the failed rows." 2. "Implication direction
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 397 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 398
matters: query predicate => index predicate. status = 'pending' => status = 'pending'
(yes). status IN ('pending','failed') => status = 'pending' (no). status =
'pending' AND amount > 1000 => status = 'pending' (yes)." 3. "Options: (a) split into
UNION of two queries, one with status = 'pending' (uses partial) and one with status =
'failed' (needs different index); (b) create a broader partial index WHERE status IN
('pending','failed'); (c) drop the partial in favour of a full index on (vendor_id, status,
created_at)." 4. "Real call depends on volumes — if 'pending' is 0.1% of payouts and 'failed' is
0.05%, two narrow partial indexes plus UNION is the cleanest. If both states together are still selective
enough, one broader partial works."
Diagnosis: Query predicate does not imply the partial index predicate; planner cannot use it.
Fix:
-- Option A: broaden the partial
DROP INDEX idx_payouts_pending;
CREATE INDEX idx_payouts_active
  ON payouts (vendor_id, created_at)
  WHERE status IN ('pending', 'failed');
-- Option B: UNION rewrite
SELECT payout_id FROM payouts WHERE vendor_id = 88012 AND status = 'pending'
UNION ALL
SELECT payout_id FROM payouts WHERE vendor_id = 88012 AND status = 'failed';
Why: Partial-index applicability is governed by predicate implication, not predicate overlap. Planner
needs proof.
NOT to say: "The planner is too strict" — using a partial index for a non-implied query would return
wrong results. "Just add a hint" — hints can't override correctness.
Follow-up: "How do I check whether a partial index will be used?" — EXPLAIN the query and look for
the index name. Postgres can also do EXPLAIN (BUFFERS) to confirm pages read.
Scenario333 · Expression Index Not Matched Literally
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Cred, Goldman, Walmart Labs · Topic: Expression indexes · Engines:
Postgres, Oracle
Setup:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 398 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 399
CREATE TABLE customers (
  customer_id   BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  full_name     VARCHAR(200),
  email         VARCHAR(120)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_customers_name_lower ON customers (LOWER(full_name));
-- Query
SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE LOWER(full_name) = 'priya sharma';
SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE LOWER(full_name) ILIKE 'priya sharma';
SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE full_name ILIKE 'priya sharma';  -- doesn't use it
Question: "The expression index on LOWER(full_name) works for WHERE LOWER(full_name)
= ... but doesn't get used for WHERE full_name ILIKE 'priya sharma'. Both seem case-
insensitive. Why?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Expression indexes are matched textually — the predicate expression must
syntactically match the indexed expression (up to a few simplifications). LOWER(full_name) =
'priya sharma' matches. full_name ILIKE 'priya sharma' is a different operator entirely
( ~~*) and the planner cannot see the equivalence." 2. "Even 
LOWER(full_name) = LOWER('PRIYA SHARMA') may not match if the planner doesn't constant-
fold the RHS. Best practice: keep both sides clean — LOWER(col) = 'lowercase_literal'." 3. 
"For ILIKE patterns, you'd either need to keep using LOWER(col) LIKE 'priya%' (which uses the
expression index for prefix patterns), or use the citext extension which makes the column case-
insensitive at the type level." 4. "Or in Postgres, the pg_trgm extension supports ILIKE patterns
directly with a GIN index — different tool for a different shape."
Diagnosis: Predicate doesn't syntactically match indexed expression; planner cannot use the expression
index.
Fix:
-- Option A: rewrite to match
SELECT customer_id FROM customers
WHERE LOWER(full_name) LIKE 'priya sharma';
-- Option B: citext column
ALTER TABLE customers ALTER COLUMN full_name TYPE citext;
CREATE INDEX idx_customers_name ON customers (full_name);
-- Now any case-insensitive comparison uses the index
Why: Expression index matching is syntactic. The planner does limited normalisation; not arbitrary
equivalence proofs.
NOT to say: "The planner should figure out equivalent expressions" — it can't, in general. "Just use ILIKE
everywhere" — it bypasses your carefully-built index.

Some planner versions constant-fold the RHS, others don't. Always test with EXPLAIN.
Scenario334 · Foreign Key Without Index — Slow Cascading DELETE
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Goldman · Topic: FK indexes · Engines: All
Setup:
CREATE TABLE customers (
  customer_id   BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  name          VARCHAR(120)
);
CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id      BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id   BIGINT REFERENCES customers(customer_id) ON DELETE CASCADE
  -- no index on customer_id!
);
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  item_id       BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id      BIGINT REFERENCES orders(order_id) ON DELETE CASCADE
  -- no index on order_id either
);
DELETE FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 7724901;  -- takes 8 minutes
Question: "Deleting one customer takes 8 minutes. Cascading deletes should be quick. What's wrong?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "When you DELETE a customer, Postgres has to find all referencing rows in 
orders and delete them, then for each deleted order find all order_items and delete those. If
there's no index on the referencing column, each lookup is a full table scan." 2. "Postgres does NOT
auto-create indexes on FK columns (only on the referenced PK side). MySQL InnoDB does auto-create
one. SQL Server doesn't. Oracle doesn't. So in most engines, you must remember to add it." 3. "For 50M
orders and 200M order_items, the cascade walks both tables linearly per customer. Add indexes on the
FK columns and the cascade becomes O(rows_to_delete) instead of O(rows_in_table)." 4. "Same issue
with UPDATE CASCADE on a PK change (rare) and with the FK validity check on INSERT (less impactful
because PK is indexed)."
Diagnosis: Foreign key columns not indexed; cascade walks each child table fully.
Fix:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer    ON orders (customer_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_order_items_order  ON order_items (order_id);
-- Cascade DELETE now uses index lookups; sub-second
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 400 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 401
Why: ON DELETE CASCADE issues a DELETE against child tables filtered by the parent key. Without an
index on the FK column, that DELETE does a full scan.
NOT to say: "FKs auto-create indexes" — only MySQL InnoDB does. "Cascade is always slow" — only
without indexes.
Follow-up: "How do I find unindexed FKs in Postgres?" — Query pg_constraint joined with 
pg_index to find FKs without a matching leftmost-prefix index. A common DBA audit query.
Scenario335 · ORDER BY Causes Sort Despite Index
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Cred, Flipkart, Walmart Labs · Topic: Sort avoidance · Engines: All
Setup:
CREATE TABLE notifications (
  notif_id      BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id       BIGINT,
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ,
  read_status   VARCHAR(10)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_notif_user_created ON notifications (user_id, created_at);
-- Want: latest 20 for a user
SELECT notif_id FROM notifications
WHERE user_id = 88012
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
Question: "EXPLAIN shows the index gets used for the WHERE but a Sort step appears after. The index
has created_at — why does the planner still sort?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "The index is ascending on (user_id, created_at). Within user_id =
88012, entries are sorted by created_at ASC. The ORDER BY wants created_at DESC." 2. 
"Postgres can read the B-tree backward — Index Scan Backward — and avoid the sort. But the
planner only does this if the ORDER BY exactly matches the index's reverse order. Sometimes it picks
Sort anyway if cost estimates differ." 3. "Cleanest fix: define the index in the order the query wants. 
CREATE INDEX ... ON notifications (user_id, created_at DESC). Now forward scan
satisfies the LIMIT directly." 4. "This also matters for composite ORDER BY with mixed directions — 
ORDER BY user_id ASC, created_at DESC. Backward scan only works if all columns flip
together. Mixed-direction ORDER BY needs an index with matching mixed directions, or a Sort step."
Diagnosis: Index sort order doesn't match ORDER BY direction; planner adds a Sort step.
Fix:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 401 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 402
CREATE INDEX idx_notif_user_created_desc
  ON notifications (user_id, created_at DESC);
DROP INDEX idx_notif_user_created;
Now LIMIT 20 returns after fetching 20 index entries; no sort.
Why: B-tree indexes have a fixed order. Reading backward works for unanimous reverse, but mixed-
direction ORDER BY needs a matching mixed-direction index.
NOT to say: "The planner should always read backward" — it does when it can; the issue is mixed
direction or cost estimates. "ORDER BY is always sortable for free" — only when the index provides the
order.
Follow-up: "What about ORDER BY user_id DESC, created_at ASC?" — Needs (user_id
DESC, created_at ASC) index, or accept a Sort. Postgres won't read part of an index in one
direction and part in the other.
Scenario336 · When to REINDEX
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Walmart Labs · Topic: Maintenance · Engines:
Postgres especially
Setup:
-- Production observability over 6 months
-- pg_stat_user_indexes shows idx_orders_customer fragmentation; bloat 45%
-- Lookups slowed from 2ms p99 to 18ms p99
Question: "When do you decide it's time to REINDEX a hot production index, and how do you do it
without taking the service down?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Indicators: index size growing faster than table size, bloat ratio (via 
pgstattuple) over 30%, latency on indexed lookups creeping up, 
pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan healthy but per-lookup time rising." 2. "Don't REINDEX on a
hunch. Measure bloat first — pgstattuple_approx(indexrelid) for cheap estimates on huge
indexes, pgstattuple for accurate (but slower) numbers." 3. "Use REINDEX INDEX
CONCURRENTLY (Postgres 12+). It builds the new index in parallel, takes only short locks at swap time.
Takes 1.5-2x longer than plain REINDEX but no exclusive lock." 4. "Schedule during low-traffic windows
even with CONCURRENTLY — the rebuild generates I/O and WAL. For very large indexes (100GB+),
consider partitioning the table so each partition's index is smaller and rebuildable independently."
Diagnosis: Heavy-write indexes accumulate bloat; periodic REINDEX restores compactness.
Fix:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 402 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 403
-- Measure first
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('idx_orders_customer'));
SELECT * FROM pgstattuple_approx('idx_orders_customer');
-- Rebuild online
REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_customer;
-- Confirm size shrank
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('idx_orders_customer'));
Why: VACUUM cleans dead tuples in the heap and marks dead index entries reusable, but doesn't
physically compact B-tree pages. REINDEX rebuilds the structure densely.
NOT to say: "REINDEX weekly on every index" — wasteful for low-write tables. "REINDEX always takes
the table down" — CONCURRENTLY exists.
Follow-up: "What if CONCURRENTLY fails halfway?" — It leaves a INVALID index behind (marked
unusable). Drop it manually and retry. pg_stat_user_indexes flags invalid indexes.
Scenario337 · VACUUM ANALYZE Cadence
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Cred, Razorpay, Goldman · Topic: Maintenance · Engines: Postgres
Setup:
-- 2TB OLTP table, 5K writes per second
-- Default autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.2 means autovacuum runs after
-- 20% of table changed = 400M rows; takes hours; floods I/O
Question: "On a 2TB Postgres OLTP table with heavy writes, default autovacuum thresholds are wrong.
How do you tune VACUUM and ANALYZE cadence?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "The default autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor is 0.2 (vacuum when 20%
of rows changed). On a 2TB table that's 400M dead tuples before autovacuum fires — bloat climbs,
queries slow, then a huge VACUUM hits and floods I/O." 2. "For large tables, tune per-table: ALTER
TABLE orders SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02); so vacuum kicks in after
2% changed instead of 20%. Smaller, more frequent VACUUMs are friendlier than infrequent huge ones."
3. "Same for ANALYZE — autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.01 on large tables keeps
stats fresh. Stats drift causes plan regressions; cheap to keep them current." 4. "Watch 
pg_stat_user_tables.last_autovacuum and n_dead_tup. If autovacuum is falling behind,
raise autovacuum_max_workers and autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit (default 200 throttles
aggressively)."
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 403 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 404
Diagnosis: Default autovacuum thresholds are tuned for medium tables; large OLTP tables need per-
table overrides.
Fix:
ALTER TABLE orders SET (
  autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor  = 0.02,
  autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.01,
  autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit    = 2000
);
Why: Autovacuum is throttled and proportional to table size. Defaults assume mid-sized tables; large
tables need tighter percentages.
NOT to say: "Disable autovacuum and run nightly VACUUM" — guarantees bloat during the day and a
thundering herd at night. "VACUUM FULL is the proper fix" — it locks the whole table; only for offline
maintenance.
Follow-up: "What's the right thing to monitor?" — n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum, 
n_mod_since_analyze, and bloat ratios from pgstattuple_approx. Alert when any of these
drift past thresholds.
Scenario338 · Indexes Bigger Than the Table
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Walmart Labs, Cred · Topic: Index sizing · Engines: All
Setup:
CREATE TABLE products (
  product_id    BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  sku           VARCHAR(40),
  name          VARCHAR(200),
  brand         VARCHAR(80),
  category_id   INT,
  price_paise   BIGINT,
  in_stock      BOOLEAN
);
-- Over time, 9 indexes added: sku, name, brand, category_id, price_paise,
-- in_stock, (brand, category_id), (category_id, price_paise), (sku, in_stock)
-- Table: 4 GB. Sum of indexes: 11 GB.
Question: "Indexes total 11GB on a 4GB table. Write throughput dropped to 60% of last quarter. What's
the assessment and what do you cut?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "Every INSERT updates every applicable index. Every UPDATE to an indexed
column updates that index. Nine indexes mean nine extra writes per row insert. That's the throughput
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 404 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 405
hit." 2. "Audit what's actually used: pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan shows lookup counts per
index. Anything with idx_scan = 0 over 30 days is dead weight — drop it." 3. "Then dedupe: 
(brand, category_id) and (category_id, price_paise) overlap nothing usable; a single
broader composite often serves both query shapes if column orders align. Check actual query patterns
first." 4. "Low-cardinality column indexes like in_stock (2 values) are almost always wasteful — partial
index WHERE in_stock = false if the rare value is queried; else drop."
Diagnosis: Index sprawl from years of one-off additions; write amplification crushes throughput.
Fix:
-- Find unused indexes
SELECT schemaname, relname, indexrelname, idx_scan, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexrelid))
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
WHERE idx_scan = 0
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(indexrelid) DESC;
-- Drop the dead weight
DROP INDEX idx_products_in_stock;
DROP INDEX idx_products_brand;        -- subsumed by (brand, category_id)
DROP INDEX idx_products_category;     -- subsumed by (category_id, price_paise)
Why: Indexes are write-amplifying. The mantra: every index has a cost; only keep ones whose lookups
pay for that cost.
NOT to say: "More indexes never hurts" — they do, on writes and on cache. "Just add storage" —
doesn't help throughput.
Follow-up: "How long should I observe idx_scan before dropping?" — At least one full business
cycle: 30 days minimum, 90 days for quarter-end report indexes.
Scenario339 · Bloat From Frequent Updates on Indexed Columns
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Cred, Razorpay, Walmart Labs · Topic: HOT updates · Engines: Postgres
Setup:
CREATE TABLE wallet_balances (
  wallet_id     BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  balance_paise BIGINT,
  last_txn_at   TIMESTAMPTZ
);
CREATE INDEX idx_wallet_last_txn ON wallet_balances (last_txn_at);
-- Every transaction updates balance_paise and last_txn_at
-- Index on last_txn_at bloats 10x in a month
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 405 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 406
Question: " last_txn_at updates every transaction. The index on it bloats badly. Postgres has HOT
updates that should help but they're not kicking in. Why, and what do you do?"
Thinking out loud: 1. "HOT (Heap-Only Tuple) updates in Postgres avoid index updates when (a) no
indexed column changes, and (b) the new tuple fits on the same page. Here last_txn_at IS indexed,
so HOT is disabled for these updates — every update writes a new heap tuple AND a new index entry." 2.
"Each new index entry pushes the dead one toward eventual VACUUM. Heavy update rate outruns
VACUUM; index grows." 3. "Two strategic options. (a) Drop the index on last_txn_at if the lookup it
supports is rare — restoring HOT eligibility. (b) Tune fillfactor lower (e.g., 70) so each page has
more free space, increasing the chance a HOT-tuple fits." 4. "For the wallet pattern specifically, a separate
wallet_activity table that's append-only often beats indexing the in-place balance column. Splits
the read pattern from the write hot-spot."
Diagnosis: Indexed column is being updated frequently, blocking HOT updates and bloating the index.
Fix:
-- Lower fillfactor to give more in-page room for HOT
ALTER TABLE wallet_balances SET (fillfactor = 70);
-- Reload existing data (CLUSTER or pg_repack) to apply
CLUSTER wallet_balances USING wallet_balances_pkey;
-- Or remove the bloat-causing index if it's not earning its keep
DROP INDEX idx_wallet_last_txn;
Why: HOT requires no indexed column to change. Index on a frequently-updated column blocks HOT,
causing index bloat and write amplification.
NOT to say: "Just REINDEX nightly" — masks the cause. "HOT is automatic in all cases" — only when
no indexed column changes and the new tuple fits.
Follow-up: "How do I check HOT update ratio?" — pg_stat_user_tables.n_tup_hot_upd /
n_tup_upd. Healthy systems are 90%+. If yours is below 50%, an indexed column is being updated
heavily.
Scenario340 · Online Index Creation Without Downtime
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Flipkart, Walmart Labs · Topic: Online DDL ·
Engines: All
Setup:
-- 800 GB orders table, p99 5ms; need to add an index on (vendor_id, created_at)
-- Cannot take downtime; cannot block writes for more than a few seconds
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 406 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 407
Question: "You need to add a multi-column index on an 800GB hot OLTP table without taking the
application down. Walk me through how you'd do it on Postgres, MySQL, and SQL Server."
Thinking out loud: 1. "Postgres: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. Takes only ShareUpdateExclusive
lock (not AccessExclusive); reads and writes proceed. Build takes 2-3x longer than blocking CREATE
INDEX because it does two table scans. Watch for INVALID index state on failure." 2. "MySQL InnoDB:
ALTER TABLE ... ADD INDEX ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE for most index types. Blocks
only briefly at the start and end. For huge tables and limits InnoDB can't handle, pt-online-schema-
change (Percona) or gh-ost (GitHub) build a shadow table and swap." 3. "SQL Server: CREATE
INDEX ... WITH (ONLINE = ON). Enterprise Edition only. Takes a brief schema-mod lock;
otherwise concurrent reads and writes work. Resumable Indexes (2017+) let you pause and resume long
builds." 4. "Across all engines: pick a low-traffic window, monitor replication lag (the WAL/binlog spike
from the build can stress replicas), set statement timeouts so a failed build doesn't hang forever, and
verify the new index name is unique before starting."
Diagnosis: Need to add an index online without blocking writes; each engine has its own primitive.
Fix:
-- Postgres
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_vendor_created
  ON orders (vendor_id, created_at);
-- Check for INVALID state
SELECT indexrelid::regclass FROM pg_index WHERE indisvalid = false;
-- MySQL 8 InnoDB
ALTER TABLE orders ADD INDEX idx_orders_vendor_created (vendor_id, created_at),
  ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE;
-- SQL Server (Enterprise)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_vendor_created
  ON dbo.orders (vendor_id, created_at)
  WITH (ONLINE = ON, RESUMABLE = ON);
Why: All major engines have online index build paths because production schema changes are
mandatory. Each uses a different mechanism (concurrent build, in-place ALTER, online index option) but
the goal is the same — no read/write downtime.
NOT to say: "Just take downtime" — unacceptable for OLTP services. "Use a maintenance window for
everything" — these primitives exist precisely so you don't have to.
Follow-up: "What if CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY fails halfway?" — Postgres leaves an INVALID
index. You must DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY it (still without blocking writes) before retrying. Always
script the retry path; never assume first-try success on multi-hour builds.

Category 6, Part A — Transaction Conflict: Deadlocks & Lock
Ordering
Two transactions enter, both want the same rows in different order, both block, the engine kills one —
that is the entire shape of every deadlock you will ever debug. Part A walks through how real-world
deadlocks form (transfers, hot rows, foreign keys, gap locks, lock escalation), how the engine detects
them (wait-for graph cycles), and the fixes you actually ship in production: deterministic lock ordering,
application-level retry with backoff, design changes that remove the conflict altogether (sharded
counters, atomic upserts, optimistic versioning), and the harder calls — when to reach for a saga instead
of a distributed transaction. Every scenario gives you a runnable two-transaction trace, the engine's
verbatim output, the diagnosis, and three fix options with trade-offs. Part B will pick up isolation-level
anomalies (lost updates, write skew, phantom reads) — read this part first; you cannot reason about
isolation bugs until the deadlock vocabulary is muscle memory.
Scenario341 · Two-Account Transfer Deadlock — The Classic
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Cred, JP Morgan · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
Two users initiate transfers at the same instant. Transaction T1 moves two thousand rupees from
account 101 to account 202. Transaction T2 moves five hundred rupees from account 202 to
account 101. Both transactions update the source account first, then the destination. Within
milliseconds the engine kills one of them with a deadlock error.
T1 (transaction 1):
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 2000 WHERE id = 101;
-- pauses here briefly while application logs the debit
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 2000 WHERE id = 202;
COMMIT;
T2 (transaction 2):
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 202;
-- pauses here briefly
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 101;
COMMIT;
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 408 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 409
What happens:
ERROR:  deadlock detected
DETAIL: Process 18421 waits for ShareLock on transaction 990012; blocked by process 18430.
        Process 18430 waits for ShareLock on transaction 990013; blocked by process 18421.
HINT:   See server log for query details.
Thinking out loud: 1. "T1 has held a row-exclusive lock on row 101 since its first UPDATE and now
wants 202." 2. "T2 has held a row-exclusive lock on row 202 and now wants 101 — that is a perfect
cycle." 3. "The wait-for graph contains an edge T1→T2 and T2→T1, so the deadlock detector picks one
victim and kills it. The other one finishes." 4. "Fix is deterministic lock ordering — lock the lower account
id first regardless of which direction the money moves."
The diagnosis: Each transaction has acquired an exclusive lock on one row and is waiting for the other.
The wait-for graph has a two-node cycle, which is the textbook deadlock. The engine's detector runs
every second or so, walks the graph, finds the cycle, and aborts the cheaper-to-rollback transaction.
The fix: - Option A — Lock ordering: Sort the two account ids before touching them. Always update the
smaller id first, then the larger. Both transactions now want 101 first, then 202; T2 waits cleanly for T1
and no cycle forms. - Option B — Application retry: Catch the deadlock SQLSTATE (40P01 in Postgres,
1213 in MySQL), wait fifty to two hundred milliseconds with jitter, then re-run the whole transaction.
Works only if the transaction is idempotent or you stamp it with a request id. - Option C — Atomic
ledger row: Insert a single row into a transfers table inside one statement, then let a trigger or a
nightly batch reconcile balances. Removes the two-row write entirely.
What NOT to say: - Do not claim "use SERIALIZABLE to fix it" — serializable makes it worse because
the engine takes more conservative locks and you get more deadlocks, not fewer.
Common follow-up: "How do you decide the lock order when the rows aren't numeric ids — say, two
UUIDs?"
Scenario342 · INSERT vs UPDATE Conflict on a Hot Row
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Swiggy, Zomato, Flipkart, Walmart Labs · Dialect: Postgres
The scenario:
A restaurant's daily_stats table has one row per (restaurant_id, date). T1 inserts a new row
for today during a midnight rollover job. T2, started a few milliseconds earlier, updates today's
row to bump the order counter. T1 sits and waits, then deadlocks.
T1 (rollover job):
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 409 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 410
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO daily_stats (restaurant_id, date, orders)
VALUES (4501, CURRENT_DATE, 0)
ON CONFLICT (restaurant_id, date) DO NOTHING;
UPDATE restaurants SET last_rollover_at = NOW() WHERE id = 4501;
COMMIT;
T2 (order ingestion):
BEGIN;
UPDATE restaurants SET total_orders = total_orders + 1 WHERE id = 4501;
INSERT INTO daily_stats (restaurant_id, date, orders) VALUES (4501, CURRENT_DATE, 1)
ON CONFLICT (restaurant_id, date) DO UPDATE SET orders = daily_stats.orders + 1;
COMMIT;
What happens: T1 holds the index lock on the new daily_stats row and wants the 
restaurants row 4501. T2 holds row 4501 in restaurants and is now waiting for the unique-
index slot on daily_stats. Postgres detects the cycle and aborts one.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Both transactions touch two tables but in opposite order — restaurant first vs
stats first." 2. "ON CONFLICT still acquires an index-level lock on the unique key while it figures out
whether to insert or update." 3. "Engine sees the cycle and kills the lower-priority transaction (Postgres
uses deadlock_timeout, default 1s)." 4. "Fix is to standardise the table order: every transaction touching
both must touch restaurants before daily_stats, or vice versa, but never mixed."
The diagnosis: This is a multi-table version of the classic deadlock. The cycle forms across tables, not
within one row. The trigger is that two transactions touched the same pair of resources in opposite order.
The fix: - Option A — Table-order convention: Document in the codebase: "Always update 
restaurants before daily_stats." Enforce in a code review checklist or a lint rule. - Option B —
Single statement: Push the counter bump into a single INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE so
the rollover job becomes a no-op when ingestion has already created the row. - Option C —
Background rollover: Drop the explicit rollover transaction entirely; let lazy creation via ON CONFLICT
in the ingestion path handle it. Run a cleanup job only for restaurants that had no orders.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "ON CONFLICT is atomic so it can't deadlock" — it is atomic at the row
level, but the surrounding transaction can still deadlock with other transactions touching different rows or
tables.
Common follow-up: "What if the unique index is on (restaurant_id, date) but you also have a partial index
on date where orders > 0 — does that change anything?"
