Scenario343 · Foreign Key Deadlock — Child INSERT Blocked by Parent UPDATE
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: PhonePe, Cred, Goldman, Wells Fargo · Dialect: MySQL InnoDB
The scenario:
An orders table has a foreign key to customers. T1 updates a customer's address. T2
inserts a new order for the same customer. The INSERT needs to verify the customer still exists,
which takes a shared lock on the parent row. T1 needs an exclusive lock on the parent, T2 needs
a shared lock. Then T1 also tries to insert an audit row — and the cycle closes.
T1 (customer update + audit):
BEGIN;
UPDATE customers SET address = 'new address' WHERE id = 7001;
INSERT INTO customer_audit (customer_id, change) VALUES (7001, 'address');
COMMIT;
T2 (new order):
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, amount) VALUES (7001, 1499);
UPDATE customers SET last_order_at = NOW() WHERE id = 7001;
COMMIT;
What happens:
ERROR 1213 (40001): Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction
Thinking out loud: 1. "T1 has an exclusive lock on customers(7001). T2's INSERT into orders
needs a shared lock on the parent for FK validation — it waits." 2. "T1 inserts into customer_audit,
which has its own FK back to customers — depending on InnoDB's lock cascade, it may need to
revalidate." 3. "Meanwhile, T2's second statement tries to take an X lock on customers(7001) — and
now there's a cycle: T1 holds X on customers, T2 waits for X, but T2 also holds the index slot on orders."
4. "InnoDB detects the wait-for cycle and aborts the smaller transaction (lowest weight, typically fewest
locks held)."
The diagnosis: Foreign-key checks acquire shared locks on parent rows. When a transaction updates
the parent and another inserts a child concurrently, the locks compete. The cycle forms when each
transaction needs both rows.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 411 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 412
The fix: - Option A — Skip FK locks: In MySQL, set foreign_key_checks = 0 for bulk inserts
(only when you can vouch for the data) — removes the shared lock acquisition on the parent. - Option B
— Defer the parent update: T2's second UPDATE on customers.last_order_at is the trigger.
Move it to an asynchronous worker that batches updates every few seconds. - Option C — Lock the
parent explicitly first: Both transactions issue SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the parent row at the
start. Everyone serializes on that lock, no cycle.
What NOT to say: - Do not advise "drop the foreign key" — it removes the symptom but loses the
integrity guarantee, and reviewers will catch it instantly.
Common follow-up: "InnoDB takes shared locks for FK checks. What about Postgres — does it behave
the same way?"
Scenario344 · Composite Key Lock Acquisition Order
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Myntra, Target, AmEx · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
An inventory table is keyed on (warehouse_id, sku). T1 decrements stock for SKU A in
warehouse 1, then SKU B in warehouse 2. T2 decrements SKU B in warehouse 2, then SKU A in
warehouse 1. Same two rows, opposite order, instant deadlock.
T1:
BEGIN;
UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE warehouse_id = 1 AND sku = 'A';
UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE warehouse_id = 2 AND sku = 'B';
COMMIT;
T2:
BEGIN;
UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE warehouse_id = 2 AND sku = 'B';
UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE warehouse_id = 1 AND sku = 'A';
COMMIT;
What happens: The engine kills one transaction with a deadlock error.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Composite keys do not help here — what matters is the order of physical row
locks, not the index structure." 2. "T1 holds (1, A), waits for (2, B). T2 holds (2, B), waits for (1, A). Cycle."
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 412 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 413
3. "The fix is the same as single-column: sort the row identifiers and acquire locks in a global order." 4. 
"For composite keys, sort by warehouse_id first, then sku — lexicographic order on the tuple."
The diagnosis: Composite keys do not change the deadlock arithmetic. The engine still holds row locks
indexed by the heap or clustered-index position. A consistent ordering rule, applied at the application
layer, eliminates the cycle.
The fix: - Option A — Lexicographic lock order: Sort the rows you intend to touch by (warehouse_id,
sku) before the first UPDATE. Both transactions converge to the same order. - Option B — Pre-flight
SELECT FOR UPDATE in order: Issue SELECT ... FOR UPDATE for all rows in sorted order at the
start of the transaction, then do the writes. - Option C — Batch operation: Replace N individual
UPDATEs with a single multi-row UPDATE statement; the engine handles locking internally and is far less
likely to deadlock.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "MySQL takes the lock on the primary key, so order doesn't matter" —
order matters at the row level, regardless of how the index is structured.
Common follow-up: "If the rows you need to lock are determined by a JOIN at runtime, how do you sort
them without first reading the data?"
Scenario345 · Index Gap Lock Deadlock — MySQL Repeatable Read
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Goldman, JP Morgan · Dialect: MySQL InnoDB
The scenario:
InnoDB at Repeatable Read takes gap locks on the index to prevent phantoms. T1 inserts an
order with id 5005. T2 inserts id 5007. Both inserts fall into the same index gap, and both
transactions get blocked on each other's gap lock — classic phantom-prevention deadlock.
T1:
BEGIN;
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id BETWEEN 5000 AND 5010 FOR UPDATE;
INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, amount) VALUES (5005, 7001, 1499);
COMMIT;
T2:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 413 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 414
BEGIN;
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id BETWEEN 5000 AND 5010 FOR UPDATE;
INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, amount) VALUES (5007, 7002, 999);
COMMIT;
What happens:
ERROR 1213 (40001): Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction
Thinking out loud: 1. "Both SELECTs at Repeatable Read take gap locks on the range (5000, 5010) on
the PK index." 2. "Gap locks are shared with other gap locks but block inserts into the gap." 3. "T1's
INSERT of 5005 needs an insert-intention lock that conflicts with T2's gap lock. T2's INSERT of 5007
conflicts with T1's gap lock. Cycle." 4. "Fix options: drop to READ COMMITTED, or use SELECT without
FOR UPDATE, or partition the id space so the two transactions never share a gap."
The diagnosis: MySQL InnoDB at REPEATABLE READ takes next-key locks (record + gap) on indexes
scanned by SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. Two transactions scanning the same range hold compatible
gap locks but their subsequent INSERTs request insert-intention locks that conflict with the other's gap
lock — instant cycle.
The fix: - Option A — READ COMMITTED: Switch the session or transaction to READ COMMITTED,
which disables gap locks. You give up phantom prevention but eliminate this entire class of deadlock. - 
Option B — Avoid the scan: Replace SELECT ... FOR UPDATE over a range with a lookup on the
exact id. Gap locks only appear on range scans. - Option C — Auto-assigned ids: Let the database
assign ids via auto-increment so each transaction inserts into a different physical position; the conflicting
gap never exists.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "REPEATABLE READ is always safer than READ COMMITTED" — in
MySQL it adds gap locks, which produce deadlocks that READ COMMITTED simply does not have.
Common follow-up: "Does Postgres have gap locks?"
Scenario346 · Both Transactions Wait on the Same Row
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Infosys, TCS, Wipro, Wells Fargo · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
T1 updates a row, doesn't commit. T2 updates the same row, waits. T3 arrives and also wants the
row, waits behind T2. Eventually T1's session times out or the application crashes — and both T2
and T3 are still waiting. No deadlock, just a stalled queue.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 414 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 415
T1:
BEGIN;
UPDATE invoices SET status = 'paid' WHERE id = 9001;
-- application hangs, never commits
T2:
BEGIN;
UPDATE invoices SET status = 'cancelled' WHERE id = 9001;
-- waiting for T1
What happens: T2 and T3 block indefinitely. The engine does not flag a deadlock because there is no
cycle — just a chain of waiters.
Thinking out loud: 1. "There is no cycle in the wait-for graph. The detector finds nothing. This is
starvation, not deadlock." 2. "The problem is T1's open transaction holding the lock. Engine has no way
to know T1 will never commit." 3. "Fix is at the connection layer: set lock_timeout or 
statement_timeout so waiters give up after, say, three seconds." 4. "Also set 
idle_in_transaction_session_timeout on Postgres so a hung T1 gets reaped automatically."
The diagnosis: A long-held lock is not a deadlock — it is a queue. The engine cannot help unless you
tell it how long you are willing to wait or how long a session may sit idle inside a transaction.
The fix: - Option A — Lock timeout: Set SET lock_timeout = '3s' per transaction so the waiter
aborts rather than blocking forever. - Option B — Idle-in-transaction timeout: Postgres has 
idle_in_transaction_session_timeout. Set it to ten seconds globally so a leaked connection
is killed. - Option C — Application-side circuit breaker: Wrap the UPDATE in a timer; if it doesn't return
in N seconds, cancel and surface the error to the user.
What NOT to say: - Do not call this a deadlock — it is a lock-wait timeout scenario, and interviewers test
whether you can distinguish them.
Common follow-up: "What's the default lock-wait timeout in MySQL? In Postgres?"
Scenario347 · SELECT FOR UPDATE Order Mismatch
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Stripe, PhonePe, Goldman · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 415 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 416
A booking service locks the seat row and the user row before issuing a ticket. T1 locks seat 42
then user 7001. T2, processing a different booking for the same user, locks user 7001 first then
seat 42. Both block, engine fires the deadlock detector.
T1:
BEGIN;
SELECT * FROM seats WHERE id = 42 FOR UPDATE;
SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 7001 FOR UPDATE;
INSERT INTO bookings (seat_id, user_id) VALUES (42, 7001);
COMMIT;
T2:
BEGIN;
SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 7001 FOR UPDATE;
SELECT * FROM seats WHERE id = 42 FOR UPDATE;
INSERT INTO bookings (seat_id, user_id) VALUES (42, 7001);
COMMIT;
What happens: Deadlock; one transaction is rolled back with the appropriate SQLSTATE.
Thinking out loud: 1. "FOR UPDATE takes explicit row-level exclusive locks. Same wait-for cycle as any
UPDATE-only deadlock." 2. "The bug is that the two code paths were written by different teams who
chose different lock orders." 3. "The fix is policy: every code path that locks multiple rows must do so in a
single documented order." 4. "Enforce with a helper function lock_for_booking(seat_id,

The diagnosis: Explicit row locks via FOR UPDATE deadlock exactly like UPDATE-induced locks. The
acquisition order is set by the application, so the fix lives in the application.
The fix: - Option A — Wrapper function: Centralise the lock acquisition in a single helper. No caller
chooses the order; the helper does, consistently. - Option B — Sort by table name: Adopt the rule
"always lock tables alphabetically by table name". Mechanical and easy to audit. - Option C —
NOWAIT: Use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT so the second waiter fails immediately and the
application can either retry in the canonical order or surface an error.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "FOR UPDATE is safer than UPDATE because the lock is explicit" — the
lock is the same row-level exclusive lock; the only difference is intent.
Common follow-up: "What does FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED do, and when would you use it for a

Scenario348 · Auto-Increment Lock Contention in MySQL
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Myntra, Walmart Labs, Goldman · Dialect: MySQL InnoDB
The scenario:
A high-throughput logging table uses id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT. Under heavy concurrent
INSERTs, throughput plateaus and you see waits on the table-level AUTO-INC lock. Occasionally
a multi-row INSERT deadlocks with a single-row INSERT.
T1 (multi-row insert):
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO event_log (event_type, payload) VALUES
  ('view', '...'), ('click', '...'), ('scroll', '...');
COMMIT;
T2 (single-row insert):
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO event_log (event_type, payload) VALUES ('purchase', '...');
COMMIT;
What happens: With innodb_autoinc_lock_mode = 1 (the traditional default), the multi-row
INSERT holds a special AUTO-INC table lock until it has reserved its block of ids. Other inserters wait.
Under specific orderings, this interacts with row locks elsewhere to form a deadlock.
Thinking out loud: 1. "AUTO-INC lock is a special table-level lock, not a row lock." 2. "Mode 0
(traditional) holds it for the whole INSERT — full serialization. Mode 1 (consecutive) holds it only until the
count is known. Mode 2 (interleaved) doesn't hold a lock but breaks statement-based replication." 3. "For
pure throughput on row-based replication, switch to mode 2." 4. "To avoid contention entirely, generate
ids in the application — UUID v7 or a Snowflake-style id."
The diagnosis: The MySQL AUTO-INC lock is a coarse-grained lock that limits concurrent INSERT
throughput. The mode controls how aggressively the lock is held; the deadlock arises only when the
AUTO-INC waiter is also waiting for a row lock held by a third transaction.
The fix: - Option A — Mode 2 (interleaved): Set innodb_autoinc_lock_mode = 2. Inserts no
longer wait on the AUTO-INC lock. Requires row-based binlog replication. - Option B — Application-
generated ids: Switch to UUIDs (preferably UUID v7 for index locality) or a Twitter-Snowflake style id.
The AUTO-INC lock disappears. - Option C — Batch the inserts: One multi-row INSERT replaces many
single-row ones. Fewer lock acquisitions per row inserted.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 417 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 418
What NOT to say: - Do not say "MySQL doesn't have a table-level lock for INSERT" — the AUTO-INC
lock is exactly that, and interviewers love when candidates know its name.
Common follow-up: "Why does UUID v4 hurt InnoDB performance, and what does UUID v7 fix?"
Scenario349 · Bulk UPDATE vs Many Single-Row UPDATEs
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Swiggy, Zomato, Target, AmEx · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A nightly job runs UPDATE orders SET status = 'archived' WHERE created_at <
NOW() - INTERVAL '90 days'. During the same window, a user-facing transaction updates
a single order in that range. The bulk job holds a wide range of row locks; the single-row update
deadlocks with it.
T1 (bulk archive):
BEGIN;
UPDATE orders SET status = 'archived'
WHERE created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '90 days';
COMMIT;
T2 (user-facing):
BEGIN;
UPDATE orders SET shipping_status = 'returned' WHERE id = 8042;
UPDATE customers SET return_count = return_count + 1 WHERE id = 7001;
COMMIT;
What happens: T1 holds a row lock on order 8042 (among thousands of others). T2 waits on order 8042
but also already holds the customer lock. T1 then needs the customer for an FK validation chain —
deadlock.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Bulk updates take a row lock per matched row. With thousands of rows, the lock
footprint is huge." 2. "The cycle forms when the bulk job needs any other resource — even an FK shared
lock — that the small transaction already holds." 3. "Fix: chunk the bulk update into batches of, say, one
thousand rows with a sleep or commit between chunks." 4. "Better: run the bulk job in a maintenance
window with a LOCK TABLE ... IN ROW EXCLUSIVE MODE that locks out the OLTP path cleanly."
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 418 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 419
The diagnosis: Bulk DML holds locks for the duration of the statement. With concurrent OLTP traffic, the
bulk job becomes a deadlock magnet because every other transaction is one row away from sharing a
resource with it.
The fix: - Option A — Chunked bulk update: Loop in batches with explicit commits between, so each
batch holds only N row locks for a short time. - Option B — Maintenance window: Schedule the bulk
job for low-traffic hours and accept the trade-off. - Option C — Move to a separate archive table: Use
partition switching (Postgres declarative partitioning or SQL Server partition swap) — flips an entire
partition into the archive table without row locks.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "use WITH (NOLOCK)" — that is SQL Server dirty-read hint, doesn't
apply to UPDATEs, and is the wrong answer to a write conflict anyway.
Common follow-up: "How would you chunk a multi-million row archive job without scanning the same
table over and over?"
Scenario350 · Lock Escalation Cascade in SQL Server
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: AmEx, JP Morgan, Goldman, Walmart Labs · Dialect: SQL Server
The scenario:
A transaction holds row locks on five thousand rows. SQL Server's lock-escalation threshold
(around five thousand locks on a single table) trips, and the row locks are escalated to a table-
level intent-exclusive lock. Another transaction holding a small number of row locks elsewhere on
the same table now blocks; if its locks are needed by the escalating transaction, you get a
deadlock.
T1 (large update):
BEGIN TRAN;
UPDATE orders SET region = 'south'
WHERE customer_state IN ('TN', 'KL', 'KA', 'AP', 'TS');
-- ~5000 rows; lock escalation to table lock triggers
T2 (small concurrent update):
BEGIN TRAN;
UPDATE orders SET status = 'cancelled' WHERE id = 99001;
-- already holds row lock on 99001
COMMIT TRAN;

PAGE 420
What happens: T1 attempts to escalate to a table-level X lock. T2 holds a row lock that conflicts with the
escalation. SQL Server fails the escalation, retries; if T2 then needs another row T1 has just locked, you
get a deadlock.
Thinking out loud: 1. "SQL Server escalates to table or partition lock when row-lock count crosses the
threshold." 2. "Escalation is opportunistic — it tries, fails, retries — but combined with a concurrent
transaction it can cycle." 3. "Disable escalation per table with ALTER TABLE ... SET
(LOCK_ESCALATION = DISABLE) if memory allows." 4. "Or partition the table so escalation only
affects one partition, not the whole table."
The diagnosis: Lock escalation reduces lock-manager memory pressure by exchanging many fine-
grained locks for one coarse lock. Under concurrent load this can cause deadlocks because the coarse
lock conflicts with row locks held by other sessions.
The fix: - Option A — Disable escalation on hot tables: ALTER TABLE orders SET
(LOCK_ESCALATION = DISABLE). Trades memory for fewer deadlocks. - Option B — Use partition-
level escalation: LOCK_ESCALATION = AUTO with a partitioned table; escalation stops at the
partition. - Option C — Chunk the large update: Keep the row-lock count under the threshold; no
escalation ever fires.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "use WITH (ROWLOCK)" hint — it is a hint, not a contract, and the
engine will still escalate under memory pressure.
Common follow-up: "What is the default lock-escalation threshold in SQL Server, and how does it
interact with trace flag 1224?"
Scenario351 · Hot Row in an Invoicing Counter
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, PhonePe, Stripe · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
Every invoice needs a sequential invoice number. The application reads the next_number from
a counters table, increments it, writes it back, and uses it. Under concurrent load, every
transaction serializes on that one row; throughput collapses to single-threaded.
T1:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 420 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 421
BEGIN;
SELECT next_number FROM counters WHERE name = 'invoice' FOR UPDATE;
-- application reads, increments to N+1
UPDATE counters SET next_number = next_number + 1 WHERE name = 'invoice';
INSERT INTO invoices (number, ...) VALUES (N, ...);
COMMIT;
T2 (identical):
BEGIN;
SELECT next_number FROM counters WHERE name = 'invoice' FOR UPDATE;
-- blocks until T1 commits
...
What happens: No deadlock — just serialization. Throughput is one transaction per round-trip. The
counter row is the bottleneck.
Thinking out loud: 1. "This is contention, not a deadlock. There is no cycle, just a queue on one row." 2. 
"Fix is to either remove the SELECT (use atomic UPDATE ... RETURNING) or shard the counter across
many rows." 3. "Atomic UPDATE shortens the lock window from two round-trips to one." 4. "Sharded
counter scales horizontally — N counter rows give roughly N times the throughput."
The diagnosis: Single-row counters are a known anti-pattern under load. Every transaction serialises on
the row's exclusive lock. The fix is to either shrink the critical section or spread the contention.
The fix: - Option A — Atomic UPDATE ... RETURNING: UPDATE counters SET next_number =
next_number + 1 WHERE name = 'invoice' RETURNING next_number. One statement; lock
held only for the UPDATE's duration. - Option B — Sharded counter: Keep N rows for the same
counter; each transaction picks one at random and increments it. Reassemble with a SUM at read time.
Trade-off: ids are no longer strictly sequential. - Option C — Sequence object: Postgres has
SEQUENCE, SQL Server has SEQUENCE, MySQL 8 has AUTO_INCREMENT or a generator function.
These are designed exactly for this.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "use a UUID instead" — invoice numbers usually have a regulatory or
human-readable requirement; UUIDs do not satisfy it.
Common follow-up: "If invoice numbers must be strictly sequential with no gaps, can you still use a
sequence?"
Scenario352 · Sharded Counter Pattern as the Fix
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Cred, Flipkart, Walmart Labs, Google · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:

hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 422
Following Scenario 11, you migrate the invoice counter to a sharded design with sixteen counter
rows. Throughput improves twenty-fold. But now a reporting query that needs the current total
scans all sixteen rows and occasionally sees an inconsistent total.
Schema:
CREATE TABLE counters_sharded (
  name TEXT,
  shard SMALLINT,
  value BIGINT,
  PRIMARY KEY (name, shard)
);
Writer:
UPDATE counters_sharded
SET value = value + 1
WHERE name = 'invoice' AND shard = MOD(ABS(HASHTEXT(SESSION_ID())), 16);
Reader:
SELECT SUM(value) FROM counters_sharded WHERE name = 'invoice';
What happens: The SUM is correct on consistent snapshots (Postgres MVCC) but may double-count or
miss under READ COMMITTED if writes happen between the per-row reads in a non-snapshot engine.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Sharding kills the deadlock and the queue but changes the read pattern." 2. 
"Reader needs a consistent snapshot across all shards — Postgres REPEATABLE READ or
SERIALIZABLE gives it." 3. "For MySQL InnoDB, REPEATABLE READ also gives a consistent snapshot
for the read." 4. "For an approximate counter, READ COMMITTED is fine and faster."
The diagnosis: Sharded counters trade write contention for read complexity. The reader needs snapshot
isolation to see a consistent sum.
The fix: - Option A — Snapshot read: Run the SUM in a REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE
transaction. - Option B — Approximate counter: Accept that the SUM is a recent-but-not-instant value.
Cache it for thirty seconds. - Option C — Two-table pattern: Increment a sharded counter for speed;
periodically materialise the SUM into a counter_totals row for cheap reads.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "use a single counter for reads" — that reintroduces the bottleneck you
just engineered around.
Common follow-up: "How would you decide between 16 shards and 64 shards?"

Scenario353 · Atomic UPDATE col = col + 1 vs SELECT-then-UPDATE
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Wells Fargo, Walmart · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A like counter on a social post is incremented as SELECT likes FROM posts WHERE id =
X; ... UPDATE posts SET likes = N + 1 WHERE id = X. Under concurrent likes, the
final count is wrong — N appears when two users liked at the same time, not 2N.
Bad pattern:
SELECT likes FROM posts WHERE id = 9001;
-- application reads likes = 10
UPDATE posts SET likes = 11 WHERE id = 9001;
Correct pattern:
UPDATE posts SET likes = likes + 1 WHERE id = 9001 RETURNING likes;
What happens: With the read-modify-write pattern at READ COMMITTED, two concurrent transactions
both read 10, both write 11, and one increment is lost.
Thinking out loud: 1. "This is the lost-update anomaly in its simplest form." 2. "Atomic UPDATE removes
the race because the read-and-write happen inside one row lock." 3. "Alternative is optimistic locking —
add a version column, only update if version matches." 4. "Or upgrade isolation to REPEATABLE READ,
which detects the lost update and aborts the second transaction."
The diagnosis: Read-modify-write across a transaction boundary leaks the intermediate value. The
engine has no idea your UPDATE depends on what you SELECTed. Atomic UPDATE compresses the
operation into a single locked statement.
The fix: - Option A — Atomic UPDATE: UPDATE posts SET likes = likes + 1 WHERE id =
X. Always correct under any isolation level. - Option B — Optimistic version: UPDATE posts SET
likes = N+1, version = version+1 WHERE id = X AND version = V. Retry on zero rows
affected. - Option C — SELECT FOR UPDATE: Lock the row at read time so the second transaction
waits. Higher latency, simpler logic.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "this is fine because the write is fast" — speed has nothing to do with it;
the race exists at any latency.

Scenario354 · Distributed Deadlock Across Two Databases
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs, Stripe · Dialect: vendor-agnostic +
distributed
The scenario:
A booking service writes to a bookings database in Mumbai. A payments service writes to a 
payments database in Singapore. T1 holds a booking row in Mumbai and waits for a payment
row in Singapore. T2 holds the payment row in Singapore and waits for the booking row in
Mumbai. Neither database can see the cycle.
T1 (booking service):
-- Mumbai DB
BEGIN;
UPDATE bookings SET status = 'pending_payment' WHERE id = 5001;
-- now calls payments service which opens transaction in Singapore
T2 (payments service):
-- Singapore DB
BEGIN;
UPDATE payments SET status = 'reconciling' WHERE booking_id = 5001;
-- now calls booking service which tries to open transaction in Mumbai
What happens: Each database holds its own lock and waits on the other. Neither has a global wait-for
graph, so neither can detect the cycle. Both transactions hang until the application timeout fires.
Thinking out loud: 1. "No single database has the global view, so neither detector triggers." 2. "Two-
phase commit with a transaction manager could detect it, but XA is operationally painful and rare in
modern Indian stacks." 3. "The pragmatic fix is the saga pattern — break the work into local transactions
with compensating actions." 4. "Alternative is to centralise all writes for one entity in one database —
single source of truth."
The diagnosis: Distributed deadlock has no automatic detector outside of a coordinated transaction
manager. You either prevent it via design (saga, single source of truth) or detect it via timeouts at the
application layer.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 424 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 425
The fix: - Option A — Saga pattern: Local transactions chained with explicit compensations. No
distributed lock state to deadlock. - Option B — XA / two-phase commit: A transaction coordinator
manages locks across both DBs and can detect cycles. Heavyweight and slow. - Option C — Strict
ordering: Always lock the booking before the payment, in every code path. Prevents the cycle by
convention.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "Postgres can detect distributed deadlocks" — it cannot; it only sees its
own wait-for graph.
Common follow-up: "Draw the saga for a booking-then-payment workflow including the compensation
transactions."
Scenario355 · Long-Running Transaction Holding Locks
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Wipro, Wells Fargo, JP Morgan · Dialect: Postgres + MySQL
The scenario:
A reporting query runs inside a transaction with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE for "consistency".
It takes thirty minutes. For thirty minutes, every OLTP write blocks behind it. The team blames the
database; the database is fine.
T1:
BEGIN;
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days' FOR UPDATE;
-- 30-minute report generation
COMMIT;
T2:
UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped' WHERE id = 9001;
-- waits 30 minutes
What happens: No deadlock — just one transaction starving every other writer that touches the locked
rows.
Thinking out loud: 1. "FOR UPDATE on a reporting query is almost always a bug. Reports should be
read-only." 2. "Remove FOR UPDATE entirely and use REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE for
snapshot consistency." 3. "Or move the report to a read replica." 4. "If you really must lock, lock only the
rows you intend to modify."
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 425 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 426
The diagnosis: Long-running transactions hold locks for their entire duration. The bug is using FOR
UPDATE on read-only work.
The fix: - Option A — Drop FOR UPDATE: Use plain SELECT inside REPEATABLE READ for snapshot
consistency without writer-blocking locks. - Option B — Read replica: Send reports to a replica; OLTP
traffic is unaffected. - Option C — Statement timeout: Set statement_timeout = '5min' so a
runaway report dies before causing damage.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "FOR UPDATE prevents the data from changing during the report" — it
does, but at the cost of blocking writes; that is rarely the trade-off you want.

Scenario356 · Idle-in-Transaction Warning in Postgres
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Swiggy, Google · Dialect: Postgres
The scenario:
A background worker opens a transaction, does one INSERT, and then waits for a Kafka message
before committing. The Kafka consumer hangs. Postgres now has a connection in idle in
transaction state for hours, holding locks and bloating MVCC.
Symptom:
$ select state, query from pg_stat_activity where state like 'idle in%';
state               | query
idle in transaction | INSERT INTO outbox (event_type, payload) VALUES ($1, $2)
What happens: The transaction holds row locks and prevents vacuum on the table. Other transactions
either block on the locks or, more insidiously, accumulate dead tuples that vacuum cannot reclaim.
Performance degrades over hours.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Idle-in-transaction is the silent killer in Postgres. No alert by default; just slow
degradation." 2. "Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '60s' globally so a stuck
connection is killed automatically." 3. "Don't hold a transaction across an external network call. Commit,
send to Kafka, then start a new transaction if you need a follow-up write." 4. "Use the outbox pattern:
write the event row inside the original transaction, let a separate worker pick it up and publish."
The diagnosis: Holding a database transaction across an external call is a structural bug. The fix is the
outbox pattern or an immediate commit.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 426 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 427
The fix: - Option A — idle_in_transaction_session_timeout: Postgres kills any session
sitting idle in a transaction past the limit. Belt-and-braces protection. - Option B — Outbox pattern:
Write the message to an outbox table inside the transaction, commit, then a separate worker reads
outbox and publishes to Kafka. - Option C — Commit before the network call: If correctness allows,
commit the DB write first, then do the network call. Accept that the network call may fail, requiring a retry.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "Postgres handles this automatically" — it does not, unless you
configure idle_in_transaction_session_timeout.

Scenario357 · Retry with Exponential Backoff
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Stripe, PhonePe, Goldman · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
The application is hitting deadlocks under load. The fix is to retry the failed transaction. A naive 
retry 3 times makes the problem worse — all victims retry simultaneously and re-collide.
Production needs exponential backoff with jitter.
Pattern (pseudocode):
for attempt in 1..max_attempts:
  try:
    BEGIN;
    ...work...
    COMMIT;
    break
  except DeadlockError:
    sleep(min(2^attempt * base_ms, cap_ms) + random_jitter_ms)
    continue
SQL hooks:
-- Postgres: SQLSTATE 40P01 (deadlock_detected) or 40001 (serialization_failure)
-- MySQL: error 1213 (deadlock) or 1205 (lock wait timeout)
-- SQL Server: error number 1205
Thinking out loud: 1. "The naive retry stampedes. Jitter spreads the retries across a time window so they
don't re-collide." 2. "Exponential backoff caps the worst-case wait but starts cheap." 3. "Always cap the
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 427 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 428
attempt count — three to five — to avoid retrying through a real outage." 4. "Distinguish deadlock from
lock timeout; both are retriable but other errors (constraint violation) are not."
The diagnosis: Deadlock is a transient condition. The right response is to retry, but the retry policy
needs jitter and caps to avoid making the problem worse.
The fix: - Option A — Exponential backoff with jitter: delay = base * 2^attempt +
uniform(0, jitter). Industry standard. - Option B — Library-level retry: Use a library (Spring
Retry, Polly, Tenacity) so policy is consistent across the codebase. - Option C — Decorrelated jitter
(AWS-recommended): delay = uniform(base, prev_delay * 3). Spreads retries even better
than full jitter.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "retry forever" — eventually the policy makes the deadlock worse and
you mask real bugs.
Common follow-up: "How do you make the transaction safe to retry — what's the idempotency story?"
Scenario358 · Idempotency Before Retry

The scenario:
The retry policy in Scenario 17 fires on a payment-creation transaction. Without idempotency, the

deadlock error fired — though usually it didn't.

CREATE TABLE payments (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,

  ...

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO payments (request_id, amount) VALUES ($1, $2)
ON CONFLICT (request_id) DO NOTHING
RETURNING id;
COMMIT;

Thinking out loud: 1. "The first deadlocked attempt aborts cleanly — but in distributed systems we
cannot always be sure." 2. "Idempotency key on a unique constraint converts a retry into a no-op." 3.

Scenario359 · Statement Retry vs Transaction Retry
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Walmart Labs, Razorpay · Dialect: vendor-
agnostic
The scenario:
Your ORM has a built-in retry that re-runs the failed statement on deadlock. The transaction
continues with subsequent statements. This is silently wrong: a deadlock aborts the entire
transaction in every major engine, and the connection is now in an error state.
Bad pattern:
# pseudo-Python with broken statement-level retry
with conn.begin():
  conn.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1")
  for attempt in range(3):
    try:
      conn.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2")
      break
    except DeadlockError:
      continue  # WRONG: transaction is already aborted
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 429 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 430
Correct pattern:
for attempt in range(3):
  try:
    with conn.begin():
      conn.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1")
      conn.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2")
    break
  except DeadlockError:
    sleep(backoff(attempt))
Thinking out loud: 1. "A deadlock aborts the whole transaction. The session must issue ROLLBACK and
start a new BEGIN." 2. "Retry must wrap the entire transaction — every statement — not just the one that
failed." 3. "Postgres explicitly errors out on subsequent statements with 'current transaction is aborted'."
4. "This is one of the most common ORM-related bugs in production Indian fintech codebases."
The diagnosis: The retry boundary must match the transaction boundary. Statement-level retry inside an
aborted transaction is invalid; the engine rejects every subsequent statement until ROLLBACK.
The fix: - Option A — Wrap the transaction: Retry loop outside the BEGIN... COMMIT block. - 
Option B — Library-level transaction retry: Use a library that understands transaction boundaries (e.g.,
Spring's @Retryable on a @Transactional method). - Option C — Stateful retry helper: A
custom helper that owns the connection, knows when it's safe to retry, and recreates the transaction
context.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "Postgres will let you retry the failed statement" — it will not; the next
statement returns SQLSTATE 25P02.
Common follow-up: "What is SQLSTATE 25P02 and when do you see it?"
Scenario360 · Read-Modify-Write Race Even at Repeatable Read
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Cred, Stripe, Goldman, Google · Dialect: Postgres + MySQL
The scenario:
A transaction at REPEATABLE READ reads a row, computes a new value, writes it back. Surely
the snapshot protects it? In MySQL InnoDB, yes — REPEATABLE READ takes locks that prevent
lost updates. In Postgres, no — REPEATABLE READ uses snapshot isolation, which detects lost
updates and aborts one transaction (the engine raises a serialization failure).
T1:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 430 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 431
-- Postgres, REPEATABLE READ
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 101;  -- reads 5000
UPDATE accounts SET balance = 5500 WHERE id = 101;
COMMIT;
T2 (concurrent):
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 101;  -- reads 5000
UPDATE accounts SET balance = 5300 WHERE id = 101;
COMMIT;
What happens (Postgres):
ERROR:  could not serialize access due to concurrent update
HINT:   The transaction might succeed if retried.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Postgres REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation. It detects the lost update and
aborts the second transaction." 2. "MySQL REPEATABLE READ is different — it uses next-key locks; the
second SELECT would block until T1 commits." 3. "This is the most surprising cross-engine difference in
isolation behavior." 4. "Fix is the standard read-modify-write fix: atomic UPDATE, optimistic version, or
SELECT FOR UPDATE."
The diagnosis: REPEATABLE READ in Postgres protects you against the lost update by aborting the
second transaction with a serialization failure. You still need to retry.
The fix: - Option A — Retry with backoff: Catch SQLSTATE 40001 and retry the entire transaction. - 
Option B — Atomic UPDATE: Replace the read-modify-write with UPDATE ... SET col =
expression. No snapshot, no failure. - Option C — Application-level optimistic: Add a version
column; UPDATE WHERE version = old_version. Retry on zero rows affected.
What NOT to say: - Do not assume "Postgres and MySQL REPEATABLE READ behave the same" —
they do not.
Common follow-up: "What does SERIALIZABLE add on top of Postgres REPEATABLE READ, and when
is the extra cost worth it?"
Scenario361 · INSERT ... ON CONFLICT Atomic Upsert
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Razorpay, Stripe, Swiggy, Walmart · Dialect: Postgres + MySQL
The scenario:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 431 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 432
A device-registration endpoint inserts a row keyed on (user_id, device_id). If the row exists,
update last_seen. The naive pattern of SELECT-then-INSERT-or-UPDATE races: two concurrent
requests both SELECT, see nothing, both INSERT, one fails with a unique-key violation. Worse, in
MySQL with auto-increment, you have already burned an id.
Bad pattern:
SELECT id FROM devices WHERE user_id = 7001 AND device_id = 'abc';
-- nothing returned
INSERT INTO devices (user_id, device_id, last_seen) VALUES (7001, 'abc', NOW());
-- ERROR: duplicate key
Correct pattern (Postgres):
INSERT INTO devices (user_id, device_id, last_seen)
VALUES (7001, 'abc', NOW())
ON CONFLICT (user_id, device_id)
DO UPDATE SET last_seen = EXCLUDED.last_seen;
Correct pattern (MySQL):
INSERT INTO devices (user_id, device_id, last_seen)
VALUES (7001, 'abc', NOW())
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE last_seen = VALUES(last_seen);
Thinking out loud: 1. "Upsert is the right primitive for 'register or refresh'." 2. "Both engines have atomic
upserts; use them instead of building one out of SELECT + INSERT/UPDATE." 3. "In MySQL, ON
DUPLICATE KEY can burn auto-increment ids; partial mitigation is INSERT IGNORE for the no-update
case." 4. "In Postgres, ON CONFLICT requires a unique or exclusion constraint to target."
The diagnosis: SELECT-then-act is a race waiting to happen. Atomic upsert compresses the decision
into a single statement under a single lock.
The fix: - Option A — Native upsert: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (Postgres) / INSERT ... ON
DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE (MySQL). - Option B — INSERT then UPDATE on conflict: Try INSERT,
catch duplicate-key, run UPDATE. Works but doubles round-trips on conflict. - Option C — MERGE
statement: SQL Server and Postgres 15+ have MERGE — see Scenario 22 for its concurrency caveats.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "wrap SELECT-then-INSERT in a transaction and it's safe" — it is not,
unless you also SELECT FOR UPDATE the key, and even then you may need to handle phantoms.

Scenario362 · MERGE INTO Concurrency Bug in SQL Server
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, AmEx, JP Morgan, Goldman · Dialect: SQL Server (and
Postgres 15+)
The scenario:
A MERGE INTO statement is used as an upsert. Under concurrent load, you start seeing primary-
key violations on the INSERT branch even though you "checked" via MERGE. SQL Server's
MERGE has a well-known concurrency hole: between the WHEN MATCHED check and the
INSERT, another transaction can insert the row.
Vulnerable pattern:
MERGE devices AS target
USING (VALUES (7001, 'abc')) AS src(user_id, device_id)
ON target.user_id = src.user_id AND target.device_id = src.device_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET last_seen = SYSUTCDATETIME()
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (user_id, device_id, last_seen)
                       VALUES (src.user_id, src.device_id, SYSUTCDATETIME());
Hardened pattern:
MERGE devices WITH (HOLDLOCK) AS target
USING (VALUES (7001, 'abc')) AS src(user_id, device_id)
ON target.user_id = src.user_id AND target.device_id = src.device_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET last_seen = SYSUTCDATETIME()
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (user_id, device_id, last_seen)
                       VALUES (src.user_id, src.device_id, SYSUTCDATETIME());
Thinking out loud: 1. "MERGE without HOLDLOCK takes shared locks that other transactions can also
take. Two MERGEs can both decide 'NOT MATCHED' and both try to INSERT." 2. "HOLDLOCK upgrades
the lock to a key-range lock that prevents phantom inserts." 3. "Postgres 15 added MERGE; check its
concurrency semantics carefully — INSERT ... ON CONFLICT is still simpler." 4. "For high-concurrency
upserts in SQL Server, many teams prefer IF EXISTS-style explicit branches with HOLDLOCK over
MERGE."
The diagnosis: MERGE without explicit lock hints in SQL Server is not atomic across concurrent
sessions. The fix is HOLDLOCK or switching to INSERT-then-UPDATE.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 433 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 434
The fix: - Option A — WITH (HOLDLOCK): Forces a key-range lock that prevents phantom inserts. - 
Option B — Use INSERT-then-UPDATE pattern: Try INSERT inside TRY/CATCH; on duplicate-key,
UPDATE. - Option C — Avoid MERGE for upserts: Many SQL Server experts (Aaron Bertrand among
them) recommend never using MERGE for upserts due to its bug history.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "MERGE is atomic by definition" — the statement is, but its semantics
regarding concurrent inserts are surprising.
Common follow-up: "Why has MERGE been called 'Microsoft's gift to people who hate their DBAs'?"
Scenario363 · Range Lock from REPEATABLE READ Scan
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: PhonePe, Cred, JP Morgan, Goldman · Dialect: MySQL InnoDB
The scenario:
A reporting transaction at REPEATABLE READ scans SELECT SUM(amount) FROM payments
WHERE created_at >= '2026-05-01'. InnoDB takes next-key locks on the index, blocking
concurrent INSERTs into that date range. A morning standup explains why "the database is slow"
— it isn't; it's locked.
T1 (report):
BEGIN;
SELECT SUM(amount) FROM payments WHERE created_at >= '2026-05-01' FOR UPDATE;
-- runs for 90 seconds
T2 (writer):
INSERT INTO payments (amount, created_at) VALUES (499, '2026-05-26 11:00:00');
-- blocks for 90 seconds
Thinking out loud: 1. "Even without FOR UPDATE, REPEATABLE READ in MySQL takes next-key locks if
the engine thinks it needs to prevent phantoms." 2. "With FOR UPDATE the locks are explicit and
definitely block writers." 3. "Fix: drop FOR UPDATE; drop to READ COMMITTED for the report; or send
the report to a read replica." 4. "Or use a covering index that lets the engine use a non-locking snapshot
read path."
The diagnosis: REPEATABLE READ in MySQL InnoDB uses next-key locks on range scans, which block
inserts into the range. The combination of REPEATABLE READ + FOR UPDATE + long-running query is a
writer-starvation pattern.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 434 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 435
The fix: - Option A — READ COMMITTED: Switch session to READ COMMITTED; uses single-row
locks, no gap locks. - Option B — Drop FOR UPDATE: Report queries are read-only; FOR UPDATE is a
bug. - Option C — Read replica: Reports run on the replica with zero impact on the OLTP primary.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "the engine should release locks faster" — locks are held until COMMIT
by design.
Common follow-up: "Postgres MVCC doesn't take read locks at REPEATABLE READ — why does

Scenario364 · Application Lock vs Database Lock — Trade-offs
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Stripe, Cred, Goldman · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A leader-election routine for a background job needs to ensure only one instance runs at a time.
Option A is SELECT pg_advisory_lock(42). Option B is a Redis SET NX EX. Option C is a
database row with an exclusive lock and a heartbeat. Which one and why?
Postgres advisory lock:
SELECT pg_advisory_lock(42);
-- holder runs the job
SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(42);
Redis lock:
SET job_lock $instance_id NX EX 30
-- holder renews every 10s
DEL job_lock when done
Database row lock:
UPDATE job_leadership
SET leader = 'instance-A', last_heartbeat = NOW()
WHERE job = 'archive'
  AND (last_heartbeat < NOW() - INTERVAL '30 sec' OR leader = 'instance-A')
RETURNING leader;
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 435 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 436
Thinking out loud: 1. "Advisory locks are cheap, but tied to the connection — if the connection dies, the
lock releases (good for liveness, bad for orphan-detection)." 2. "Redis is fast but introduces an extra
dependency and is famously hard to make correct under partition (see Martin Kleppmann on Redlock)." 3.
"Database row with heartbeat is most portable; you control the timeout." 4. "For multi-process leader
election within one DB, advisory locks are the sweet spot."
The diagnosis: "Lock" is overloaded. Pick the right kind for the use case: in-process for in-memory
state, advisory for inter-process coordination, row-level for data, distributed for cross-service.
The fix (option = recommendation per use case): - Advisory lock (Postgres pg_advisory_lock,
MySQL GET_LOCK): Best for leader election within one database, low overhead. - Row lock with
heartbeat: Best when you need explicit ownership tracking, take-over after crash, audit log. - Redis (or
Etcd, ZooKeeper): Best when coordination spans services that don't share a database.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "Redlock is the standard for distributed locks" — its correctness is hotly
debated, and many teams have moved to Etcd or ZooKeeper for hard locks.
Common follow-up: "Walk through one scenario where Redlock loses the lock guarantee."
Scenario365 · Deadlock Timeout vs Lock Timeout
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Goldman, JP Morgan, Wells Fargo, AmEx · Dialect: Postgres +
MySQL + SQL Server
The scenario:
Engineering wants to "lower the deadlock timeout to fix slow transactions". But deadlock timeout
and lock-wait timeout are different settings with different effects. Confusing them is a common
interview trap.
Postgres: - deadlock_timeout (default 1s): how long to wait before running the deadlock detector.
Lower means faster detection, higher CPU. - lock_timeout (default 0 = wait forever): how long a
statement waits for a lock before aborting with an error.
MySQL InnoDB: - innodb_deadlock_detect (ON/OFF): whether to run the detector at all. - 
innodb_lock_wait_timeout (default 50s): how long to wait for a lock.
SQL Server: - Deadlocks detected by a continuously running monitor; no timeout setting. - SET
LOCK_TIMEOUT 5000 (ms): per-session lock wait timeout.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Deadlock timeout in Postgres is detector frequency, not a wait-for-deadlock
timeout." 2. "Lock timeout is the right knob for 'don't wait forever'." 3. "For an OLTP app, lock_timeout of
two to five seconds is sane." 4. "For batch jobs, longer is fine, but document the choice."
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 436 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 437
The diagnosis: The two timeouts solve different problems. Use lock_timeout to bound waiter latency;
leave deadlock_timeout alone unless you have specific evidence.
The fix (no single fix — choice depends on goal): - For latency-sensitive OLTP: SET lock_timeout
= '3s' per transaction. - For Postgres deadlock detection latency: Lower deadlock_timeout to
500ms only if your workload is highly contended. - For MySQL: Tune innodb_lock_wait_timeout
down from 50s — typical default is too long.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "lowering deadlock_timeout fixes deadlocks faster" in Postgres — it
makes the detector run more often, but the deadlock itself is not resolved any sooner than the next
detection cycle.
Common follow-up: "Postgres runs the deadlock detector lazily. What's the worst-case latency from
cycle formation to deadlock-error?"
Scenario366 · Deferred Constraints and Commit-Time Failure
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Goldman, Stripe · Dialect: Postgres (primarily)
The scenario:
A transaction inserts rows in an order that temporarily violates an FK, expecting to fix it later in
the same transaction. With normal constraints, the first insert fails immediately. With
DEFERRABLE constraints (Postgres), the check is held until COMMIT — and if it fails then, you
get an error at commit, after all your work.
Schema:
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id BIGINT REFERENCES customers(id) DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED
);
T1:
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id) VALUES (7001);  -- customer doesn't exist YET
-- ...other work...
INSERT INTO customers (id) VALUES (7001);  -- creates the parent
COMMIT;  -- FK is checked here; succeeds because parent now exists
What happens: If the parent insert is forgotten, the COMMIT fails:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 437 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 438
ERROR:  insert or update on table "orders" violates foreign key constraint
DETAIL: Key (customer_id)=(7001) is not present in table "customers".
Thinking out loud: 1. "Deferrable constraints are useful for bulk loads and circular FK structures." 2. "The
cost is that errors surface at COMMIT, not at the offending statement — debugging is harder." 3. "Use
DEFERRABLE INITIALLY IMMEDIATE to allow per-transaction SET CONSTRAINTS ALL DEFERRED
when needed." 4. "Don't make every FK deferrable by default — production debugging suffers."
The diagnosis: Deferred constraints trade earlier failure for circular-reference flexibility. Be deliberate.
The fix: - Option A — Use DEFERRABLE selectively: Only on tables where circular FKs or bulk loads
require it. - Option B — DEFERRABLE INITIALLY IMMEDIATE: Default to immediate check; opt into
deferred behavior per transaction with SET CONSTRAINTS. - Option C — Restructure the schema: A
truly circular FK is often a smell. Consider whether the relationship is really bidirectional.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "deferred constraints are a free win" — they make debugging harder
when errors fire at COMMIT.
Common follow-up: "MySQL doesn't support DEFERRABLE constraints. How do you load circular FK
data in MySQL?"
Scenario367 · Saga Pattern When Distributed Transactions Are Infeasible
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Goldman, Stripe · Dialect: distributed
The scenario:
A booking flow spans three services: bookings, payments, notifications. Each owns its own
database. A two-phase commit across all three is operationally painful. The team adopts the saga
pattern: each step is a local transaction with a compensating action defined for failure.
Forward saga: 1. Create booking (T1: INSERT into bookings.bookings) 2. Charge payment (T2: INSERT
into payments.charges) 3. Send confirmation (T3: INSERT into notifications.outbox)
Compensations (reverse order on failure): 1. If T3 fails: refund payment, cancel booking 2. If T2 fails:
cancel booking
Sketch:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 438 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 439
-- T1 (bookings DB)
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO bookings (id, status, idempotency_key) VALUES (...);
INSERT INTO outbox (event_type, payload) VALUES ('BookingCreated', ...);
COMMIT;
-- worker picks up outbox, calls payments service
Thinking out loud: 1. "Sagas convert distributed locking into local transactions plus compensation
logic." 2. "Each step is its own local ACID transaction; the engine handles deadlock recovery within
each." 3. "Compensations must be idempotent because retries are inevitable." 4. "Outbox pattern
publishes the event reliably without holding cross-service locks."
The diagnosis: Distributed transactions cost more than they pay. Saga + outbox is the pragmatic Indian-
fintech standard for cross-service consistency.
The fix: - Option A — Orchestration saga: Central coordinator (a state machine) drives each step.
Easier to reason about, single point of state. - Option B — Choreography saga: Each service publishes
events; others react. More decoupled, harder to debug. - Option C — Outbox pattern as a building
block: Pair with either orchestration or choreography for reliable event delivery.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "use 2PC, it's safer" — XA in production is rare in Indian-stack
microservices for good reason; performance and operational complexity kill it.
Common follow-up: "What's the difference between orchestration and choreography sagas, and which
one would you pick for a payment flow?"
Scenario368 · Two-Phase Commit Reality Check
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: JP Morgan, Goldman, Wells Fargo, Walmart Labs · Dialect: distributed
The scenario:
A senior engineer suggests 2PC for the cross-DB booking + payment transaction. The new
engineer is excited — atomic across two DBs! Then they read the failure modes: blocked
transactions on coordinator failure, in-doubt transactions requiring manual resolution, dramatic
throughput drop.
2PC outline: 1. Coordinator sends PREPARE to all participants. 2. Each participant writes prepared state
to its log and replies PREPARED or ABORT. 3. If all PREPARED, coordinator writes COMMIT, then sends
COMMIT to all. 4. If any ABORT or timeout, coordinator sends ROLLBACK.
Failure modes: - Coordinator crashes after PREPARE but before COMMIT — participants are blocked
indefinitely with locks held. - Network partition between coordinator and one participant — same. -
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 439 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 440
Recovery requires the coordinator's log to be intact and the DBAs to manually resolve in-doubt
transactions.
Thinking out loud: 1. "2PC trades availability for atomicity. Under failure, it picks blocked-and-correct
over available-and-possibly-wrong." 2. "It's not theoretically broken — it's operationally heavy." 3. 
"Postgres supports it (PREPARE TRANSACTION / COMMIT PREPARED) but most ops teams avoid it." 4.
"In Indian fintech, only certain bank-to-bank integrations use 2PC; everything else is saga."
The diagnosis: 2PC is correct but operationally painful. The blocking problem is fundamental — see
Three-Phase Commit, which trades safety for availability and is also rarely used.
The fix (when 2PC is genuinely required): - Option A — Use a battle-tested transaction manager:
Java's JTA + Atomikos or Narayana; .NET's MSDTC. - Option B — Saga: Replace the 2PC with a saga +
compensations. - Option C — Single source of truth: Restructure so the cross-DB write isn't needed.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "2PC is unsafe" — it is safe but blocking; the trade-off is documented
and clear.
Common follow-up: "What's the FLP impossibility result, and how does it relate to 2PC's blocking
property?"
Scenario369 · Optimistic Locking with a Version Column
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Walmart Labs, Goldman · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A product-catalog editor allows multiple admins to edit the same product. Pessimistic locking
(FOR UPDATE) would block one admin while another is editing. Optimistic locking lets both work;
the second to save sees "stale version, please reload".
Schema:
CREATE TABLE products (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT,
  price NUMERIC,
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);
Update:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 440 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 441
UPDATE products
SET name = $name, price = $price, version = version + 1
WHERE id = $id AND version = $expected_version;
-- check affected_rows: 1 = success, 0 = stale
Thinking out loud: 1. "Optimistic locking is wait-free in the success path." 2. "Loser gets affected_rows =
0; application surfaces a reload prompt." 3. "Works at any isolation level — the WHERE clause is the
synchronisation." 4. "Trade-off: under heavy contention, lots of retries; pessimistic locking may be

The diagnosis: Optimistic locking pushes conflict detection into the WHERE clause. Cheap when
conflicts are rare, costly when they're common.
The fix (here, the pattern is the fix): - Option A — Version column: Simplest; increment on every
UPDATE. - Option B — Timestamp column: Use last_modified_at instead of version. Slight risk
of clock skew. - Option C — Hash of row contents: ETag-style; only update if the current hash
matches. Useful for HTTP-driven editors.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "optimistic locking is always better than pessimistic" — under heavy
write contention, retries cost more than waits.
Common follow-up: "How would you handle merging two admins' edits instead of just rejecting one?"
Scenario370 · Pessimistic SELECT FOR UPDATE Pattern
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Wells Fargo, Goldman · Dialect: vendor-
agnostic
The scenario:
A money-transfer service uses SELECT FOR UPDATE to lock both source and destination
accounts before computing the new balances. It's the textbook pessimistic-locking pattern for
fintech, and it works — provided you remember to lock in a deterministic order (Scenario 1) and
to use FOR UPDATE, not FOR SHARE.
Pattern:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 441 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 442
BEGIN;
-- Sort by id to avoid deadlock with the reverse transfer
SELECT id, balance FROM accounts WHERE id IN (101, 202)
ORDER BY id
FOR UPDATE;
-- Application reads both balances, computes new ones
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 2000 WHERE id = 101;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 2000 WHERE id = 202;
INSERT INTO transfers (from_id, to_id, amount) VALUES (101, 202, 2000);
COMMIT;
Thinking out loud: 1. "FOR UPDATE acquires row-level exclusive locks. Other readers can proceed (in
Postgres MVCC); other writers wait." 2. "FOR SHARE is wrong here — it allows another reader to also
take a share lock and read stale data." 3. "Always sort the ids before locking — deterministic order
prevents deadlock." 4. " FOR UPDATE NOWAIT fails immediately if another transaction holds the lock; 
SKIP LOCKED skips locked rows (useful for queue workers)."
The diagnosis: Pessimistic locking is the default for high-stakes financial workflows. Combine FOR
UPDATE with deterministic ordering and idempotent retries for production-grade correctness.
The fix (this is the recommended pattern): - Option A — FOR UPDATE + sorted ids: As shown above.
Battle-tested. - Option B — FOR UPDATE NOWAIT: Fail fast for user-facing flows where waiting is
unacceptable. - Option C — FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED: For queue workers — pick the next
unlocked job.
What NOT to say: - Do not say "FOR SHARE prevents writes" — it prevents writes from acquiring
exclusive locks but allows concurrent shared readers, which is rarely what you want for read-modify-
write.
Common follow-up: "How does SKIP LOCKED interact with isolation levels — does it give you the same
correctness as a full FOR UPDATE?"
Category 6, Part B — Isolation Level Fixes & Anomaly Scenarios
Part B is about diagnosing concurrency anomalies (dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, write skew,
lost update) and picking the right isolation level to fix them — without over-paying with Serializable when
Snapshot would suffice. Every scenario below interleaves two transactions and asks you to spot what
slipped through, then reason about the cheapest correctness fix. The trap is symmetric: candidates
either reach for Serializable on every problem (kills throughput) or stay on Read Committed and learn the
hard way that not all anomalies are visible at that level. Indian payment, inventory, and booking systems
run very hot on Read Committed by default, so these scenarios mirror the production landmines that get
filed as "ghost transactions", "double booking", or "stock went negative". For each scenario: read the
interleaving, name the anomaly, then prescribe the minimal fix.

Scenario371 · Dirty Read — Reporting Picks Up Uncommitted Salary
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro · Dialect: SQL Server (READ UNCOMMITTED),
Postgres (does not exist) · Topic: Dirty Read
The scenario:
Finance runs a payroll summary report. Around month-end, the totals it prints sometimes do not
match the totals when the same query is rerun ten seconds later. No rows were deleted in
between. The report runs at isolation READ UNCOMMITTED to "avoid blocking the OLTP
system."
-- Txn A (payroll admin, accidentally still open)
BEGIN;
UPDATE salaries SET amount = 200000 WHERE emp_id = 42; -- typo, meant 20000
-- ...long pause while admin notices typo...
-- Txn B (report, READ UNCOMMITTED)
SELECT SUM(amount) FROM salaries; -- includes 200000
-- Txn A
ROLLBACK;
What happens: Txn B reads Txn A's uncommitted update and the rollback erases it. Report is wrong by
180000 and there is no row that ever existed which would explain it.
Thinking out loud: 1. "The numbers shift without any DML happening between runs — that's the classic
dirty-read smell." 2. "Report is on READ UNCOMMITTED, so it sees uncommitted writes from other
sessions." 3. "If the other session rolls back, the report's value never reflects any committed state." 4. 
"This is the only anomaly that can produce a value the database never agreed to."
Diagnosis: Dirty read. READ UNCOMMITTED on the reporting side allows visibility of uncommitted
writes. A rollback then leaves the report holding a phantom number.
Fix options: - Move the report to READ COMMITTED (default on SQL Server and Postgres). Cost: small
reader-writer blocking on SQL Server unless you enable READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT. - On Postgres,
dirty reads do not occur even if you ask for READ UNCOMMITTED — the engine silently treats it as
READ COMMITTED. So the bug only reproduces on engines that honour the request (SQL Server, older
MySQL configurations). - Design fix: keep reports out of OLTP and run them off a replica or a snapshot
table; do not use isolation level to paper over architecture choices.
What NOT to say: - "Just retry the report" — it can land on a different rollback next time. - "Wrap the
admin's UPDATE in a stored procedure" — does not address the reader's isolation contract.

Scenario372 · Non-Repeatable Read — Audit Sees Two Balances
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, ICICI · Dialect: vendor-agnostic (default READ
COMMITTED) · Topic: Non-Repeatable Read
The scenario:
An audit job under READ COMMITTED reads a customer's balance, performs a series of
compliance checks, then re-reads the balance to confirm it has not changed during the check.
The job sometimes fails the consistency assertion even when no fraud is occurring.
-- Txn Audit (READ COMMITTED)
BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE acct_id = 9001; -- returns 50000
-- ...runs sanctions checks, KYC lookups...
-- Txn UPI (commits between the two reads)
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 12000 WHERE acct_id = 9001;
COMMIT;
-- Txn Audit
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE acct_id = 9001; -- now returns 62000
COMMIT;
What happens: The same row read twice in the same transaction returns two different committed
values. The audit assertion read1 == read2 fails.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Two reads of the same row in one transaction, two different values — that's non-
repeatable read by definition." 2. "READ COMMITTED only guarantees you never see uncommitted data
— it says nothing about stability across reads." 3. "Each statement under READ COMMITTED takes its
own snapshot." 4. "Either I need a stable snapshot for the whole transaction or I need to lock the row."
Diagnosis: Non-repeatable read. READ COMMITTED allows committed writes from other transactions to
appear between two statements of the same reader.
Fix options: - Raise audit to REPEATABLE READ (MySQL InnoDB, Postgres) or SNAPSHOT (SQL
Server). The whole transaction now sees one consistent view. - Use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on
the row at the start of the audit — locks out concurrent writers until commit. - Design fix: copy the
balance into a local variable at the start; the assertion var == reread() is the wrong test in any
case — write the audit against an immutable snapshot.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 444 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 445
What NOT to say: - "READ COMMITTED is broken" — it gives exactly what it promises, no more. - "Use
SERIALIZABLE" — works but is overkill for a single-row stability requirement.
Common follow-up: "How does Postgres's REPEATABLE READ differ from the SQL standard's
REPEATABLE READ?"
Scenario373 · Phantom Read — Loan Cap Bypassed By Concurrent Insert
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: HDFC, Bajaj Finserv, IDFC First · Dialect: SQL Server (REPEATABLE
READ), Oracle (REPEATABLE READ) · Topic: Phantom Read
The scenario:
A loan-approval flow checks how many active loans a customer already holds, and refuses if they
have three or more. Under REPEATABLE READ on SQL Server, two concurrent applications
occasionally both succeed even though their combined effect breaks the cap.
-- Txn A (REPEATABLE READ)
BEGIN;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM loans WHERE cust_id = 71 AND status = 'active'; -- returns 2
-- decides 2 < 3, will insert
-- Txn B (REPEATABLE READ, concurrent)
BEGIN;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM loans WHERE cust_id = 71 AND status = 'active'; -- returns 2
INSERT INTO loans(cust_id, status, principal) VALUES (71, 'active', 50000);
COMMIT;
-- Txn A
INSERT INTO loans(cust_id, status, principal) VALUES (71, 'active', 80000);
COMMIT;
-- Customer now has 4 active loans
What happens: Both transactions saw count of two, both decided to insert, both committed. The cap of
three was breached.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Each transaction's individual rows did not change between its reads —
REPEATABLE READ held them stable." 2. "But a new row appeared in the same predicate range — that's
a phantom, not a non-repeatable read." 3. "REPEATABLE READ in non-MVCC engines locks the rows it
read, not the rows it would have read." 4. "The only standard fix is SERIALIZABLE, or a range lock
equivalent."
Diagnosis: Phantom read. REPEATABLE READ keeps existing rows stable but does not prevent new
rows from entering the predicate.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 445 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 446
Fix options: - SERIALIZABLE — SQL Server takes range locks, Oracle uses serialization, Postgres uses
SSI. - MySQL InnoDB's REPEATABLE READ is unusual: it uses gap locks and next-key locks, so
phantoms are already prevented at REPEATABLE READ (a deliberate strengthening above the SQL
standard). - Design fix: enforce the cap with a CHECK against a maintained counter column protected by
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the customer row, so concurrent inserts serialise on that single lock.
What NOT to say: - "Just use REPEATABLE READ harder" — there is no "harder", you must climb a
level on this engine. - "Add a unique constraint on (cust_id, status)" — kills the data model, customers
legitimately have multiple active loans.
Common follow-up: "Why does MySQL InnoDB not need SERIALIZABLE to prevent this phantom?"
Scenario374 · Lost Update — Wallet Top-Up Vanishes
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Paytm, Mobikwik, PhonePe · Dialect: vendor-agnostic · Topic: Lost
Update
The scenario:
A wallet top-up service runs at READ COMMITTED without row locking. Two simultaneous top-
ups for the same user — one for 500, one for 800 — sometimes leave the wallet showing only
one of the two amounts added, not both.
-- Txn A (top-up 500, READ COMMITTED)
BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM wallets WHERE user_id = 555; -- reads 1000
-- application computes 1000 + 500 = 1500
-- Txn B (top-up 800, READ COMMITTED, concurrent)
BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM wallets WHERE user_id = 555; -- reads 1000
UPDATE wallets SET balance = 1800 WHERE user_id = 555;
COMMIT;
-- Txn A
UPDATE wallets SET balance = 1500 WHERE user_id = 555;
COMMIT;
-- Final balance: 1500. The 800 top-up was overwritten.
What happens: Txn A read 1000, computed 1500 in app memory, and wrote that value back —
clobbering Txn B's committed 1800. The 800 top-up is gone but the customer has the SMS receipt.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Both reads saw 1000 because they happened before either commit." 2. 
"Application-side arithmetic means the database has no idea each transaction depended on the value
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 446 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 447
being 1000." 3. "Whichever transaction commits last wins, the other's effect disappears — that's a lost
update."
Diagnosis: Lost update. Read-modify-write done in application memory under READ COMMITTED, with
no locking or version check.
Fix options: - Use SQL arithmetic so the database does the read-modify-write atomically: UPDATE
wallets SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE user_id = 555; — the row lock during
UPDATE forces serial execution. - Pessimistic lock: SELECT balance FROM wallets WHERE
user_id = 555 FOR UPDATE; before the application read. - Optimistic concurrency: add a 
version column; UPDATE ... SET balance = ?, version = version + 1 WHERE
user_id = ? AND version = ?; — zero rows updated means retry. - Raise to REPEATABLE READ
on Postgres/MySQL — these engines abort one of the conflicting transactions automatically (Postgres
raises "could not serialize access due to concurrent update").
What NOT to say: - "It's a race condition, add a sleep" — please no. - "Use SERIALIZABLE for
everything" — REPEATABLE READ already catches this on MVCC engines.
Common follow-up: "Which of these fixes survives the application crashing between read and write?"
Scenario375 · Write Skew — Two Doctors Both Go Off-Call
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Practo, 1mg, PharmEasy · Dialect: Postgres (SSI), MySQL (does not

The scenario:
A hospital roster rule says at least one doctor must remain on call at all times. Two doctors, both
currently on call, simultaneously request to go off duty. Under REPEATABLE READ, both requests
succeed and the ward is left uncovered.

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM oncall_doctors WHERE shift_id = 17 AND on_call = TRUE; -- returns 2
-- 2 > 1, safe to go off
-- Txn B (Dr Reddy, REPEATABLE READ, concurrent)
BEGIN;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM oncall_doctors WHERE shift_id = 17 AND on_call = TRUE; -- returns 2
UPDATE oncall_doctors SET on_call = FALSE WHERE doctor_id = 'reddy';
COMMIT;
-- Txn A
UPDATE oncall_doctors SET on_call = FALSE WHERE doctor_id = 'iyer';
COMMIT;
-- 0 doctors on call
What happens: Each transaction read a snapshot showing two on-call doctors. Each made a decision
based on that snapshot. Each wrote a different row. No write-write conflict; no row was read and then
modified by the same transaction. Yet the invariant is broken.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Neither transaction overwrote the other's write — they touched different rows." 2. 
"Both made a decision off a snapshot that was true when they read but false by the time they
committed." 3. "That's write skew — the classic invariant-violation anomaly." 4. "MVCC at REPEATABLE
READ does not detect this because no row both wrote."
Diagnosis: Write skew. Two transactions read overlapping data, made disjoint writes that together
violate an invariant. Only SERIALIZABLE (or explicit locking) catches it.
Fix options: - Postgres SERIALIZABLE (Serializable Snapshot Isolation, SSI) — detects the read-write
dependency cycle at commit and aborts one transaction with serialization failure. - Materialise the
conflict: have each transaction SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on every row that is currently on_call =
TRUE, so the rows being read are locked and a write skew becomes a write-write conflict. - Maintain a
counter row protected by a row lock — both transactions update the same counter, the second blocks. -
MySQL InnoDB at SERIALIZABLE acquires shared locks on read, which prevents the skew but at
significant concurrency cost.
What NOT to say: - "REPEATABLE READ should prevent that, the database is buggy" — REPEATABLE
READ never promised invariant preservation across disjoint writes. - "Just use a unique constraint" —
there is nothing unique to constrain.
Common follow-up: "What is the simplest invariant that survives write skew at REPEATABLE READ?"
Scenario376 · Read Skew — Inconsistent View Across Two Tables
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Zerodha · Dialect: vendor-agnostic · Topic: Read
Skew

PAGE 449
The scenario:
An end-of-day reconciliation reads the total of accounts.balance for a customer, then reads
the running total of ledger_entries.amount for the same customer. The two should be
equal. Under READ COMMITTED they are sometimes off by a single recent transfer.
-- Txn Recon (READ COMMITTED)
BEGIN;
SELECT SUM(balance) FROM accounts WHERE cust_id = 12; -- snapshot 1: 30000
-- Txn Transfer (commits between the two reads)
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 5000 WHERE acct_id = 100;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 5000 WHERE acct_id = 101;
INSERT INTO ledger_entries(cust_id, acct_id, amount) VALUES (12, 100, -5000), (12, 101, 5000);
COMMIT;
-- Txn Recon
SELECT SUM(amount) FROM ledger_entries WHERE cust_id = 12; -- snapshot 2: includes the new ±5000
COMMIT;
What happens: The recon job's two reads landed on either side of the transfer commit. Account sum is
the "before" state, ledger sum is the "after" state. Recon flags a spurious mismatch.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Each statement under READ COMMITTED takes a fresh snapshot." 2. "A
consistent cross-table read needs both statements to see the same instant of the database." 3. "That's
read skew — closely related to non-repeatable read but spread across multiple objects."
Diagnosis: Read skew. Each statement saw a consistent state by itself, but together they did not see a
consistent state.
Fix options: - REPEATABLE READ on Postgres or SNAPSHOT on SQL Server pins the whole transaction
to one snapshot. - SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; at the start of the
recon transaction is enough. - Design fix: precompute the ledger sum and account sum into a single
materialised view refreshed atomically.
What NOT to say: - "Add a delay between the two reads" — makes it worse. - "Run recon at
SERIALIZABLE" — works but no need to pay the abort cost.
Common follow-up: "Why is REPEATABLE READ enough here when SERIALIZABLE was needed for
write skew?"
