Scenario377 · Concurrent Inserts Both Trying To Reserve The Same Username
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Flipkart, Meesho, Nykaa · Dialect: vendor-agnostic · Topic: Uniqueness
Race
The scenario:
A signup flow first checks if a username exists, then inserts a new user. Under load, two
concurrent signups for the same username both pass the existence check, and one of the inserts
later fails with a duplicate key violation — but only after expensive downstream work (welcome
email, KYC start) was already triggered.
-- Txn A
SELECT 1 FROM users WHERE username = 'arnav99'; -- 0 rows
-- triggers welcome email pipeline
INSERT INTO users(username) VALUES ('arnav99'); -- succeeds
-- Txn B (concurrent)
SELECT 1 FROM users WHERE username = 'arnav99'; -- 0 rows (before A committed)
-- triggers welcome email pipeline
INSERT INTO users(username) VALUES ('arnav99'); -- fails with unique violation
What happens: Check-then-act on a uniqueness predicate is racy. Both transactions found nothing,
both did work, one failed at insert time.
Thinking out loud: 1. "The existence check is informational, not enforcing — anything can change
between SELECT and INSERT." 2. "The actual gatekeeper is the unique index on username — that
always wins." 3. "I should let the database be the source of truth, not pre-validate in app code."
Diagnosis: TOCTOU on a uniqueness predicate. The SELECT and INSERT are not atomic.
Fix options: - Drop the SELECT, attempt the INSERT, catch the duplicate-key error and return
"username taken" to the user. Cheaper and correct. - INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
RETURNING id; (Postgres) — if RETURNING is empty, the username was taken. - INSERT IGNORE
(MySQL) returns row count zero for taken usernames. - If the downstream work is expensive, defer it until
after the INSERT succeeds — the welcome email pipeline should be triggered from the row, not from the
check.
What NOT to say: - "Add a transaction wrapper around SELECT and INSERT" — doesn't help unless
you lock the table or use SERIALIZABLE. - "Use a distributed lock on the username string" — over-
engineering, the unique index already serialises this.
Common follow-up: "Is the unique constraint enough if usernames can differ by case?"

Scenario378 · Increment-Counter Race Despite "Atomic" Single Statement
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred · Dialect: vendor-agnostic · Topic: Counter Race
The scenario:
A daily_metrics table tracks API call counts per endpoint per day. The increment is done
with count = count + 1, but only after a SELECT establishes the row exists — otherwise an
INSERT is issued. Under load, two concurrent first-call-of-the-day requests sometimes both
insert, producing duplicate key errors or duplicate rows.
-- Txn A
SELECT count FROM daily_metrics WHERE endpoint = '/login' AND day = '2026-05-26'; -- 0 rows
INSERT INTO daily_metrics(endpoint, day, count) VALUES ('/login', '2026-05-26', 1);
-- Txn B (concurrent)
SELECT count FROM daily_metrics WHERE endpoint = '/login' AND day = '2026-05-26'; -- 0 rows
INSERT INTO daily_metrics(endpoint, day, count) VALUES ('/login', '2026-05-26', 1); -- duplicate key error
What happens: Two transactions both saw no row, both inserted, the second failed at the unique index.
The increment for that call is lost.
Thinking out loud: 1. "The SELECT-then-INSERT-or-UPDATE pattern is a textbook race." 2. "I should be
using upsert — let the database decide insert vs update." 3. " UPDATE count = count + 1 on a
single row is atomic because of the row lock during UPDATE."
Diagnosis: Upsert race. SELECT-then-INSERT-or-UPDATE has a window where both transactions decide
to insert.
Fix options: - Postgres: INSERT INTO daily_metrics(endpoint, day, count) VALUES ('/
login', '2026-05-26', 1) ON CONFLICT (endpoint, day) DO UPDATE SET count =
daily_metrics.count + 1; - MySQL: INSERT INTO daily_metrics(endpoint, day,
count) VALUES (...) ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE count = count + 1; - SQL Server: 
MERGE or IF EXISTS (...) UPDATE ELSE INSERT inside an explicit transaction with 
HOLDLOCK hint. - Design fix: ensure the row exists for all endpoints at the start of day (a cron seeds the
rows) so only UPDATE is ever needed.
What NOT to say: - "Use SERIALIZABLE" — sledgehammer for a tack. - "Catch the duplicate and retry
the UPDATE" — works but the upsert idiom is one statement, not two.
Common follow-up: "What happens to ON CONFLICT under high contention on the same key?"

Scenario379 · Balance Check + Debit Race (TOCTOU)
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: HDFC, Axis, RBL · Dialect: vendor-agnostic · Topic: TOCTOU
The scenario:
A debit flow checks the account balance is sufficient before debiting. Under READ COMMITTED,
two concurrent debits of 600 each, against a balance of 1000, sometimes both succeed —
leaving a negative balance of -200.
-- Txn A
BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE acct_id = 70; -- 1000
-- app: 1000 >= 600, proceed
-- Txn B (concurrent)
BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE acct_id = 70; -- 1000
-- app: 1000 >= 600, proceed
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 600 WHERE acct_id = 70;
COMMIT;
-- Txn A
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 600 WHERE acct_id = 70;
COMMIT;
-- final balance: -200
What happens: Each transaction made the sufficient-balance decision on a stale read. Both UPDATEs
used balance - 600, so both subtractions applied — leaving a negative balance.
Thinking out loud: 1. "The UPDATE arithmetic is atomic — the row lock means each - 600 is applied
serially. But the decision to debit was made in app code on a stale read." 2. "That's classic TOCTOU: the
value that gates the decision is no longer the value when the action executes." 3. "I need to put the check
inside the database, where it sees the locked, current value."
Diagnosis: TOCTOU on balance check. Application checked, database executed — the gap allowed
overspend.
Fix options: - Pessimistic lock: SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE acct_id = 70 FOR
UPDATE; — blocks the second transaction until the first commits, the second then reads the updated
400 and refuses. - Push the check into the UPDATE: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance
- 600 WHERE acct_id = 70 AND balance >= 600; — zero rows updated means refuse. App
must check rowcount. - Add a CHECK constraint: CHECK (balance >= 0) — both UPDATEs
run, the second errors out, transaction rolls back automatically. - Combine: the CHECK is the belt, the in-
statement WHERE is the braces.

What NOT to say: - "Add SELECT FOR UPDATE NOWAIT" — non-blocking lock acquisition will fail
immediately, blocks user experience. - "Use SERIALIZABLE" — works, but the targeted fixes are
cheaper.
Common follow-up: "Why is UPDATE ... WHERE balance >= 600 safe even at READ
COMMITTED?"

Scenario384 · Optimistic Locking With Version Column
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Zerodha · Dialect: vendor-agnostic · Topic:

The scenario:
A trading app lets two devices edit the same order draft. Without locking, the slower device's
save can clobber the faster device's edits — but the user has no idea their changes were

-- Edit pattern with version column
SELECT order_id, qty, price, version FROM draft_orders WHERE order_id = 'ord_77';
-- returns (qty=10, price=500, version=3)
-- user edits qty to 12
UPDATE draft_orders
   SET qty = 12, version = version + 1
 WHERE order_id = 'ord_77' AND version = 3;

Scenario385 · Pessimistic SELECT FOR UPDATE
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: HDFC, Axis, Yes Bank · Dialect: vendor-agnostic · Topic: Pessimistic
Locking
The scenario:
An inter-account transfer must read both source and destination balances, validate the source
has enough, then update both. Under load, multiple transfers between the same pair sometimes
interleave badly.
BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE acct_id IN (101, 102) FOR UPDATE;
-- both rows locked exclusively
-- ... app does validation ...
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 1000 WHERE acct_id = 101;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 1000 WHERE acct_id = 102;
COMMIT;
What happens: The FOR UPDATE lock blocks concurrent transactions trying to lock the same rows.
They queue, run serially, no anomalies.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Pessimistic locking assumes conflict is likely and pre-empts it by blocking the
second writer." 2. "FOR UPDATE acquires exclusive row locks, held until commit or rollback." 3. 
"Deadlock risk: always lock in a consistent order (e.g. by acct_id ascending)."
Diagnosis: Without FOR UPDATE, the read is non-locking — concurrent transactions can read the same
balances and base decisions on stale values.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 458 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 459
Fix options: - SELECT ... FOR UPDATE — exclusive, blocks both readers and writers (in InnoDB) or
just writers (in Postgres, where readers can still read). - SELECT ... FOR NO KEY UPDATE
(Postgres) — slightly weaker, allows concurrent reads that don't touch key columns. - 
SELECT ... FOR SHARE (Postgres) or LOCK IN SHARE MODE (MySQL) — shared lock, blocks
writers but not other readers. Useful for read-validate-then-write patterns where many txns can read
concurrently. - Deadlock prevention: order locks by primary key, set lock_timeout so a deadlocked
transaction errors out rather than waiting indefinitely.
What NOT to say: - "Lock the entire table" — kills throughput. - "FOR UPDATE prevents all anomalies"
— only the ones whose rows you actually locked; phantoms still need SERIALIZABLE on most engines.
Common follow-up: "How do you avoid deadlock when two transfers go in opposite directions on the
same pair of accounts?"
Scenario386 · SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED For Queue Processing
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Dunzo · Dialect: Postgres, MySQL 8+ · Topic: Queue
Pattern
The scenario:
A job-queue table holds pending jobs. Multiple worker processes need to pick "the next available
job" without two workers grabbing the same job. The naive SELECT ... LIMIT 1 FOR
UPDATE causes workers to block each other and serialise — throughput drops to one worker
effectively active at a time.
-- Worker pattern
BEGIN;
SELECT job_id, payload FROM jobs
 WHERE status = 'pending'
 ORDER BY created_at
 LIMIT 1
 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
-- process the job
UPDATE jobs SET status = 'done' WHERE job_id = ?;
COMMIT;
What happens: With SKIP LOCKED, each worker grabs a different row — if the first row is locked by
worker A, worker B silently picks the next unlocked row instead of waiting. Throughput scales with
worker count.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 459 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 460
Thinking out loud: 1. "Plain FOR UPDATE makes workers queue on the same row — exactly what I'm
trying to avoid." 2. "SKIP LOCKED says: don't wait on rows already locked, pretend they aren't there." 3. 
"Combined with LIMIT 1, each worker gets the next row no other worker is currently working on."
Diagnosis: Without SKIP LOCKED, FOR UPDATE serialises workers on the first row of the queue. SKIP
LOCKED parallelises them.
Fix options: - Postgres: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED — available since 9.5. - MySQL: FOR UPDATE
SKIP LOCKED — available since 8.0. - Oracle: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED — original implementer
of the pattern. - SQL Server: READPAST hint with UPDLOCK — equivalent. - Pair with LIMIT
(Postgres/MySQL) or FETCH FIRST 1 ROW ONLY (Oracle/SQL Server) so each worker takes a small
batch. - Design fix: dedicated queue systems (RabbitMQ, SQS) handle this natively; database-as-queue
works for low scale and avoids extra infra.
What NOT to say: - "Use NOLOCK and just hope" — NOLOCK is dirty read, will let two workers pick the
same job. - "Have workers pick by job_id MOD worker_count = my_id" — works but loses
ordering and breaks if worker count changes.
Common follow-up: "What happens if a worker crashes after locking a job but before updating its
status?"
Scenario387 · READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT vs READ COMMITTED on SQL
Server
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: TCS GCC, Infosys GCC, Capgemini GCC (BFSI clients) · Dialect: SQL
Server · Topic: SQL Server Isolation
The scenario:
A SQL Server OLTP system shows reads blocking writes and writes blocking reads under load.
Enabling READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT (RCSI) eliminates the blocking, but a senior engineer
flags that this changes semantic guarantees.
Default behaviour (READ COMMITTED, locking): - Readers acquire shared locks, writers acquire
exclusive locks. Each blocks the other. - A reader sees the latest committed data but blocks any in-flight
writer until its statement completes. - Statement-level consistency only — two statements in one
transaction see different snapshots.
With READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT enabled: - Readers do not take shared locks. They read the last
committed version of each row from the tempdb version store. - Writers do not block readers; readers do
not block writers. - Semantic difference: a reader sees a snapshot of each row as of the start of the
statement, even if a writer subsequently commits during the read.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 460 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 461
Thinking out loud: 1. "Default SQL Server isolation is lock-based — concurrent readers and writers
contend." 2. "RCSI is MVCC-flavoured READ COMMITTED — readers see versioned snapshots, writers
don't block them." 3. "Same statement-level consistency contract, but reached via versions instead of
locks." 4. "The trade is tempdb pressure for reduced blocking — usually worth it on OLTP."
Diagnosis: The locking READ COMMITTED is the source of the reader-writer contention. RCSI removes
it but moves the cost to tempdb version-store maintenance.
Fix options: - ALTER DATABASE my_db SET READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON; — flips all READ
COMMITTED transactions to use snapshots. - Use ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION ON separately to
enable explicit SNAPSHOT isolation level (full-transaction snapshot, equivalent to Postgres REPEATABLE
READ). - Tradeoff: tempdb size grows with version-store volume; long-running transactions cause
version-store bloat.
What NOT to say: - "RCSI is the same as Postgres MVCC" — Postgres versions live in the table, SQL
Server's live in tempdb — operational behaviour differs. - "RCSI removes all anomalies" — it removes the
locking artefacts; non-repeatable reads and phantoms still apply at the READ COMMITTED level.
Common follow-up: "What happens to tempdb if a long-running report runs while RCSI is on?"
Scenario388 · Postgres SSI Catching Write Skew
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred · Dialect: Postgres · Topic: Serializable Snapshot
Isolation
The scenario:
A two-doctor-on-call scenario (like Scenario 5) is implemented in Postgres at SERIALIZABLE.
Both transactions appear to commit successfully — until the second one is suddenly aborted
with ERROR: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies
among transactions.
Postgres SSI behaviour: - SERIALIZABLE in Postgres is implemented as Serializable Snapshot Isolation
(SSI). - Each transaction runs at REPEATABLE READ semantics PLUS tracks read-write dependencies
between concurrent transactions. - At commit, Postgres checks for a dangerous dependency cycle; if
one exists, one transaction is aborted with serialization_failure (SQLSTATE 40001). - The application's
responsibility is to retry the aborted transaction.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Postgres SSI gives serializable semantics without taking shared read locks — it
tracks dependencies instead." 2. "The cost is paid at commit time as a serialization failure on the loser
transaction." 3. "Applications must be retry-aware — every SERIALIZABLE transaction needs a retry
wrapper."
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 461 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 462
Diagnosis: SSI is the only practical way Postgres prevents write skew without app-level locking. The
retry loop is part of the contract.
Fix options: - Wrap SERIALIZABLE transactions in a retry loop: catch serialization_failure,
reset state, retry up to N times with exponential backoff. - Keep transactions short — long transactions
increase SSI's tracking overhead and the chance of detected cycles. - Use SERIALIZABLE only on the
transactions that actually need write-skew protection; keep the rest at READ COMMITTED. - Don't mix
SERIALIZABLE and lower-level transactions casually — SSI's guarantees apply to interactions between
SERIALIZABLE transactions; a concurrent READ COMMITTED writer can still cause anomalies for a
SERIALIZABLE reader.
What NOT to say: - "SERIALIZABLE in Postgres is the same as in SQL Server" — SQL Server uses
range locks, Postgres uses SSI. Different cost models. - "Just retry forever on failure" — bound the
retries and surface persistent conflicts to the user.
Common follow-up: "What is the difference between SSI's serialization failure and a deadlock abort?"
Scenario389 · MySQL InnoDB Gap Locks Preventing Phantoms
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Flipkart, Myntra, MakeMyTrip · Dialect: MySQL · Topic: Gap Locking
The scenario:
A booking system at MySQL InnoDB's default REPEATABLE READ never appears to suffer
phantoms — but the same code on SQL Server's REPEATABLE READ does. The team wonders if
MySQL is silently using SERIALIZABLE.
InnoDB REPEATABLE READ behaviour: - InnoDB uses next-key locks: a row lock plus a gap lock on
the gap before the row. - A range scan like SELECT ... WHERE x BETWEEN 5 AND 10 FOR
UPDATE locks the rows in that range AND the gaps between them, preventing inserts. - This is stricter
than the SQL standard's REPEATABLE READ, which only requires existing rows be stable.
Thinking out loud: 1. "InnoDB intentionally over-delivers on REPEATABLE READ — gap locks prevent
phantoms even though the standard doesn't require it." 2. "The price: gap locks reduce insert
concurrency in ranges being read." 3. "This is why MySQL apps often don't need SERIALIZABLE for
invariant safety."
Diagnosis: InnoDB's REPEATABLE READ is strictly stronger than the standard. Gap locks close the
phantom window that other engines leave open.
Fix options: - Stay at REPEATABLE READ on MySQL — phantoms already prevented for locking reads
(FOR UPDATE / LOCK IN SHARE MODE). - For non-locking reads, MySQL takes a snapshot at the first
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 462 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 463
read and reuses it for the transaction — also prevents phantoms via MVCC. - To get insert concurrency
back on a range, switch to READ COMMITTED — disables gap locks but reintroduces phantom risk.
What NOT to say: - "MySQL REPEATABLE READ is broken because it doesn't match the SQL standard"
— it's a deliberate, documented strengthening. - "Disable gap locks for performance" — they exist for
correctness; replace with explicit locking strategy first.
Common follow-up: "How do gap locks contribute to InnoDB deadlocks?"
Scenario390 · Choosing Snapshot Over Serializable For Performance
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Cred, Razorpay, Zerodha · Dialect: vendor-agnostic · Topic: Isolation
Trade-off
The scenario:
A long-running analytics query needs to scan millions of rows for a consistent view. The team
initially set it to SERIALIZABLE for safety, but it conflicts with concurrent writers and frequently
aborts with serialization failures. The right answer is usually Snapshot, not Serializable.
The trade-off: - SERIALIZABLE (Postgres SSI, SQL Server with range locks): protects against write skew
and other dependency-cycle anomalies; conflicts manifest as aborts or blocking. - SNAPSHOT /
REPEATABLE READ on MVCC engines: gives a consistent transaction-long snapshot; no read-write
blocking; vulnerable to write skew but read-only queries cannot cause write skew by definition.
Thinking out loud: 1. "A read-only analytics query cannot suffer write skew — write skew requires both
transactions to write." 2. "All I need is a consistent snapshot — REPEATABLE READ delivers that without
the SSI overhead." 3. "Reserve SERIALIZABLE for transactions that read-and-write invariants."
Diagnosis: SERIALIZABLE was over-specified. The query is read-only and only needs snapshot
consistency.
Fix options: - Postgres: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; or SET
TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY; — read-only hint allows
additional optimisations. - SQL Server: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SNAPSHOT; —
explicit snapshot, full-transaction consistency. - Decide per-transaction, not per-database — SET
TRANSACTION applies only to the current transaction. - For very long analytics, consider a snapshot
copy on a read replica to avoid impact on OLTP.
What NOT to say: - "SNAPSHOT and SERIALIZABLE are the same thing" — Snapshot does not protect
against write skew; Serializable does. - "Just SERIALIZABLE everything for safety" — over-paying for
correctness you don't need.
Common follow-up: "Name a workload where SNAPSHOT is wrong and SERIALIZABLE is required."

Scenario391 · REPEATABLE READ Inside A Long Batch — Bloat Consequence
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, BillDesk, Juspay · Dialect: Postgres · Topic: MVCC Bloat
The scenario:
A nightly batch processes millions of orders inside a single REPEATABLE READ transaction. The
next morning, the database is sluggish — query plans are unchanged but everything is slow. A
DBA notices the table has 10x its expected on-disk size.
What happens: Postgres MVCC keeps old row versions alive as long as any open transaction's
snapshot could see them. A long REPEATABLE READ batch holds a snapshot for hours; VACUUM
cannot reclaim any row updated or deleted during the batch. The table bloats.
Thinking out loud: 1. "REPEATABLE READ pins a snapshot for the whole transaction." 2. "VACUUM can
only free row versions older than the oldest snapshot." 3. "Hours-long batch transactions hold snapshots
that block VACUUM hours behind."
Diagnosis: Long-running REPEATABLE READ transaction caused MVCC version retention, blocking
VACUUM and producing table bloat.
Fix options: - Break the batch into smaller transactions — each commit releases its snapshot and allows
VACUUM to make progress. - Use a server-side cursor with WITH HOLD if you genuinely need to
iterate a single result across many transactions. - Schedule batches during low-OLTP windows so
VACUUM has slack to recover afterwards. - Run pg_stat_activity checks for xact_start
older than N minutes and alert; long transactions are operational smells.
What NOT to say: - "Run VACUUM FULL nightly" — locks the table, OLTP downtime. - "REPEATABLE
READ is fundamentally broken for batches" — the isolation level is fine; the transaction scope is wrong.
Common follow-up: "How does autovacuum decide which tables to vacuum, and what tuning helps in
this case?"
Scenario392 · Postgres VACUUM Behaviour With Long Transactions
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred · Dialect: Postgres · Topic: MVCC / Vacuum
The scenario:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 464 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 465
A monitoring dashboard shows pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup climbing steadily on a
hot table. Autovacuum runs frequently but the dead tuple count keeps growing. A 
pg_stat_activity query shows a user's reporting session open for the past four hours.
What happens: A reporting transaction holding a snapshot prevents VACUUM from removing row
versions that other transactions deleted or superseded. Even though VACUUM runs, it cannot reclaim
anything older than what the snapshot still needs.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Dead tuples are stale versions awaiting reclamation by VACUUM." 2. "VACUUM

Diagnosis: An idle-in-transaction or long-running transaction held the xmin horizon and prevented

Fix options: - idle_in_transaction_session_timeout — auto-terminates sessions idle inside a

get "snapshot too old" errors. - Monitor pg_stat_activity for state = 'idle in
transaction' and alert. - Educate developers: open transactions only when needed, commit
promptly, never hold a transaction across user input.
What NOT to say: - "Just run VACUUM more often" — frequency doesn't help if the horizon hasn't
moved. - "Restart Postgres to clear it" — works in panic, but the underlying habit will repeat.

Scenario393 · Connection Pool + Transaction Scope (Leaking Transactions)

Pool Discipline
The scenario:
An application using HikariCP randomly experiences "transaction state from another request"
symptoms — a query that should see a freshly inserted row sometimes does not, and rows from
a previous user's session occasionally appear in the current user's request. The bug is
intermittent and hard to reproduce.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 465 / 586

PAGE 466
What happens: A connection was returned to the pool with an open transaction. The next checkout-

Scenario394 · Read Replica + Transaction Visibility Lag

Replication
The scenario:
A user updates their profile on the primary, gets a success response, navigates to the profile page

What happens: The primary has the new value; the replica is N ms behind. The read for the page

Diagnosis: Read-your-writes anomaly due to replica lag. The transaction committed on primary but the
user's next read was served from a stale replica.

Scenario395 · Multi-Statement Transaction Holding Read View Too Long

Transaction Scope
The scenario:
A user-facing checkout transaction includes a call to an external SMS provider while a row is

Concurrent transactions trying to read or write the same row queue up, request timeouts
cascade.

-- ... call SMS API (4 seconds) ...

COMMIT;
What happens: The row lock acquired by FOR UPDATE is held until commit. The external call extends
the lock's lifetime to seconds. Concurrent transactions block, downstream timeouts ensue.

lock is the contention point; everything queues on it." 3. "Move the external call out of the transaction or
use compensating actions if it fails."
Diagnosis: Transaction scope extends across an external API call, holding locks for far too long.
Fix options: - Restructure: do the database work (commit), then do the SMS call. If the SMS fails, log it
and retry asynchronously — most flows can tolerate eventual SMS delivery. - If the SMS must succeed
before commit, use the outbox pattern (see Scenario 29) — insert a row to send the SMS, commit, then a
background worker reads the outbox and sends. - Set lock_timeout so a transaction holding a lock

PAGE 468
too long is aborted (treats the disease, not the cause). - Monitor longest-held lock duration as a database
SLI.
What NOT to say: - "Make the SMS call async with a thread pool inside the transaction" — the thread
returns but the transaction still holds the lock. - "Increase the lock timeout" — makes the problem worse.

Scenario396 · Application Retry Pattern After Serialization Failure
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred · Dialect: Postgres SERIALIZABLE · Topic: Retry
Loop
The scenario:
A team enables SERIALIZABLE for a critical transfer flow on Postgres. Some transactions now fail
with serialization_failure (SQLSTATE 40001). The team's "fix" is to log the error and
surface a 500 to the user. The right pattern is to retry transparently.
-- Pseudocode
for attempt in 1..MAX_RETRIES:
    try:
        BEGIN;
        -- ... transaction body ...
        COMMIT;
        return success
    catch SerializationFailure:
        ROLLBACK;
        sleep(backoff * 2^attempt)
    catch DeadlockError:
        ROLLBACK;
        sleep(backoff * 2^attempt)
raise FailureAfterMaxRetries
Thinking out loud: 1. "Serialization failures are a normal outcome of SERIALIZABLE under contention —
they're a signal to retry, not an error to surface." 2. "Deadlocks at any isolation level are similarly retry-
able." 3. "Exponential backoff and a retry cap prevent thundering-herd retries."
Diagnosis: Treating serialization_failure as a terminal error misuses the abstraction. SSI's contract is
"either succeed or abort and retry."
Fix options: - Centralise the retry logic in a transactional helper. Every SERIALIZABLE transaction is
wrapped automatically. - Distinguish error classes: serialization failures and deadlocks are retry-able;
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 468 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 469
constraint violations are not. - Cap retries (e.g. 3) and surface a user-facing "please try again" only after
exhausting them. - Metric: count retries per endpoint; persistent high counts indicate hot conflicts to
redesign. - Make the transaction body idempotent so retries are safe — no externally visible side effects
until after commit.
What NOT to say: - "Retry forever" — unbounded retries cascade into capacity issues. - "Disable
SERIALIZABLE to avoid the failures" — gives up the correctness guarantee that motivated
SERIALIZABLE.
Common follow-up: "What does the SQL state 40001 mean across Postgres, MySQL, and SQL Server?"
Scenario397 · Idempotency Key + At-Least-Once Delivery
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Stripe, Cashfree · Dialect: vendor-agnostic · Topic:
Idempotency
The scenario:
A payment-create endpoint can be retried by the client on network errors. Without an
idempotency key, two retries result in two charges on the customer's card.
-- Client provides idempotency_key in request header
CREATE TABLE idempotency_records (
  idempotency_key TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  response_body JSON,
  status_code INT,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);
-- Handler flow
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO idempotency_records(idempotency_key, response_body, status_code)
  VALUES (:key, NULL, NULL)
  ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO NOTHING
  RETURNING idempotency_key;
-- if RETURNING is empty: the key was used before; SELECT the stored response and return it
-- if RETURNING is non-empty: proceed with the actual work, then UPDATE the record with the response
COMMIT;
What happens: First attempt inserts the key, processes the payment, stores the response. Retries hit the
conflict path, find the stored response, return it unchanged. The customer sees one charge, the
integrator's retries are absorbed safely.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 469 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 470
Thinking out loud: 1. "At-least-once is the only realistic delivery contract for network APIs." 2. "The
server must enforce idempotency — clients cannot." 3. "An idempotency key is the contract: same key,
same outcome, regardless of how many times you call."
Diagnosis: Endpoint is not idempotent. Retries cause duplicate side effects.
Fix options: - Idempotency key per request, indexed in a dedicated table with the response cached. -
Store the response so retries return the original response — clients see exactly the same data as the first
call. - TTL the keys (e.g. 24 hours) to bound storage growth. - Pair with a unique constraint on the
underlying domain object where possible (e.g. payment unique on (order_id, attempt_no)).
What NOT to say: - "Tell clients not to retry" — they will, and they should. - "Use a UUID as the
idempotency key on the server side" — defeats the purpose; the client must supply the key for retries to
share it.

Scenario398 · Outbox Pattern To Prevent Dual-Write Inconsistency
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Swiggy, Flipkart · Dialect: vendor-agnostic · Topic: Dual-Write
The scenario:
An order-placement handler inserts into the orders table, then publishes an event to a message
broker. Sometimes the database insert commits but the broker publish fails (network blip).
Downstream services that listen to the event never know the order exists.
-- Broken pattern: dual write
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders(...) VALUES (...);
COMMIT;
-- now publish to Kafka
broker.publish("order_placed", payload); -- may fail; we have no way to retry consistently
What happens: The database commit and the broker publish are two separate writes to two systems.
There is no shared atomic boundary, so any partial failure leaves the systems inconsistent.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Two-phase commit between databases and brokers is rarely available and rarely
fast enough." 2. "Outbox pattern: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the
order. A relay polls the outbox and publishes." 3. "Single transaction means either both the order and the
outbox row commit, or neither does."
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 470 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 471
Diagnosis: Dual-write inconsistency. No atomicity across database and broker.
Fix options: - Outbox table: CREATE TABLE outbox (id BIGSERIAL, aggregate_id TEXT,
event_type TEXT, payload JSONB, published BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE); - Insert into
outbox inside the same transaction as the domain change. Atomic. - A separate relay process polls
outbox WHERE published = FALSE FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, publishes, marks as 
published = TRUE. - At-least-once delivery is acceptable because downstream is built to be
idempotent. - Alternative: Change Data Capture (Debezium) reads the WAL and emits events — no
application-side outbox needed.
What NOT to say: - "Use a distributed transaction (XA)" — operationally painful, slow, often unavailable
for brokers. - "Retry the publish in a finally block" — does not survive process crash between commit
and publish.

the outbox in parallel?"
Scenario399 · Saga Compensation Pattern
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Swiggy, Flipkart, Razorpay · Dialect: vendor-agnostic · Topic: Distributed
Transaction
The scenario:
A travel booking spans three services: flight, hotel, payment. If the payment fails after the flight
and hotel are booked, both bookings need to be reversed. There is no shared database
transaction that spans the three services.
The pattern: - Each step is its own local transaction in its own service. - For each step, a corresponding
compensating transaction is defined. - If any step fails, the orchestrator invokes the compensating
actions for all completed prior steps in reverse order.
forward:    flight.book → hotel.book → payment.charge
compensate: payment.refund ← hotel.cancel ← flight.cancel
Thinking out loud: 1. "Distributed atomicity is hard; the saga gives up atomic rollback for explicit
compensation." 2. "Each service is responsible for its own consistency; the orchestrator coordinates the
choreography." 3. "Compensation is not always perfectly inverse — refund may charge a fee, cancellation
may leave audit traces. Domain decides."
Diagnosis: No global transaction is possible across services. Sagas decompose the workflow into local
transactions plus compensations.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 471 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 472
Fix options: - Orchestrator-based saga: a central coordinator (e.g. AWS Step Functions, Camunda,
Temporal) drives the steps and compensations. - Choreography-based saga: each service listens for
events and reacts. No central coordinator. Harder to reason about, easier to scale. - Each step must be
idempotent (retries are inevitable). - Compensations must also be idempotent — retrying a refund must
not refund twice. - Persist saga state so a crash mid-workflow can resume.
What NOT to say: - "Use a distributed transaction (XA) across the services" — usually impractical with
HTTP services and brokers. - "Just wrap everything in a try-catch" — does not address process crashes
or partial network failures.
Common follow-up: "How does a saga handle the case where a compensating action itself fails?"
Scenario400 · Eventual Consistency vs Strong Consistency Choice
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Flipkart · Dialect: vendor-agnostic · Topic: Consistency
Model
The scenario:
A product manager asks whether to use eventual consistency for a "follower count" feature on a
social product, vs strong consistency for the "wallet balance" feature on a payments product. The
engineering team needs to articulate the trade-off and decide.
Strong consistency: - After a write completes, all subsequent reads everywhere see the new value. -
Achieved via single-leader synchronous replication, consensus protocols, or distributed locks. - Cost:
higher latency, lower availability during partitions (CAP theorem trade).
Eventual consistency: - Reads may see stale values for a bounded period after a write. - All replicas
converge given time and no further writes. - Cost: application must tolerate staleness, handle reordering,
design for read-your-writes via session affinity.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Follower count being off by 30 seconds is fine — UX impact is invisible." 2. 
"Wallet balance being off by 30 seconds enables double-spend — UX impact is a refund queue and
possibly fraud." 3. "Strong consistency is paid for in latency and availability; pay only where the business
actually needs it."
Diagnosis: Consistency model is a per-domain choice, not a global database setting. Pick strong where
invariants are financial or safety-critical; pick eventual where staleness is invisible to users.
Fix options: - For wallet: single-region single-writer Postgres / Spanner. Synchronous replication.
SERIALIZABLE for the critical writes. - For follower count: write to primary, propagate asynchronously to
replicas; serve reads from replicas. Tolerate brief staleness. - Per-feature decision: same database can
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 472 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 473
host both, with isolation level chosen per transaction. - Document the consistency contract in the API
spec so consumers know what to expect.
What NOT to say: - "Always strong consistency for safety" — gives up scale and latency unnecessarily.
- "Always eventual for performance" — leads to data corruption in financial or safety-critical paths.
Common follow-up: "For an Indian UPI payment, which consistency model does NPCI require, and
why?"
Category 7, Part A — Data Quality: Duplicate Investigations
There is one question that every product company, analytics team and data role in India eventually asks
you — and it is rarely written down in a job description. It goes something like this: "I see duplicates in
this report. Find the cause." No schema is shared upfront. The query may or may not be shown.
Sometimes you only get the output and a Slack screenshot from a panicking founder. The interviewer is
not testing whether you know window functions; they are testing whether you can think like a data
engineer — form a hypothesis, narrow the search space, isolate the offending row, and propose a fix that
survives the next deployment. The 25 scenarios below cover the most common duplicate investigations
you will face: join multipliers, migration leftovers, at-least-once delivery, case sensitivity, encoding
mismatches, ETL race conditions, materialised view drift, and a few sneaky ones that have ruined many a
Monday standup. Work through them out loud — the interview is as much about your narration as it is
about the final SQL.
Scenario401 · Daily revenue report doubled overnight
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Razorpay, Meesho, CRED · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
You run a daily revenue report for a D2C brand. Yesterday it showed roughly ₹12 lakh, today it

       SUM(o.total_amount) AS revenue
FROM orders o

PAGE 474
What's wrong: Revenue is roughly doubled compared to the previous day, yet no surge in traffic, ad

Thinking out loud: 1. "Anything that suddenly doubles points to a join multiplier, not a real revenue

FROM orders o
WHERE o.id IN (SELECT DISTINCT order_id FROM order_items WHERE sku_category = 'apparel')
  AND DATE(o.created_at) = CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 day'
GROUP BY DATE(o.created_at);

above the query: -- grain: one row per order_item saves hours. - Add a CI check that flags

What NOT to say: - "Maybe yesterday's number was wrong." Anchoring on the wrong day is the most

SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS row_count

         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY created_at ASC) AS rn
  FROM users
)
DELETE FROM users WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM ranked WHERE rn > 1);

Scenario404 · Duplicate webhook deliveries inflating GMV

The scenario:

FROM payment_events
WHERE event_type = 'payment.captured'
  AND DATE(received_at) = CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 day';
What's wrong: Webhook providers offer at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once. Some payments
captured once will arrive 2–5 times.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Webhooks are at-least-once. If the network burped or our 200 was slow, the PSP

SELECT SUM(amount) AS gmv

  FROM payment_events
  WHERE event_type = 'payment.captured'
    AND DATE(received_at) = CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 day'
  ORDER BY payment_id, received_at ASC
) deduped;

Scenario405 · Race condition on INSERT — missing UNIQUE constraint
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Swiggy, Zomato, Dunzo · Dialect: Postgres
The scenario:
Your signup endpoint does a SELECT … WHERE email = ? then INSERT if not found.
Most days it is fine. On a flash sale day, you find 84 rows where two users have the same email
registered within 200ms of each other.
SELECT email, COUNT(*) FROM users
WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2026-05-10'
GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
What's wrong: Two concurrent requests both ran the SELECT, both got "not found", both inserted.
Thinking out loud: 1. "This is a classic check-then-act race. SELECT and INSERT are not atomic." 2. 
"Under low traffic the window is small enough to never trigger; under flash-sale traffic it bites." 3. "The
application logic cannot fix this reliably — the database has to enforce uniqueness." 4. "Add a UNIQUE
constraint, switch the INSERT to use ON CONFLICT, and the race becomes a no-op."
The diagnosis: TOCTOU (time-of-check vs time-of-use) race; uniqueness enforced in app code, not in
the schema.
The fix:
ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT users_email_unique UNIQUE (email);
INSERT INTO users (email, created_at, source)
VALUES ($1, NOW(), $2)
ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING
RETURNING id;

Dedupe existing rows first using a ROW_NUMBER cleanup like Scenario2.

constraint at schema level. - Application code never decides uniqueness.
What NOT to say: - "We'll add a Redis lock." Locks across services are notoriously hard to get right;
database constraints are bulletproof.

Scenario406 · Same email registered twice — case sensitivity

-- returns 2 rows

most providers. Treating it as case-sensitive lets duplicates in.
Thinking out loud: 1. "MySQL's default collation utf8mb4_unicode_ci is case-insensitive, but if the

pasted from another schema." 4. "Fix is twofold: lower-case all emails on write, and change the collation."
The diagnosis: Column collation was binary, allowing two casings of the same email to coexist.
The fix:
-- Postgres equivalent: use CITEXT or LOWER() at write time.
ALTER TABLE users
  MODIFY COLUMN email VARCHAR(255) COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
-- Then normalise:
UPDATE users SET email = LOWER(email);
-- Then dedupe.

silently merge accounts on the back of that.

Scenario411 · Recursive CTE looping and inflating rows
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Microsoft India, Oracle, SAP Labs · Dialect: Postgres
The scenario:
An org-chart query that walks a manager_id hierarchy returns 47,000 rows for a company of
1,200 employees. The query has been adding rows on every refresh.
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS depth FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, o.depth + 1
  FROM employees e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id
)
SELECT * FROM org;
What's wrong: Someone introduced a circular manager_id (A reports to B, B reports to A) by
mistake during an org restructure. The recursive CTE walks the cycle until the recursion depth limit, then
stops — but the row count balloons.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Recursive CTEs blow up if the graph has cycles. Postgres has no cycle detection
unless you ask for it." 2. "Use CYCLE clause (Postgres 14+) or maintain a visited set manually." 3. "First,

ideally via a check or a trigger."
The diagnosis: Cycle in the hierarchy + recursive CTE with no cycle detection.
The fix:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 484 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 485
-- Find cycles:
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, ARRAY[id] AS path FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, o.path || e.id
  FROM employees e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id
  WHERE e.id <> ALL(o.path)  -- cycle guard
)
SELECT * FROM org;
-- Fix the offending row:
UPDATE employees SET manager_id = NULL WHERE id = <cycle_root>;
Prevention going forward: - Trigger that rejects updates which would create a cycle. - All recursive
CTEs in the codebase carry an explicit cycle guard.
What NOT to say: - "Set max_recursive_depth lower." That hides the bug.

Scenario413 · Dupes from re-running an upsert without conflict handling

Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 486 / 586

PAGE 487

SELECT CURRENT_DATE - 1, 'gross_revenue', SUM(amount)
FROM orders WHERE DATE(created_at) = CURRENT_DATE - 1
ON CONFLICT (kpi_date, metric) DO UPDATE SET value = EXCLUDED.value;

Scenario414 · Customer 360 view double-counting orders + refunds

The scenario:
The "lifetime value" column in your CRM shows ₹84,000 for a customer who has actually spent

SELECT o.customer_id,
       SUM(o.total_amount) - SUM(r.refund_amount) AS ltv
FROM orders o

GROUP BY o.customer_id;
What's wrong: If an order has 2 partial refunds, the join produces 2 rows for that order, doubling

The fix:

hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 488
SELECT o.customer_id,
       COALESCE(SUM(o.total_amount), 0) - COALESCE(SUM(r.refund_total), 0) AS ltv

  FROM refunds
  GROUP BY order_id

What's wrong: The web frontend was shipped two weeks ago with a useEffect that fires

actually the count is bloated identically on both sides? No — the bug here is the other direction: 
checkout_complete fires once, checkout_start fires repeatedly, so the ratio looks good. The
inverse bug exists too.
Wait — re-reading: COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) collapses the dupes back to one per user. So a re-
render bug actually does not inflate this query. The real problem: a checkout_complete event also
fires from the "thank-you" page on every reload, but you are counting distinct users — so the actual
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 488 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 489
issue is users reloading after success and being counted only once, masking the bug entirely.
Conversion is 84 percent of users who started, but most "starts" are accidental.
Thinking out loud: 1. "The numerator looks too high. Either the denominator is undercounted or the
numerator is over." 2. "Inspect raw event counts before DISTINCT — checkout_start has 1.4M rows
for 280K users. That's 5 fires per user." 3. "DISTINCT on user_id hides the re-fire issue but reveals a
different one: starts include accidental fires from re-renders that never had real intent." 4. "Either filter to
the first fire per user per session, or fix the client."
The diagnosis: Client-side event was firing on every re-render; DISTINCT user_id papered over the
duplication but made the funnel look unrealistically efficient because trivial "starts" were counted as
intent.
The fix:
-- Take first event per user per session:
WITH first_events AS (
  SELECT user_id, session_id, event,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, session_id, event ORDER BY ts) AS rn
  FROM events WHERE event_date = CURRENT_DATE - 1
)
SELECT
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event = 'checkout_start' AND rn = 1 THEN user_id END),
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event = 'checkout_complete' AND rn = 1 THEN user_id END)
FROM first_events;
Prevention going forward: - Client SDK debounces events. Every event has a client-generated UUID for
dedupe. - Analytics warehouse dedupes on (user_id, session_id, event, client_uuid).
What NOT to say: - "Just remove the DISTINCT." That makes the number even more wrong.
Common follow-up: "How would you instrument the client to distinguish true intent from re-render
fires?"
Scenario416 · Daily snapshot table written twice for same day
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: TCS, Capgemini, Cognizant · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
Your daily_inventory_snapshot table has 2,840,000 rows for May 14 and 1,420,000 rows
for every other day in the month. The schema has no unique constraint on (sku,
snapshot_date).
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 489 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 490
SELECT snapshot_date, COUNT(*) FROM daily_inventory_snapshot
GROUP BY snapshot_date ORDER BY snapshot_date;
What's wrong: The snapshot job ran twice on May 14 — probably someone re-ran it manually after a
'failure' that had already succeeded.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Row count for one day is exactly double. The snapshot job ran twice." 2. "Each
snapshot row should be unique per (sku, snapshot_date)." 3. "Delete one set of duplicates and add the
constraint."
The diagnosis: Snapshot job re-run without idempotency.
The fix:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT ctid, sku, snapshot_date,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY sku, snapshot_date ORDER BY ingested_at) AS rn
  FROM daily_inventory_snapshot WHERE snapshot_date = '2026-05-14'
)
DELETE FROM daily_inventory_snapshot
WHERE ctid IN (SELECT ctid FROM ranked WHERE rn > 1);
ALTER TABLE daily_inventory_snapshot ADD CONSTRAINT inv_snap_uk UNIQUE (sku, snapshot_date);
( ctid is Postgres; on MySQL use the primary key column.)
Prevention going forward: - Snapshot job uses DELETE WHERE snapshot_date = ? THEN
INSERT inside a transaction. - UNIQUE constraint blocks the second insert.
What NOT to say: - "We can leave it — downstream reports take the first value." Downstream reports
likely SUM, so the day is doubled.
Common follow-up: "How would you write the snapshot job so a partial failure can be safely retried?"
Scenario417 · Cron job ran twice in parallel
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Juspay, Pine Labs · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
The settlement report for May 18 contains every transaction twice. Cron logs show the job started
at 02:00 and again at 02:01 because the previous day's run took 25 hours to finish.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 490 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 491
SELECT settlement_id, COUNT(*) FROM settlements
WHERE settlement_date = '2026-05-18'
GROUP BY settlement_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
What's wrong: Two instances of the same cron ran concurrently. Both finished, both wrote.
Thinking out loud: 1. "This is a 'cron is not a job runner' problem. cron just runs the command; if a run

The fix: At the start of the job:
SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(hashtext('settlement_job'));

Or use flock on a file at the OS level.

What NOT to say: - "Just run cron every 25 hours." That introduces drift.

released?"
Scenario418 · ETL idempotency missing — partial reruns inflate
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Walmart Labs, Target India, Lowe's · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
Your ETL processes hourly shards from a Kafka source into a warehouse fact table. A shard failed
midway — 60 percent ingested, then the process died. Operator re-ran the shard. Now 60
percent of that hour is doubled.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 491 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 492
SELECT event_uuid, COUNT(*) FROM fact_events
WHERE event_hour = '2026-05-19 14:00:00'
GROUP BY event_uuid HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
What's wrong: The ETL appends rows by event_uuid, but does not check whether the uuid is
already present. A partial rerun doubles the partial slice.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Idempotency requires either (a) deterministic deletion + reinsert per shard, or (b)
merge-on-uuid." 2. "For high-throughput inserts, the staging-then-merge pattern is standard." 3. "Fix the
existing dupes; switch the load to merge on UUID."
The diagnosis: ETL was not idempotent. Partial failure plus retry inflated.
The fix:
-- Clean up:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT id, event_uuid,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY event_uuid ORDER BY ingested_at) AS rn
  FROM fact_events WHERE event_hour = '2026-05-19 14:00:00'
)
DELETE FROM fact_events WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM ranked WHERE rn > 1);
-- Going forward: stage into a temp table, then MERGE.
MERGE INTO fact_events AS target
USING staging AS src
  ON target.event_uuid = src.event_uuid
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (...) VALUES (...);
Prevention going forward: - Every fact table has a natural deduplication key (event_uuid). - Every
ETL load is MERGE or INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, never plain INSERT. - Shard
boundaries are documented so retries are bounded.
What NOT to say: - "We'll add a LIMIT 1 somewhere." That has no relevance to idempotency.
Common follow-up: "How do you handle the case where the same event_uuid arrives with two different
payloads?"
Scenario419 · Materialised view + source table both queried by report
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Microsoft India, Adobe, Salesforce India · Dialect: Postgres
The scenario:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 492 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 493
A dashboard joins mv_daily_sales (a materialised view aggregating from orders) with 
orders itself to "enrich" with recent orders. Today's total is wildly inflated because some
recent orders appear in both.
SELECT region, SUM(revenue) AS total
FROM (
  SELECT region, total_amount AS revenue FROM orders WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE
  UNION ALL
  SELECT region, gross AS revenue FROM mv_daily_sales WHERE sales_date = CURRENT_DATE
) x GROUP BY region;
What's wrong: The mat view is refreshed every hour. Orders placed in the last hour appear once in 
orders and (after refresh) again in mv_daily_sales.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Two sources of truth for the same window: live table + materialised aggregate.
Overlap is inevitable." 2. "Standard fix: live-tail from orders for the time window after the last MV

The diagnosis: Time-window overlap between materialised view and live source.

WITH mv_max AS (
  SELECT MAX(refreshed_at) AS as_of FROM mv_refresh_log WHERE mv_name = 'mv_daily_sales'
)

  SELECT region, total_amount AS revenue FROM orders, mv_max
   WHERE created_at > mv_max.as_of
  UNION ALL
  SELECT region, gross AS revenue FROM mv_daily_sales WHERE sales_date = CURRENT_DATE
) x GROUP BY region;
Prevention going forward: - Maintain a refresh log table. Every report that mixes MV + live uses it. - Or
refresh more frequently and accept the slight latency, querying only the MV.
What NOT to say: - "Drop the materialised view." MVs exist for a reason; the problem is how the report
mixes sources.

Scenario421 · Bridge table missing a primary key
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Infosys, Wipro, TCS · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A user_roles bridge table maps users to roles. Rohit Shetty shows three "admin" rows.
Permissions audit fails because the role count is off.
SELECT user_id, role_id, COUNT(*)
FROM user_roles
GROUP BY user_id, role_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
What's wrong: The bridge table has no primary key, just two FK columns. Re-running the role-

Thinking out loud: 1. "Bridge tables must have a composite PK on the two FK columns. Otherwise

Scenario422 · Many-to-many join inflation in a wide table
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Flipkart, Myntra, Ajio · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A "customer summary" view joins customers → addresses → orders → tags. Each
customer has multiple addresses, multiple orders, and multiple tags. The view returns 3.4 million
rows for 12,000 customers.
SELECT c.id, c.name, a.city, o.total_amount, t.tag
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN addresses a ON a.customer_id = c.id
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
LEFT JOIN tags t ON t.customer_id = c.id;
What's wrong: A customer with 3 addresses × 12 orders × 4 tags produces 144 rows. The wide join
multiplies all child tables together.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Three independent child tables fan out the Cartesian product." 2. "You almost
never want this. Either aggregate each child before joining, or use lateral subqueries to get a single 'most
recent' value." 3. "Or model it as JSON aggregation in the SELECT."
The diagnosis: Multiple independent child joins produced a multiplicative explosion.
The fix:
SELECT c.id, c.name,
       (SELECT array_agg(city) FROM addresses WHERE customer_id = c.id) AS cities,
       (SELECT SUM(total_amount) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.id) AS lifetime_value,
       (SELECT array_agg(tag) FROM tags WHERE customer_id = c.id) AS tags
FROM customers c;
Or aggregate-then-join each side.
Prevention going forward: - "Wide" customer views are never built with raw multi-joins. Use CTE-per-
child-aggregate or JSON aggregation.
What NOT to say: - "Add DISTINCT to the SELECT." DISTINCT over a wide projection is wildly
expensive and still wrong if any column is an aggregate.
Common follow-up: "How would you build this same view in BigQuery using STRUCT and
ARRAY_AGG?"

Scenario423 · A/B test exposure counted in control + treatment via cookie collision
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Swiggy, Zomato, Meesho · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
Your A/B test results show 12 percent overlap — users appearing in both control and treatment.
Your assignment is supposed to be deterministic via cookie hash, but the overlap is real.
SELECT user_id, COUNT(DISTINCT variant) AS variants
FROM ab_exposures
WHERE experiment_id = 'checkout_v3'
GROUP BY user_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT variant) > 1;
What's wrong: Users hit the experiment from web and from app — different cookie / device ID — and
got bucketed independently on each.
Thinking out loud: 1. "A/B assignment must be keyed on a stable identity (logged-in user_id), not on a
per-device cookie." 2. "For logged-out users, you accept some bucket drift; for logged-in users it's a
bug." 3. "Mitigation: drop those users from analysis (they pollute both arms), and fix the assignment logic
to key on user_id when known."
The diagnosis: Bucketing keyed on cookie rather than on stable user identity.
The fix:
-- Exclude polluted users from the analysis:
WITH polluted AS (
  SELECT user_id FROM ab_exposures
  WHERE experiment_id = 'checkout_v3'
  GROUP BY user_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT variant) > 1
)
SELECT variant, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS exposed, SUM(converted::int) AS converted
FROM ab_exposures
WHERE experiment_id = 'checkout_v3'
  AND user_id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM polluted)
GROUP BY variant;
Prevention going forward: - A/B assignment service prefers user_id over cookie when available;
falls back to cookie only for logged-out traffic. - Exposure events are deduplicated per (experiment_id,
user_id, variant) at the warehouse layer.
What NOT to say: - "Just keep both buckets and weight." That biases the test in unpredictable ways.
Common follow-up: "How would you have caught this before launching the experiment?"

Scenario424 · Affiliate click dupes from refresh and back-button
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Cuelinks, INRDeals, EarnKaro · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
Affiliate payouts are calculated per unique click. Your top affiliate is showing 4.2× the clicks of last
month with no campaign change. Browsing patterns reveal users hitting refresh on the redirect
page.
SELECT affiliate_id, COUNT(*) AS clicks
FROM affiliate_clicks
WHERE click_date = CURRENT_DATE - 1
GROUP BY affiliate_id
ORDER BY clicks DESC;
What's wrong: The redirect endpoint logs a click on every hit. Browser back-button + refresh on the
destination produces phantom clicks.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Affiliate clicks need a session-level dedupe, not raw-hit counting." 2. "The dedupe
key is usually (affiliate_id, visitor_id, day) — at most one click per visitor per affiliate per day."
The diagnosis: Raw hit counting without dedupe on visitor + day.
The fix:
SELECT affiliate_id, COUNT(DISTINCT visitor_id) AS unique_clicks

Better: enforce at write time using INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING with a UNIQUE on

affiliate T&C so payouts are unambiguous.
What NOT to say: - "Pay them anyway, it's good for the relationship." You will be subsidising bot-like
behaviour and the next affiliate will exploit it.

Scenario425 · Same address marked primary for multiple users
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: BigBasket, Grofers, Zepto · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A "household" feature shows that 47 customers share the same primary address. The team
thinks it is a data quality smell — but is it noise, families, or shared sellers?
SELECT address_hash, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS users
FROM user_addresses
WHERE is_primary = TRUE
GROUP BY address_hash
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) > 5
ORDER BY users DESC;
What's wrong: Hard to tell without context. The query is correct — but the interpretation requires you to
think like a data engineer.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Five users on one address could be a joint family (legitimate) or a hostel
(legitimate) or fraud rings (not legitimate) or normalisation noise (street address parsed two ways)." 2. 
"First, check whether the addresses are actually the same string or just the same hash — bug in the hash
function would collapse different addresses." 3. "Then segment by household size distribution: top-1
percent might be fraud; the middle bulk is families."
The diagnosis: This is not a single bug — it is a data quality investigation. The "duplicate" is real but the
meaning depends on segment. Most production data has at least 3 distinct sources of address dupes:
fraud, families, and parsing noise.
The fix:
SELECT address_hash,
       address_line1,
       pincode,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS users,
       MIN(created_at) AS first_user_seen,
       MAX(created_at) AS last_user_seen
FROM user_addresses
WHERE is_primary = TRUE
GROUP BY address_hash, address_line1, pincode
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) > 5
ORDER BY users DESC;
-- Then sample 20 rows and eyeball.

Category 7, Part B — Data Quality: Missing Rows & Counts
Mismatch
"The dashboard says 9,87,432 orders, the app says 9,91,108, and finance says 9,89,200 — which one is
right and who do I have to call?" That is the kind of message that lands in your DM on a Monday
morning when nothing technically broke but every system has a slightly different version of reality.
Counts not matching across systems and "where did these rows go" investigations are the most
common, most underrated kind of data work. They look like trivia. They are actually how a data person
earns their salt — because the answer is almost never "the database is wrong"; it is almost always a join,
a filter, a timezone, a partition, a replication lag, or a definition drift that someone treated as obvious. The
25 scenarios below walk through the detective playbooks for these — the questions to ask, the
diagnostic queries to run, the prevention to put in place, and the things not to say in the meeting before
you have evidence.
Scenario426 · DB Count vs GA4 Count Mismatch — 12% Gap
Tags: intermediatedq-investigationanalytics-toolsattributionvendor-
agnostic
Business context: You run an Indian D2C skincare brand on Shopify. The marketing lead pings you on
Slack — "GA4 is showing 8,742 purchases yesterday, but our DB is showing 9,931. Which one is
correct? We are about to scale ad spend based on GA4 ROAS." The 12% gap is too big to ignore.
SQL:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS db_orders, SUM(total_amount) AS db_revenue
FROM orders
WHERE order_status = 'paid'
  AND created_at >= '2026-05-25' AND created_at < '2026-05-26';
Suspicious output: db_orders = 9931, db_revenue = 47,82,650. GA4 reports purchases
= 8742. Discrepancy of 1,189 orders (~12%).
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 500 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 501
Thinking out loud: 1. First, are we comparing the same definition? GA4 counts purchase events fired
client-side; DB counts paid orders server-side. These are structurally different sources, so some gap is
expected — but 12% is high. 2. Common reasons GA4 under-counts: ad-blockers (10-15% in India is
normal), users who close the browser before the thank-you page fires, single-page checkout glitches,
consent-banner rejections, and Safari ITP. 3. Common reasons DB over-counts vs GA4: server-to-server
reorders (COD confirmations, retry payments), backend imports, manual orders entered by the support
team, B2B/wholesale orders. 4. The right diagnostic is to bucket the gap — how many orders had no
GA4 client_id, came from COD, came from manual channel, came from mobile-app (which fires different
events).
Diagnosis: Of the 1,189 missing orders — 612 were COD (GA4 purchase fires only on thank-you page,
which COD users often skip), 287 had ad-blocker (no client_id captured), 198 came from native mobile
app (separate GA4 property not aggregated), 92 were manual orders by support.
Fix or diagnostic query:
SELECT
  CASE WHEN payment_method = 'cod' THEN 'cod'
       WHEN ga4_client_id IS NULL THEN 'no_client_id'
       WHEN source_channel = 'mobile_app' THEN 'mobile_app'
       WHEN created_by_user_id IS NOT NULL THEN 'manual' ELSE 'web' END AS bucket,
  COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
WHERE order_status = 'paid' AND created_at::date = '2026-05-25'
GROUP BY 1;
Prevention: Send server-side purchase events via Measurement Protocol with the order_id as
deduplication key. Stamp ga4_client_id on the order record at checkout. Treat DB as source of
truth for revenue, GA4 only for attribution.
NOT to say: "GA4 is wrong, ignore it." Both are right for what they measure — GA4 measures client-side
behaviour, DB measures money received.
Follow-up: "How would you bucket the gap by acquisition channel to see if one channel has a worse
data loss rate than another?"
Scenario427 · App Reports 1,000 Orders, DB Shows 950 — Find the 50
Tags: intermediatedq-investigationpending-statesvendor-agnostic
Business context: A food-delivery startup in Bengaluru — the operations dashboard inside their internal
app says 1,000 orders placed today, but the analytics DB count says 950. The CEO asks in standup:
"Where are the 50 orders?"
SQL:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 501 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 502
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM analytics_orders WHERE order_date = CURRENT_DATE;
-- returns 950
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ops.orders_live WHERE order_date = CURRENT_DATE;
-- returns 1000
Suspicious output: Difference of exactly 50 orders. The fact that the gap is round-ish is suspicious —
possibly a single batch or a single failure.
Thinking out loud: 1. The ops app is reading from the live OLTP system; the analytics DB is downstream
after an ETL. So the gap could be (a) ETL hasn't finished yet, (b) ETL filter is excluding some orders, (c)
some orders are in a state that ETL skips. 2. The first thing I'd check is the ETL last-run timestamp. If it
ran at 22:00 yesterday and we're querying at 14:00 today, the day isn't "done" yet. 3. Second, what
status are those 50? Pending, cancelled, failed? Many ETLs intentionally skip non-terminal states. 4.
Third, do they share a common feature — same restaurant, same payment method, same city? A
correlated cluster usually points to a single bug.
Diagnosis: ETL filter was WHERE order_status IN ('placed','delivered','cancelled').
The 50 missing orders were in order_status = 'pending_payment' — a state added to the
source schema last week but never added to the ETL filter. The ETL is technically running fine, just blind
to the new state.
Fix or diagnostic query:
SELECT order_status, COUNT(*)
FROM ops.orders_live
WHERE order_date = CURRENT_DATE
  AND order_id NOT IN (SELECT order_id FROM analytics_orders WHERE order_date = CURRENT_DATE)
GROUP BY order_status;
Prevention: ETLs should ingest all rows and let the BI layer filter — never apply business filters at
ingestion. Add a CI check that fails if a new status appears in source but isn't in the analytics dimension
table.
NOT to say: "It's probably a sync delay, let's check tomorrow." That defers the diagnosis; the gap might
be persistent and not delay-related.
Follow-up: "How would you build a reconciliation report that runs hourly and alerts when the gap
exceeds 1%?"
Scenario428 · Timezone Mismatch Between Source and Report

Business context: A Mumbai-based SaaS company runs on AWS Mumbai region but their data

  AND created_at <  TIMESTAMP '2026-05-26 00:00:00' AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata'

Scenario429 · Cron Job Cuts Off at Midnight, Loses 30 Minutes of Rows
Tags: intermediatedq-investigationcron vendor-agnostic
Business context: A logistics company runs a nightly ETL that aggregates the day's shipments. The ETL
runs at 23:30 IST and is supposed to capture "today." But every morning, the reconciliation report shows
~80 shipments missing compared to the OLTP system.
SQL:
-- ETL filter (runs at 23:30 IST on 25-May)
INSERT INTO daily_shipments_summary
SELECT shipment_id, status, created_at
FROM shipments
WHERE created_at >= '2026-05-25 00:00:00'
  AND created_at <  '2026-05-26 00:00:00';
Suspicious output: Summary table has 4,217 shipments for 25-May. Source shipments table for the
same date range has 4,298. Gap of 81.
Thinking out loud: 1. The ETL runs at 23:30, but the day isn't over yet — there are still 30 minutes left in
the day, plus all the late-arriving rows after the cron starts. 2. The cron is filtering for the entire day, but it
can only see rows up to the moment it runs. The 80-shipment gap matches the typical 23:30-00:00
traffic. 3. Two clean fixes: (a) run the cron after midnight (e.g., 01:30 next day) for "yesterday", or (b) keep
the 23:30 schedule but re-run a "catch-up" job at 01:00 for any late rows. 4. There's also a subtle one —
rows created at 23:30:15 while the cron is running may or may not be captured depending on transaction
isolation level.
Diagnosis: Cron starts at 23:30 IST, scans rows up to its query start time. The 30 minutes between cron
start and midnight produce ~80 shipments that never get into the summary.
Fix or diagnostic query:
-- Either shift the cron schedule:
-- crontab: 30 1 * * *   (run at 01:30 the NEXT day for "yesterday")
-- And filter:
WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 day'
  AND created_at <  CURRENT_DATE;

Prevention: Never run a "today" aggregation while today is still happening. Always aggregate
"yesterday" the next morning. Add a sentinel check: assert row_count_in_summary =
