Scenario431 · Status Casing Bug — 'Completed' vs 'completed'
Tags: intermediatedq-investigationcasingvendor-agnostic
Business context: A B2B invoicing platform reports 1,820 "completed" payments for the week. The
CFO does a spot-check by exporting the raw table and finds 1,847 rows with completed status. Gap of
27.
SQL:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM payments
WHERE status = 'completed' AND week_of = '2026-05-19';
-- returns 1820
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM payments
WHERE LOWER(status) = 'completed' AND week_of = '2026-05-19';
-- returns 1847
Suspicious output: 27 rows have status = 'Completed' (capital C) instead of 'completed'.
The original query is case-sensitive and misses them.
Thinking out loud: 1. In PostgreSQL and most databases with case-sensitive string equality, 
'completed' != 'Completed'. In MySQL with default collation, they'd be equal — so the
behaviour depends on the engine. 2. Where would inconsistent casing come from? Multiple ingestion
sources writing to the same column — perhaps a legacy app writes 'Completed' while the new API
writes 'completed'. 3. The fix is twofold: short-term, use LOWER() in the filter; long-term, normalise the
casing at write time and add a CHECK constraint. 4. Worth checking what other statuses are affected —
could be 'Refunded' vs 'refunded', 'Cancelled' vs 'cancelled', etc.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 506 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 507
Diagnosis: 23 of the 27 were written by an older mobile-app version that didn't standardise casing. 4
were written by a third-party integration that uses TitleCase by convention.
Fix or diagnostic query:
SELECT status, COUNT(*) FROM payments
WHERE week_of = '2026-05-19'
GROUP BY status ORDER BY 2 DESC;
-- See all variants. Then:
UPDATE payments SET status = LOWER(status) WHERE status != LOWER(status);
ALTER TABLE payments ADD CONSTRAINT status_lowercase CHECK (status = LOWER(status));
Prevention: Use a CHECK constraint or trigger to enforce lowercase. Better — use an enum type if your
database supports it. Even better — make the column a foreign key to a payment_statuses lookup
table.
NOT to say: "Just always use LOWER() in queries." Defensive but doesn't fix the root cause; the next
engineer will write a non-LOWER query and the bug returns.
Follow-up: "What if the column also has leading/trailing whitespace — how would you find and fix that?"
Scenario432 · INNER JOIN Silently Drops Rows
Tags: intermediatedq-investigationjoinsvendor-agnostic
Business context: A travel booking startup. The marketing team asks for "all bookings with the user's
signup source." The data analyst joins bookings to users and reports 4,200 bookings for the
month. The product team insists there were 4,580.
SQL:
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM bookings b
INNER JOIN users u ON b.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE b.booked_at >= '2026-05-01';
-- returns 4200
Suspicious output: Bookings table standalone count is 4,580. Joined count is 4,200. Gap of 380.
Thinking out loud: 1. INNER JOIN drops bookings whose user_id doesn't match any row in 
users. So 380 bookings have a user_id that doesn't exist in users. 2. Possible reasons: (a) guest
checkouts where user_id is null, (b) users who were hard-deleted from the users table but their
bookings remain, (c) FK isn't enforced and there's data corruption, (d) user_id in bookings table points to
a different table (e.g., admin_users). 3. The fix is to use LEFT JOIN and add a flag column so the gap is
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 507 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 508
visible, not silent. 4. Also need to investigate why those 380 are orphaned — could be a real bug or could
be expected (guest bookings).
Diagnosis: 290 are guest checkouts (user_id IS NULL in bookings), 87 are users who deleted their
account (cascade-deleted from users but bookings remained), 3 are corrupted (user_id points to
nothing).
Fix or diagnostic query:
SELECT
  COUNT(*) AS total_bookings,
  COUNT(u.user_id) AS bookings_with_user,
  COUNT(*) - COUNT(u.user_id) AS bookings_missing_user
FROM bookings b
LEFT JOIN users u ON b.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE b.booked_at >= '2026-05-01';
Prevention: Default to LEFT JOIN when one side is "facts." Only use INNER JOIN when you explicitly
want to exclude unmatched rows, and document why. Add a data-quality alert for orphaned bookings.
NOT to say: "INNER JOIN is faster, so I used it." Correctness > performance, especially for reports.
Follow-up: "What if you wanted to count bookings whose user signed up in the last 30 days — would
INNER JOIN be appropriate there?"
Scenario433 · WHERE Clause Excludes NULL Silently
Tags: intermediatedq-investigationnull-handlingvendor-agnostic
Business context: A health-tech app reports the number of appointments where the doctor is NOT a
cardiologist. The number looks low. On review, the gap is around 600 appointments.
SQL:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM appointments
WHERE doctor_specialty != 'cardiology'
  AND appointment_date = '2026-05-25';
-- returns 1240
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM appointments
WHERE appointment_date = '2026-05-25';
-- returns 2100
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM appointments
WHERE doctor_specialty = 'cardiology' AND appointment_date = '2026-05-25';
-- returns 260
-- 1240 + 260 = 1500, not 2100 — 600 missing
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 508 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 509
Suspicious output: Total 2,100 appointments. Cardiology = 260. Non-cardiology = 1,240. Sum = 1,500.
600 are unaccounted.
Thinking out loud: 1. Classic SQL three-valued-logic bug. NULL != 'cardiology' evaluates to
NULL, not TRUE. So rows with doctor_specialty IS NULL are excluded from both queries. 2.
The 600 missing rows are appointments where the doctor's specialty was never recorded — possibly
walk-ins, telemedicine, or general physicians. 3. The fix is to either: (a) treat NULL as "non-cardiology" by
using IS DISTINCT FROM (Postgres) or doctor_specialty != 'cardiology' OR
doctor_specialty IS NULL, or (b) coalesce to a sentinel value. 4. The deeper question is — should
NULL be allowed at all in this column? If every appointment must have a specialty, make it NOT NULL.
Diagnosis: 600 rows have doctor_specialty IS NULL. The != filter silently excluded them.
Fix or diagnostic query:
-- Postgres
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM appointments
WHERE doctor_specialty IS DISTINCT FROM 'cardiology'
  AND appointment_date = '2026-05-25';
-- Vendor-agnostic
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM appointments
WHERE (doctor_specialty != 'cardiology' OR doctor_specialty IS NULL)
  AND appointment_date = '2026-05-25';
Prevention: When writing exclusion filters, always think "what about NULL?" Add a unit test that asserts 
cardiology_count + non_cardiology_count = total_count.
NOT to say: "I'll just add IS NOT NULL to fix it." That excludes NULLs entirely, which may not be the
intent.
Follow-up: "What if the column is doctor_specialty[] (an array) and you want appointments
where cardiology is NOT in the array — how does the NULL logic change?"
Scenario434 · Source Stored in Local Time, Report Assumes UTC
Tags: intermediatedq-investigationtimezonevendor-agnostic
Business context: A pan-Asia logistics SaaS. Some warehouses are in Singapore, some in Bengaluru,
some in Dubai. The OLTP stores event_time as TIMESTAMP (no timezone) in each warehouse's
local time. The central warehouse aggregates and assumes UTC. Daily counts are wrong for every
warehouse.
SQL:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 509 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 510
SELECT warehouse_id, COUNT(*) AS scans_today
FROM scans
WHERE event_time >= '2026-05-25 00:00:00' AND event_time < '2026-05-26 00:00:00';
Suspicious output: Bengaluru warehouse usually has ~12,000 scans/day. Today it shows 9,800.
Singapore shows 14,200 instead of typical 13,000.
Thinking out loud: 1. The query is in UTC. Bengaluru scans happen in IST (UTC+5:30). A scan at 02:00
IST is at 20:30 UTC the previous day. So a UTC-day filter chops off the early-morning IST hours and
adds late-evening hours from the previous IST day. 2. Singapore is UTC+8. Same problem in the
opposite direction — the UTC day includes some of yesterday's Singapore evening and misses today's
Singapore morning. 3. This is worse than it sounds because each warehouse is shifted by a different
amount. There is no single timezone you can convert to without splitting per-warehouse. 4. The fix is to
store the warehouse timezone explicitly and convert when querying.

query treated all timestamps as UTC, causing per-warehouse day shifts.

SELECT
  s.warehouse_id,
  COUNT(*) AS scans_today
FROM scans s
JOIN warehouses w ON s.warehouse_id = w.warehouse_id
WHERE s.event_time >= TIMESTAMP '2026-05-25 00:00:00' AT TIME ZONE w.timezone
  AND s.event_time <  TIMESTAMP '2026-05-26 00:00:00' AT TIME ZONE w.timezone
GROUP BY 1;
Prevention: Always store timestamps in UTC (TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE). Store the entity's
timezone separately. Never use naive TIMESTAMP for events from multiple regions.
NOT to say: "Let's just convert all warehouses to IST." Doesn't help — the underlying data is in mixed
timezones; conversion needs the warehouse timezone, not a single uniform one.
Follow-up: "What if the warehouse moves to a new timezone (DST or a regulatory change) — how would
you handle historical data?"
Scenario435 · Daylight Saving Time Drops Rows
Tags: advanceddq-investigationdst vendor-agnostic
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 510 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 511
Business context: A US-India hybrid SaaS — Indian users are unaffected, but US users in spring see
their daily activity reports drop one hour's worth of data. The product manager in Boston complains
every March.
SQL:
SELECT
  generate_series(
    TIMESTAMP '2026-03-08 00:00:00' AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York',
    TIMESTAMP '2026-03-09 00:00:00' AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York',
    INTERVAL '1 hour'
  ) AS hr;
Suspicious output: The series skips the 02:00-03:00 ET hour (because DST jumped forward at 02:00).
When aggregating hourly buckets, that hour has zero rows — but the user-facing report shows it as "no
activity," misleading the PM.
Thinking out loud: 1. DST spring-forward means 02:00 doesn't exist on that day in US time zones. Fall-
back means 01:00-02:00 happens twice. 2. If the underlying data is stored in UTC (which it should be),
no rows are actually lost — it's the bucketing that's wrong. 3. If the underlying data is stored in local time
as a naive timestamp, then the spring-forward hour literally has no rows because those moments don't
exist locally — but also some rows are ambiguous in fall-back. 4. The diagnostic is to query in UTC and
confirm the row counts are continuous, then fix the local-time presentation.
Diagnosis: Data is stored in UTC, but the hourly bucketing is converting to America/New_York and then
bucketing — which produces a gap on spring-forward and a duplicate on fall-back.
Fix or diagnostic query:
-- Don't bucket on local time. Bucket on UTC, then convert the bucket label.
SELECT
  DATE_TRUNC('hour', event_time) AS utc_hour,
  DATE_TRUNC('hour', event_time AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York') AS local_hour_label,
  COUNT(*) AS events
FROM user_events
WHERE event_time >= '2026-03-08' AND event_time < '2026-03-09'
GROUP BY 1, 2;
Prevention: For continuous time-series, always bucket in UTC. Only convert for human-facing labels.
Document DST handling in the schema notes.
NOT to say: "Indian users are fine, ignore the US one." DST bugs compound — fall-back duplicates also
break sum-of-hourly equals daily-total.
Follow-up: "What if your data warehouse uses DATE_TRUNC in local time and you can't change it —
how do you patch the report?"

-- Postgres: list partitions
SELECT child.relname AS partition_name
FROM pg_inherits
JOIN pg_class parent ON pg_inherits.inhparent = parent.oid
JOIN pg_class child ON pg_inherits.inhrelid = child.oid
WHERE parent.relname = 'cdr_records'
ORDER BY child.relname;
-- Attach the missing one:
ALTER TABLE cdr_records ATTACH PARTITION cdr_records_2026_05_25
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-05-25') TO ('2026-05-26');

Scenario439 · Read Replica Lag Hides Recent Rows
Tags: intermediatedq-investigationreplicationvendor-agnostic
Business context: A B2C app. Customer support runs a "recent orders" query against a read replica. A
customer placed an order 30 seconds ago and is now on the phone — but the support agent's query
returns nothing. They tell the customer "we don't see your order," and the customer escalates.
SQL:
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE customer_email = 'priya@example.com'
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 5;
-- returns nothing (recent order not yet replicated)
Suspicious output: The order exists on the primary but not on the replica. Replica lag is currently ~45
seconds during peak hours.
Thinking out loud: 1. Read replicas are async. Any query against a replica can be slightly stale. 2. For
most analytics use cases this is fine; for customer-support real-time queries it's a disaster. 3. The fix is to
route certain queries (recent orders, recent payments, account status) to the primary, or to use a "recent
reads from primary" policy. 4. Could also use a read-your-own-writes pattern — check replica first, fall
back to primary if not found.
Diagnosis: Read replica lag of 45s. Recent orders haven't replicated yet. Support tool was configured to

Scenario440 · Outbox Events Stuck, Downstream Missing Rows
Tags: advanceddq-investigationoutboxvendor-agnostic
Business context: An e-commerce platform uses the outbox pattern — orders are written to an 
outbox table, then a worker publishes them to Kafka, then a downstream warehouse ingests.
Warehouse shows 12,400 orders. App DB shows 12,580. Gap of 180.
SQL:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM app.orders WHERE order_date = CURRENT_DATE;
-- 12580
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM warehouse.fact_orders WHERE order_date = CURRENT_DATE;
-- 12400
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM app.outbox WHERE event_type='order_created' AND published_at IS NULL;
-- 180
Suspicious output: Exactly 180 unpublished events in the outbox. The downstream is missing exactly
those 180.
Thinking out loud: 1. The outbox pattern is precisely what's broken — events written to the outbox,
never published. The publisher worker has fallen behind or died. 2. Why? Could be (a) worker crashed
and didn't restart, (b) Kafka topic at capacity / unhealthy, (c) the worker's poll loop is stuck on a poison
message, (d) the worker is running but its filter is wrong. 3. Check the worker process status, the Kafka
topic lag, and the most recent successful publish time. 4. After fixing the worker, the events need to be
re-driven — but ensure idempotency on the consumer side.

PAGE 517
Diagnosis: Publisher worker crashed at 14:30 due to OOM. Auto-restart wasn't configured. 180 events
accumulated unpublished.
Fix or diagnostic query:
-- Find oldest unpublished event
SELECT MIN(created_at), MAX(created_at), COUNT(*)
FROM app.outbox
WHERE published_at IS NULL;
-- Drive the publisher manually or wait for it to catch up after restart
Prevention: Health check on publisher worker (alert if no publish in 60 seconds). Limit outbox backlog

SELECT SUM(p.amount * er.rate_to_inr) AS total_revenue_inr

Scenario446 · Attribution Model — Last-Click vs First-Click
Tags: advanceddq-investigationattributionvendor-agnostic

SQL:
-- Performance team: last-click
SELECT last_click_channel, COUNT(*) FROM conversions
WHERE converted_at >= '2026-05-01' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;
-- Brand team: first-click
SELECT first_click_channel, COUNT(*) FROM conversions
WHERE converted_at >= '2026-05-01' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 522 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 523
Suspicious output: Last-click puts Google Ads first; first-click puts Instagram first. Both totals equal the
same overall conversion count, so the sum is consistent — but the per-channel attribution differs.
Thinking out loud: 1. This is structurally correct — different attribution models produce different per-
channel numbers. The bug is treating one as definitive. 2. Real attribution should be multi-touch (linear,

attribution number without the model name attached.

Fix or diagnostic query:
SELECT
  channel,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE first_click_channel = channel) AS first_click_attributions,
  COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE last_click_channel = channel) AS last_click_attributions,
  SUM(linear_weight) AS linear_attributions
FROM conversions c
JOIN UNNEST(c.touchpoints) t(channel, linear_weight) ON TRUE
WHERE c.converted_at >= '2026-05-01'
GROUP BY channel;
Prevention: Always label attribution numbers with the model used. Build a single attribution dashboard
with a model toggle. Document the org-default model (usually multi-touch for budget allocation).
NOT to say: "Last-click is the right model." It depends on the business; brand vs performance teams
legitimately need different models.
Follow-up: "If a conversion has 7 touchpoints across 4 channels over 14 days, how does a time-decay
model weight each?"
Scenario447 · Funnel Step Counted Differently Downstream
Tags: intermediatedq-investigationfunnelvendor-agnostic
Business context: An ed-tech platform measures signup-to-payment funnel. The "added to cart" step
shows 14,200 users in the product analytics tool but 13,800 in the data warehouse. Same event.
SQL:
-- Product analytics: distinct users who fired add_to_cart event
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) FROM events WHERE event_name='add_to_cart' AND event_date='2026-05-25';
-- Warehouse funnel mart: users with at least one cart row created
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) FROM cart_items WHERE created_at::date='2026-05-25';
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 523 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 524
Suspicious output: Events table: 14,200. Cart_items table: 13,800. Gap of 400.
Thinking out loud: 1. The events table records the user firing the add_to_cart event (client-side
tracking). The cart_items table records the server-side cart row creation. 2. The gap of 400 likely

  AND c.created_at::date = e.event_date
WHERE e.event_name = 'add_to_cart'
  AND e.event_date = '2026-05-25'
  AND c.user_id IS NULL;
Prevention: Reconcile client-side events with server-side actions daily. Treat server-side as source of
truth for funnel metrics. Use client-side only for cohort discovery.
NOT to say: "Product analytics is wrong." Both are recording real things; the question is which is the
truth source for the funnel.

SQL:

WHERE status != 'inactive' AND last_seen_at >= week_starting
GROUP BY 1;
-- Mon-Tue: ~24,000/day. Wed onwards: ~19,700/day.

hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 526
Suspicious output: A clean step-change on Wednesday — not a gradual decline, which would indicate
a real business issue.
Thinking out loud: 1. A sharp step-change in a metric, dated exactly to a deployment or migration, is

Tags: advanceddq-investigationfederationvendor-agnostic

-- Federated query (simplified)
SELECT 'sub_a' AS source, COUNT(*) FROM ext.sub_a_customers
UNION ALL

Scenario451 · Revenue Line Went Flat — Upstream Pipeline Silently Broken
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Flipkart · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
The CFO's daily revenue dashboard shows a flat line for the last nine days. Bookings are
happening — support is fielding tickets, customers are receiving order confirmations — yet 
fact_revenue_daily has not advanced. The query that powers the chart returns rows for
every date, the bar just plots at the same height because the underlying total has not moved.
SELECT booking_date, SUM(amount_inr) AS revenue_inr
FROM fact_revenue_daily
WHERE booking_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30' DAY
GROUP BY booking_date
ORDER BY booking_date;
Expected: Daily revenue that tracks reality — visible day-over-day swings. Actual: Flat line; the most
recent nine booking_date values all sum to a value identical to the value nine days ago.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Flat means either (a) no new rows landing for those dates, or (b) the rows that exist
are stale duplicates of an older snapshot." 2. "Let me count rows per booking_date — if it is zero for
the last nine days, the load stopped. If row counts are normal but amounts are identical, the source has
frozen but the loader kept copying the same snapshot." 3. "Either way the dashboard cannot tell — it just
renders what is in the warehouse."
The diagnosis: Row count per recent date is zero; MAX(load_ts) on the table is nine days old. The
upstream Airflow DAG has been red since a credential rotation but the alerting rule was set up against a
different DAG name after a recent rename, so nobody got paged. The chart silently re-rendered the last
good day at the right edge of the window because the y-axis auto-scaled.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 528 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in

The fix:
-- Daily freshness guard — runs on a schedule, raises if breached

  MAX(booking_date)                     AS latest_business_date,
  CURRENT_DATE - MAX(booking_date)      AS days_behind,
  MAX(load_ts)                          AS latest_load_ts,
  CURRENT_TIMESTAMP - MAX(load_ts)      AS hours_since_last_load
FROM fact_revenue_daily;

FROM fact_revenue_daily
WHERE booking_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '14' DAY
GROUP BY booking_date
HAVING COUNT(*) = 0 OR COUNT(*) < 0.5 * AVG(COUNT(*)) OVER ();
Why this works: Freshness checks treat the absence of data as a first-class signal rather than an

Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 538 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 539
-- Postgres: ALTER TYPE is metadata-only for INT → BIGINT in newer versions,
-- but the sequence behind it needs widening too
ALTER TABLE transactions ALTER COLUMN txn_id TYPE BIGINT;

-- pt-online-schema-change --alter "MODIFY txn_id BIGINT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT" \
--   D=payments,t=transactions --execute

       2147483647 AS signed_int_max,

Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Cred, Swiggy · Dialect: Postgres, MySQL
The scenario:
Service A writes UUIDs as b1f2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890 (lowercase,
hyphenated). Service B writes UUIDs as B1F2C3D4E5F67890ABCDEF1234567890
(uppercase, no hyphens). The join between their tables returns no rows; the two systems are
talking past each other.
SELECT *
FROM service_a_orders a
JOIN service_b_shipments b ON b.order_uuid = a.order_uuid;
Expected: A row for every order with a corresponding shipment. Actual: Empty.
Thinking out loud: 1. "The columns might be VARCHAR instead of native UUID, in which case the
join is a string comparison and string comparison is case-sensitive in most collations." 2. "Even if one
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 539 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 540
side is UUID and the other VARCHAR, casting on either side normalises only one direction." 3. "I will
canonicalise both sides on read."
The diagnosis: Service A column is UUID, Service B column is VARCHAR(32) with no hyphens and
uppercase letters. The implicit cast on the join either fails outright or silently produces zero matches
depending on the dialect.
The fix:
-- Normalise both sides to canonical UUID
SELECT *
FROM service_a_orders a
JOIN service_b_shipments b
  ON a.order_uuid::TEXT = LOWER(
    REGEXP_REPLACE(b.order_uuid, '^([0-9a-fA-F]{8})([0-9a-fA-F]{4})([0-9a-fA-F]{4})([0-9a-fA-F]{4})([0-9a-fA-F]{12})$',
                                 '\1-\2-\3-\4-\5'));
-- Long-term fix: convert service_b_shipments.order_uuid to native UUID type
ALTER TABLE service_b_shipments
  ALTER COLUMN order_uuid TYPE UUID
  USING LOWER(REGEXP_REPLACE(order_uuid, '^([0-9a-fA-F]{8})([0-9a-fA-F]{4})([0-9a-fA-F]{4})([0-9a-fA-F]{4})([0-9a-fA-F]{12})$', '\1-\2-\3-\4-\5'))::UUID;
Why this works: Converting the rogue column to native UUID makes the format mismatch impossible
going forward — the database enforces canonical representation on insert.
What NOT to say: - "Just LOWER() both sides" — that does not insert the hyphens. - "Add another
column for the canonical form" — possible, but the type fix is cleaner.
Common follow-up: "How would you detect this drift across all UUID columns in the schema?"

The scenario:
Compliance reviews show that customers_audit has rows for every change made through
the application, but is missing entries for the monthly bulk update job that imports 50,000 KYC

Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 540 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 541
CREATE TRIGGER customers_audit_trg
AFTER UPDATE ON customers
FOR EACH ROW
EXECUTE FUNCTION customers_audit_fn();
Expected: One audit row per updated customer. Actual: Audit rows for application traffic only; bulk-
import path leaves no trail.
Thinking out loud: 1. " FOR EACH ROW should fire 50,000 times, not zero." 2. "Unless the bulk path
uses COPY (Postgres) or LOAD DATA INFILE (MySQL) which bypass triggers, or TRUNCATE +

The fix: Cover all DML paths and consider statement-level triggers for bulk:
-- Fire on INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE
CREATE TRIGGER customers_audit_ins_trg
AFTER INSERT ON customers
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION customers_audit_fn();
CREATE TRIGGER customers_audit_del_trg
AFTER DELETE ON customers
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION customers_audit_fn();
-- For Postgres COPY, application code must call the audit function explicitly
-- because COPY bypasses row-level triggers by design in some configurations.
-- Verification: bulk-load row count vs audit row count for the same window
SELECT
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE last_modified_ts BETWEEN $1 AND $2) AS data_changes,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers_audit WHERE audit_ts BETWEEN $1 AND $2)   AS audit_rows;
Why this works: Triggers on every DML verb close the obvious gap; the reconciliation query is the safety
net that detects future bypasses (a new bulk path that skips triggers shows up immediately).
What NOT to say: - "The trigger looks correct, must be a permissions issue" — the trigger is correct for
UPDATE, the bug is that the bulk path is not UPDATE. - "Just add the audit rows manually for the
missing months" — fix the leak first, then back-fill from logs if possible.
Common follow-up: "How do you design an audit pattern that survives bulk replaces?"

The scenario:
A compliance request asks for who edited customer KYC records in the last 18 months. The audit

Thinking out loud: 1. "Audit data is regulated — retention is usually defined externally." 2. "Some team

-- (Disable the cron / unschedule the Airflow DAG / drop the EVENT in MySQL)
-- Move audit to a cold-storage table partitioned by month
CREATE TABLE customers_audit_archive (LIKE customers_audit INCLUDING ALL)
  PARTITION BY RANGE (audit_ts);
-- Restore from backup the 90-day to 18-month window, then attach as historical partitions
-- Going forward: hot table holds 90 days, archive holds the regulated tail
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW customers_audit_full AS
SELECT * FROM customers_audit
UNION ALL
SELECT * FROM customers_audit_archive
WHERE audit_ts < (SELECT MIN(audit_ts) FROM customers_audit);
Why this works: Splitting hot and cold storage keeps the OLTP cost down while preserving the audit tail
for the regulated retention period. The view gives consumers one query surface.

Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Myntra, Nykaa · Dialect: Postgres, MySQL
The scenario:
The application implements soft deletes by setting is_deleted = TRUE. The audit trigger is

CREATE TRIGGER orders_audit_del_trg
AFTER DELETE ON orders
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION orders_audit_fn();
Expected: Audit trail for every effective deletion. Actual: Audit captures only hard deletes; soft deletes
are invisible.
Thinking out loud: 1. "A soft delete is technically an UPDATE — set is_deleted = TRUE." 2. "The 
AFTER DELETE trigger does not fire on UPDATE." 3. "I need an UPDATE trigger with a WHEN
(NEW.is_deleted IS DISTINCT FROM OLD.is_deleted) clause."
The diagnosis: Audit pattern was designed when deletes were hard. When the team moved to soft-

The fix:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 543 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 544
-- Postgres: WHEN clause restricts to actual deletion transitions
CREATE TRIGGER orders_audit_softdel_trg
AFTER UPDATE ON orders
FOR EACH ROW
WHEN (OLD.is_deleted IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.is_deleted)
EXECUTE FUNCTION orders_audit_fn();
-- MySQL: no WHEN, gate inside the trigger body
DELIMITER //
CREATE TRIGGER orders_audit_softdel_trg
AFTER UPDATE ON orders
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  IF NOT (OLD.is_deleted <=> NEW.is_deleted) THEN
    INSERT INTO orders_audit (...) VALUES (...);
  END IF;
END //
DELIMITER ;
Why this works: The trigger now fires precisely when the soft-delete flag flips, capturing every effective
deletion regardless of physical DML verb.
What NOT to say: - "Convert soft deletes back to hard deletes" — defeats the recoverability
requirement. - "Audit every UPDATE" — wasteful, the WHEN clause keeps the audit table tight.
Common follow-up: "How do you audit a soft-restore (un-delete) as well?"

Scenario467 · Customer ID Space Collision After Migration
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Cred · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 547 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 548
The scenario:
Two regional databases were consolidated into a single customer master. Both used sequential
integer IDs starting at 1. After the merge, customer_id = 12345 could mean one customer
from the South region or a completely different customer from the North region. Downstream
reports double-count.
Expected: A unique ID per customer. Actual: Collisions on natural-key joins.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Two ID spaces that both start at 1 will collide unless re-keyed during merge." 2. 
"The fix is a surrogate key in the unified table, with the legacy region-qualified key kept as an attribute." 3.
"All downstream joins must move to the surrogate."
The diagnosis: The consolidation copied both tables into a single customer_master preserving the
original customer_id. The migration team thought "we will dedupe later." Later never came. Reports
now show inflated counts because joins on customer_id match across both populations.
The fix:
-- Add a surrogate primary key
ALTER TABLE customer_master ADD COLUMN customer_uid UUID DEFAULT gen_random_uuid();
ALTER TABLE customer_master ADD COLUMN source_region VARCHAR(10);
ALTER TABLE customer_master ADD CONSTRAINT customer_master_legacy_uk UNIQUE (source_region, customer_id);
-- Backfill source_region from the merge metadata
UPDATE customer_master SET source_region = 'S' WHERE migrated_from = 'south_db';
UPDATE customer_master SET source_region = 'N' WHERE migrated_from = 'north_db';
-- Downstream tables need a customer_uid column joined via (source_region, customer_id)
ALTER TABLE fact_orders ADD COLUMN customer_uid UUID;
UPDATE fact_orders f
SET customer_uid = cm.customer_uid
FROM customer_master cm
WHERE cm.source_region = f.source_region
  AND cm.customer_id   = f.customer_id;
Why this works: Surrogate keys are immune to source-system collisions. The composite uniqueness on
(source_region, customer_id) prevents future regression.
What NOT to say: - "Renumber one region's customer_ids" — breaks every external reference to those
IDs. - "Add a region prefix to customer_id" — changes the type and breaks integrations.
Common follow-up: "How would you detect this collision without explicit knowledge of the merge?"

Scenario468 · Currency Conversion Table Stale
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Flipkart, Nykaa · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A cross-border revenue dashboard shows USD revenue translated to INR at last quarter's
exchange rate. The FX table is updated quarterly via a manual upload that someone forgot to do
this quarter. The INR figure is materially understated.
SELECT order_date, SUM(amount_usd * fx.usd_to_inr) AS revenue_inr
FROM fact_orders o
JOIN dim_fx_rates fx ON fx.fx_date = (SELECT MAX(fx_date) FROM dim_fx_rates)
GROUP BY order_date;
Expected: Each order translated at the rate effective on its order_date. Actual: Every order
translated at one stale rate.
Thinking out loud: 1. " MAX(fx_date) returns whatever the latest available rate is — that is a single
rate, not a per-day rate." 2. "Even if the table had daily rates, a manual upload is fragile." 3. "I need an
effective-date join and an automated source."
The diagnosis: Two bugs in one place. First, the join collapses all dates to one rate. Second, the rate
that one date returns is months old. Either one alone would be wrong; together they produce confidently
incorrect output.
The fix:
-- Effective-dated join
SELECT o.order_date,
       SUM(o.amount_usd * fx.usd_to_inr) AS revenue_inr
FROM fact_orders o
JOIN dim_fx_rates fx
  ON fx.fx_date = (
    SELECT MAX(fx_date) FROM dim_fx_rates WHERE fx_date <= o.order_date
  )
GROUP BY o.order_date;
-- Automate the load from RBI reference rates daily, and assert freshness
SELECT MAX(fx_date) AS latest_fx_date,
       CURRENT_DATE - MAX(fx_date) AS days_behind
FROM dim_fx_rates;
-- raise if days_behind > 1

Why this works: Each order is translated at the rate effective on its own date, not a single point-in-time
rate. The freshness check catches the next stale-load incident on day two, not day ninety.
What NOT to say: - "FX moves slowly enough that this does not matter" — not after multi-percent
monthly moves. - "Lock in the quarterly rate as policy" — a finance decision, not a data-quality decision.

The fix:
-- Data-side freshness monitor (runs every hour, independent of the cron)
SELECT
  MAX(fx_date) AS latest_fx_date,
  CURRENT_DATE - MAX(fx_date) AS days_behind,
  CASE WHEN CURRENT_DATE - MAX(fx_date) > 1 THEN 'BREACHED' ELSE 'OK' END AS sla_status
FROM dim_fx_rates;
-- Cron-side fix: stop swallowing errors, page on failure
-- (Shell): set -e ; curl --fail https://vendor/api/v2/latest ...
Why this works: A data-side SLA monitor is independent of cron health. If the data is fresh, the cron is
by definition working; if the data is stale, something is wrong regardless of cron exit codes.

Scenario470 · Holiday Calendar Drift (Multiple Regions, Multiple Calendars)
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Swiggy, Zomato, Ola · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A business-day calculator uses a single holiday calendar. Operations in Kerala observe Onam, in
Maharashtra Ganesh Chaturthi, in West Bengal Durga Puja, and in Delhi the national holidays
only. SLA calculations on shipments are wrong in every state because the calendar is one-size-
fits-all.
SELECT shipment_id,
       business_days_between(dispatch_date, delivery_date) AS bd_to_deliver
FROM fact_shipments;
Expected: A regionally aware business-day count. Actual: Single national calendar misses state-specific
holidays; SLAs look better or worse than reality.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Regional holiday observance varies meaningfully — Kerala alone has ~20 public
holidays vs Delhi's ~17 with very different dates." 2. "A composite calendar dimension keyed by (region,
date) is the only correct structure." 3. "The function needs to take a region argument."
The diagnosis: The calendar table is keyed only by date. Functions consuming it cannot distinguish a
Kerala-only holiday from a national one. SLA breaches in Kerala under-count when Onam week is treated
as business days; in Delhi, over-count when Onam is mistakenly excluded.
The fix:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 551 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 552
CREATE TABLE dim_holiday_calendar (
  region_code VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,
  holiday_date DATE NOT NULL,
  holiday_name VARCHAR(100),
  PRIMARY KEY (region_code, holiday_date)
);
-- Region-aware business-day calculation
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION business_days_between(p_from DATE, p_to DATE, p_region VARCHAR)
RETURNS INT AS $$
  SELECT COUNT(*)::INT
  FROM generate_series(p_from, p_to - INTERVAL '1' DAY, INTERVAL '1' DAY) AS d(dt)
  WHERE EXTRACT(DOW FROM dt) NOT IN (0,6)   -- exclude Sun, Sat
    AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM dim_holiday_calendar h
      WHERE h.region_code IN (p_region, 'IN')   -- region-specific OR national
        AND h.holiday_date = dt::DATE
    );
$$ LANGUAGE SQL;
Why this works: A composite key (region, date) lets the same calendar table serve every region. National
holidays are stored once with region_code = 'IN'; state holidays add a row per state that
observes them.
What NOT to say: - "Use a third-party API for holidays" — viable, but the data model is still the problem.
- "Just always use the national calendar" — that is precisely the bug.
Common follow-up: "How do you handle moveable feasts like Eid where the date varies year to year?"

hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 554
SELECT sensor_id, reading_ts, temp_c
FROM fact_sensor_readings
WHERE sensor_id = 'WH-BLR-12';
Expected: A consistent measurement scale across time. Actual: A 1.8 °C step at the calibration date;
downstream "in spec" determinations are wrong on both sides.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Calibration is not just a future-facing change — it implies an offset to past
readings if we want a single comparable series." 2. "I need a dim_sensor_calibration table that

The diagnosis: The sensor recall came with a calibration certificate documenting a +1.8 °C bias. The
certificate was filed; no one fed it into the warehouse. The fact table contains uncorrected raw readings.
The fix:
CREATE TABLE dim_sensor_calibration (
  sensor_id VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  effective_from TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  effective_to   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  offset_c DECIMAL(5,2) NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (sensor_id, effective_from)
);
INSERT INTO dim_sensor_calibration VALUES
  ('WH-BLR-12', '2025-01-01', '2026-04-15', -1.80, /* pre-recall, subtract 1.8 */),
  ('WH-BLR-12', '2026-04-15', '9999-12-31',  0.00 /* post-recall, no offset */);
-- Corrected view
CREATE VIEW fact_sensor_readings_corrected AS
SELECT s.sensor_id, s.reading_ts, s.temp_c + c.offset_c AS temp_c_corrected, s.temp_c AS temp_c_raw
FROM fact_sensor_readings s
JOIN dim_sensor_calibration c
  ON c.sensor_id = s.sensor_id
 AND s.reading_ts >= c.effective_from
 AND s.reading_ts <  c.effective_to;
Why this works: Raw readings are preserved (forensics), corrected readings are derived (reporting).
Future calibration events add rows without rewriting history.
What NOT to say: - "Just subtract 1.8 from all old readings" — destroys the raw value. - "Throw out pre-
recall data" — over a year of cold-chain history would be lost.
Common follow-up: "How would you back-test the corrected series against ground-truth thermometers
if any are available?"

FROM fact_transactions t
JOIN dim_merchant_category_code mcc_dim ON mcc_dim.merchant_id = t.merchant_id
WHERE txn_date BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2026-04-30'
GROUP BY mcc;

Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 555 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 556
-- Convert to SCD Type 2
CREATE TABLE dim_merchant_category_code_scd2 (
  mcc_surrogate BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  merchant_id INT NOT NULL,
  mcc CHAR(4) NOT NULL,
  effective_from DATE NOT NULL,
  effective_to   DATE NOT NULL DEFAULT '9999-12-31',
  is_current BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE,
  UNIQUE (merchant_id, effective_from)
);
-- Fact joins on the effective window
SELECT d.mcc, SUM(t.amount_inr)
FROM fact_transactions t
JOIN dim_merchant_category_code_scd2 d
  ON d.merchant_id = t.merchant_id
 AND t.txn_date >= d.effective_from
 AND t.txn_date <  d.effective_to
WHERE t.txn_date BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2026-04-30'
GROUP BY d.mcc;
Why this works: Each historical transaction joins to the MCC that was in force on its own date. Updating
a merchant's MCC creates a new row, never overwriting the old one.

problem. - "Store the MCC on the fact" — denormalises but works; SCD2 is more flexible.

Thinking out loud: 1. "Type 1 dimensions overwrite history. They are correct for attributes that have no

someone will ask, Type 2 is the answer." 3. "I can recover some history from the shipment table if
shipping address was denormalised onto the shipment row."
The diagnosis: The original modelling team chose Type 1 to keep the dimension small. Address was
treated as a "current state" attribute. Operations now needs historical accuracy for dispute resolution.
The fix:
-- Recover what is recoverable from the shipment row itself (denorm address)
SELECT s.shipment_id, s.shipped_to_address, s.ship_date

  customer_id INT NOT NULL,

  city VARCHAR(80),
  pincode VARCHAR(6),
  effective_from DATE NOT NULL,
  effective_to   DATE NOT NULL DEFAULT '9999-12-31'
);

  REFERENCES dim_customer_address_scd2 (address_sk);
Why this works: Two defences: SCD2 going forward so address history survives, plus a denormalised
foreign key on the fact so the answer to "what address on day X" is a single column read.
What NOT to say: - "Address never matters historically" — it does, for disputes, refunds, fraud
investigations. - "Convert all dimensions to SCD2" — overkill; choose based on temporal relevance.

Scenario475 · Late-Arriving Dimension Confused Fact-Table Joins
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Swiggy, Zomato, Razorpay · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A new merchant signs up on March 1 and processes 200 transactions in the first hour. The
dimension load runs at midnight, so the merchant does not exist in dim_merchant until March
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 557 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 558
2. Every transaction from March 1 joins to NULL on the merchant side; the dashboard shows 200
transactions for "Unknown Merchant."
SELECT m.business_name, COUNT(*)
FROM fact_transactions t
JOIN dim_merchant m ON m.merchant_id = t.merchant_id
WHERE t.txn_date = '2026-03-01'
GROUP BY m.business_name;
Expected: Every transaction attributed to its merchant. Actual: New-merchant transactions appear
under NULL / are dropped by INNER JOIN.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Late-arriving dimensions are a classic data-warehouse problem." 2. "Two patterns:
(a) insert a placeholder row with merchant_id only and back-fill attributes when they arrive, or (b)
outer-join and tolerate NULLs in the report." 3. "Pattern (a) preserves fact integrity; pattern (b) admits the
gap on every read."
The diagnosis: The fact-table load runs hourly; the dimension load runs nightly. Transactions for
merchants registered today arrive at the warehouse 24 hours before their dimension row does. The
INNER JOIN drops them; the LEFT JOIN preserves them but with NULL attributes.
The fix:
-- Pattern A: create a placeholder dim row at fact-load time
INSERT INTO dim_merchant (merchant_id, business_name, load_status)
SELECT DISTINCT t.merchant_id, '(pending dimension load)', 'pending'
FROM fact_transactions t
LEFT JOIN dim_merchant m ON m.merchant_id = t.merchant_id
WHERE m.merchant_id IS NULL
  AND t.load_ts >= NOW() - INTERVAL '1' HOUR;
-- The nightly dim load then upserts real attributes onto the placeholder rows
MERGE INTO dim_merchant d
USING staging_merchant s ON d.merchant_id = s.merchant_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET business_name = s.business_name,
                              load_status = 'loaded',
                              ...
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (merchant_id, business_name, load_status, ...) VALUES (...);
-- Sanity check: anything still 'pending' after 48h is investigated
SELECT merchant_id, load_status, first_seen_ts
FROM dim_merchant
WHERE load_status = 'pending' AND first_seen_ts < NOW() - INTERVAL '48' HOUR;
Why this works: Placeholder rows keep the join working on day one. The MERGE on the nightly load fills
in the real attributes. The watchdog query catches stragglers.

What NOT to say: - "Run the dimension load every minute" — fixes the race for the cost of more
upstream load. - "Drop new merchants from the report until tomorrow" — silently under-counts revenue.

window changes after the fact?"
Category 7, Part D — Data Quality: Timezone, Encoding, Locale &
NULL Issues
The last bucket of DQ — the boring-but-painful issues that cost real money in production. Timezones
split orders across days and make Monday's revenue spill into Sunday's report. Encoding silently breaks
string equality so "Mumbai" and "Mumbai" stop joining when one row came in as Latin1 and the other as
UTF-8. NULL semantics double-count or miss rows depending on which clause they hide in, and
downstream Excel readers turn them into zeroes without anyone noticing. The interviewer asks these
because you'll hit them in week one — a cron at 23:59 IST will silently process "today" as yesterday's
UTC date, a payments file with a trailing space won't reconcile, a COUNT(col) will silently change the
denominator of a key metric, and the CFO will ask you why the dashboard moved 4%. The 25 scenarios
below walk through the symptom, the diagnosis, and the fix you'd narrate on a screen-share — including
the dialect quirks that make these issues so dialect-dependent.
Scenario476 · Daily Order Count Off By One Day For Some Users
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Flipkart, Swiggy, Zomato · Dialect: vendor-agnostic, with
PostgreSQL/MySQL call-outs
The scenario:
The product team runs a daily report grouping orders.created_at by date. For most users
the numbers tie out, but a subset of orders consistently appear on the wrong calendar day —
yesterday's order shows up in today's bucket. The pattern: it's always orders placed late at night
IST.
SELECT DATE(created_at) AS order_date, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders
WHERE DATE(created_at) = CURRENT_DATE
GROUP BY DATE(created_at);
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 559 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 560
Expected: Today's IST orders grouped under today's date. Actual: Orders placed between 00:00 and
05:29 IST land in yesterday's bucket.
Thinking out loud: 1. "The orders table almost certainly stores created_at in UTC — that's the
AWS-RDS default." 2. " DATE(created_at) extracts the UTC date, not the IST date." 3. "An order
placed at 02:00 IST is 20:30 UTC the previous day — so DATE() returns yesterday." 4. "The fix is to
convert to IST before extracting the date."
The diagnosis: The column is stored as UTC (either timestamp without time zone interpreted
as UTC, or timestamptz). Calling DATE() on it extracts the UTC calendar date. India is UTC+5:30,
so orders placed in the first 5.5 hours of each IST day are still on the previous UTC date. The grouping
then bucketing them yesterday is correct from the database's point of view but wrong from the
business's.
The fix (PostgreSQL with timestamptz):
SELECT (created_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date AS order_date,
       COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders
WHERE (created_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date = CURRENT_DATE
GROUP BY (created_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date;
In MySQL: DATE(CONVERT_TZ(created_at, '+00:00', '+05:30')).
Why this works: AT TIME ZONE shifts the instant onto the IST clock before the date is extracted, so
an IST-evening order stays on its IST date. Make sure CURRENT_DATE on the right side is also IST-
based — either set the session timezone or wrap it the same way.
What NOT to say: - "Just add 5.5 hours to created_at" — works until DST in a multi-region app and
lies if you ever onboard a non-IST tenant. - "Store created_at as IST going forward" — fixes new
rows, breaks historical comparisons and breaks the first time you serve a Singapore customer.
Common follow-up: "How would you avoid hand-writing AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata' in every
query in the codebase?"
Scenario477 · Cron At 23:59 IST Processing "Today" But DB Is UTC
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Paytm · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A reconciliation cron runs at 23:59 IST every night. It computes "today's" settlements by filtering 
WHERE settlement_date = CURRENT_DATE. The job is occasionally missing settlements
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 560 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 561
that the operations team can see in the UI, and the mismatch always happens on the last 30
minutes of the day.
SELECT merchant_id, SUM(amount) AS settled_today
FROM settlements
WHERE settlement_date = CURRENT_DATE
GROUP BY merchant_id;
Expected: All settlements that show "today" in the UI. Actual: Settlements created in the last ~30
minutes of the IST day are missing.
Thinking out loud: 1. "23:59 IST is 18:29 UTC — CURRENT_DATE in a UTC session is still yesterday's
UTC date." 2. "But settlement_date was stamped using the application's IST clock, so it's today's
IST date." 3. "Filter is comparing a UTC date to an IST date. Mismatch by one for the IST evening." 4. 
"And the run is starting at 23:59 — if a settlement lands at 23:59:45, the run probably already started,
double-trouble."
The diagnosis: Two bugs stacked. First, CURRENT_DATE resolves against the session timezone (UTC
on most managed databases), while settlement_date was written using IST. Second, a cron that
runs at the boundary is racing the data it's trying to summarise.
The fix:
SELECT merchant_id, SUM(amount) AS settled_today
FROM settlements
WHERE settlement_date = (CURRENT_TIMESTAMP AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date
GROUP BY merchant_id;
And schedule the cron at 00:15 the next day, processing today - 1, not at 23:59 of the current day.
Why this works: The filter and the data now agree on what "today" means. Running the job after the day
has fully closed removes the race.
What NOT to say: - "We'll subtract a day in the WHERE clause." — fragile, and now you have to
remember which side has the offset. - "Just run the cron more often." — masks the boundary bug rather
than fixing it.
Common follow-up: "Could you have caught this in CI? What would the test look like?"
Scenario478 · DST Transition Losing An Hour Of Events
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Multinationals operating in US/EU · Dialect: vendor-agnostic,
PostgreSQL examples
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 561 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 562
The scenario:
Your event pipeline ingests clickstream from a US-based partner. Every March, the partner's daily
counts dip noticeably for a 24-hour window. You're tasked with explaining the dip before the
QBR. The data is real, not corrupted.
SELECT date_trunc('hour', event_time) AS hr, COUNT(*)
FROM events
WHERE event_time >= '2026-03-08'
  AND event_time <  '2026-03-09'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
Expected: 24 hourly buckets for that day. Actual: 23 buckets — the 2 AM bucket is missing for that one
day.
Thinking out loud: 1. "March is when US DST springs forward — clocks jump from 02:00 to 03:00." 2. "If
event_time is local US time, there is no 02:00 row that day — the hour doesn't exist." 3. "My hourly
bucketing didn't fail, it correctly produced a non-existent hour with zero rows."
The diagnosis: The events are timestamped in the partner's local civil time (US/Eastern). On the spring-
forward Sunday, 02:00–02:59 local does not exist. There's no data to be lost — there is no such hour —
but reports comparing year-over-year see "23 hours" of activity.
The fix: Always store and reason in UTC. If display in local time matters, convert at query time and
document the discontinuity:
SELECT date_trunc('hour', event_time_utc AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York') AS hr_local,
       COUNT(*)
FROM events
WHERE event_time_utc >= '2026-03-08 05:00:00+00'   -- 00:00 EST
  AND event_time_utc <  '2026-03-09 05:00:00+00'   -- 00:00 EDT next day
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
Why this works: UTC has no DST. Year-over-year comparisons stay honest; the missing local hour is a
presentation artefact, not a data gap.
What NOT to say: - "Linearly interpolate the missing hour." — invents data. - "We lost an hour of data,
file a partner ticket." — there is no data to recover.
Common follow-up: "What about the fall-back, when 01:00–01:59 happens twice in the same local
day?"

Scenario479 · Multi-Region App, Single DB Timezone, Regional Reports Wrong
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Freshworks, Zoho, Postman · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A SaaS product serves customers in India, the US, and Germany. The database is in UTC. Every
regional sales lead is complaining that "today" on their dashboard doesn't match their local
"today".
SELECT COUNT(*) AS leads_today
FROM crm_leads
WHERE created_at::date = CURRENT_DATE
  AND tenant_country = :country;
Expected: Each lead sees the count for their local "today". Actual: Everyone sees the UTC count, which
is wrong for everyone.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Single DB timezone, three audiences. The query is ignoring the audience entirely."
2. "I need a per-tenant timezone, applied at query time." 3. "And CURRENT_DATE on the right side has
to be in the same timezone."
The diagnosis: A single global filter cannot serve three different "todays". The query needs to know the
tenant's timezone (stored on tenants) and apply it both to the timestamp column and to the
boundary expression.
The fix:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS leads_today
FROM crm_leads l
JOIN tenants t ON t.tenant_id = l.tenant_id
WHERE (l.created_at AT TIME ZONE t.timezone)::date
    = (CURRENT_TIMESTAMP AT TIME ZONE t.timezone)::date
  AND t.country = :country;
Why this works: Each tenant's "today" is computed against its own timezone, so the comparison is
apples to apples for that tenant. Storing the IANA name (Asia/Kolkata, not IST) on tenants
keeps DST correct for the regions that have it.
What NOT to say: - "Run three separate dashboards in three separate timezones." — works but doesn't
scale to 50 tenants. - "Store everything in local time." — sounds tidy, breaks the moment a customer
moves regions or expands.
Common follow-up: "What if a single user belongs to multiple tenants in different timezones?"

Scenario480 · "Yesterday's" Report Different Depending On User's Locale
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Razorpay, Stripe-India, Zoho · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A daily email goes out at 09:00 IST with "yesterday's" revenue. Customer-success reps in
different cities see different totals when they open the dashboard at the same moment —
Bangalore and Delhi agree, but the Singapore office (UTC+8) disagrees.
SELECT SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM transactions
WHERE created_at::date = CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 day';
Expected: One "yesterday" for the whole org. Actual: Each session timezone produces a different
"yesterday".
Thinking out loud: 1. " CURRENT_DATE follows session timezone — a session in SGT and one in IST
disagree." 2. "There's no single answer to 'yesterday' across timezones without a reference point." 3. 
"The business wants 'yesterday in IST' for India ops — make that explicit, not implicit."
The diagnosis: "Yesterday" is timezone-dependent. The query, the data, and the reporter must agree on
a single canonical zone. Right now each session implicitly imposes its own answer.
The fix: Pin "yesterday" to the business calendar (IST for an India ops report):
WITH ist_today AS (
  SELECT (CURRENT_TIMESTAMP AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date AS d

FROM transactions t, ist_today
WHERE (t.created_at AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::date = ist_today.d - 1;
Why this works: Whoever runs the query, wherever they sit, gets the same "IST yesterday." The output
is deterministic.
What NOT to say: - "Set the session timezone in the BI tool." — works for that one tool, fragile across
users. - "Send three different emails." — solves the symptom, not the inconsistency.

Scenario481 · Same String Fails JOIN — Collation Mismatch
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: TCS, Infosys, Wipro — also product cos. inheriting legacy MS-SQL ·
Dialect: SQL Server / MySQL specific
The scenario:
You join orders.customer_email to users.email and you get zero rows for some
legitimate matches. The strings are visibly identical. You copy-paste them into a comparison and
get True. But the join still drops them.
SELECT u.user_id, o.order_id
FROM orders o
JOIN users  u ON o.customer_email = u.email;
Expected: Match on every shared email. Actual: A subset of perfectly-equal-looking emails don't match.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Visually identical strings, JOIN fails. That smells like collation." 2. "One column is 
utf8_bin, the other utf8_general_ci — bin treats case as significant; ci doesn't." 3. "When two
collations meet in a comparison and they disagree on case sensitivity, the engine sometimes refuses or
silently picks the stricter one."
The diagnosis: The two columns have different collations. In MySQL the engine may either error out or
coerce in a way that changes equality behaviour; in SQL Server you get an "Cannot resolve the collation
conflict" error or, worse, a silent mismatch when explicit COLLATE clauses are added without thought.
The fix (vendor-agnostic — pick one):
SELECT u.user_id, o.order_id
FROM orders o
JOIN users  u
  ON LOWER(TRIM(o.customer_email)) = LOWER(TRIM(u.email));
Or pin the collation explicitly:
-- MySQL
ON o.customer_email COLLATE utf8mb4_general_ci = u.email COLLATE utf8mb4_general_ci
Why this works: Both sides are now normalised by the same function (or the same collation), so equality
means the same thing on both sides.
What NOT to say: - "Just ALTER one of the columns to match." — okay long-term, terrible for hotfixing
a join. - "Convert one to BINARY." — opposite of what you want; makes it case-sensitive.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 565 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 566
Common follow-up: "What's the performance cost of LOWER() in the JOIN, and how would you keep
the index usable?"
Scenario482 · "Mumbai" vs "mumbai" vs "MUMBAI" As Different Cities
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Swiggy, Zomato, Dunzo · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A logistics dashboard groups deliveries by city. The city dropdown shows "Mumbai", "mumbai",
"MUMBAI", "Mumbai ", and "mumbai-india" as five distinct cities. The product manager is upset.
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS deliveries
FROM deliveries
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY deliveries DESC;
Expected: One row for "Mumbai". Actual: Five rows, three of which are casing/whitespace variants.
Thinking out loud: 1. "The column is free-text and was never normalised on insert." 2. "GROUP BY
treats each variant as distinct because the bytes are distinct." 3. "Either fix on write (preferred) or
normalise on read for the report."
The diagnosis: City strings came in from multiple ingestion paths (mobile app, partner API, manual data
entry) with no normalisation contract. The grouping is correct given the data; the data is the bug.
The fix (read-side, quick win):
SELECT INITCAP(LOWER(TRIM(city))) AS city_clean, COUNT(*) AS deliveries
FROM deliveries
GROUP BY INITCAP(LOWER(TRIM(city)))
ORDER BY deliveries DESC;
Write-side (the actual fix): a normalised city_id foreign key into a curated cities table, with the
free-text field still retained for audit.
Why this works: Read-side collapses variants for the report; write-side prevents the next variant from
appearing.
What NOT to say: - "We'll add a CHECK constraint listing every valid city." — unmaintainable for 4,000
Indian cities. - "Let the BI tool clean it up." — happens once, then breaks the next week.

Scenario483 · Latin1 vs UTF-8 Silent Corruption On Insert
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Older enterprise stacks, legacy MySQL shops · Dialect: MySQL-heavy
The scenario:
A name field stores Indian names with diacritics ("Pooja Khannã"). Some rows render correctly,
others display as "Pooja Khannã" or "????". The corruption is consistent per-source: the mobile
app's rows are fine, the partner CSV import's rows are mangled.
SELECT user_id, full_name FROM users WHERE user_id IN (101, 202);
-- 101: 'Pooja Khanna' (correct)
-- 202: 'Pooja Khannã' (mojibake)
Expected: Both render correctly. Actual: Bytes from one path were interpreted as Latin1 when they were
UTF-8 (or vice versa) and were silently re-encoded on the way in.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Mojibake is the calling card of double-encoding or wrong-encoding-on-write." 2. 
"Different sources, different corruption — the CSV import declared the wrong encoding." 3. "At read time
the bytes are wrong, no SQL fix can recover them perfectly."
The diagnosis: The CSV import opened the file as Latin1 but the file was UTF-8. Each multi-byte UTF-8
character got expanded into two Latin1 characters, which were then re-encoded as UTF-8 for storage.
The result is mojibake bytes that don't decode back cleanly.
The fix: - Future imports: declare SET NAMES utf8mb4; LOAD DATA ... CHARACTER SET
utf8mb4. - Historical: attempt a best-effort repair: sql UPDATE users SET full_name =
CONVERT(CAST(CONVERT(full_name USING latin1) AS BINARY) USING utf8mb4) WHERE
full_name LIKE '%Ã%' OR full_name LIKE '%â%'; And spot-check before committing.
Why this works: The repair undoes the wrong decode-then-encode chain. The cure is fragile, so the real
fix is to set encoding correctly at every ingress.
What NOT to say: - "I'll just delete the bad rows." — loses data, doesn't fix the source. - "Strip non-
ASCII." — discards every Indian name with a diacritic.
Common follow-up: "What's your check-list before turning on a new ingestion pipeline?"

Scenario484 · Emoji Breaks MySQL utf8 (Need utf8mb4)
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Consumer apps with chat features · Dialect: MySQL specific
The scenario:
A chat feature throws "Incorrect string value: '\xF0\x9F\x98\x80' for column 'message'" on
certain inserts. The user is typing an emoji. The schema declares utf8.
INSERT INTO chat_messages (room_id, body) VALUES (10, 'great call 😀');
-- ERROR 1366 (HY000): Incorrect string value
Expected: Insert succeeds, emoji round-trips. Actual: Error or silent truncation at the emoji.
Thinking out loud: 1. "MySQL's utf8 is historically a 3-byte alias — it can't store 4-byte code points."
2. "Emoji is in the supplementary planes, needs 4 bytes — that's utf8mb4." 3. "The fix is column
charset, connection charset, and server-side default — all three."
The diagnosis: MySQL's utf8 is the legacy 3-byte variant; full Unicode requires utf8mb4. Emoji,
several historical Indic combining sequences, and many uncommon symbols need the 4-byte range.
The fix:
ALTER TABLE chat_messages
  CONVERT TO CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci;
-- Also pin the connection:
SET NAMES utf8mb4;
-- And the server / database defaults:
ALTER DATABASE myapp CHARACTER SET = utf8mb4 COLLATE = utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci;
Why this works: All three layers — server, connection, column — now speak the same 4-byte-capable
charset, so emoji and rare characters survive end to end.
What NOT to say: - "Strip emojis at the app layer." — product hostile and breaks user content. - "Use
BLOB." — bypasses the charset entirely; loses the ability to text-search, sort, or collate.
Common follow-up: "How would you migrate a 200 GB messages table to utf8mb4 with minimal
downtime?"

Scenario485 · Trailing Whitespace Defeating Equality
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Most data engineering interviews · Dialect: vendor-agnostic, with SQL
Server / Oracle call-outs
The scenario:
A reconciliation job matches payments.reference_id to 
bank_settlements.reference_id. About 2% of payments fail to match. When you eyeball
them in a query result, they look identical. The CFO has been asking about the 2% for a week.
SELECT p.payment_id
FROM payments p
LEFT JOIN bank_settlements s ON s.reference_id = p.reference_id
WHERE s.reference_id IS NULL;
Expected: Zero unmatched. Actual: 2% unmatched, all visually identical to a matched row.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Invisible characters — trailing space, leading space, NBSP, zero-width-space." 2. 
" LENGTH(reference_id) will tell me — if it differs from LENGTH(TRIM(reference_id)),
gotcha." 3. "In CHAR columns SQL Server pads; in VARCHAR it doesn't. Either could bite."
The diagnosis: The bank settlement file has trailing spaces on the reference. = in standard SQL is
case- and whitespace-sensitive. SQL Server's = actually treats trailing spaces as equal for VARCHAR,
which complicates the picture — but on a join from a true CHAR(20) to a VARCHAR(20) with
explicit collation overrides, the behaviour is unreliable.
The fix:
SELECT p.payment_id
FROM payments p
LEFT JOIN bank_settlements s
  ON TRIM(s.reference_id) = TRIM(p.reference_id)
WHERE s.reference_id IS NULL;
And add a write-time normaliser so the file's trailing spaces never enter the table.
Why this works: TRIM strips all leading/trailing whitespace on both sides, making the comparison
purely on content.
What NOT to say: - "Set ANSI_PADDING off." — fixes one corner of one dialect, makes future joins
surprise everyone. - "Compare with LIKE." — slower and still wrong if the trailing chars include _ or 
%.

hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in

Scenario486 · CHAR vs VARCHAR Padding Inflating Storage
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Database-focused interviews, Oracle/DB2 shops · Dialect: Oracle/
DB2 examples, MySQL/Postgres comparison
The scenario:
A status_code CHAR(20) column was used to store values like 'OK' or 'FAILED'. The table
is 4x larger than the size predicted by row count × column count of meaningful data. Storage
budget overrun.
SELECT status_code, LENGTH(status_code)
FROM transactions
LIMIT 5;
-- 'OK                  '  20
-- 'FAILED              '  20
Expected: LENGTH('OK') = 2. Actual: CHAR(20) pads to 20 on every row; LENGTH returns the
padded value in some dialects.
Thinking out loud: 1. " CHAR(N) is fixed-width — every row is stored as N bytes regardless of
content." 2. "For short enum-ish values that's huge waste." 3. "And comparing CHAR to VARCHAR
invites the trailing-space ambiguity from the previous scenario."
The diagnosis: CHAR(20) allocates 20 bytes per value (or 20 character-widths after charset, often
more). For a status code, this is a 10x storage and IO penalty. The choice of CHAR was historical —
likely copied from an old COBOL-era schema.
The fix: Migrate to VARCHAR (or TEXT in Postgres):
ALTER TABLE transactions
  ALTER COLUMN status_code TYPE VARCHAR(20)
  USING TRIM(status_code);
For a true enum, use a lookup table or your dialect's ENUM type if applicable.
Why this works: VARCHAR stores only the actual length plus a small length prefix, eliminating the
padding waste. The TRIM during alter cleans up the existing padding.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 570 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 571
What NOT to say: - "It doesn't matter, disk is cheap." — compressed backups, IO bandwidth, and
cache hit ratios still suffer. - "Just shrink CHAR to CHAR(6)." — still pads to 6, still wastes on 2-char
values.
Common follow-up: "In Postgres, does VARCHAR(20) actually save space versus TEXT?"
Scenario487 · Currency: ₹ vs INR vs Rs As Three Representations
Tags: Difficulty: Easy · Asked at: Razorpay, PhonePe, Cashfree · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
The amount field is numeric but a sibling display_amount field is free-text. Some rows show
"₹500", others "INR 500", others "Rs. 500", others "500/-". A search-by-amount feature returns
wildly different results depending on which prefix the user typed.
SELECT * FROM invoices
WHERE display_amount LIKE '%500%';
-- Returns rows for 500, 1500, 2500, 50000…
Expected: A single normalised representation, or no free-text at all. Actual: Four representations of the
same value, plus a LIKE-search bug on top.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Currency should never live in display text in a database — it's a derived value." 2. 
"Store amount + currency code separately, render at the edge." 3. "The search bug is also LIKE-based;
substring matching on numbers is dangerous (500 matches 5000)."
The diagnosis: Two conflated problems. The first is that human-readable currency strings should never
be the source of truth — they should be derived from amount_minor (integer paise) and 
currency_code ('INR') at presentation time. The second is that LIKE on a number-as-string is a
substring search, which matches all "500"-containing values.
The fix:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 571 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 572
ALTER TABLE invoices
  ADD COLUMN amount_minor BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  ADD COLUMN currency_code CHAR(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'INR';
-- Drop display_amount once views are migrated to render from the canonical columns.
SELECT * FROM invoices
WHERE amount_minor = 50000  -- ₹500 stored as paise
  AND currency_code = 'INR';
Why this works: Numeric equality on integers is unambiguous and fast. The display string is computed
at the edge ("₹" || (amount_minor / 100.0)) and never enters the WHERE clause.
What NOT to say: - "Strip the symbol with regex." — works until someone types "RS.500" with no
space. - "Store as DECIMAL with the symbol." — DECIMAL can't hold a symbol; the symbol then leaks
back into a text column.
Common follow-up: "Why minor units (paise) instead of DECIMAL(10,2)?"
Scenario488 · Number Formatting Locale: "1,000.50" vs "1.000,50"
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Multinational SaaS, fintech with EU customers · Dialect: vendor-
agnostic
The scenario:
A CSV upload accepts amounts. Indian users type "1,00,000" (lakh comma grouping) and
German users paste "1.000,50". The pipeline parses both with the same logic and produces
garbage for one of them.
INSERT INTO refunds(amount) VALUES (CAST('1.000,50' AS DECIMAL(10,2)));
-- ERROR or unexpected 1.00050
Expected: Parsed correctly per locale. Actual: One locale parses fine, the other corrupts.
Thinking out loud: 1. "The database doesn't know about locale — it expects 1234.56 plain." 2. 
"Locale-specific parsing must happen at the app/import layer, before the cast." 3. "Storage is always
locale-free; display is locale-aware."
The diagnosis: SQL CAST(string AS DECIMAL) uses the database's invariant numeric format (.
as decimal, no thousands separator). Locale formatting must be stripped or interpreted before the SQL
boundary.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 572 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 573
The fix: Normalise at ingestion (pseudocode for the import layer):
amount = locale_parse(raw, user_locale)  # returns 1000.50 as float/Decimal
Then insert the plain number:
INSERT INTO refunds(amount) VALUES (1000.50);
Inside SQL, when stuck with locale-formatted strings, normalise explicitly:
-- Indian: remove commas
SELECT CAST(REPLACE('1,00,000', ',', '') AS DECIMAL(12,2));
-- German: replace dots with empty, comma with dot
SELECT CAST(REPLACE(REPLACE('1.000,50', '.', ''), ',', '.') AS DECIMAL(12,2));
Why this works: The database sees a single canonical numeric format, eliminating ambiguity. Locale-
handling lives where locale is known: at the user's edge.
What NOT to say: - "Force everyone to use Indian formatting." — alienates users. - "Try both parses and
pick the bigger one." — silent corruption waiting to happen.

The scenario:
A user signs up with Abhi@example.com. Tries to log in next week with

ticket of the day.
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'abhi@example.com';
-- 0 rows — but the row stored 'Abhi@example.com'.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 574 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 575
Expected: Login works regardless of capitalisation. Actual: Case-sensitive comparison; user is locked
out of their own account.
Thinking out loud: 1. "RFC 5321 says the local-part may be case-sensitive; the domain is not." 2. "In
practice, virtually no mail server treats it as case-sensitive — Gmail, Outlook, AWS, all case-fold." 3. "So

The diagnosis: The application stored email as-typed and compares case-sensitively. The RFC

The fix:

Why this works: Equality is now defined on the canonical form. Indexing the generated column keeps
lookups fast.
What NOT to say: - "We're respecting the RFC." — technically true, practically harmful. - "Force users to
remember the original case." — UX-hostile, doesn't reflect reality of how email works.
Common follow-up: "What about dots-and-plus-signs aliasing — abhi+work@gmail.com vs
abhi@gmail.com?"

The scenario:

different households because their address is typed slightly differently each delivery. Marketing's

-- Three rows that are the same place
'12, MG Road, Bangalore - 560001'
'12 M.G. Road, Bengaluru, 560001'
'No. 12, Mahatma Gandhi Road, Bangalore 560001'
Expected: Same household recognised. Actual: Three "households" in the system.

 AND a1.pincode = a2.pincode

Scenario492 · NULL Counted As Zero In A Downstream System
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: BI-heavy interviews · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
SQL says AVG(rating) = 4.6. An Excel export of the same data says AVG = 3.2. The
finance team has been making decisions off the Excel number.
SELECT AVG(rating) FROM reviews;
-- 4.6 in SQL — NULL ratings excluded from the average.
-- 3.2 in Excel — NULLs read as 0 by the BI exporter, pulling the mean down.
Expected: Same number in both systems. Actual: Excel coerced NULLs to 0; the average is wrong by a
lot.
Thinking out loud: 1. "SQL AVG(col) ignores NULL — denominator and numerator both skip NULL
rows." 2. "Many BI exporters / Excel readers treat empty cells as 0, not NULL." 3. "So the downstream
system computes SUM/N where N includes the NULL-as-zero rows."
The diagnosis: Semantic mismatch at the SQL-to-Excel boundary. SQL's NULL means "unknown";
Excel's empty cell often gets coerced to 0 in numeric formulas. The averaging behaviour diverges
accordingly.
The fix: At the export boundary, decide explicitly: - If "no rating" means "not rated yet", export NULL as
text "N/A" so Excel doesn't coerce. - If business says "no rating = 0", make that explicit in SQL: 
AVG(COALESCE(rating, 0)) — and accept the consequence.
Best: produce an exported column for the user with the explicit denominator: AVG_rated, 
COUNT_rated, COUNT_unrated.
Why this works: The downstream consumer can't silently misinterpret what they're shown when the
columns force the intent.
What NOT to say: - "Fix Excel." — not yours to fix. - "Filter out NULLs in the export and don't tell
anyone." — hides the problem and shifts the mean differently.
Common follow-up: "What if some reviewers rated 0 deliberately? How do you tell that apart from 'not
rated'?"

Scenario493 · NULL Excluded From COUNT(col) Silently Changing The
Denominator
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Most data interviews · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
A funnel report shows "conversion rate = paid / signed_up". Conversion has been climbing
steadily and the team is celebrating. You spot a new column being added to the signed_up
count's denominator that's silently shrinking it.
SELECT COUNT(email)        AS signed_up,    -- ignores NULL emails
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE plan = 'paid') AS paid
FROM users;
Expected: signed_up = total users. Actual: signed_up excludes users with NULL email — the
denominator dropped after a recent schema change that made email optional.
Thinking out loud: 1. " COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values of col. COUNT(*) counts rows." 2. 
"If email became nullable last sprint, COUNT(email) quietly drops those users." 3. "Conversion
rate paid / signed_up goes up because the denominator shrunk, not because more people paid."
The diagnosis: The denominator definition was tied to a specific column's non-NULL count. When that
column's semantics changed, the metric changed without any code change to the metric itself.
The fix:
SELECT COUNT(*)                                       AS signed_up,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE plan = 'paid')          AS paid,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE plan = 'paid')::float
         / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0)                         AS conversion_rate
FROM users;
And document: "conversion = paid users / all rows in users". Any change to user definition triggers a
metric review.
Why this works: COUNT(*) is decoupled from any column nullability change. The metric definition is
now stable against schema drift.
What NOT to say: - "Add WHERE email IS NOT NULL." — same bug, written more explicitly. -
"Lock the schema." — doesn't address the underlying brittleness.
Common follow-up: "What's the difference between COUNT(*), COUNT(1), and COUNT(col) in
execution and semantics?"

Scenario494 · NULL In A Foreign Key — Unknown vs Not-Applicable
Tags: Difficulty: Hard · Asked at: Schema-design interviews · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
The orders table has coupon_id as a nullable FK to coupons. Reporting can't agree:
some queries treat NULL as "no coupon used", others treat it as "coupon was used but is
missing in the table." Two different interpretations produce two different revenue impact numbers.
-- "Orders that used a coupon"
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE coupon_id IS NOT NULL;
-- Some teams say: that's orders with known coupon.
-- Others say: NULL coupon_id means we lost the coupon link.
Expected: One unambiguous meaning of NULL. Actual: NULL is being asked to carry two semantic
meanings.
Thinking out loud: 1. "NULL in a nullable FK can mean either 'not applicable' (no coupon used) or
'unknown' (we don't know which coupon, but one was used)." 2. "You can't tell them apart from the value
alone." 3. "Schema must make the distinction explicit — separate boolean or sentinel value."
The diagnosis: A single NULL value is being asked to encode two different business concepts. Without
explicit modelling, every query has to guess which one was meant.
The fix:
ALTER TABLE orders
  ADD COLUMN used_coupon BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE;
-- Backfill: assume the historical NULLs = "no coupon used"
UPDATE orders SET used_coupon = (coupon_id IS NOT NULL);
-- Now queries are unambiguous
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE used_coupon = TRUE;
-- Orders with a coupon, regardless of whether coupon_id is present.
Why this works: The boolean carries intent; the FK carries identity. Their NULL states are independently
meaningful.
What NOT to say: - "Use a sentinel coupon_id = 0 for 'no coupon'." — pollutes the coupons table
and breaks FK semantics. - "Document the convention." — humans forget, queries don't.
