Scenario495 · NULL Handling In AVG — Denominator Changes
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Analytics interviews · Dialect: vendor-agnostic
The scenario:
Two queries that look identical produce different averages. One uses AVG(col), the other uses
SUM(col) / COUNT(*). The numbers diverge whenever col has NULLs.
SELECT AVG(discount_amount)                            AS avg_v1,
       SUM(discount_amount) / COUNT(*)                 AS avg_v2,
       SUM(discount_amount) / COUNT(discount_amount)   AS avg_v3
FROM orders;
Expected: All three equal. Actual: v1 = v3 (NULLs excluded), v2 lower (NULLs in denominator, not
numerator).
Thinking out loud: 1. " AVG(col) = SUM(col) / COUNT(col) — NULLs excluded from both." 2. 
" SUM(col) / COUNT(*) includes NULL rows in the denominator but not the numerator — pulls the
average toward zero." 3. "Both are valid for different questions; the bug is using one as if it were the
other."
The diagnosis: SQL aggregates skip NULL inputs. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) counts
non-NULL values. Dividing the SUM by the wrong denominator changes what the metric means.
The fix: Be explicit about intent:
-- "Average discount among orders that had a discount"
SELECT AVG(discount_amount) FROM orders WHERE discount_amount IS NOT NULL;
-- "Average discount per order (treating NULLs as zero discount)"
SELECT AVG(COALESCE(discount_amount, 0)) FROM orders;
Name the columns in the output to match the intent — avg_discount_when_applied vs 
avg_discount_per_order.
Why this works: The query name and the formula now agree on what's being asked. The reader can't
accidentally misread.

What NOT to say: - "AVG is broken; let me reimplement it." — AVG is correct; the metric definition was

Thinking out loud: 1. "COALESCE turns NULL into 0 — that's correct only if NULL means zero." 2.

FROM transactions
WHERE date_trunc('day', created_at) = CURRENT_DATE - 1;

Scenario498 · Empty String vs NULL — Pick One And Enforce

The scenario:
A middle_name column has rows with NULL, rows with '', and rows with ' '

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE middle_name IS NULL;        -- 4,000
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE middle_name = '';           -- 2,500
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE TRIM(middle_name) = '';     -- 2,700
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE COALESCE(NULLIF(TRIM(middle_name), ''), NULL) IS NULL; -- 6,700

different counts.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Empty string and NULL are technically different in standard SQL — Oracle is the

enforce." 3. "Whitespace-only is a third bug — normalise on write."
The diagnosis: The write path has no normalisation contract. Forms submit '' for blank fields, the mobile
app submits NULL, and an old import path submits ' '.
The fix:
-- Normalise existing data
UPDATE users
SET middle_name = NULL
WHERE TRIM(COALESCE(middle_name, '')) = '';
-- Enforce going forward
ALTER TABLE users
  ADD CONSTRAINT chk_middle_name_no_empty
  CHECK (middle_name IS NULL OR LENGTH(TRIM(middle_name)) > 0);

Scenario499 · ANSI vs MySQL Behaviour On NULL In WHERE col != value
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Dialect-aware interviews · Dialect: vendor-agnostic, MySQL/
Postgres/Oracle differ on edge cases
The scenario:
A query WHERE status != 'cancelled' excludes cancelled orders but also silently
excludes orders whose status is NULL. The product manager expected NULL-status orders to be
included because "they're not cancelled."
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status != 'cancelled';
-- Excludes NULL-status rows along with 'cancelled' rows.
Expected: Anything not literally 'cancelled' — including NULL-status. Actual: NULL-status orders are
dropped because NULL != 'cancelled' evaluates to NULL, not TRUE.
Thinking out loud: 1. "Three-valued logic: NULL != 'x' is UNKNOWN, not TRUE." 2. "WHERE
keeps rows where the predicate is TRUE — UNKNOWN is treated as FALSE for filtering." 3. "To include
NULLs, you need explicit OR status IS NULL or IS DISTINCT FROM."
The diagnosis: Standard SQL applies three-valued logic. WHERE NULL = anything and WHERE
NULL != anything are both UNKNOWN, both filtered out. The intuition "NULL is not cancelled, so
include it" doesn't match the language semantics.
The fix:
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM orders
WHERE status IS DISTINCT FROM 'cancelled';   -- Postgres
-- Or vendor-agnostic:
WHERE (status IS NULL OR status != 'cancelled');
MySQL has the null-safe equality operator <=>, so NOT (status <=> 'cancelled') also works.
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 584 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 585
Why this works: IS DISTINCT FROM (or the explicit OR) treats NULL as a distinct value, so the
predicate evaluates to TRUE for NULL-status rows.
What NOT to say: - "Just COALESCE the status to a sentinel string." — invents data and pollutes
downstream queries. - "Set status NOT NULL and backfill 'unknown'." — sometimes right, but a schema
change for a query bug is overkill.
Common follow-up: "What does the same query do in Oracle, where empty string == NULL?"
Scenario500 · IS DISTINCT FROM As The NULL-Safe Equality Fix
Tags: Difficulty: Medium · Asked at: Senior-level, dialect-aware · Dialect: PostgreSQL/SQL Standard with
MySQL equivalents
The scenario:
A change-data-capture pipeline diffs old and new row versions to detect updates. It misses
updates where a column went from 'A' to NULL or from NULL to 'B', because the diff uses
old.col != new.col. Customer-success has been chasing ghost bugs for a week.
SELECT *
FROM old_snapshot o
JOIN new_snapshot n USING (id)
WHERE o.email != n.email
   OR o.phone != n.phone;
-- Misses cases where one side is NULL.
Expected: Detect any change, including to/from NULL. Actual: Changes involving NULL slip through the
diff.
Thinking out loud: 1. " a != b returns NULL if either side is NULL — three-valued logic strikes again."
2. "For change detection I need NULL-safe equality." 3. "That's exactly what IS DISTINCT FROM was
designed for."
The diagnosis: The diff predicate uses standard !=, which is NULL-unsafe. NULL-to-value and value-
to-NULL transitions evaluate to UNKNOWN and are filtered out, masking real changes.
The fix:
Learn & Excel · Scenario-Based SQL Library — 500 Scenarios 585 / 586
hello@learnandexcel.in · learnandexcel.in
PAGE 586
SELECT *
FROM old_snapshot o
JOIN new_snapshot n USING (id)
WHERE o.email IS DISTINCT FROM n.email
   OR o.phone IS DISTINCT FROM n.phone;
MySQL equivalent using the <=> operator:
WHERE NOT (o.email <=> n.email)
   OR NOT (o.phone <=> n.phone);
For wide tables, generate a row hash on both sides and compare hashes (still treating NULL explicitly).
Why this works: IS DISTINCT FROM returns FALSE when both sides are NULL, TRUE when one
side is NULL and the other isn't, and otherwise behaves like !=. It is total — never returns UNKNOWN.
What NOT to say: - "Wrap every column in COALESCE." — works but invents a sentinel that might
collide with real data. - "Use a hash and compare." — fine pattern, but the hash function still has to
handle NULL consistently.
Common follow-up: "How would you efficiently diff two snapshots of a 200-column table?"
